# Sūrah Āl ʿImrān (Chapter 3) — Expanded Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Introduction to the Sūrah

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second of the Radiant Ones**

Sūrah Āl ʿImrān, "The House of ʿImrān," is the third chapter of the Qur'an and, by the consensus of the scholars of readings and chronology, a Madinan sūrah — revealed after the Hijrah to a community that was now building a civilization rather than merely surviving persecution. It comprises two hundred verses. Its name honors the blessed family — the house, or line, of ʿImrān — whose story the sūrah unfolds in verses 33–63: the grandmother who consecrated her unborn child to God, the daughter Mary who grew up "in a beautiful way" under the care of Zachariah, and the son, Jesus the Messiah, born of a word from God. No other sūrah of the Qur'an is named after a prophetic household, and the choice is deliberate: this chapter is the Qur'an's most sustained address concerning the family in whom the earlier covenant reached its flowering, and concerning the claims made in the name of that family's most famous son.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself bound this sūrah forever to the one before it. Muslim records in his Ṣaḥīḥ, from Abū Umāmah:

> *"Recite the Qur'an, for on the Day of Resurrection it will come as an intercessor for its companions. Recite the two illuminated ones (al-zahrāwayn), al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān, for on the Day of Resurrection they will come as two clouds, or two shades, or two flocks of birds arrayed in ranks, pleading for their companions."* (Muslim 804)

They are the "radiant ones" — and the pairing is structural, not merely devotional. Al-Baqarah laid down the constitution of the new community: its creed, its law, its rituals, its economics. Āl ʿImrān, revealed in its earliest portions around the second and third years after the Hijrah, takes up the two great external questions that constitution raised: how the new community is to stand before the older religious communities around it, and how it is to stand in battle before the enemies who seek its annihilation. The sūrah's two great arenas are thus the debate-hall and the battlefield — the delegation from Najrān and the field of Uḥud.

**The Delegation from Najrān and the Opening of the Chapter**

The commentators, beginning with the reports preserved by al-Ṭabarī and al-Wāḥidī, relate that the first portion of the sūrah — between thirty and eighty-plus verses, according to different opinions — was revealed in connection with a delegation of Christians from Najrān, the great Christian center of South Arabia, who came to Madinah to question the Prophet ﷺ. In the traditional accounts the delegation's argument ran in three steps: Jesus must be divine, for he revived the dead, healed the leper, and told of unseen things; he must be son of God, for he had no human father; and God must be three, for scripture habitually says "We did," "We created," whereas a solitary speaker would say "I." The accounts then record the Prophet's methodical response, a model of rational engagement that the sūrah itself will echo and surpass: he asked them, point by point, whether God lives and does not die while Jesus is subject to passing away; whether God alone sustains, guards, and provides for all things, and whether Jesus did any of that; whether anything in heaven or earth is hidden from God, and whether Jesus knew aught of it save what he was taught; whether Jesus was borne in a womb, born, nursed, and fed as children are. To each they could only answer yes — and he concluded, "So how can it be as you allege?" The opening movement of Āl ʿImrān — the letters, the twin names the Living and the Self-Subsisting, the sending down of the Book, Torah, Gospel, and Criterion, the forming of every child in the womb — reads in this light as revelation taking up, in God's own voice, precisely the questions the Prophet had put to the delegates: Who truly lives and does not die? Who truly sustains? What is Jesus, really, beside Adam (v. 59)? The sūrah is thus, from its first line, a work of theology conducted on the highest level: not invective, but the presentation of evidence and the invitation to judgment (vv. 61, 64).

**The Education of Mary and the Education of a Community**

The sūrah's center of gravity then becomes the sacred history of the House of ʿImrān (vv. 33–63): a woman consecrates what is in her womb; God accepts a daughter where a son was expected, "and the male is not like the female"; a child grows in a sanctuary provisioned from beyond natural means; an aged prophet, Zachariah, learns from the girl's miracle to ask for his own impossible son; angels address Mary by name twice; and the Word is announced — a Messiah whose likeness before God "is as that of Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him, 'Be!' and he was" (v. 59). The narrative is not decorative. In a sūrah that will later demand of the believers that they stand firm at Uḥud, spend their wealth, and march out when called, the story of Mary is the curriculum of the soul: consecration, unexpected divine preference, provision without reckoning, answered prayer at the point of hopelessness, purity of intention, and the command to "be devoutly obedient, prostrate, and bow with those who bow" (v. 43). The community that must later be told *iṣbirū, ṣābirū, rābiṭū* — "be patient, vie in patience, persevere" (v. 200) — has already been shown what such steadfastness looks like in a young woman alone in a sanctuary.

Between the narrative and the battle stretches the sūrah's long central address to the People of the Book (vv. 64–120): an invitation to "a word common between us and you" (v. 64), a setting right of Abraham's identity (v. 67), a warning against a party who feign belief in the morning and disbelieve at day's end (v. 72), praise of the trustworthy among them (v. 75), a reminder of the covenant over all the prophets (v. 81), the condition of those who prefer disbelief after belief (vv. 86–91), the legislation of pilgrimage at the first House (vv. 96–97), the great command to hold fast together to the rope of God (v. 103), the constitution of a community that commands what is right (vv. 104, 110, 114), and the forecast of the hurts the believers will hear and the patience by which they will endure them (vv. 111, 118–120, 186).

**Uḥud: The Sūrah's School of Defeat**

Then, from verse 121 through 179 — nearly a third of the chapter — the sūrah becomes the Qur'an's own commentary on the Battle of Uḥud, fought in the year 3/625 at the foot of the mountain north of Madinah. Badr had been the victory of the few over the many (v. 123); Uḥud was the near-catastrophe of the many through the failure of a few: fifty archers left their station against orders, a tactical gap opened, the tide reversed, and some seventy believers were killed, among them Ḥamzah, the Prophet's uncle. The sūrah does not flinch. It names the waverers by their wavering (v. 122), the deserters by their desertion (v. 155), the hypocrites by their interior speech (vv. 154, 156, 167–168), and the martyrs by their genuine state — alive with their Lord, provided for (v. 169). It teaches the law of alternation: "such days We rotate among mankind" (v. 140); the difference between the slumber of God-given security and the agitation of self-absorption (v. 154); the gentleness of prophetic leadership at the moment it had most excuse for severity (v. 159); the exposure of fraud in the spoils (v. 161); and the meaning of divine love and divine pardon for an army that had disobeyed and been forgiven (vv. 152, 155). No other extended passage of the Qur'an turns a military reversal into so complete an education in psychology, leadership, collective responsibility, and the theology of victory and defeat. The Prophet ﷺ loved that mountain to the end of his life, saying:

> *"Uḥud is a mountain that loves us and that we love."* (al-Bukhārī 2889; Muslim 1365)

**The Closing Ascension**

The sūrah closes as it opened — with the Book's signs and the minds that read them. Verses 190–194 form one of the most profound doxologies in scripture: the alternation of night and day as signs "for the possessors of intellect," who remember God standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, whose reflection upon creation ends not in pride but in supplication — "Our Lord, Thou hast not created this in vain" — and whose prayer is answered in verse 195 with one of the Qur'an's most sweeping declarations of the equal worth of every worker's work, male and female. It is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās that when he spent the night in the house of his aunt Maymunah, he saw the Prophet ﷺ rise for the night prayer, and after preparing himself, he recited these closing verses of Āl ʿImrān as he stood in the darkness (al-Bukhārī 183; Muslim 763). The chapter that began with letters only God fully understands ends with minds fully awake — "possessors of intellect" who turn the whole cosmos into remembrance; and the final verse gathers the whole sūrah, debate and battle alike, into three commands and one promise: *be patient, vie in patience, hold your post, and reverence God, that you may prosper* (v. 200).

**A Word on Method**

What follows is a verse-by-verse expanded commentary in which every one of the two hundred verses receives its own complete treatment, in the manner of the earlier volumes of this series on Sūrah al-Fātiḥah and Sūrah al-Baqarah. Where the source groups verses together (as with vv. 3–4, 8–9, 16–17, 33–34, and others), the verses have been separated and treated individually, as the method of this series demands. Each commentary draws upon the Arabic language and its roots, the transmitted views of the classical commentators — al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, and the reports of Ibn ʿAbbās among them — the authenticated words of the Prophet ﷺ with their collections identified, the occasions of revelation where they are soundly transmitted, and the living reasoning that connects this Madinan revelation to the conditions of every reader, in every age, who must decide what to do with a Book, a battlefield, and a heart.

## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:1

> **Alif. Lām. Mīm.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Letters Return, and the Debate Deepens**

The sūrah opens with the same three disjointed letters — *alif, lām, mīm* — that opened Sūrah al-Baqarah, and the repetition is a summons to attention. Twenty-nine sūrahs of the Qur'an begin with such isolated letters (al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿah), recited as separate alphabetical names rather than as words, and they constitute the most famous of the Book's openings. The commentators have transmitted a range of interpretations across the centuries. Some, like al-Ṭabarī's preferred posture and the constant practice of the early community, hold them to be among the matters whose interpretation belongs to God — *Allāhu aʿlam*, "God knows best" — a reading that itself is deeply instructive: at the very threshold of a chapter that will soon distinguish determined signs from symbolic ones (v. 7), the reader is handed a text whose first line already trains him in intellectual humility. Others proposed that the letters gesture toward names: *alif* for Allāh, *lām* for Jibrīl (Gabriel), *mīm* for Muḥammad — God, the carrying angel, the receiving messenger, the three stations of revelation's descent. Still others, in the interpretive tradition of al-Sulamī, heard in them qualities: *alif*, the first letter, for God's oneness and priority; *lām* for *luṭf*, kindness — the attribute the sūrah will stamp at the end of its thirtieth verse, "God is Kind unto His servants"; *mīm* for *mulk*, sovereignty — the attribute the sūrah will enthrone at verse 26, "O God, Master of Sovereignty." Whether or not one adopts these expansions, note what they share: all of them take letters whose sounds a child can pronounce and unfold them into theology.

**Miracle Made from the Alphabet**

The deepest classical explanation, repeated from Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Rāzī and Ibn Kathīr, binds these letters to the Qur'an's inimitability (*iʿjāz*). The Qur'an is composed of nothing but these letters — the same twenty-nine letters the Arabs used for their letters, contracts, and poems. The isolated letters at the head of a sūrah are like a craftsman displaying his raw material before displaying the artifact: here is the alphabet you possess; here, immediately following, is what God builds out of it — and no one has ever built the like. The structure is a standing challenge (cf. 2:23; 10:38; 11:13; 17:88) delivered not as an argument but as a fact of experience: fourteen centuries of Arabic letters, and the text remains unmatcHed. There is also a subtler pedagogy. Speech worthy of God and speech habitual to man are made of identical elements; the difference between them is not material but compositional — meaning, order, truth, and divine origin. So too the sūrah will soon argue about Jesus: his material was the same dust as Adam's (v. 59); it is absurd to worship the material when the marvel lies in the command "Be!" that ordered it.

**A Threshold Trained in Reverence**

Finally, the letters function at the level of the reciter's soul. A sūrah that will demand much — patience in defeat, honesty about hypocrisy, the spending of beloved wealth, the releasing of cherished claims about Jesus — opens with three sounds that no one can rush past, because no one can skim what one cannot paraphrase. They slow the tongue and quiet the interpretive ego. The reader who begins *alif, lām, mīm* has already conceded that this Book contains more than his reading of it; and that concession is the first gate of every verse that follows.
**The Letters Across the Qur'an: A Census of Sacred Openings**

*Alif-Lām-Mīm* belongs to the Qur'an's own class of *fawātiḥ* — the disconnected letters (*al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿah*) opening twenty-nine sūrahs, from al-Baqarah's identical opening to Qāf and Nūn. The earliest authorities received them with disciplined reverence: the position reported of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, and Ibn Masʿūd is that they are *mysteries (asrār) of God in the Qur'an*, whose key rests with Him; Ibn ʿAbbās transmitted that they stand as *abbreviated oaths and names from the Most Beautiful Names* — taking *Alif-Lām-Mīm* as a vocative-form of God's name itself; and al-Ṭabarī, after cataloguing the opinions (letters of the Book's names; letters forming half of every alphabet by which the nations write; tokens that the Book is built from the speech-signs of the Arabs themselves), preferred the reading that sustains the others without violence: the letters are among the names of the Qur'an and its sūrahs, as the Prophet ﷺ himself named them — he recited "Alif-Lām-Mīm al-Raḥmān" and "Ḥā-Mīm al-Qur'ān al-Karīm" in invocations.

A further lesson is fixed in their *function*: they arrive as a deliberate mystery at the very gate of the two longest recitations of revelation — training the reciter, before a single legible sentence, in the posture the whole Book demands: *reception before mastery*. The community that begins its reading with letters it cannot decode begins it rightly — humbled, open, listening. As the sages said: the Lord placed at the head of His speech a sign that speech touches places reason does not finish mapping.

**From Mystery to Majesty: The First Two Translations**

Only then does the train of meanings begin: *Allāh — lā ilāha illā huwa, al-ḥayy al-qayyūm*. The letters admit us; the Names crown us. And the Prophet's own practice made this sequence a supplication-file: in the pre-dawn prayer he would open with *"Alif-Lām-Mīm — Allāhumma innī aʿūdhu bika..."* among his beginnings, treating the sūrah-opener as a doorway for the tongue. The believer reciting these two verses at any daybreak thus stands in the oldest liturgy of Islam: mystery first, Majesty named; then the Book descends.

## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:2

> **God, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Creed of the Chapter in Seven Words**

After the letters, the sūrah's first full sentence is the shortest and the heaviest in all revelation: *Allāhu lā ilāha illā huwa, al-Ḥayyu al-Qayyūm* — "God: there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting." The sentence does three things at once. It names God with His essential Name, Allāh, which gathers every attribute of perfection. It then negates and affirms in a single breath: *lā ilāha illā huwa* — no object of worship whatsoever, except Him — the formula of tawḥīd on which Islam stands, which Ibn Taymiyyah described as a sentence whose negation clears the field of every false claimant so that the affirmation may stand alone, unobstructed. Then it seals the affirmation with two names that operate like a proof: *al-Ḥayy*, the Ever-Living, whose life is essential, uncaused, and undying; *al-Qayyūm*, the Self-Subsisting who subsists by Himself and sustains — *qayyūm* intensifying the root *qāma*, to stand — everything other than Himself. He stands needing none; all things stand needing Him. This is precisely the pairing enthroned in the greatest verse of the Qur'an: *"God — there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting. Neither slumber overtakes Him nor sleep"* (2:255), and the full discussion of these two names given in this series' commentary on Āyat al-Kursī applies here. The Prophet ﷺ indicated the eminence of this very line when he instructed that the most magnificent Name of God — the Name by which, when He is asked, He gives — is found in these two places. It is reported from Asmāʾ bint Yazīd in the Jāmiʿ of al-Tirmidhī:

> *"The greatest Name of God is in these two verses: 'And your God is One God; there is no god but He, the Compassionate, the Merciful' (2:163), and the beginning of Āl ʿImrān: 'Alif. Lām. Mīm. God, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting.'"* (al-Tirmidhī 3478; he graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ)

**An Answer to Najrān Written into the Opening**

Read against the sūrah's occasion, the verse is not an abstraction. The delegation whose arguments occasioned this revelation had proposed divinity for a man who was born from a womb, ate food, and would pass away. God's answer opens the chapter: the true God is *al-Ḥayy* — a life that death has never touched and never will — and *al-Qayyūm* — the very sustainer whose continuous upholding of Mary and her son was itself the proof that they were creatures, not creators. Ibn Kathīr notes the point explicitly: the Messiah, honored as he is, was sustained by the Sustainer; whoever is upheld by another cannot himself be the upholder of the worlds. And the Prophet's reported questioning of the delegates — "Do you not know that our Lord is Living and does not die, and that Jesus is subject to passing away?" — is this verse turned into a courtroom exchange. Theology here is logical hygiene: attributes belong to their proper bearer, and when they are transferred to one who manifestly lacks them, the error is not merely in loving the wrong being but in misreading the evidence of one's own eyes.

**What the Two Names Do to a Human Life**

The two names also work inwardly. To know that ultimate reality is *al-Ḥayy* is to be cured of the despair that whispers that life is a dying flame between two darknesses; the believer's existence is grounded in One whose life cannot flicker, and whose gift therefore cannot be exhausted. To know He is *al-Qayyūm* is to be cured of managerial anxiety: you are not the one holding the universe together, nor even your own household; you sleep nightly in the custody of One whom sleep never touches. The sūrah will later tell an army that slept on the field of Uḥud — "He sent down upon you, after sorrow, security, a sleepiness" (v. 154) — and the believer who has internalized verse 2 understands that sleep: hearts can let go because the Sustainer does not. Every muscle that unclenches in trust, every plan handed over after exhaustive effort, is verse 3:2 lived rather than merely recited.

## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:3

> **He sent down the Book upon thee in truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel**

**Expanded Commentary**

**One God, One Chain of Revelation**

Having named Himself as the Living, Self-Subsisting One, God immediately names His act toward mankind: the sending down of speech. *Nazzala ʿalayka al-kitāba bi-l-ḥaqq* — "He sent down the Book upon thee in truth" — and then, in the same sentence, the Torah and the Gospel. The structure is itself the chapter's first argument. The Qur'an is not announced as a rival scripture entering a market of religions; it is announced as the latest and sealing link in a single chain whose earlier links God Himself forged. To those Christians of Najrān who might hear this Book as an outsider's accusation, the opening answer is continuity: the God of Jesus is speaking, and He is the one who sent the Gospel to Jesus. Verse 4, continuous with this verse, will date those earlier scriptures "aforetime, as a guidance to mankind" — the chain is old, genuine, and honored.

The commentators note the two verbs: *nazzala* for "the Book upon thee," *anzala* (v. 4) for the Torah and the Gospel. Some, including al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī, hear a distinction: *tanzīl* with a doubled rhythm hints at the piecemeal descent of the Qur'an — apportioned over twenty-three years, verse answering event, law accompanying growth — while *īnzāl* befits books delivered to their prophets whole. Al-Ṭabarī, ever cautious, records the view that the two verbs function interchangeably in Qur'anic usage, so the safer ground is the fact itself: Muhammad ﷺ receives his Book in measures, as Moses and Jesus received theirs. Either way the verse carries a hidden mercy for the Prophet ﷺ personally: the assembly-line of revelation he had been undergoing — promptings that came with battle, marriage, treaty, and scandal alike — was not an anomaly but a mode of God.

**"In Truth, Confirming What Was Before It"**

The phrase *muṣaddiqan limā bayna yadayhi* — "confirming what was before it" — establishes the Qur'an's posture toward prior revelation: *taṣdīq*, attestation of truth. The Qur'an sets its seal to the originals of Torah and Gospel; what it later corrects, it corrects in the name of that attestation, distinguishing the revealed kernel from accretions of interpretation and transcription — "a party of them used to hear the words of God, then distort them knowingly after understanding" (2:75). Al-Rāzī pauses over "what was before it" (*mā bayna yadayhi*, literally "what is before its face"), for the idiom can mean what precedes in time or what lies present before one; the revealed past, he answers, is spoken of as present because it is so widely possessed and known. Either way, the image is of a Book facing the earlier books, looking at them directly — not a rumor about other scriptures but a verdict delivered in their sight. This is why the sūrah can soon invite Jews and Christians alike to be judged by their own texts (vv. 23, 93, 187), and why the Prophet ﷺ could adjudicate among the Jews of Madinah by the Torah they carried.

**The Unbroken Curriculum of Heaven**

There is a profound psychological rest in this verse for any believer who has ever wondered whether God changes His mind about human beings. The God of 3:3 is a teacher who has held the same class — *līl-nās*, for mankind, not for one tribe — since the first prophet, updating the materials as the students matured, never once abandoning the subject. "In truth" (*bi-l-ḥaqq*) guards the whole process from the suspicion of caprice: each descent was just, warranted, and proportionate. And for the individual reader there is a mirror here: a book "in truth" can only be received "in truth." One does not approach a chain of revelation stretching across millennia with the casualness of a browser tab; one comes the way the sūrah has just taught — letter by letter (v. 1), before the Living and the Self-Subsisting (v. 2), and with the humility to be confirmed and corrected at once.

## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:4

> **Aforetime, as a guidance to mankind. And He sent down the Criterion. Truly those who disbelieve in the signs of God shall have a severe punishment. And God is Mighty, Possessor of Vengeance.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Criterion and the Cost of Refusing It**

The verse completes the sentence of verse 3 and then turns, abruptly, from gift to warning. First the completion: Torah and Gospel came *min qablu* — aforetime — *hudan lil-nās*, "as a guidance to mankind." The universality of the phrase deserves pause. Mosaic law was addressed to a particular people, yet its guidance is here declared for *al-nās*, mankind: the light of the earlier scriptures was never a private lantern but a public one, in principle open to any human being who sought God through them. Then comes the third sending-down: *wa anzala al-furqān* — "and He sent down the Criterion." *Furqān* derives from the root *farqa*, to separate, divide, discriminate: it is that by which truth is sundered from falsehood, licit from forbidden, the saved from the ruined. Most commentators take the Criterion here to be the Qur'an itself, since it is elsewhere titled *Furqān* — *"Blessed is He Who sent down the Criterion upon His servant, that he may be a warner to the worlds"* (25:1) — and since God makes *furqān* the very fruit of reverence: *"O you who believe! If you reverence God, He will appoint for you a criterion"* (8:29). Others, noting that Moses and Aaron are each called possessors of *furqān* (2:53; 21:48), widened the term to discernment generally — the God-given faculty or document by which a community distinguishes. Al-Ṭabarī records a pointed reading for this context: since "the Book" of verse 3 already names the Qur'an, the Criterion may here name the decisive clarification concerning Jesus — the very sorting of truth from falsehood about him that this sūrah proceeds to perform. Whatever the exact referent, the theology is fixed: God's revelatory activity is not only instruction but *separation*. Every genuine descent of His word sorts humanity around itself.

**Why the Warning Arrives This Early**

The verse then closes with the first thunderclap of the chapter: *"Truly those who disbelieve in the signs of God shall have a severe punishment. And God is Mighty, Possessor of Vengeance."* The placement is deliberate. Having just established that Qur'an, Torah, and Gospel are one chain of His gifts, the verse declares the standing of those who respond to that chain with *kufr* — a word that in its root means to cover, to bury: to disbelieve in signs is to throw earth over evidence. The penalty is described as *ʿadhāb shadīd*, severe punishment, and then grounded in two attributes: might (*ʿazīz*), which none can overpower or escape, and *dhū intiqām*, Possessor of Vengeance — *intiqām* being the exacting of just retribution upon the one who has arrogantly persisted, never mere vindictiveness; the Qur'an reserves it for contexts of obstinate, knowing refusal. There is a logic here the believer should not rush past: guidance given publicly, cordially, and with evidence creates responsibility. The danger of revelation is not that it exists but that it was *heard*. Hence the sūrah's audience in Madinah — people of scripture, hearing God's freshest speech — is warned first among mankind. The principle generalizes: knowledge widens both the gate and the ledger. This is why the scholars taught that the proof of God stands against a person only once the message has truly reached him, and why concealment of clear truth is treated, later in this very sūrah (v. 187), as among the gravest of betrayals.
**Furqān: The Criterion That Splits the Road**

The third scripture named is *al-furqān* — from *farq*, separation: that which *separates* between truth and falsehood. Upon it the commentators differ harmoniously: many of the earliest (and al-Qurṭubī's review of them) take it as a title of the Qur'an itself — the Sent-Down that came *after* Torah and Gospel as their *confirmer and criterion over them* (the exact office named at 5:48: *muhaymin — guardian over* what preceded); others take it as the revealed distinction *within* each Book, by which each community knew right from wrong. Either way, the gentle trilogy of guidance (Torah, Gospel, Criterion) is followed immediately by the verse's grim twin-clause, and the juxtaposition is the whole doctrine: *inna alladhīna kafarū bi-āyāti Allāhi lahum ʿadhābun shadīd, wa-Allāhu ʿazīzun dhū intiqām* — "truly those who deny God's signs, theirs is a severe punishment; and God is Almighty, Lord of Retribution."

**ʿAzīz Dhū Intiqām: The Two Hands of the Lord**

*Intiqām* — from *naqama*: to punish with the taking-back of rights — completes the name-pair: *ʿazīz*, Might unapproachable, and *dhū intiqām*, possessor of exacting repossession. The verse thereby fixes, at the sūrah's opening, the full frame of its theology of scripture: God *gives guidance* — three Books, one light — and God *holds accountability* for its reception: the Furqān that sorts the roads also marks who walked which. Between these two hands the whole chapter will move — every call it sounds (v. 23, v. 64, v. 98) heard under His mercy, every refusal it records answered under His requital. The believer reads and takes both ends: the guidance is given free; the return is audit complete.

## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:5

> **Truly naught is hidden from God on earth or in Heaven.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Exposure That Frames the Whole Chapter**

Seven words, and the privacy of the universe evaporates: *inna Allāha lā yakhfā ʿalayhi shayʾun fī al-arḍi wa lā fī al-samāʾ* — nothing whatsoever is hidden from God, neither on earth nor in heaven. The comprehensiveness is achieved by rhythm as much as by words: *shayʾ*, "a thing," the most indefinite noun the language possesses, arrived at through the negation of hiding — so that no thing, in any place, escapes into concealment. And the geography is exhaustive: the earth beneath, where secrets are buried in vaults and hearts; the heaven above, where the affairs of angels and decrees unfold. Between the two there is no third realm to hide in.

Why here? The commentators read the verse as a seal upon the warning of verse 4. A threat of "severe punishment" is only as serious as the knowledge of the punisher; every human system of deterrence fails at the same point — the unseen act. God's, the verse declares, never fails, because there is no unseen. But verse 5 also plants a seed whose harvest fills the sūrah. This is the chapter in which men will hide in their souls what they do not disclose to the Prophet ﷺ (v. 154), in which a party will say with their mouths what is not in their hearts (v. 167), in which deceivers will whisper "had we any decision, we would not have been slain here" — all of it governed by 3:5, repeated almost verbatim near the close of the section: *"And God knows what lies within breasts"* (v. 154). The hypocrisy that Uḥud exposed was, in a sense, verse 5 acted out in history: what was hidden on earth from even the Messenger of God was never hidden from God for an hour. The same is true of the earlier theater of the sūrah: the Najrān delegation's private misgivings after the public debate, the party that planned to "believe at the morning and disbelieve at day's end" (v. 72) — verse 5 had already read those scripts.

**Knowledge Without Gap, and the Calm It Gives**

It is worth dwelling on *why* nothing is hidden from Him, because the logic of the verse carries its own comfort. Things are hidden from us because we stand outside them; our knowledge must travel across a gap. But God is the maker of everything known to Him, and a maker is not outside his making. The knot in the wood does not hide from the carpenter; the counter in the program does not hide from the programmer. Hiddenness is a relation between creatures, not between the Creator and His work. This is why the Qur'an can say elsewhere: *"Do they not know that God knows their secret and their private converse, and that God is Knower of the Unseen?"* (9:78) and *"Truly naught is hidden from God on earth or in Heaven. He it is Who forms you in the wombs however He will"* — the very juxtaposition our own verse 6 makes next.

And the comfort: a heart fully known need never perform. Much of human exhaustion is the exhaustion of managing appearances — curating the visible fraction of ourselves for employers, congregations, families. Verse 5 confronts and relieves at once. Confronts, because the hidden ledger is open somewhere; relieves, because the One holding it sees also the intentions, the beginnings, the buried tenderness, the repentance whispered at 3 a.m. that no human chronicler recorded. The believer's response to total exposure is not terror but honesty: since nothing can be hidden, nothing need be staged. Confession to Him is never news to Him; and that is precisely why it can be the beginning of mercy rather than the end of standing.
**Khafāʾ: The Root of Un-hiding**

*Lā yakhfā* — the verb from *khafāʾ*, concealment — arrives in the negative: *nothing hides from Him*. The universe's own sandwich of clauses — *in the earth nor in the heaven* — seals the totality at both poles of creation: nothing beneath, nothing above, escapes. The companions of this verse across the Book assemble their own chorus: "He knows the secret and the more hidden" (20:7); "with Him are the keys of the Unseen — none knows them but He; and He knows what is on land and in sea; not a leaf falls but He knows it" (6:59); and the intimacy-verse the Prophet's ﷺ generation heard as nearness: "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein" (50:16).

**No Privacy, No Abandonment: The Twin Reading of Total Knowledge**

Total knowledge terrifies until it is read as God intends it — and this sūrah itself supplies the key at every turn: the God from Whom nothing hides is the same Who forgives the repenters (v. 89), counts the seeds (v. 61), and feeds the birds of the air He counts (v. 49). The psychology of the believer converts surveillance into *companionship*: He Who knows all is thereby also the One Whose knowledge guarantees that no injustice done to you is unwitnessed, no hidden intention of yours unrewarded. Al-Rāzī's remark on these verses runs in this channel: knowledge-all-encircling is simultaneously the ground of accountability and the deepest of consolations — the two mature responses of the two humanities: to the unjust, a warning; to the striving, a Witness who never sleeps.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:6

> **He it is Who forms you in the wombs however He will. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Argument Every Person Carries in His Own Body**

The verse that follows the declaration of total knowledge names the most hidden workshop on earth: the womb. *Huwa alladhī yuṣawwirukum fī al-arḥāmi kayfa yashāʾ* — "He it is Who forms you in the wombs however He will." The verb *yuṣawwiru* comes from *ṣawwara*, to form, fashion, shape — one of God's own names is *al-Muṣawwir*, the Fashioner (59:24) — and its choice is exquisite. Of all human beginnings, the womb is the one place no parent, physician, or criminal could reach to direct the work; it is the innermost secrecy of the innermost creature. A verse about nothing being hidden from God (v. 5) is sealed by proof at the origin of every single reader: the concealed One was never concealed from the Concealer. Before you kept your first secret, He had already shaped your face, your sex, the span of your life, in a workshop sealed against every eye but His. There is therefore no such thing as a self-made human being. Every critic who would later dispute with this revelation — every delegate from Najrān, every schemer of Madinah, every reader today — arrives in the argument carrying in his own body the signature of the One he disputes with.

The clause *kayfa yashāʾ*, "however He will," guards the sovereignty of the work. The Qur'an unfolds the detail elsewhere: *"We created man from an extract of clay; then We placed him as a drop in a secure lodging; then We made the drop a clinging clot; then We made the clot a lump; then We made the lump bones, and clothed the bones with flesh; then We brought him forth as another creation — blessed be God, the best of creators"* (23:12–14); and: *"He forms you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in threefold darkness"* (39:6). *How* He wills also embraces the individuality of formation: no two wombs deliver the same person; faces, temperaments, and allotments differ by His wisdom, not by cosmic accident. The verse thus quietly forbids two common modern despairs — the despair of the person ashamed of his making, and the pride of the person congratulating himself for it. Both are answered in advance: the shaping was willed, and the Willer was wise.

**The Womb as Refutation**

Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī both draw the verse's immediate polemical edge: it strikes at the deification of Jesus at its root. The one about whom divine sonship was alleged *was himself formed in a womb however God willed*. The Qur'an will say it explicitly later in the sūrah — Jesus is created by the same "Be!" as Adam (v. 59) — but the argument is already laid down here, in the sūrah's second sentence of theology: the workshop of the womb belongs exclusively to the Mighty, the Wise. Whoever passed through that workshop as its product cannot be its Owner. The delegation's own concession, in the traditional account — that Mary bore Jesus as women bear children — is this verse's verdict conceded by the other side. And the closing pair of names, *al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm*, the Mighty, the Wise, fixes the point: His fashioning cannot be thwarted (Mighty) and cannot be random (Wise). Form follows wisdom; every reader's existence is therefore a message, and the first act of reading oneself rightly is gratitude toward the Fashioner.

**A Contemporary Mirror**

In an age that has made "identity" a project of self-fabrication, 3:6 offers a startlingly restful doctrine: the core of what you are was crafted before you could act, choose, or speak; it came to you as sheer gift, *kayfa yashāʾ*, from a will wiser than yours and mightier than any critic's. The practical fruit is not passivity — the same sūrah will soon demand striving, spending, persevering — but the end of self-contempt and of the anxious performance of being self-invented. You begin owned, formed, and intended. The question the sūrah poses for the rest of its length is only this: what will you do with the form He chose for you?

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:7

> **He it is Who has sent down the Book upon thee; therein are signs determined; they are the Mother of the Book, and others symbolic. As for those whose hearts are given to swerving, they follow that of it which is symbolic, seeking temptation and seeking its interpretation. And none know its interpretation save God and those firmly rooted in knowledge. They say, "We believe in it; all is from our Lord." And none remember, save those who possess intellect.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verse That Legislates How the Book Is Read**

This verse is the Qur'an's own treatise on hermeneutics — the most direct discussion in the Book of how sacred text is to be interpreted, by whom, and with what inner equipment. Every school of Islamic thought, from the jurists to the philosophers to the Sufis, has anchored its theory of reading in these few clauses, and every misuse of scripture from the first schism to the present day can be located somewhere in its diagnosis. It begins with *āyāt*, "signs" — the word western languages flatten into "verses," though Arabic reserves other words for the lines of poetry. A sign is something that points, and signs are naturally of kinds: some point so directly that all competent observers take the same direction; others point in ways that require return, depth, and qualification. The Qur'an itself, the verse declares, contains both species, and knowing which is which is among the master-skills of religion.

**Determined and Symbolic: What the Words Mean**

The *muḥkam* signs are the "determined" — from *ḥakama*, whose lexical field includes curbing a mount with a bit, judging, and rendering solid; a well-tied knot and a well-built structure are both *muḥkam*. These are the verses braced against misreading: the abolishing and the abolished in law, the everlasting moral commands — worship of One God, justice, honesty, generosity, prohibition of murder and adultery — the univocal creedal truths like the oneness declared in verse 2. They are, the verse says, *umm al-kitāb*, the Mother of the Book: the word *umm* serving, as it does in "Mother of Cities" for Makkah (6:92), to mean the origin, the flag around which a force rallies, the principal instances. Elsewhere the Book identifies the Mother of the Book with what is with God Himself — *"God effaces what He will and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book"* (13:39); *"truly it is with Us in the Mother of the Book"* (43:4) — identified by many with the Preserved Tablet (85:22). The *muḥkam*, then, are the Book's ground floor and load-bearing walls: what every other passage must be brought back to, the test by which interpretations stand or fall.

The *mutashābih* are the "symbolic," from the root of resemblance and similitude: things that resemble one another, and hence admit more than one face. The Qur'an describes itself as wholly *mutashābih* in one place — *"God has sent down the most beautiful discourse, a Book consimilar (mutashābih)"* (39:23) — and wholly *muḥkam* in another — *"a Book whose signs have been determined (uḥkimat)"* (11:1) — and the commentators (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr) harmonize the three descriptions: wholly determined because every line of it is genuinely God's word; wholly consimilar because its parts resemble one another in beauty and mutual confirmation; and, in the sense of our verse, partly univocal and partly multivalent. Multivalent does not mean murky or expendable. When the Book says *"the Hand of God is over their hands"* (48:10), no sound interpreter thinks the sentence expendable; they understand that "hand" here cannot be terminated at the literal sense of flesh and bone, because the Mother of the Book has already ruled that "there is nothing like unto Him" (42:11). The determined verses govern the symbolic; the symbolic invite depths the determined frame. Some placed the isolated letters of verse 1 in this category; some added matters like the exact hour of the world's end, which "none shall reveal at its time save He" (7:187).

**The Diagnosis of the Swerving Heart**

The verse's pivot is not intellectual but moral: *"As for those whose hearts are given to swerving (zaygh), they follow that of it which is symbolic, seeking temptation (fitnah) and seeking its interpretation (taʾwīl)."* *Zaygh* is a swerving from the straight — used of hearts (9:117; 61:5) and of eyes famously at the climax of terror (33:10). Al-Ṭabarī glosses the swerving ones as those in whom doubt and hypocrisy have taken hold; the verse thereby locates the abuse of scripture not in the text's ambiguities but in the reader's condition. Two occasions are transmitted for these words, and both are paradigms. The Christians of Najrān pressed the Prophet ﷺ: "Do you not say that Jesus is 'the Word of God and a Spirit from Him' (4:171)?" When he answered yes, they cried, "That suffices us!" — seizing a symbolic description as though it had closed the very question the determined verses reopen. And some Jews reportedly probed the isolated letters for the hidden duration of the Muslim community, treating the Book as a cryptographic code rather than a guidance. In both cases the pattern is identical: an agenda precedes the reading; the ambiguous is mined to serve it; *fitnah* — here both temptation and strife, the fires (2:217; 8:39) that ambiguity can be used to light — is the harvest. The al-Rāzī and al-Thaʿlabī both warn of the interpreter's oldest self-deception: to call "determined" whatever agrees with one's school and "symbolic" whatever does not. The verse stands guard over that maneuver: the diagnosis comes before the discussion — ask first whether the heart is swerving, then ask what the verse means.

**Who Knows the Interpretation? The Two Recitations of a Comma**

*Taʾwīl* — rendered "its interpretation" — carries in its root the sense of *returning a thing to its origin*, its ultimate reality; hence it is used of dreams (Sūrah 12) and of the end to which matters return (17:35). The verse then makes its most contested statement: *"And none know its interpretation save God — and those firmly rooted in knowledge (al-rāsikhūna fī al-ʿilm). They say, 'We believe in it; all is from our Lord.'"* The whole science of Islamic reading turns on where one pauses. Stop after "save God," and the deeply rooted are characterized not by mastery of the symbolic but by their *response* to it: "We believe in it; all is from our Lord" — the posture of faith before acknowledged mystery, acting by the determined and entrusting the rest (so al-Ṭabarī reports the rule: we believe in the *mutashābih*, but act only by the *muḥkam*). Read straight through, and the firmly rooted in knowledge are granted participation in the interpretation — the charter, as it were, of the entire learned tradition, for as al-Thaʿlabī observed, in practice no school has ever passed over any part of the Book in silence. The difference between the two readings is, in the end, one of humility's degree, not of method's content: both agree that the servant's share is *faith first* ("all is from our Lord"), and that any interpretation claiming finality about the depths has overstepped. Later centuries formalized the work: doctrinal and legal reading (*tafsīr*, broadly), and the deeper return of symbols to their spiritual realities (*taʾwīl*, broadly) — though the early masters, al-Ṭabarī included, used the words nearly interchangeably, and the hard professional distinction belongs to the maturity of the sciences.

**The Extremes It Forbids, and the Mind It Crowns**

Around this verse the commentators map the great fault-lines. At one extreme stands the flat literalism that reads every sign as determined, collapsing the symbolic into a single surface — even when that surface implies for the transcendent God the very created attributes His own determined verses deny He has. At the opposite extreme stands the allegorism that treats nearly everything as symbolic, dissolving the plain sense — and with it, law, promise, and history — into whatever the interpreter finds plausible. The first impoverishes God; the second impoverishes His Book. Between them stands the broad tradition: affirm the plain sense, then plumb it. The Sufis and philosophers — Ibn ʿArabī, Rūmī, Mullā Ṣadrā — insisted on holding all the levels at once: for them the error is not depth but monopoly, the claim of any single level to be the only one. And they add, precisely in the spirit of this verse's psychology, that access to the deeper levels is not a technique but a condition: the heart that is pure of swerving reads further, not because it is cleverer but because it is clearer — glass transmits more light when less colored.

The verse ends by crowning its own lesson: *"And none remember — none truly take admonition — save those who possess intellect (ulū al-albāb)."* The *lubb* is the kernel, the pith — the pure core of the mind after the shell of agitation and agenda is cracked away. It is the same word God will use for the sūrah's closing heroes, who read the creation of the heavens and the earth and conclude, "Our Lord, Thou hast not created this in vain" (v. 190). The chapter thus opens and closes with the same persons: not the pedants of ambiguity, not the enemies of depth, but the possessors of kernels — hearts stilled enough to let determined signs determine them, and reverent enough to let symbolic signs lead them further in.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:8

> **"Our Lord, make not our hearts swerve after having guided us, and bestow upon us a mercy from Thy Presence. Truly Thou art the Bestower."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prayer of Those Who Know How Hearts Behave**

Most of the commentators, following the flow of verse 7, place these words on the lips of *al-rāsikhūna fī al-ʿilm* — those firmly rooted in knowledge. The placement is itself a lesson in what knowledge does to a person. A shallow learning puffs; a deep one trembles. The people described a moment ago as the most steadfast of all readers open their mouths, and the first thing they ask for is not mastery, rank, or insight into the symbolic, but *steadfastness of heart*: "make not our hearts swerve *after having guided us*." The phrase "after having guided us" holds the rope of their fear: guidance is not a possession acquired once, like a deed of property, but a relation that must be renewed hourly; what was received can be reversed. They use the very word — *zaygh*, swerve — that the previous verse hung around the necks of the misreaders: the deeply rooted know that the disease of the misreaders is a cardiac disease, and that cardiac diseases are not conquered by certificates.

**The Ḥadīth of the Turned Hearts**

The Prophet ﷺ lived this supplication so constantly that his companions noticed it and asked about it. ʿĀʾishah, Anas, and others transmit that the most frequent of his oaths and prayers included the plea *Yā muqalliba al-qulūb, thabbit qalbī ʿalā dīnik* — "O Changer of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion." Anas relates in the Jāmiʿ of al-Tirmidhī:

> *"We said: O Messenger of God, we believe in you and in what you have brought — do you fear for us? He said: 'Yes; for the hearts are between two of the Fingers of God — He turns them as He wills.'"* (al-Tirmidhī 2140; graded ṣaḥīḥ)

Muslim records the matching imagery from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr:

> *"Verily the hearts of the children of Adam, all of them, are between two of the Fingers of the Merciful, as one heart; He directs them however He wills." Then the Messenger of God said: "O God, Director of hearts, direct our hearts to obedience to You."* (Muslim 2654)

Ponder who is praying: a prophet, sinless, already guided, already promised paradise — afraid nonetheless of *zaygh*; "do you fear for us?" his companions ask, astonished. If the firmest heart ever created asked for firmness, the supplication is not a liturgy of the weak but the daily maintenance of the strong, like a pilot re-checking his trim in clear air. The heart (*qalb*) in Arabic is named, the linguists observe, from *taqallub*, turning — its very name confesses its volatility. Verse 8 is therefore the prayer fitted to our anatomy: a turning organ, praying to the Turner to be turned rightly.

**"A Mercy from Thy Presence" — the Grammar of God's Nearness**

The request has two halves, and their pairing is subtle: protection from swerving is asked first; then positive bestowal — *wa hab lanā min ladunka raḥmah*, "and bestow upon us a mercy from Thy Presence." The preposition *ladun* is one of the Qur'an's treasures of nearness: not merely *min*, "from," but *ladun*, "from at Your own side," from Your very Presence — the same word used when God grants the saintly companion of Moses *raḥmah* from His Presence and teaches him *knowledge from Our Presence* (18:65). From this usage the tradition derived the term *al-ʿilm al-ladunī*: ladunnī knowledge, learning that arrives not through the usual conveyer-belts of book, teacher, and inference but as direct bestowal upon a purified heart. The deeply rooted evidently know the difference between information and gift. They ask not merely "teach us more," but "let mercy issue from the proximity of You" — for knowledge without mercy is the very formula of the swerving scholars verse 7 described.

And the closing name seals the request with the perfect attribute: *innaka anta al-Wahhāb* — "Truly Thou art the Bestower," the intensive form of giving, *wahhāb* from *hiba*, a gift with no obligation, no invoice, no return demanded. God's giving in this sūrah is repeatedly marked as measureless — "He provides for whomsoever He will without reckoning" (v. 27, v. 37) — and here the givers' own petition is addressed to the Giver's own name. The logic is delicate: we ask to be kept from swerving; but since even the wishing to be kept is itself a turning of the heart that only He can accomplish, we must borrow the strength to ask from the One we ask. All is gift, top to bottom — which is exactly what the firmly rooted said in the verse before: "All is from our Lord."

**For the Modern Heart That Turns for a Living**

Never in history have human hearts been engineered to turn as relentlessly as they are today — turned by feeds tuned to outrage, by markets tuned to appetite, by the thousand daily invitations to drift an inch from what one vowed at dawn. Verse 8 is the counter-practice the sūrah installs at its threshold: a short, repeatable prayer by which the guided acknowledge their physics. Not "make me never tempted" — temptation will come to prophets and saints — but "make not our hearts swerve after having guided us": let the turn stop at the shore of the vow. The companion-habit that Muslim piety built around this verse — morning and evening recitation, the Prophet's frequent plea taught verbatim to his followers — instructs that the medicine is taken in doses, daily, preventatively. Hearts do not hold; they are held. And the Hand that holds them is, the verse ends by reminding us, the most generous Hand in existence.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:9

> **Our Lord, Thou art the Gatherer of mankind unto a Day about which there is no doubt." Truly God will not fail the tryst."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Guidance Forward Looks Toward a Gathering**

The prayer of the deeply rooted closes with its third petition, and this time it is not exactly a request but a remembrance folded into an address: "Our Lord, Thou art the Gatherer of mankind unto a Day about which there is no doubt." Notice the sequence of the three cries of verses 8–9: keep our hearts from swerving; give us mercy from Your Presence; we know You will gather us. The order is the psychology of the journey. First, the present battle of the heart; then, the need of supply for the road; then, the destination that explains why the first two matter so urgently. People pray best when the ending is in view. A community that genuinely believes in its assembling before God prays differently, spends differently, endures differently — and a chapter that is about to march its readers through Uhud wants the destination fixed in their mouths from the beginning.

The verb for the gathering, *jāmiʿ*, carries the sense of assembling what is scattered: mankind, dispersed across centuries, continents, graves, and oceans, will be re-collected as though a shepherd were gathering a far-flung flock. "About which there is no doubt" (*lā rayba fīhi*) echoes the Book's own self-description at 2:2 — a Book "wherein is no doubt," leading to a Day "wherein is no doubt." The two certainties mirror each other: doubtless guidance, doubtless meeting. All the doubt-mongering of the chapter — the swerving hearts of verse 7, the numbered-days delusion of verse 24, the whispers at Uḥud — is answered before it begins: the rendezvous is fixed.

**The Tryst God Never Misses**

The verse seals with a divine attribute none of us have ever consciously named but all of us rely on: *inna Allāha lā yukhlifu al-mīʿād* — "Truly God will not fail the tryst." *Mīʿād* is an appointed meeting — a date set and guaranteed; the Qur'an uses it for the moment of judgment (34:30: "For you is the tryst of a Day you cannot hold back by an hour, nor put forward"), and for God's sworn promises generally (13:31; 39:20). Around this word cluster the theologians built the celebrated pair *al-waʿd wa-l-waʿīd* — the Promise and the Threat — the axis on which classical debates about the fate of sinners turned: God has pledged felicity to faith and retribution to obstinate disbelief, and His pledge never lapses. Human appointments lapse constantly; we miss them through weakness, forgetfulness, changed minds. Each failure-mode is excluded in God: no weakness in the Mighty (v. 4), no forgetfulness in the Living and Self-Subsisting (v. 2), no change of mind in the Wise (v. 6). The tryst stands.

There is a devotional genius in ending the supplication this way. We beg for steadfast hearts and for mercy from His Presence — but both requests ride finally on His fidelity, not ours. The deeply rooted do not conclude with "we shall never swerve"; they conclude with "Thou wilt never fail." Their confidence is relocated from self to Lord. In an age of canceled appointments and quietly broken contracts — statistic and ethos both — the verse calls its reader to build his entire interior architecture on the one appointment that has never been, and can never be, broken; and then to order every lesser appointment — prayers, debts, promises, treaties — as so many rehearsals for the keeping of that one.
**Yawm al-Jamʿ: The Day of Three Gatherings**

*Jāmiʿ al-nās* — Gatherer of mankind — builds on the root *j-m-ʿ*, and the commentators open the gathering's three directions: peoples gathered to one plain ("the Day the earth splits from about them, hasting — that is a muster easy for Us," 50:44); generations gathered across time — first and last in one assembly, no century excused; and deeds gathered to their authors — every mailed work arriving at its addressee, per the chapter's own forwarding-language (vv. 25, 30, 182). *Li-yawmin lā rayba fīh* — "for a Day in which there is no doubt": the doubt-negation is categorical — *rayb* being the suspicion that unsettles certainty — for the Day's reality stands on God's own announcement, doubly sealed.

**The Tryst Kept: God Does Not Fail Appointments**

*Inna Allāha lā yukhlifu al-mīʿād* — "God does not fail the Promised-Date": the mīʿād-word is the word of a fixed rendezvous, a planned meeting. Its use here, at the sūrah's first eschatological beat, installs the chapter's reigning assurance: every date God has set holds. The Book rings the same bell wherever appointments are spoken of: "God's promise — God does not break the tryst, but most people know not" (39:20); and at 3:194 — the prayer of the wise at the sūrah's close — the faithful will quote this very title back to Him: *"Truly You do not fail the tryst."* The distance between v. 9 and v. 194 is two hundred verses of proof, but the doctrinal line is one sentence: what is dated by God is as done as the past; only the calendar conceals it.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:10

> **As for those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them aught against God. And it is they who shall be fuel for the Fire.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Investments That Cannot Be Cashed**

The address now turns from the praying hearts of verses 8–9 to the opposite condition, and the turn is marked by a shift of grammatical person that the commentators habitually note: God speaks to the believers directly, and *about* the disbelievers — distance itself drawn in grammar. The verse names the two assets in which human beings across all cultures place their ultimate earthly security: *amwāl*, wealth — the asset that buys protection, status, medicine, lawyers, and time; and *awlād*, children — the asset that extends the self beyond death, fights for the old, avenges the wronged, and recites the family's name into the future. Against *God*, the verse rules, both portfolios yield nothing: *lan tughniya ʿanhum ... shayʾan* — they will avail them nothing whatsoever. The definite object of the availing — "against God" (*min Allāh*) — is precise. Wealth avails against poverty, children against loneliness; neither avails "against God," because the transaction required at the end is not of the currency they circulate in.

The Qur'an returns to this audit repeatedly, and the commentators of this verse marshall the ledger. Wealth and children are themselves His gifts in the first place (16:72: "God has made for you spouses of your own kind, and made for you from your spouses children and grandchildren, and provided you of the good things"); they become trials as easily as they become pride — *"Your wealth and your children are but a trial"* (64:14; 8:28); they distract — *"O you who believe! Let not your wealth and your children divert you from the remembrance of God"* (63:9); and what actually endures is named plainly: *"Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world, but the enduring good works are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope"* (18:46). The warning is never against owning but against *banking* — mistaking the decorative liquidity of the world for the capital of the next. It is the difference between a traveler who uses foreign currency at the market and one who hoards it past the border, where the exchange window no longer exists.

**Fuel, and the Hadith That Burns Complacency**

Then the image turns severe: *ulāʾika hum waqūdu al-nār* — "it is they who shall be fuel for the fire." *Waqūd* is what a fire consumes to keep burning — wood, coke. The economies of earth, inverted: the man who amassed and fathered and neglected God discovers that what he built fed nothing but the flame, and that he himself is the load it burns. The verse stands in a family of like severity — *"fear the Fire whose fuel is people and stones"* (2:24; 66:6); *"you and what you worship apart from God are fuel of Hell; you are bound for it"* (21:98).

And lest the believers file the warning under "other people," the Prophet ﷺ brought it inside the mosque. In a hadith transmitted in the Musnad and the Sunan literature he described a coming generation of Qur'an-reciters and teachers who would count no one above them on account of their learning — and named them, in the most sobering possible extension of our verse, "fuel for the Fire": offices of religion carried without the substance of religion. The warning travels the whole distance from the wealthy pagan to the decorated hypocrite: whatever the asset class — gold, sons, titles, or tajwīd — nothing avails against God except what was transacted *for* God alively. The next verse will show the principle in history: Egypt's house had wealth and heirs aplenty.
**The Furnishing That Failed: Āl Firʿawn as Standing Type**

The verse names the exemplars by dynasty: *ka-daʾbi āli firʿawna wa-lladhīna min qablihim* — "after the wont of Pharaoh's folk and those before them": the *daʾb* — wont, habitual course — of a house that possessed everything the chapter has just declared helpless: the Nile's agriculture, the granaries, the armies, the monuments. Their destiny-clause is terminal in its scantness: *kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā fa-akhadhahumu Allāhu bi-dhunūbihim* — "they denied Our signs, and God seized them for their sins." *Akhadha* — seized — is the verb of a grip that closes on availability: no chase, no siege; the Lord of all simply *seized*.

**Seizure for Sins: The Causality the Empires Missed**

*Bi-dhunūbihim* — "for their sins" — is the moral pivot the Book refuses to surrender: the seizure was never naked power; it was billed to their own account. The Qur'an walks through Firʿawn's history in scores of verses to document the billing — nine signs (17:101), the flood and locusts (7:133), the prolonged call of Moses — and then the verdict: "so We seized him and his hosts, and cast them into the sea; behold how was the end of the wrongdoers" (28:40). For the first audience in Madinah the pointedness was immediate: the Quraysh of Badr were the local Āl Firʿawn — their scholars' pride, their merchants' confidence — and verse 11 makes the address explicit with the Badr-day slaying: *as had been the wont before, so be warned*. Every later age re-reads the verse in its own mirror: any establishment whose signs-of-God-denial proceeds while its treasuries still perform has purchased, not exemption, but *sequence*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:11

> **[It is] like the affair of the House of Pharaoh and those who were before them; they denied Our signs. So God seized them for their sins, and God is severe in retribution.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Precedent Set in Pharaoh's Ruins**

The abstract law of verse 10 — wealth and children avail nothing — is immediately given its historical exhibit. *Ka-daʾbi āli Firʿawn* — "like the affair of the House of Pharaoh." The word *daʾb* is worth unpacking, for it is chosen with surgical breadth: it means a matter, a case, an affair, but also a *wont*, a custom, a repeated way of proceeding. So the comparison runs in two directions at once: their affair — the historical case study, documented and closed; and their *wont* — a repeatable pattern of behavior that later generations can slide into without noticing they have joined an old procession. The House of Pharaoh was the ancient world made confident: granaries full, armies massed, a dynasty that had conflated longevity with legitimacy so thoroughly that its king could say "I am your most high lord" (79:24). "And those who were before them" widens the exhibit — ʿĀd, Thamūd, the cities overturned — a gallery of the powerful who discovered that scale is not shelter.

The indictment is specified: *kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā* — "they denied Our signs." The ruin of a civilization is here traced not to economics, weather, or geopolitics, but to a spiritual verb: the covering that follows recognition, the *takdhīb* — calling true things false because their truth is expensive. God's signs had arrived to Pharaoh's court not as whispers but as nine public signs (cf. 17:101; 27:12); his house had the very thing verse 3 honored — revelation's chain — and sold it for the continued enjoyment of being unreformable. Then comes the seizure: *fa-akhadhahumu Allāhu bi-dhunūbihim* — "God seized them for their sins." *Akhadha* in Qur'anic usage is never a casual taking; it is the closed fist of justice — *"and such is the seizure of your Lord when He seizes the cities that are doing wrong; indeed His seizure is painful, severe"* (11:102). Note the causal precision: *for their sins*. The seizure was not arbitrary wrath but earned harvest; a law, not a tantrum. The verse ends with the attribute that matches the act: *wa Allāhu shadīdu al-ʿiqāb* — "God is severe in retribution," the same note struck at verse 4, forming a frame around the chapter's teaching of revelation and refusal.

**Why Believers Are Told This Story at All**

One might ask why a sūrah addressing the Madinan believers — people already Muslims — spends its eleventh verse on Pharaoh. The answer lies in the sociology of warning. Faith does not immunize a community against the *disease* of Pharaoh — the confidence of the established. Madinah in year three was acquiring exactly what Pharaoh once owned: treasury, treaties, an army, neighbors who flattered. The verse instructs the new commonwealth to read every Pharaoh as a mirror held up in advance: buildup is not blessing by itself; continuity is not covenant. In our terms: GDP is not guidance. The believer reading 3:11 audits his own institutions — mosque, company, party, family — with a single question: are our signs being denied here, politely, procedurally, by people whose granaries are full? And the private audit follows: every sin I persist in while my storehouses stand is a small rehearsal of the House of Pharaoh, whose wont (*daʾb*) began — as everyone's does — with one denied sign it was inconvenient to obey.
**Daʾb: The Wont-Word and Its Chain of Dynasties**

The participle *ka-daʾbi* — "in the manner of the wont of" — contains a whole philosophy of history in one noun. *Daʾb* is doing-by-habit, the settled course of an actor: the Qur'an's dynastic term for the *repeating behavior-pattern* of civilizations before God. Pharaoh's folk had a daʾb: hear the signs, call them sorcery, persist, boast, drown. The nations before them had theirs. The pattern's *predictability* is precisely the prophet-office's burden and consolation: nothing the warners meet is new; nothing the seizers do is arbitrary: "you will find no alteration in the wont (sunnah) of God" (35:43) — the Book's twin-term for the same ledger.

**Why the First Readers Were Shown Pharaoh**

For the Muslims of year 2–3 the verse was not archaeology but *intelligence*: the Makkan establishment, with its commerce-networks and poets and idols garrisoned round the House, stood exactly in the daʾb-line — and the exact matching detail arrives in v. 12–13: *the gathering at Badr*, where "a company fought in God's way, and another disbelieving — seeing them twice their own number by the eye's own sight." God therefore reminds the young ummah, in the grammar of dynasties: Pharaoh's Nile afforded no more exemption than Quraysh's wells of Badr; the seizure precedes the monument. And the believer receives the verse's private edition: any heart that builds its Firʿawn — pride's dynasty over God's signs — books the same appointment.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:12

> **Say to the disbelievers, "You shall be vanquished and gathered unto Hell, an evil resting place!"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Defeat Dated Twice: In This World and the Next**

The first direct command of the sūrah to the Prophet ﷺ is a commission to deliver bad news: *qul lilladhīna kafarū sa-tughlabūna wa tuḥsharūna ilā jahannam* — "Say to those who disbelieve: you shall be vanquished, and gathered unto Hell." Two verbs, two theaters. *Tughlabūn* — you will be overcome, defeated — in time, on earth, in the arena they trust. *Tuḥsharūn* — you will be herded, mustered, gathered — in eternity, in the custody they deny. The twin certainty is declared to their faces, and the commentators identify two audiences. Al-Thaʿlabī and others take it as addressed to the idolaters of Makkah, forecast of the sequence that was in fact fulfilled — Badr, then the breaches of treaty, then the bloodless conquest. Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī preserve the account that it was addressed first to the Jews of Madinah, whom the Prophet ﷺ, returning victorious from Badr, warned that the fate of Quraysh could be theirs; they dismissed the warning with a merchant's disdain — we know war; these men are unlettered grazers — and verses 12–13 answered their confidence. On either reading, the verse is an announcement of outcome before the battle, the sort of statement that can only be made safely by the Omniscient.

The destination is then named with grim irony: *jahannama, wa biʾsa al-mihād* — "Hell — an evil resting place." *Mihād* is a prepared bed, a smoothed resting-spot, related to *mahd*, a cradle; the language of comfort is repossessed for horror, as though to say: they were offered rest and chose a bed prepared in fire. The Qur'an names the same resting place for the same people elsewhere — "an evil resting place" (2:126; 3:162, 197) — and the recurrence creates a vocabulary of homelessness at the heart of rejection: the one who refuses his Lord's direction finally comes to rest, but in the last place rest can be found.

**Forecast as Mercy**

It is worth asking why God commands His Prophet to tell an opponent in advance that he will lose. There is mercy embedded in the forecast. A warning delivered while there is still time to change the outcome is not taunting but an open door: the verse is a threat, but a threat announced is an invitation in disguise — leave the column marching to defeat, and the prophecy concerning you is canceled by your leaving. The pattern holds across the Book: the warner (*nadhīr*) and the bringer of good news (*bashīr*) are one office. Nor is the believer who carries such news permitted to relish the ruin; he is commanded to *say* it, no more. The Prophet's own tears over enemies are part of the record. The commission of 3:12 is the purest possible duty of truth-telling: deliver the whole sentence — defeat and bed of fire — then step back, for the rest is theirs. Every age gives the faithful versions of this duty: speaking unpopular verdicts — about exploitation, about addiction, about godless prosperity — not from superiority but from the terrifying knowledge of Someone who keeps every appointment (v. 9) and misses no hidden thing (v. 5).
**Tughlabūn: The Passive Voice of a Prophecy Already Signed**

The address-command — *qul li-lladhīna kafarū* — "say to those who disbelieve" — is one of the Qur'an's boldest exercises in foretelling: issued in Madinah, before Badr, to a community of scarcely three hundred fighters, it declares in the passive of perfect certainty: *sa-tughlabūna wa tuḥsharūna ilā jahannam* — "you shall be overcome and gathered into Hell." The passives deserve their weight: *tughlabūn* leaves the Overcomer unnamed, for every agency of the overcoming — angels, rain, terror, a handful of believers — is but His instrument; and *tuḥsharūn* — gathered — links the earthly defeat to muster-day, as though the battle's outcome were itself a gate into the assembly of judgment. Ibn ʿAbbās's report, treasured in all the tafsīr, records that ʿUmar said on the day of Badr: *who promised this? — God promised this* — as the prophecy's word turned visible in the dust of the well.

**Wa Biʾsa al-Mihād: The Bedding of the Proud**

The verse seals with the same *mihād* — resting-spread — that awaits the disbelieving caravan at v. 197's close of the chapter. The word is domestic, deliberately: men march to secure their *beddings* — estates, cushions, heirlooms — and the Book names the final bedding of the sign-deniers. *Sa-tughlabūn* is thus not only information for its first addressees but a standing rule of address: truth's messenger may say to every open enemy of God's signs, in every century, the same sentence — not as threat hurled but as physics recited: *the sequence is fixed: sign-offered, sign-denied, overcome, gathered.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:13

> **There was a sign for you in the two hosts that met, one host fighting in the way of God and the other disbelieving, whom they [the former] saw as twice themselves as the eye sees. And God strengthens by His help whomsoever He will. Truly in that is a lesson for those who possess insight.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Badr as Permanent Evidence**

The promised defeat has already had its rehearsal in history: *qad kāna lakum āyatun fī fiʾatayn iltaqatā* — "there was a sign for you in the two hosts that met." The consensus of the commentators — al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī — fixes the reference: Badr, in the second year after the Hijrah, the first large clash of the new community with the establishment of Makkah. Some three hundred and thirteen believers, provisioned for a raid on a caravan, met a professional army of near a thousand. The Qur'an here turns that morning into standing evidence — an *āyah* — placed deliberately at the head of a chapter whose center will be the harder morning of Uḥud. The pairing matters: before the sūrah teaches the community how defeat works, it grounds them in how victory worked; before it warns "you shall be vanquished" (v. 12) to the enemy, it shows the believers the One by whom the vanquishing of the stronger came to pass.

**Seen as Twice: The Optics of Trust**

The most debated detail is the perception clause: the disbelieving host was seen by the believers "as twice themselves, as the eye sees" — *raʾya al-ʿayn*, in plain ocular sight, not as rumor or estimate. Elsewhere God says He *showed* each side the other as few (8:44: "when He showed them to you, when you met, as few in your eyes, and made you appear few in their eyes, so that God might accomplish a matter already enacted"). The commentators reconcile the two reports along two lines. One: the perception shifted — seen small while marching (to steel the believers' resolve to advance), then seen at double on contact, yet still borne with, because the smaller certainty of God's help outweighs ocular arithmetic; al-Rāzī notes the sight is expressly qualified "as the eye sees," meaning there was no illusion — the actual discrepancy was simply not as terrifying as it should have been, and that is the miracle of morale. Two: "twice" can be heard as doubling-over, closer to the traditionally given ratio of three to one. But the effort spent on reconciling numbers risks muffling the verse's own conclusion, which is not numerical at all: *wa Allāhu yuʾayyidu bi-naṣrihi man yashāʾ* — "God strengthens with His help whomsoever He will." The help of God (*naṣr*) is a causal power that does not read headcounts. The arithmetic of 313 against a thousand was designed to show all later arithmeticians of God's religion what the term "in the way of God" (*fī sabīl Allāh*) is worth as a combat multiplier.

**A Lesson for the Proprietors of Insight**

The verse ends with its target audience: *inna fī dhālika la-ʿibratan li-ulī al-abṣār* — "truly in that is a lesson for those who possess insight." *ʿIbrah*, a lesson, is literally a crossing — something by which you cross (*ʿabara*) from the seen to the unseen, from an event to its meaning. And the eyes named are *abṣār*, inner sight: the perception that evaluates. Badr is staged as a standing exercise in seeing straight. The world will always present its evaluations in terms of hosts and numbers — market shares, battalions, majorities, banks. The eye trained by 3:13 looks past the census to the Co-efficient: withness (*maʿiyyah*) of God, by which He, and not the arithmetic, decides. The believer does not disdain preparation — this same sūrah will commend resolve and consultation (vv. 159–160) and blame the archers for abandoned positions — but he refuses to let census outrank covenant. This is the exact education Uḥud will require: the same God, a different morning, an army this time chastised for trusting a number and a hill. The possessors of insight learn Badr's lesson so they will not have to learn Uḥud's twice.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:14

> **Made to seem fair unto mankind is the love of passions, among them women, children, hoarded heaps of gold and silver, horses of mark, cattle, and tillage. Those are the enjoyment of the life of this world. And God, with Him is the beautiful return.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Beautification Machine**

The sūrah turns from the battlefield of numbers to the subtler battlefield that precedes and explains it: desire. *Zuyyina lil-nāsi ḥubbu al-shahawāt* — "made to seem fair unto mankind is the love of passions." The passive — *zuyyina*, "was beautified" — is the verse's thesis in a single word. The attractiveness of these things is real, not hallucinated, but it is *dressed*: presented by an agent — Satan adorning (cf. 8:48; 15:39), the soul's own love of adornment, the consensus of a consumer civilization — in a manner that exaggerates the glow and conceals the terms. The Qur'an does not deny the glitter; it names the jeweler. Elsewhere the same verb describes how evil deeds are "made fair" to a man "so that he sees them as good" (35:8). The first step in religious seriousness is not hatred of the world but recognition of the styling department.

The catalogue that follows is a cross-section of a seventh-century Arabian's dream-portfolio, and — structurally — of every portfolio since.
