> **Say, "If you love God, follow me, and God will love you and forgive you your sins. And God is Forgiving, Merciful."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Litmus Test of Love**

Few verses compress an entire spiritual science into one sentence as this one does. *Qul in kuntum tuḥibbūna Allāha fa-ttabiʿūnī yuḥbibkumu Allāh* — "Say: If you love God, follow me; God will love you." The logic is that of a test — the grammarians call the structure a conditional whose two limbs define each other: the claim of love is the protasis; the imitation of the Messenger ﷺ is the verification; God's love in return is the outcome. The early Muslims called it *āyat al-miḥnah* — the Verse of the Test. The commentators transmit its backdrop: whispered claims that love of God needed no law — the Najrān Christians saying they worshiped the Messiah *out of love* for God; the pagan Arabs saying of their idols, *"we do not worship them save to bring us nigh in nearness unto God"* (39:3). To every such claim of devotion detached from obedience, the verse replies with the only instrument that distinguishes love from mood: conformity of the life of the lover to the way of the beloved's chosen one. The Christian claim is answered with precision: your love for God must run in the channel God *Himself* dug — if the latest prophet is God's, love demands following *him*; if it refuses the channel, the love is for one's own idea of God, not for God. Al-Thaʿlabī transmits the penetrating hadith: *"Idolatry (shirk) is more hidden than the creeping of an ant on a black stone in a dark night; and the least of it is to love something tyrannical or to hate something just. Is religion aught but loving in God and hating in God? God said: Say, 'If you love God, follow me, and God will love you.'"* Love, sorted by its object and proven by its ethics, is either worship or shirk with pious vocabulary.

**Love Rendered a Verb: Follow**

Note the imperative's choice: not "believe me" or even "obey me" (that comes in v. 32) but *ittabiʿūnī* — *follow* me. *Ittibāʿ* is to walk behind someone, matching his steps — a discipleship of gait. A follower is on a path; the way beloved becomes the way taken. The Book's praise of the Prophet is framed precisely as exemplary walk: *"Indeed you have in the Messenger of God a beautiful example (uswah ḥasanah) for whoever hopes in God and the Last Day"* (33:21). Following differs from obedience as travel differs from transaction: obedience can be episodic; following is a life-pattern. And the distinction between this verse and the next — *follow me* (v. 31) versus *obey God and obey the Messenger* (v. 32) — the commentators savor: one cannot ordinarily "follow" God the way one follows a human guide; with God, the relation must be obedience and worship; with the Messenger, who walked on earth as we do, it can be *imitation* — God arranged to make the abstract love of the Unseen practicable by giving love a visible road.

**The Return Love, and the Forgiveness That Travels With It**

The verse's promise is two gifts, ordered. First: *yuḥbibkumu Allāh* — God will *love you*. In the Qur'an's economy of love, God's love for human beings is mentioned more often than their love for Him, and the spiritual masters make the reason a principle: our love is response; His is gift. The very first movement of love was His — "He brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing" (16:78), before you could love anything at all. To become *beloved of God* — the Prophet's own title was Ḥabīb Allāh — is the highest station a creature can hear; the famous hadith qudsī describes its completion: *"When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his seeing with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks; and if he asks Me, I shall surely give him"* (al-Bukhārī 6502). Second: *wa yaghfir lakum dhunūbakum* — and forgive you your sins. Forgiveness is attached to love's promise because the follower remains imperfect: his following stumbles, and divine love in the Qur'an is never the love of a cold admirer of the flawless — it is the love that covers, restores, and repeats. Hence the seal: *wa Allāhu ghafūrun raḥīm* — "God is Forgiving, Merciful" — the two names that answer to the two fears of every sincere lover: that one's past disqualifies one (Ghafoor: covered), and that one's present is unworthy (Raheem: cherished anyway).

**For Every Modern Claimant of Devotion**

The verse is permanently contemporary. Every age manufactures loves of God that bypass His Messenger: spirituality without Sunnah, sentiment without law, "God in my heart" without God in the conduct. Verse 3:31 is the standing audit — a sentence intentional enough to be terrifying and gracious enough to be a door: *prove it, and be loved*. The follower's program is not imitation at the level of costume but at the level of the covenant-virtues the sūrah has been teaching: truthfulness when it costs (v. 17), spending from the beloved shelf (v. 14), keeping covenant (v. 76), piety hidden at dawn (v. 17). Love that stops at the feeling is, by this verse's standard, not yet love; love that becomes following is *met* — the way a road meets a traveler — by the Love it walked toward.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:32

> **Say, "Obey God and obey the Messenger." If they turn away, then truly God loves not the disbelievers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Proof of Love to the Practice of Command**

Verse 31 ended in love's promise; verse 32 descends to command's form: *qul aṭīʿū Allāha wa-l-rasūl* — "Say: obey God and obey the Messenger." The shift is deliberate. Love was the *interior* test (v. 31); obedience is the *exterior* shape love takes in law and life. The two are not rivals but the inside and outside of one thing — a point the early theologians made when distinguishing the terms: *ittibāʿ* (following) aims at the heart's orientation and the life's pattern; *ṭāʿah* (obedience) aims at the concrete act under a concrete command. The verse pairs God and Messenger in one breath — and here lies a structural pillar of Islam. In the earliest community, and ever since, God's command comes not by way of vague inspiration but by way of *wahy* — the revealed Book — and the Messenger's command is its executrix; hence the normal prophetic task itself, delivered in exactly these terms in 4:59 and 4:80: *"Whosoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God."* The pairing legislates the Sunnah's very authority: the Prophet's guidance is not a commentary by a first believer but the living form of the command. Al-Qurṭubī underscores that the verse's grammar is not "obey God and the Messenger" as one compound object, but the verb repeated — *obey... and obey* — an emphatic doubling the lawyers read as a full, independent command-address to each: God's command directly in the Book; the Messenger's command in what he legislated and exemplified. This is among the verses (with 4:59; 4:65; 4:80; 33:36; 59:7) from which the entire architecture of Islam's second source — the normative precedent of the Prophet ﷺ — is built.

**Turning Away: The Diagnosis Sentences Itself**

Then the verse states the alternative with clinical brevity: *fa-in tawallaw fa-inna Allāha lā yuḥibbu al-kāfirīn* — "if they turn away, truly God loves not the disbelievers." The conditional is beautiful in its revelation: turning away is itself the identifier — refusal of the channel of command *is* kufr in action; it needs no creedal disclaimer from a pulpit. And the sentence pronounced is not "God will punish the disbelievers" (true elsewhere) but *God loves them not* — the direct antithesis of verse 31's promise: follow, and be loved; turn, and forfeit love. The trading-floor of verses 31–32 has two prices and one coin. To internalize the severity: Islam's measure of ruin is not primarily God's anger but the withdrawal of His love — for love in His speech means election, care, drawing-near (cf. the chain of "God loves not": the transgressor, 2:190; the arrogant boaster, 4:36; the traitor, 4:107; the corrupter, 5:64); its opposite is exposure — the soul left to its own managers, the very catastrophe the deeply rooted prayed against in verse 8.

For the believer who recites it, the verse operates as a daily summons to coherence: obedience is love's body; where obedience is chronically refused, the love-talk has a leak. And yet — the mercy of the pairing with verse 31 must not be missed — the road back is never a new religion; it is the same road, *follow me*, permanently open, sealed with "Forgiving, Merciful" (v. 31). Between the two verses the whole pattern of the religion stands: God's love offered through a Messenger, refused only by turning, and restored only by returning.
**Love-Obama? No — Love Negated: The Form and Its Reach**

*Wa-Allāhu lā yuḥibbu al-kāfirīn* — "and God does not love the disbelievers": the sūrah's love-register, opened so warmly in v. 31 (*follow me, God will love you*), now shows its other hand. The class-negation — *kāfirīn*, disbelievers *as a category* — is among the Book's strongest verdicts, and the commentators mark its jurisprudence exactly: God's love is the goal toward which every command aims and the prize of every relinquishment; its negation, therefore, defines the disobedient direction *itself*. Al-Ṭabarī: *He does not love them means He does not approve them nor their works nor does He reward them in the Hereafter*. The love that the chapter lays in sequence — love of God (v. 31's goal), love of the reverent (v. 76), of the muḥsinīn (v. 134), of the patient and the reliant (v. 146), of the pure and just (v. 150's environment; 5:42; 9:7) — has now its stated negative pole, and the believer measures his direction by it: *to be moving toward God's love, or moving outward from it.*

**Obeisance, or Aversion: The Sentence's Either/Or**

The imperative paired the Messenger with God — *obey God and the Messenger* — because revelation's chain is continuous: what the Messenger conveys *is* God's obedience-portion. Refusal's second clause — *if they turn away* — hence the necessity of the verdict-clause: turning is itself named; disbelief of the ones turning stipulated. Obedience is not ritual garnish upon love but *evidence in love's trial*: the believer's claim of loving God stands or falls in the docket of obedience — as v. 31 set the claim and v. 32 now sets its test — a parity the Book insists upon wherever love is put in evidence.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:33

> **Truly God chose Adam, Noah, the House of Abraham, and the House of ʿImrān above the worlds,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Family Tree of Guidance**

With this verse the sūrah begins its central sacred history, and it opens not with a person but with a principle: divine election. *Inna Allāha iṣṭafā Ādama wa Nūḥan wa āla Ibrāhīma wa āla ʿImrāna ʿalā al-ʿālamīn* — "Truly God chose Adam, Noah, the House of Abraham, and the House of ʿImrān above the worlds." The verb *iṣṭafā* — chose, elected, selected out — from *ṣafw*, the pure extract of a thing — is a profound way to describe God's favorites: they are the clarified portion of humanity, refined for His purposes. It is the same root that gives the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ one of his dearest titles among Muslims: *al-Muṣṭafā*, "the Chosen One." Election, in Qur'anic logic, is never genealogical accident nor earned résumé; it is an act of divine wisdom that chooses vessels and then fills them — *"God knows best where to place His message"* (6:124). The verse gathers four nodes of the one chain: Adam, the first man and first prophet, chosen as the species' root; Noah, chosen as the species' second root after the Flood; the House of Abraham, trunk of prophethood in the enduring line, in whose loins the covenant ran (2:124; 19:58); and the House of ʿImrān — the family whose story this sūrah is about to tell: the dedicated grandmother, the consecrated daughter Mary, her guardian Zachariah, and at its crown, Jesus — *ʿĪsā ibn Maryam* — the last great messenger of the Israelite line.

The phrase *ʿalā al-ʿālamīn* — "above the worlds" — means above all the peoples of their ages, as the same phrase honors other prophets (2:47; 6:86–90). Note the care of the list: it is not "all Israelites" but a distilled succession — Adam to Noah to Abraham's house to ʿImrān's house. Election is personal and covenantal, not ethnic and automatic. The sūrah has already dismantled the idea that descent itself saves (vv. 10, 23–24); now it shows what descent from the chosen actually is: a *trust* that runs in families and is discharged or betrayed person by person.

**Who Is Blessed to Be Named? — Mary, the Mother of the Chapter**

Of the four names, one is a surprise by worldly measure: not a king, not a conqueror-prophet, but a household unknown to history until revelation honored it — the family of ʿImrān. Ḥadīth and the sīrah record no worldly exploit of ʿImrān himself; his glory is his daughter and his daughter's Son. The sūrah itself will proceed to explain why this house was chosen: because within it a woman prayed one of the most beautiful prayers of scripture (v. 35), and God answered with "a beautiful acceptance" (v. 37). There is a teaching here for every believer who measures worth by visible scale: God's roll of honor counts sanctity, not size. The House of ʿImrān — ordinary by Nazareth's or Jerusalem's registers — is named in one breath with Adam, Noah, and Abraham, in a Book read until the end of the world. Election is God's commentary on the world, delivered in the world's own valleys.

And the placement of the verse is precise: it comes directly after the commands of love and obedience (vv. 31–32), as though to answer the inevitable question — *what does a following look like when God loves it back?* The answer is the next thirty verses: a grandmother who vowed, a child who grew pure, an old prophet who dared to ask, a virgin who trusted, and a boy called a Word from God.
**Iṣṭafā: Selection from Purity, Not Privilege**

The verb governing the whole register is *iṣṭafā* — He selected — from the root *ṣ-f-w*, purity and clarified-selection: to choose by purifying — the clarified oil, the pick of the flock. God's *selection* therefore is never a lottery of blood-lines; it is *purification made election*: Adam named and taught (2:31) and repented-and-guided (*fa-jtahāhu rabbuhu fa-tāba ʿalayhi wa hadā*, 20:122); Noah, gratefulest servant (17:3); Abraham, taken as *khalīl* — intimate friend (4:125); and the House of ʿImrān pulled into light by a woman's vow (v. 35). Al-Rāzī treats the four as the Qur'an's *epochs of the covenant*: one father of humanity, one under the Flood, one father of the nations of prophecy, one mother-house of the Messiah — four angles from which the world has seen God choose.

**Chosen Above the Worlds: In Their Worlds**

The phrase *ʿalā al-ʿālamīn* — "above the worlds" — carries its standing qualification from the commentators, and its removal of every remnant of racial reading: each is selected *above the worlds of his own epoch* — as 2:47 makes explicit for Israel in their age, and as al-Baqarah caps for the whole argument: *favor was for their time and their trust*, never a perpetual patent. The perpetual line runs elsewhere — to faith, which any century may enter, as vv. 103 and 110 make the present community's own election explicit (*"the best community brought forth for mankind"* — not a strain but a task). Election is a calling before a crown.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:34

> **As progeny, one from another. And God is Hearing, Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**One Vine, Many Branches**

The four elected names of verse 33 are now bound together by a single clause: *dhurriyyatan baʿḍuhā min baʿḍ* — "as progeny, one from another." Outwardly the phrase certifies lineage: Adam's line runs to Noah, Noah's survivors father the post-flood world, from that humanity Abraham is raised, and within Abraham's loins — through Israel — comes the house of ʿImrān. The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī) add interiorly what outward genealogy only adumbrates: the deeper filiation is *faith*. These are a progeny in religion — one spiritual substance descending through the houses, "one from another" the way light passes candle to candle without loss. Thus the verse does double duty: it honors bloodline while subordinating it to doctrine. Kinship in God outranks kinship in flesh — the Qur'an will say of Abraham's father and of Noah's son that blood without faith does not belong to the elected house: *"He is not of your family; indeed, it was unrighteous conduct"* (11:46). The House of ʿImrān is a house of ʿImrān's *God* first, and only therefore of ʿImrān.

There is also in *baʿḍuhā min baʿḍ* a quiet equalizer, as some commentators (among them al-Māturīdī's reading preserved in the tradition) observed: the same phrase appears at 4:25 as "you are one of another" — the human family itself. Election, then, does not found an aristocracy of a different species; the chosen are drawn from the same clay, and the remaining door — submission, deed, reverence — stands open to every descendant of Adam. Election distinguishes vocation, not biological essence.

**"And God Is Hearing, Knowing" — The Seal Above the Story**

The verse closes with a pair of divine names whose position here is a foreword to verses 35–41: *wa Allāhu samīʿun ʿalīm* — "and God is Hearing, Knowing." The names are not decorative tags; they are the two faculties the coming narrative will rest upon. *Samīʿ*: because the next verse is a woman's whispered prayer — "My Lord, I dedicate to Thee what is in my belly" — deliberately cast past every human audience, into ears that do not miss. *ʿAlīm*: because the prayer will be answered in a form the suppliant did not foresee — a girl instead of a boy, a gift instead of a servant — and only comprehensive Knowledge could have authored *that* answer. Before the story begins, the verse posts its two guarantees: no whisper in the house of ʿImrān goes unheard; no mistaking in their plans escapes correction. In a single line God has told us how to read all that follows: every prayer in the chapter — Ḥannah's, Zachariah's, Mary's, and later the believers' at Uḥud — is spoken into hearing, and every human plan crosses a knowing.

The believer is thereby given the smallest complete charter of supplication: *He hears* the call you are too ashamed to voice aloud; *He knows* the answer you could never design. Pray, then, and let election — of outcomes, not just of houses — belong to the Knowing.
**Dhurriyyah: Descent Preserved by Design**

*Dhurriyyatan baʿḍuhā min baʿḍ* — "descendants, one of another" — reads like a genealogy-clause and works like an argument: the Qur'an's lineage of prophecy is *continuous by design* — 6:84–87's long roll from Noah through Abraham's branches to Jesus and beyond — so that no era of the world stands without a link in the chain. The link's blood-exactness mattered here for its dignifying of one mother's anxiety: the woman of ʿImrān, coming in v. 35 with a child in her womb and a doubt in her plea (*"my Lord, I have delivered a female"*), receives first the doctrine and then the answer — her child enters the chain *itself*: Mary, mother of the Messiah; and through Mary's cousin's house, John the son of Zachariah — *one of another*, indeed. Al-Qurṭubī reads the clause against the biblical levirate; Ibn Kathīr against the Abrahamic dispersion; the plain reader against his own hopes: *generations in God's hand do not miscarry*.

**Samīʿ ʿAlīm Beside the Cradle**

The verse's seal joins the two Names the whole scene needs: *wa-Allāhu samīʿun ʿalīm* — "and God is Hearer, Knower." The al-samīʾ answers the vow next verse — *a woman's whispered dedication in the temple* — the al-ʿalīm answers what she could not: the child's sex, fitness, and destiny. The Name-pair then re-appears at the vow's resolution (v. 37: *fa-taqabbalahā rabbuhā* — her Lord accepted her): God *heard* the offer and *knew* the value. The sealing stands for every afterward petition of the story — Zachariah (v. 38: *samīʿu al-duʿāʾ*) and for every vow since ʿImrān's house: the Samīʿ does not*misis* a single dedication uttered in His houses, nor the ʿAlīm a single female-child misestimated by her mother.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:35

> **[Remember] when the wife of ʿImrān said, "My Lord, truly I dedicate to Thee what is in my belly, in consecration. So accept it from me. Truly Thou art the Hearing, the Knowing."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Mother's Vow Becomes Scripture**

The story opens — as the immense events of God so often open — not with kings or angels but with a woman speaking to God about the child inside her. *Idh qālat imraʾatu ʿImrāna rabbi innī nadhartu laka mā fī baṭnī muḥarraran fa-taqabbal minnī* — "When the wife of ʿImrān said: My Lord, I have vowed to Thee what is in my belly, in consecration; so accept it from me." Tradition names her Ḥannah — Anne — and relates that ʿImrān died before the child was born, so that the vow was a widow-to-be's (or a widowed mother's) offering, made in the privacy of grief and hope at once. The child yet unborn, sex unknown, wholly hers by every human title — and she gives it away before holding it. *Nadhar* is a vow: a voluntary self-imposition of a duty not otherwise owed. And *muḥarraran* — consecrated, set free — is from *ḥurr*, freedom: freed from *her*, from all her own claims on the child, from every worldly employment, liberated for God alone; dedicated to the service of the sanctuary Temple of Jerusalem, to learning and worship. The mother's offering is thus not possession-transferred but liberation: she *frees* her child into God's service — the purest interpretation of parenthood this Book knows.

Note the address and the seal: *Rabb* — "my Lord," the nurturing, sustaining face of God; and the names of verse 34 reappear verbatim — *innaka anta al-samīʿu al-ʿalīm* — "Truly Thou art the Hearing, the Knowing": as though Ḥannah were herself echoing the editorial seal of the previous verse. God heard her calling; God knew both what she meant and what she did not yet know.

**The Prayer of "Accept," Not the Prayer of "Grant"**

The theology of petition in this one sentence is worth dwelling upon, for it corrects a common instinct of religious bargaining. Ḥannah does not pray, "make my child righteous, strong, famous," nor "give me comfort from him in my old age" — she prays only *fa-taqabbal minnī*: "accept it from me." The child is already offered; the entire burden of the prayer is laid upon *acceptance*. Here is a subtlety the commentators illuminate: good things can be given and not accepted — the Book teaches it of offerings exactly: *"say: expend willingly or unwillingly, it will not be accepted of you"* (9:53); *"God accepts only from the reverent"* (5:27). Between the giving and the accepting lies God's will — the true battlefield of devotion is not the act's size but its acceptance, and no one can secure acceptance from the supply side alone. So the most the most consecrated of mothers can do is what Ḥannah does: *offer completely, then beg.* The form is the model of all Islamic *qurbān*: the servant gives the best he cannot keep, prays *taqabbal*, and resigns the issue to Divine pleasure.

**Vows and Their Modern Echoes**

Jurists drew from this narrative the rulings of *nadhar* — that a vow to God, if it is vow of obedience, binds and must be fulfilled, as the story's continuation shows her fulfilling it; the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Whoever vows to obey God, let him obey Him; and whoever vows to disobey God, let him not disobey Him"* (al-Bukhārī 6696; Muslim 1639). But the verse's wider address is simpler and sharper. Many people bargain with God only *after* they get what they want — I'll be better if...; Ḥannah speaks in the opposite tense, consecrating *before* receiving, trusting while still barren of certainty. The believer who learns her grammar finds that the deepest prayers are not requests but returns: placing the nearest "mine" — a child, a career, a talent, a year of one's life — into God's service *first*, and asking, with her word, acceptance. The next verses will show what acceptance looks like when God is pleased with an offering: not always the expected shape, but always the beautiful one (v. 37).

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:36

> **And when she bore her, she said, "My Lord, I have borne a female," and God knows best what she bore, and the male is not like the female, "and I have named her Mary, and I seek refuge for her in Thee, and for her progeny, from Satan the outcast."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"I Have Borne a Female": When Answers Arrive in Unexpected Forms**

The vow called for a son — in the logic of seventh-century-before-Christ Temple service, a male would minister — and the delivery room of God's providence produced a daughter. The verse shows Ḥannah at the crossing of her plan and God's plan, and her first word is frank surprise carried in prayer: *rabbi innī waḍaʿtuhā unthā* — "My Lord, I have borne a female." The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī) read her tone with tenderness: not complaint — the vow stands and will be fulfilled with a girl — but a mother's honest report of the gap between expectation and decree. God's answer in the verse is one of the Qur'an's most quietly majestic parentheticals: *wa Allāhu aʿlamu bi-mā waḍaʿat* — "and God knows best what she bore." The mother knows the delivered child; God knows what was *delivered*: the vessel of the Messiah, the seal of purity over the women of the worlds (v. 42), the sign to all nations (21:91). What she bore exceeded both her vow and her gender-expectation by more than heaven and earth. The Book then utters, on His own authority, the clause that has been discussed ever since: *wa laysa al-dhakaru ka-l-unthā* — "and the male is not like the female."

That brief verdict holds two layered truths the commentators draw out, and the verse welcomes both. At one level it is realism: the sexes differ — in ritual roles, in bodily callings, in histories of service — and piety does not need to pretend otherwise; differences built by the Creator are data, not injustices. At the other level, it is reversal: take the clause with its outcome — "accepted her with a beautiful acceptance" (v. 37) — and it reads as quiet chastening of the preference for sons: *the male you expected is not like the female I gave*; God's "not like" is intrinsically superior to her "like." Al-Qurṭubī notes the whole point of the narrative is that this female was chosen over all males of her era to be the mother of a Word from God. The verse thus sits serenely against both extremes of every later age: against the cultures that despised daughters (the Qur'an has earlier crushed that particular ignorance at 16:58–59 and 43:17) and against the modern flattening that can see only interchangeability; the Book honors difference and overturns hierarchy in one clause.

**A Name and an Entrustment: The First Prayer of Refuge for a Child**

Then the mother performs two acts of prophetic instinct: she names, and she shelters. *Wa innī sammaytuhā Maryam* — "I have named her Mary." The name, preserved in the sister traditions as *Maryam* (related to the Hebrew *Miryam*), is glossed by some of the philologists of commentary as "the worshipping one," "the servant" — the mother writes her vow into her daughter's name: she wanted a servant of God; God gave her the word itself. And then the petition that Muslims have recited over their own children ever since: *wa innī uʿīdhuhā bika wa dhurriyyatahā mina al-shayṭāni al-rajīm* — "I seek refuge for her in Thee and for her progeny from Satan the outcast." The scope is tenderly ominous: she asks protection not only for the child but for *progeny* — a descendant who, humanly speaking, could not yet exist for a consecrated virgin; the commentators note faith already reaching toward what the vow could not calculate (Ibn Kathīr: the progeny is Jesus and all who follow in her line of purity). *Al-rajīm* — the stoned, cast-out one — names Satan by his expulsion from mercy; refuge-seeking is the Qur'an's standing protocol against him (16:98: "when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the outcast Satan"), a protocol the mother deploys here as a child's life-insurance.

And God answered, in a report that stands in the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections, beyond even her prayer's design. Abū Hurayrah relates:

> *"Every child of Adam is touched (*massa*) by Satan at birth, and the child bursts out crying at Satan's touch — except Mary and her son."* (al-Bukhārī 3431; Muslim 2366 — and al-Bukhārī adds: "...and if you wish, recite: 'and I seek refuge for her in Thee and for her progeny from Satan the outcast'")

The Prophet ﷺ himself linked the verse and the miracle: Ḥannah's sentence of refuge became a standing shield at the Messiah's birth — proof that the "Hearing" of verse 35 had heard every syllable, and that an accepted mother's prayer can be written, forensically, into history's most protected infancy.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:37

> **So her Lord accepted her with a beautiful acceptance, and made her to grow in a beautiful way, and placed her under the care of Zachariah. Whenever Zachariah entered upon her in the sanctuary he found provision with her. He said, "Mary, whence comes this unto thee?" She said, "It is from God. Truly God provides for whomsoever He will without reckoning."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Accepted Beautifully, Grown Beautifully**

The petition of verses 35–36 — "so accept it from me" — receives heaven's receipt in a phrase the Arabic makes unforgettably doubled: *fa-taqabbalahā rabbuhā bi-qabūlin ḥasan* — "her Lord accepted her with a beautiful acceptance" — *wa anbatahā nabātan ḥasanan* — "and made her grow with a beautiful growth." The double *ḥasan* (beautiful, good) is the chapter's tenderness made grammatical: acceptance is not mere admission into service — it is stamped *beautiful*; growth is not mere bodily increase — the child in the sanctuary thriving under every unseen hand — it is stamped *beautiful*. The commentators dwell on both: acceptance beautiful in its manner — protected, provided, honored — and growth beautiful in its fruits — devotion, wisdom, purity, God-given dignity that multiplied faster than years. A child given freely to God is then grown by God; when the consecration is complete, God becomes the gardener. Every parent who entrusts a child to Him reads this verse as charter.

Zachariah, the prophet-priest of the sanctuary, husband of Mary's maternal kinswoman (her "aunt" in the commentators' phrasing), is appointed her guardian — *wa kaffalahā Zakariyyā* — God's own designation, as v. 44 will show, contested by others until the lots chose. The custody of the most consecrated child on earth is placed in the safest prophetic care in creation: an arrangement of divine precision — the aged prophet who has no child now raises a girl who will bear the greatest child.

**The Provision in the Sanctuary: A Standing Miracle in Small Scale**

Then comes the repeated scene — *kullamā dakhala ʿalayhā Zakariyyā al-miḥrāba wajada ʿindahā rizqan* — *whenever* Zachariah entered the sanctuary upon her, he *found* provision with her. The miḥrāb was her chamber of devotion (from the word Islamic architecture later borrowed for the prayer-niche — and indeed this very verse is inscribed upon miḥrābs across the Muslim world, over the very spot where the believer stands as Zachariah stood); the provision (*rizq*) was food that had no natural supply-chain — fruits out of their season, the commentators say: winter's fruit in summer and summer's in winter; or, amounts outlasting their quantities. Either way, the chamber of a secluded girl was feeding on the table of heaven. Zachariah — himself a prophet, familiar with miracles — is astounded: *yā Maryamu, annā laki hādhā?* — "Mary, whence is this for you?" The question is the natural one every rational mind asks of any garden without a gardener. Her answer is the thesis of the entire House of ʿImrān, and of this sūrah: *huwa min ʿindi Allāh* — "it is from God" — *inna Allāha yarzuqu man yashāʾu bi-ghayri ḥisāb* — "Truly God provides for whom He wills without reckoning."

Two things must be noted. First, the clause *bi-ghayri ḥisāb* — without reckoning, beyond auditing — appeared six verses back in the prayer of the believers (v. 27): Mary now speaks it as her own creed from experience; the chain of the House of ʿImrān learns scripture by living it. Second, her sentence is a lesson for the sūrah's battlefield listeners later: economy — whether of an army, or a family, or an empire — is not closed against God. Provision arrives by rule of His will, not by rule of stock and store. The spiritual masters of Islam drew from this chamber a standing principle of grace: God plants a portion of His *kharq al-ʿādah* — the breaking of custom — in the lives of His secluded servants, so that authority's hope never dies: *there is still a door no one walls off*.

**A Niche That Still Speaks**

The Prophet ﷺ never married the idea of sanctuary to a special caste. The chamber's theology democratized instantly: wherever a believer withdraws in sincerity, the *rizq* argument holds — because the clause escaping Mary's lips is not "God provides *me* without reckoning" but *man yashāʾ*, *whomsoever He wills*. And indeed the Muslim devotion has ever since inscribed "Whenever Zachariah entered... He provides without reckoning" over the *miḥrāb* of the ordinary mosque: the place where any soul stands alone at dawn is Mary's room, under the same Provider. The verse teaches its reader to stop asking, in hard seasons, "whence can this come?" — the arithmetic of despair; and to start answering, as the girl of the sanctuary answered: "it is from God," the arithmetic of faith.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:38

> **Then and there, Zachariah called upon his Lord. He said, "My Lord, grant me from Thy Presence a good progeny. Truly Thou hearest all calls!"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Triggered Prayer of an Old Man**

The verse opens with two of the loveliest small words of the Qur'an: *hunālika* — "then and there" — there, in the miḥrāb, upon that sight. Zachariah sees out-of-season fruit kept for a consecrated girl, and something decisive turns in him: if God can provision a child beyond nature, why not provision *him* beyond nature? *Hunālika daʿā Zakariyyā rabbah* — "thereupon Zachariah called upon his Lord." Al-Ṭabarī's reading — "upon seeing the blessing bestowed upon Mary" — captures the chain of causality exactly: witnessing another's grace becomes the legitimate spark of one's own request. Envy corrodes; *imitation of aspiration* builds. Zachariah does not resent Mary's sanctuary-table; he reads it as an argument addressed specifically to his own closed hope and takes it up: *rabbi hab lī min ladunka dhurriyyatan ṭayyibah* — "My Lord, grant me from Thy Presence a *good* progeny."

**The Grammar of His Asking**

His petition deserves slow reading, for it is a masterpiece of prophetic etiquette. He asks by name the relation and not merely the gift — *Rabb*, "my Lord," namer of nurture; *hab lī* — "grant," from *hiba*, the unearned gift, the same root as *al-Wahhāb*, the Bestower named at verse 8; *min ladunka* — from Your own Presence, the *ladun* of verse 8, asking not for the ordinary issue of biology but for a gift issued from the treasury directly beside God Himself; and he qualifies the offspring with the only criterion that matters: *ṭayyib* — good, pure, wholesome — not numerous, not male, not famous, but *sound*. The fuller parallel account in Sūrah 19:2–15 lets us overhear the heart behind the words: "I fear my kinsfolk after me" — his anxiety was covenantal, not dynastic; he wanted a trustee for the sanctuary and the covenant, not a vanity-heir. And the seal of the prayer names the faculty he is betting on — *innaka samīʿu al-duʿāʾ* — "Truly Thou art the Hearer of supplication": not the Hearer of words (v. 34 taught that) but the Hearer of *calls* — the very act of calling is already addressed.

**Why "Then and There" Matters to Every Suppliant**

Two spiritual laws announce themselves here. First: the moment of witnessing grace is the moment of highest receptivity for prayer — the heart is soft with evidence, and evidence of God's hand in another's life precedes trust in His hand in ours. Muslim wisdom discovered from this verse the etiquette of supplicating *immediately* upon sights of divine generosity: the birth of another's child, the rescue of another's enterprise, rain on another's field. Second: bold asking is not prescribed only to the strong situations. Zachariah was "in the most hopeless case of all," by the terms the next verse itself will state — age overtaken, wife barren — and his consolation was the miḥrāb-argument. The Book thereby teaches: let impossibility *occasion* the request rather than close it. Most people regulate their prayers to their probabilities, and thereby pray small; prophets regulate their prayers to God's promises, and thereby pray large. The very next verse proves the law at once — while he is yet standing in prayer in that same sanctuary, heaven is already answering.
**Hunālika: A Place That Turned Into a Moment**

The verse opens with the unassuming adverb *hunālika* — "there" — and the commentators have always loved its weight: *there*, in the miḥrāb, in the house that had so recently seen Mary fed from the Unseen, Zachariah *prayed*. Place became occasion: the old priest, daily visited by evidences of impossible provision, finally *asked for his own*. It is one of the Qur'an's quiet instructions on the *geography of supplication*: some places are older than our need in God's hearing — the Prophet ﷺ worked the same doctrine with Uways's homeland, with the spots of the valley of al-Ṣafā, and the community learned it as *seeking the hours and houses of answer* (the last third of the night; the day of Friday's hidden hour; the miḥrābs of the world). Zachariah asks: *rabbi hab lī min ladunka dhurriyyatan ṭayyibah* — "my Lord, grant me from Your presence a good offspring."

**Samīʿ al-Duʿāʾ: The Title at the End of the Ask**

The seal is itself a received liturgical title — *innaka samīʿu al-duʿāʾ*: "truly You are Hearer of prayer" — the believers' standard capping-phrase of petition in the Prophet's own practice, and the Qur'an keeps it here as Zachariah's own. From Ṭabarī to Ibn Kathīr the clause is glossed simply: the One to Whom petitions are addressed without intermediary, Who singles out requests from tumult as the hearer singles threads — *samīʿ* in the intensified form, the Hearer of every call. And the Prophet's definition of prayer seals the doctrine where Zachariah stood — that duʿāʾ is not preparation for worship but its marrow:

> *"Duʿāʾ is worship"* — then he recited: *"Your Lord has said: call upon Me; I will answer you"* — (al-Tirmidhī 3372, from al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr; the *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ* of the supplicants' canon).

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:39

> **Then the angels called to him while he was praying in the sanctuary, "God gives thee glad tidings of John, confirming a word from God, noble and chaste, a prophet, from among the righteous."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**An Answered Call, Overheard by Heaven**

The prayer of verse 38 is answered in the posture it was made — standing in prayer, in the miḥrāb: *fa-nādatahu al-malāʾikatu wa huwa qāʾimun yuṣallī fī al-miḥrāb* — "then the angels called to him while he was standing praying in the sanctuary." The rapidity itself is the teaching: God does not answer the prayers of His friends by post; the interval between *innaka samīʿu al-duʿāʾ* and the angelic voice is a verse-break, nothing more. The agents are angels — heaven's own couriers — and the opening word of the message is the word of joy: *yubashshiru* — "gives thee glad tidings" — because the response to an old man's hope is announced as festival, not appointment.

**The Child Described Before the Child Promised**

The tidings name the son first — *Yaḥyā*, John — and then arrange over the infant's future four titles, each a finished portrait of what the old man is actually being given. *Muṣaddiqun bi-kalimatin min Allāh* — "confirming a word from God": John is fore-designated as the confirmer of the coming Word — Jesus — who is Himself named a Word from God in verse 45. The chain is exquisite: father prays; son is promised; son's first feature is that he will stand as witness to his cousin. *Taṣdīq*, confirming, is the work of every real witness — he reaffirms what God sends, he does not compete with it. The commentators (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī) note the precision: before John exists, he is enrolled in the service of the one greater than himself — *he came as a herald of light*, as the sister traditions also record; John's historic mission, to bear witness and to prepare, is folded into his very annunciation.

Then *sayyidan* — "noble": the master, the leader. The commentators unfold its meaning as the full moral majesty: learned, clement, self-mastered, generous, a man men naturally gathered to — the leadership of magnetism rather than office. *Wa ḥaṣūran* — "and chaste": from *ḥaṣara*, to restrain, withhold — the soul that has itself bridled; read by the majority as mastered against unlawful desire, self-contained in the presence of temptation; by many as a chosen abstention from marriage altogether, a life walled for God — either way, a title of *containment*: the passions serving, not driving. There is a deliberate echo for the reader of this sūrah: John is the male mirror of Mary's purity — the house of ʿImrān now has both its paragons, and both are marked by *ḥiṣār al-nafs*, the bridling of the self. And then the crown: *wa nabiyyan mina al-ṣāliḥīn* — "a prophet, from among the righteous." Prophethood is announced separately, and then the class into which he is admitted — *al-ṣāliḥīn*, the righteous, the assembly of all who are sound and made-sound; more than his office, his corporation: prophets are named among the righteous so that no one confuses office with exemption; John is righteous *first-class*.

**The Fullness of an Answer**

Step back and behold the exchange of verses 38–39. Zachariah asked for *dhurriyyah ṭayyibah* — good offspring, singular, unspecified, humble in scope. He receives *more* than asked: a named child, already designated to serve a Word of God, already titled morally and prophetically. The law is the one the sūrah has advertised all along: *He provides whom He wills without reckoning* (v. 37) — the answer outruns the ask. The learned in prayer have ever since marked the etiquette: ask generically for the *good* and leave the engineering to Him who gives "without reckoning"; the believers' *ẓann* — their estimate of God — is itself a ceiling on what they receive, as the hadith qudsī says: *"I am as My servant thinks of Me"* (al-Bukhārī 7405; Muslim 2675). *Estimate boldly.* The old man in the sanctuary had estimated boldly, and heaven answered — while he was still, as it were, in the act of asking.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:40

> **He said, "My Lord, how shall I have a boy when age has overtaken me and my wife is barren?" He said, "Thus does God do whatsoever He will."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Prophet's "How?" Is Not a Skeptic's "No"**

Zachariah has just received from angels, mid-prayer, the most improbable good news of his life, and his response is a question: *rabbi annā yakūnu lī ghulāmun wa qad balaghaniya al-kibaru wa-mraʾatī ʿāqir* — "My Lord, how shall I have a boy, when old age has overtaken me and my wife is barren?" The commentators carefully distinguish this *annā* — "how?" — from disbelief. Abraham had asked in the same register: *"My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead"* (2:260) — not doubting *that* God acts, but years-deep in wonder at *how* the impossible arrives. Mary in a few verses will ask the exact sibling-question: "how shall I have a child while no human being has touched me?" (v. 47). The "how?" of prophecy is inquiry into means; the "how?" of unbelief is denial of possibility. God answers the prophets with reassurance and manifestation; He answers denial with silence or threat. The difference is a pastoral treasure: the believer need not fear his astonishment. Zachariah is a prophet receiving an angelic announcement in a sanctuary and still his mind reaches for probability — and God bears with it beautifully, because the astonishment is not rebellion against God but astonishment at *nature*, which is itself God's habit.

**Submitting Probability to Will**

Now the answer, and it is one of those short Qur'anic utterances that is, in effect, the whole doctrine of creation: *kadhālika Allāhu yafʿalu mā yashāʾ* — "Thus does God do whatsoever He wills." *Kadhālika* — "thus," "even so," like *that* — points back at the very astonishment: thus — in this manner, from cases deemed closed — does God act. Age is data within nature; will is above nature. Old age and barrenness describe the ordinary expected path of *creation*; they bind nothing for the *Creator*. God does not here abolish Zachariah's data; the maidenhead of Mary will also be overcome without data being abolished (v. 47); He merely discloses the layered causation: nature's statistics are His habits, not His limits. The principle was preached earlier in the sūrah itself — "Thou providest for whom Thou wilt without reckoning" (v. 27; v. 37) — and is here heard, by one member of the House of ʿImrān, at the pivot of his own biography.

**The Consolation for Every Closed Case**

Muslims have ever since sent this verse like medicine to every heart confronting a "statistically impossible" good: the childless couple reading Zachariah; the sinner who deems his own reform barren soil; the reformer watching the ossified polity; the old who think their accounts closed. "Thus does God do whatsoever He will" does not license presumption — Zachariah does not receive a license but a gift — but it refuses despair the last word, because it relocates the operative force of events from our *barrenness* to His *will*. And there is a second, subtler consolation for the old in particular: *qad balaghaniya al-kibar* — "age has overtaken me" — was spoken by a prophet; there is no age at which one becomes ineligible for the new thing God might do. In the economy of this sūrah the oldest couple in it receives the chapter's first miracle-son; and the late-born, long-delayed goods of life are announced by angels regardless of the biological date. God keeps offices of mercy that do not consult our calendars.
**The Question of Wonder and the Answer of Fiat**

Zachariah's question — *annā yakūnu lī ghulām* — "how shall a boy be mine?" — with its establishment of impossibilities (*old age has reached me, and my wife is barren*), is among the Book's school-texts for distinguishing *the question of wonder* from *the question of doubt*. Abraham asked after resurrection-doubtless yet asked: *"my Lord, show me how You give life to the dead"* — and the Lord, knowing His friend's heart, asked: *"do you not believe?"* — *"yes — but that my heart may be at rest"* (2:260); the question was permitted, answered, indulged. Zechariah's stands in that class: he asks *mechanism*, not *possibility* — evidenced by the answer's directness rather than rebuke: *kadhālika Allāhu yafʿalu mā yashāʾ* — "thus God does what He wills."

**The Fiat Clause and Mary's Verse to Come**

The fiat-sentence — *God does what He wills* — will meet the reader again in v. 47, when Mary's question — *"how shall a child be mine, and no man has touched me?"* — brings the same reply at even higher register: *"when He decrees a matter, He only says to it: Be — and it is."* Planted in Zachariah's verse first, the clause teaches the story's pedagogic ladder: the natural-impossibility (old age and barrenness) yields to the fiat; the total-impossibility (no man has touched me) yields to *Be*. The school of Abraham's house is thereby passing its arc down three generations in as many verses — Sarah laughed (11:71–72), Zachariah wondered, Mary stood silent — and the Book teaches the believer: *ask your impossibilities of Him; the grammar of heaven has a verb for them all.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:41

> **He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said, "Your sign is that you shall not speak to the people for three days, save through signs." And remember your Lord much, and glorify [Him] at eventide and at dawn.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Asking for a Sign, Receiving a Fast of the Tongue**

The announcement of a son to an old, barren couple is met with one more request: *rabbi ijʿal lī āyah* — "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." As with verse 40's "how shall I have a boy?", the commentators defend the request from any suspicion of weak faith: signs were the pedagogy of prophecy — Moses was given the staff and the hand to strengthen him for the mission; Zachariah asks for an outward token by which the gift can be *felt* and the waiting disciplined. God's answer is as astonishing as the promise itself: *āyatuka allā tukallima al-nāsa thalāthata ayyāmin illā ramzan* — "your sign is that you shall not speak to people for three days, save by gestures" — *ramz*, signal, sign-language. Parallel Sūrah 19:10 makes explicit that his tongue was not afflicted with illness: "your sign is that you shall not speak to people for three nights, *being sound* (ṣawiyyan)." He prays for a token of joy and is given — silence. The sign is not fire from heaven but the abdication of speech: a prophet made temporarily mute, fluent only with God.

**The Sign Is Also a Training**

Why this sign, and not another? The commentators and the spiritual tradition perceive several wisdoms folded together. First, the gift matches the occasion: Zachariah, about to receive Yahya — Yahya whose very existence proclaims God's mastery over natural closure — is given three days of *natural closure* in his own body: his tongue, the instrument by which a teacher serves his people, halted. Overwhelmed joy, like overwhelming news at Badr or Uḥud, tends to clamor for speech; God schools him instead in restraint — gratitude *performed* rather than broadcast. Second, it is consecration: the nine-month waiting on the promised son begins with a three-day fast of the tongue, a miniature *iʿtikāf* of the sanctuary-man in his own miḥrāb. The pattern of the house repeats: mother consecrates the unborn (v. 35); God consecrates the expectant father. Third, it is public evidence: a prophet who suddenly cannot speak to his people while remaining healthy is a walking koan — the sign is not only *for* him but signals through him to the community that something from God has come upon him.

**From Speech to Remembrance: The Substitution Command**

The verse does not merely stop his mouth; it reroutes the flow: *wa-dhkur rabbaka kathīran, wa sabbiḥ bi-l-ʿashiyyi wa-l-ibkār* — "and remember your Lord much, and glorify Him at eventide and at dawn." Words barred from people are replaced with words toward God — human speech converts into *dhikr*. The two hours named are scripture's prime hours: *ʿashiyy*, the sun's decline into evening, and *ibkār*, the dawn — the hinges of the day. The instruction embeds a universal law of spiritual economy: silence from creation is only fruitful when it becomes address to the Creator; otherwise it curdles into brooding. Zachariah's three days are thus the first *silent retreat* in the Qur'an's prophetic chronicles — speech embargoed, remembrance commanded. Every later practitioner who has fasted from speech, shuttered the phone, or taken a morning without commentary walks Zachariah's corridor. The miracle your tongue cannot announce, *your heart can glorify* — and glorification, unlike announcement, performs the news back where it came from.
**Ramz: The Gesture-Language of the Servant Under Vow**

*Innaka lā tukallimu al-nāsa thalāthata ayyāmin illā ramzan* — "you shall not speak to men three days except by gesture": *ramz* is the sign-speech of the muted — lips and eyes and hand composing the sentence the tongue withholds. The commentators record what the vow-cost looked like in Zachariah's days: silence-vows had preceded Islam (Mary's own at 19:26 — "I have vowed to the Merciful a fast, so I shall not speak today to any human") — but Islam, al-Qurṭubī concludes, *retired the silence-fast and kept the instruction*: the sign was for three days, not a life-rule, and was sealed by the tongue's release into remembrance — *"and remember your Lord much, and glorify at dusk and dawn."*

**Bukrah and ʿAshiyy: The Two Book-Ends of Glorification**

*Wa-sabbiḥ bi-l-ʿashiyyi wa-l-ibkār* — two words for day's edge: the *ʿashiyy* span from afternoon into dark, the *ibkār* the first cool hours. Priestly silence is thereby no blankness: the verse itself prescribes how muted days are spent — *much remembrance* and the two-edged tasbīḥ — a complete liturgy for a mouth in quarantine. The Prophet's own teaching gave the same shaped-silence to the whole community:

> *"Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him speak good or be silent."* (al-Bukhārī 6018; Muslim 47, from Abū Hurayrah)

Between Zachariah's gesture-days and this ahadith stands one principle: speech is rationed under heaven's careful administration — sometimes taken (three days), sometimes fenced (speak good or hush), always converted into remembrance. The believer who memorizes the two book-end phrases carries the old priest's vow sanely: *glorify at the two edges; let the middle serve.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:42

> **And [remember] when the angels said, "O Mary, truly God has chosen thee and purified thee, and has chosen thee above the women of the worlds."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Angels Speak Her Name**

The narrative now turns from the father-to-be to the young woman at the chapter's center, and the form of address is breathtaking: *wa idh qālati al-malāʾikatu yā Maryam* — "and when the angels said: O Mary!" Human beings are addressed by angels rarely across sacred history, and here a woman receives the vocative twice in a single narrative (vv. 42, 45). The historical texture matters: this honor descends upon a vulnerable figure — fatherless from birth, consecrated by a widowed mother, in a culture with its own ideas about women's place in prophecy's domain. The Qur'an's own correction of every such idea is announced from heaven: *inna Allāha iṣṭafāki* — "truly God has chosen you."

**Chosen, Purified, Chosen Again: Reading the Double Election**

The verse places two elections around one purification: chosen — *iṣṭafāki* — and purified — *ṭahharaki* — and chosen above the women of the worlds — *wa iṣṭafāki ʿalā nisāʾi al-ʿālamīn*. The commentators (al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr) discern the two elections as two stages of one destiny: the first choice — her consecration from the womb, her acceptance in the sanctuary, the out-of-season provisions (v. 37), God's shield over her already prophesied through her mother's prayer of refuge (v. 36; and the Ṣaḥīḥ report that she and her son alone escaped Satan's touch at birth); the second — her selection as the bearer of a Word from God, the mother of the Messiah. Between them stands purification — *ṭahhara*: emptied of defilements, inward and outward; protected from the contaminants of others' evil as well as her own; spiritual *and* physical purity — the ancients discuss whether the purification means from the stains of guilt, or from the crafting of the blame, or from what custom marks as impure; the widest and soundest reading gathers them all: God made her pure and guarded pure.

The phrase *ʿalā nisāʾi al-ʿālamīn* — "above the women of the worlds" — al-Rāzī and the jurists of doctrine have discussed whether the superlative is of her age or of all time; noteworthy is that the expression *nisāʾ al-ʿālamīn* — the women of the worlds — had already been used by the Prophet ﷺ in the definitive pairing of female exemplars, in the well-known hadith:

> *"Sufficient for you among the women of the worlds are: Maryam daughter of ʿImrān, Khadījah daughter of Khuwaylid, Fāṭimah daughter of Muhammad, and Āsiyah wife of Pharaoh."* (al-Tirmidhī 3878; graded ṣaḥīḥ)

And in the Ṣaḥīḥayn, from Abū Hurayrah:

> *"Many men have attained perfection, but among women none attained it except Āsiyah the wife of Pharaoh and Maryam daughter of ʿImrān."* (al-Bukhārī 3411; Muslim 2431)

The "perfection" (*kamāl*) — prophethood's gender, says the tradition — is thus confirmed, in the mouth of the last Prophet, for these two women: the one who raised Moses under a tyrant's roof, and the one who bore Jesus under God's roof alone.

**The Theology of This Honor**

Stepping back, the verse is a quiet theological earthquake for two audiences at once. Against the materialism of Nazareth's social eye (and every age's), heaven declares: the summit of this age's humanity is a woman in a prayer-chamber, not the armed savior of nationalist dream, nor the high priest in his vestments. Against every doctrine that would later make Mary herself divine or semi-divine, the verse fixes her rank *as a creature-favorite, not a god*: *iṣṭafā* — *God chose her* — she is the object of election, not its source. The same Book that demolishes the world's scale of value also demolishes the exaggerations that would later be built on Mary's own fame (cf. the refutation, 5:17, 5:72–75: "the Messiah, son of Mary, was but a messenger... and his mother was a woman of truth — they both ate food"). The chapter of people who ask how a thing can be will now be taught by the chapter's first mother that the summit of humanity is receptivity to God — and in verse 43, *her* curriculum is given.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:43

> **O Mary! Be devoutly obedient to thy Lord, prostrate, and bow with those who bow.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Curriculum of the Chosen: Qunūt, Sujūd, Rukūʿ**

Angels often announce; here they *assign*. Having been told she is chosen and purified over the women of the worlds, Mary is immediately given her regimen — as though divine election, the moment it is declared, requires a matching discipline to bear its weight: *yā Maryamu, uqnutī li-rabbiki wa-sjudī wa-rkaʿī maʿa al-rākiʿīn* — "O Mary! Be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate, and bow with those who bow." Three commands, and their order is a ladder of meaning.

First, *uqnutī* — "be devoutly obedient." *Qunūt*, the commentators note, carries a field of meanings that braid into one character: steadfast obedience, long-standing in prayer, humility, silence, constancy in worship — the settled posture of one perpetually turned to God. It is the highest verb of worship-disposition in the chapter — the same disposition named as a badge of the blessed at verse 17 (*al-qānitīn*) — and its grammar as a durative command means constancy, not episode: not "pray sometimes" but "be one who *stands devoted*." Before any miracle is asked of her, constancy is asked of her: God's special destinies have their foundation in unremarkable perseverance.

Second, *wa-sjudī* — "prostrate" — the crown of Islamic prayer, where forehead (body's highest) meets ground (earth's lowest) — the surrender-form of the body matching the surrender-verb of the religion (*islām*, v. 19). The Prophet ﷺ said the servant is *nearest* to his Lord in sujūd — *"the closest the servant is to his Lord is while he is prostrate, so make much supplication"* (Muslim 482) — and Mary, who had just been told she is nearest to God's favor, is pointed to the posture of nearness.

**"With Those Who Bow": Community for the Solitary**

Third, *wa-rkaʿī maʿa al-rākiʿīn* — "bow with those who bow." The command is Qur'anically resonant: it was the standing address to Israel — "bow with those who bow" (2:43) — and it echoes the earlier consecrating command over Abraham's house at the first sanctuary (2:125: "purify My House for... those who bow and prostrate"). For Mary the phrase carries special poignancy: who had bowed alone in her chamber until now is inducted into *rākiʿīn* — the company of the bowing. Election is not isolation: the most solitary soul in revelation is commanded to join the rank. Commentators past and present note the gentleness of this: she is not ordered to found a form, but to *enter one*; God's religion gives even its most exceptional children the mercy of shared movement. There is a body of worshippers, and her place is inside it — a sign of what the sūrah later legislates for the whole community: hold fast, *all together*, to the rope of God (v. 103).

**Why the Assignment Follows the Honor**

The sequence across verses 42–43 is a condensed theology of grace and responsibility. Favor precedes command (chosen, purified) — grace is first; command follows favor (obey, prostrate, bow) — gratitude is the assignment; and the commands, strikingly, are not supernatural: no miracles are demanded of Mary, only qunūt, sujūd, rukūʿ — everything already within human capacity fourteen centuries later. The spiritual masters drew the verse's rule: God does not ask His elect for *more than* worship; He asks them for more *of* worship — deeper, longer, steadier. The special ones are distinguished not by exemption from the ordinary forms but by their fidelity inside them. And for every reader honored by some gift — knowledge, family, provision — the verse is a persistent template: when God marks you, mark yourself *with Him*, in the oldest posture there is.
**Qunūt: Devotion as Mary's Daily Bread**

*Yā maryamu uqnutī li-rabbiki* — "O Mary, be devout toward your Lord": *qunūt* is the standing-devotion of unbroken obedience — the word the Prophet ﷺ placed in his own dawn-prayer and the word for long-held standing in recitation (the commentators of 2:238's *qānitīn* and 33:31's address to the Prophet's house install the lane: stillness with obedience). Her commission string then binds the three acts in the order of a rakʿah's anatomy: *usuqud — prostrate; wa-rkaʿī maʿa al-rākiʿīn — and bow with the bowing ones*. Devotion is interior, prostration is floor-contact, and the bowing is *with the congregation* — *maʿa* — the preposition of community in an address to a solitary woman in a temple.

**Maʿa al-Rākiʿīn: The With-ness of Worship**

The little *maʿa* carries the pew-theology of the whole pilgrimage of prayer: Mary, uniquely graced, is not exempt from the *maʿa* — commanded, rather, to join the ordinary ranks of the ritual bowers. Al-Qurṭubī reads there a general principle his school has cited ever since: *the specially favored stand in the same row* — no private dispensation from congregation for the elites of devotion. The Prophet ﷺ pressed the same into the community's habit:

> *"The prayer with the people is twenty-seven degrees above a man's prayer alone."* (al-Bukhārī 645; Muslim 650, from Ibn ʿUmar)

Mary's *maʿa*-bowing thereby reaches the reader in every mosque-row and living-room-line since: the woman of ʿImrān's house performed alone is never performed *apart* — she bows with the bowing ones, across every century her story is read.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:44

> **This is from the tidings of the Unseen, which We reveal unto thee. And thou wast not with them when they cast their lots [to choose] who among them would care for Mary, and thou wast not with them when they were disputing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Signature of Revelation Stamped Across the Narrative**

The story pauses as God addresses His Messenger ﷺ directly across the centuries: *dhālika min anbāʾi al-ghaybi nūḥīhi ilayk* — "this is from the tidings of the Unseen which We reveal unto thee." The word *anbāʾ* — tidings, momentous news — of *al-ghayb* — the Unseen: everything absent from human reach, whether hidden behind veils of distance, of the unseen world, or — as here — of *time*: events from a past no man in Arabia had witnessed. The verse then documents the proof with two plain sentences: *wa mā kunta ladayhim idh yulqūna aqlāmahum ayyuhum yakfulu Maryam, wa mā kunta ladayhim idh yakhtaṣimūn* — "and you were not with them when they cast their lots — which of them would care for Mary — and you were not with them when they were disputing." The narrative is accompanied by its own chain-of-custody: this knowledge comes not from archives, learning, or proximity (the Prophet ﷺ was an unlettered — v. 20 — man of Mecca and Madinah, centuries after the events), but by *waḥy* — revelation — "We reveal unto thee."

The historical detail that God here certifies is itself vivid: the priests of the Temple, desiring the honor of the consecrated girl's guardianship, cast their *aqlām* — their pens, lots, the reed-arrows of sortition — and disputed. The majority of the commentators (Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī) take it as a true contest of lots; some hold Zachariah's legal claim (as kinsman by marriage) was always clear, and the dispute concerned the honor of *serving* her. But the story's point in the Qur'an is not antiquarian: God's hand selected Zachariah — the same Zachariah about to be taught to ask for Yahya — as guardian, over the head of every other claimant.

**A Proof Addressed to Audiences Both Present and Future**

Why does God interrupt a beautiful narrative to say *you were not there*? Several wisdoms converge. First, it is an authentication clause for the Prophet ﷺ against the constant charge of manufacture or borrowing: precise report of hidden events, without human source, is itself a sign of prophethood — the same device appears after Joseph's saga: *"that is from the tidings of the Unseen We reveal unto you; and you were not with them when they resolved upon their affair and were plotting"* (12:102), and concerning Moses: *"We recite unto thee from the tidings of Moses and Pharaoh in truth"* (28:3). God is effectively saying: *your report of the miḥrāb, the lots, the angels, the annunciation, carries heaven's own warranty.* Second, it comforts: the Messenger receives every such story with this seal — a standing emblem that his was not the labor of research but the gift of speech from the All-Knowing (v. 34). Third, it instructs every reader how to treat sacred history — not as legend decorating doctrine, but as testified knowledge: what is recited here is *nabaʾ* — *news* — with the solidity of fact.

And the detail of the *lots* whispers one more lesson: Zachariah was chosen though others contested — custody of Mary, like empires in verse 26, is God's to bestow; and the small drama of the sanctuary mirrors the great one of history: God's elect are chosen *from above the lots*, and those prepared by Him are brought to their guardianships "when the pens are cast" and the disputants are loud. The house of ʿImrān receives what it never campaigned for; the story knows how much of what is most decisive in a life is decided beyond the disputed field of our canvassing. The believer's prayer after this verse writes itself: *Lord, You who bestowed in the unseen of that sanctuary, allot for me in my own unseen what is best — and teach me, like Mary, to be worthy of the allotting.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:45

> **When the angels said, "O Mary, truly God gives thee glad tidings of a Word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, high honored in this world and the Hereafter, and one of those brought nigh."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Annunciation: A Word Is Promised**

For the second time, heaven opens upon Mary with her name: *idh qālati al-malāʾikatu yā Maryamu inna Allāha yubashshiruki bi-kalimatin minhu* — "O Mary! Truly God gives you glad tidings of a *Word* from Him." The annunciation given to Zachariah was of a son named and numbered among the righteous; to Mary it is of something stranger and prior: a *kalimah* — a *word* — from God. Every child is formed by God's creative command; this child is so identified with the command itself that he is named for it. The best commentary on the phrase is the Qur'an's own, two verses later: "when He decrees a thing, He only says to it, 'Be!' (kun) — and it is" (v. 47), and at v. 59: the likeness of Jesus before God is as Adam — "He created him from dust, then said to him, Be! and he was." Jesus is "a Word from Him" because his very existence was a direct divine fiat — "Be!" — issued without the mediation of a father. Al-Rāzī mentions the idioms of Arabic honor: as one calls a magnanimous man "generosity itself," so is Jesus "a Word from Him" — the perfect venue through which God's creative speech became visible in the world. The opening passage of Sūrah 19:16–21, the fuller annunciation narrative, identifies the carrying angel specifically — Gabriel in the form of a "well-proportioned man," saying: *"I am only the messenger of your Lord, that I may bestow on you a pure boy"* (19:19).

**The Name Descends with the Child**

The announcement then denominates him in full: *ismuhu al-Masīḥu ʿĪsā ibnu Maryam* — "whose name is the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary." Three designations folded in one. *Al-Masīḥ* — the Messiah: the anointed one (Hebrew *mashiach*). Classical commentators offered derivations from the Arabic root: one *masaḥa* — one who was anointed or whom God anointed for blessing; another heard *masīḥ* as the *traveling* one (*sāʾiḥ*) who journeys the earth in God's service, or one "wiped clean" of sin (Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah among the transmitters of these understandings). Whatever the linguistic path, the office in Israelite scripture was regal and priestly — anointed king, anointed servant — and Jesus, in the Qur'an's presentation, carries it without crown or altar-politics: a Messiah whose domain is truth and healing. *ʿĪsā* — Jesus — the personal name by which the Qur'an names him twenty-five times, never in idolizing hush, always as prophet and sign; Islamic tradition retains al-Ghazālī's note that his was among the ancient noble Hebrew names. Then the matronymic, which is this chapter's theological signature: *ibn Maryam* — *son of Mary* — a deliberate, repeated designation (the Qur'an calls him "son of Mary" some two dozen times) that performs doctrine as naming: he is forever identified by his *mother*, which both honors her to the end of the world and denies, in the very name, the attribution of him to any father — human or divine.

**Honored in Both Abodes, Brought Near**

The angels conclude with his rank: *wajīhan fī al-dunyā wa-l-ākhirah wa min al-muqarrabīn* — "high-honored in this world and the Hereafter, and among those brought nigh." *Wajīh* — from *wajh*, face — is the person of standing, the one held in regard, face-forward in honor. In the world: his miraculous speech and table, his mission confirmed from cradle to maturity; in the Hereafter: his station with God, his intercession on behalf of his people by God's leave, as among the resolute messengers (*ulū al-ʿazm*, 46:35). *Al-muqarrabūn*, "those brought nigh," is the Qur'an's own highest circle — the foremost drawn-near (56:11: "the foremost, the foremost — they are the ones brought nigh"; 83:21), applied by the commentators here to the most honored of angels and prophets; Jesus is enrolled, in the veil of annunciation, *already* among them. Christian devotional language often wrapped him in metaphysics; the Qur'an keeps every superlative and names him — honored, near, chosen — as *servant*. The glory of the greatest member of the House of ʿImrān is thereby fully affirmed, and entirely re-anchored: the Messiah is God's gift through Mary, not God's entry into biology.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:46

> **He will speak to people in the cradle and in maturity, and will be among the righteous."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Podiums Across a Life: The Cradle and Manhood**

The annunciation's portrait of Jesus ends with a marvel of prophetic biography: *wa yukallimu al-nāsa fī al-mahdi wa kahlan* — "and he shall speak to the people in the cradle, and in maturity." *Mahd* is the cradle — infancy's bed; *kahl* is mature manhood — between thirty and forty, when strength and judgment join. The commentators read the two podiums as the delimitation of his mission's witnesses: the first speech, God's defense of his mother's honor; the last, God's commissioning of Israel's reform. Both are speeches God gave; both served the same message.

The event at the cradle is told at length in Sūrah 19, and is among the most astonishing signs in all revealed narrative. The Qur'an's Mary returns to her people carrying the newborn; they confront her with the cruelest suspicion a consecrated woman could face: *"O sister of Aaron! Your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother unchaste"* (19:28). Mary, divinely instructed, does not argue her case — she points to the child. The scandalized crowd protests: *"How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?"* — at which the infant opens his mouth with his creed:

> *"He said: 'Truly I am the servant of God. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet. He has made me blessed wherever I am, and charged me with prayer and almsgiving so long as I live; and dutiful to my mother; and He has not made me a tyrant, wretched. And peace be upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive.'"* (Qur'an 19:30–33)

The child from the crib utters "I am the servant of God" — *ʿabd Allāh* — the precise designation that forever closes the door on divinizing him; his first words in history are his own definitive christology. And he utters, in the same cradle-speech, the doctrine his honored mother needed most: *peace upon me, the day I was born* — the day the crowd condemned as evidence of guilt is declared the day of peace.

**The Bookend of Maturity, and the Frame of the Book**

"And in maturity" — prophecy's full station: his fluent wisdom among men, his Torah, his Gospel, his confrontation of the learned, his proofs and his patience; the commentators note that the phrase *fī al-mahdi wa kahlan* is also a quiet chronology: between two speeches comes a silence, the hidden years, in which the sign walked among people and ate food as they did. And the verse seals with the class-verdict the entire chapter has been building: *wa mina al-ṣāliḥīn* — "and he shall be among the righteous" — enrolled in the corporation of the sound into which John was enrolled in verse 39: the repeated designation performs jurisprudence as creed: every angelic biography in this chapter terminates in *ṣalāḥ* — God-given soundness — not ontological otherness.

For the believer, this cradle-and-maturity pattern bears a deep consolation: God's defense of the innocent can arrive through the least expected instruments, at the least expected time. Mary did not defend herself; a cradle did. Those who hand their case to God — as she did, pointing silently — find that He appoints for them advocates beyond the reach of calculation: "Truly God defends those who believe" (22:38). The Messiah's first miracle was not a cure or a storm stilled — it was *testimony*: that truth, at the crucial hour, spoke.
**Mahd and Kahl: The Two Voices of the Word**

The promise's fifth act fixes the miraculous across the whole age-spectrum: *wa yukallimu al-nāsa fī al-mahdi wa kahlan* — "and he speaks to people in the cradle and in maturity." *Mahd* (cradle) and *kahl* (the strength-season of life's middle — glossed by the early authorities as the thirties, when Jesus' ministry opened) span existence from its weakest crib to its strongest hour — *both* made pulpits. The cradle-speech, proclaimed in the next verses, is the world's one childhood-sermon, and the Prophet ﷺ counted it among the three soundest infant-speeches preserved:

> *"None spoke in the cradle but three: Jesus son of Mary; and the companion of Jurayj... and the child who spoke for the prophet Joseph's innocence."* (al-Bukhārī 3434&ndash;3435 et al., from Abū Hurayrah)

— the three infants each vindicating a wronged party: a prophet accused, a monk accused, a prophet accused. Even the nursery's mouths, in God's court, open only for the defense.

**Wa ka-Kahlan: The Ptarmigan of Ministry Prepared**

*Kahlan* — the Word speaks *when mature* — guards the second half of the marvel: the same Jesus whose infant-tongue confessed *servant, prophet-in-trust* would, at his strength's peak, stand in the temple the elders used to close to wanderers — words as if of birds made men by his preaching. Between the cradle and the kahl lies a hidden span the Gospels dearly fill and the Qur'an deliberately leaves — the boy between the two miracles growing "in wisdom and favour" — and the salīs-sensed reader understands: God's proofs do not need a paper-trail between miracles; *Be* at the cradle and *Be* in the temple suffice.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:47

> **She said, "My Lord, how shall I have a child while no human being has touched me?" He said, "Thus does God create whatsoever He will." When He decrees a thing, He only says to it, "Be!" and it is.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Chaste Woman's "How?" — Paragon of a Legitimate Question**

Mary's response to the annunciation is the sibling of Zachariah's (v. 40): *rabbi annā yakūnu lī waladun wa lam yamsasnī bashar* — "My Lord, how shall I have a child, when no human being has touched me?" Her *annā* — "how?" — is the model of a lawful question posed to the impossible. It is not doubt of God; Mary, chosen and purified, speaking with angels in a chamber where provision arrives out of season, had no creed-uncertainty. It is the mind's natural request for the *how* before an entirely unprecedented mode of event: male-less conception had no precedent in all of nature. Note too the purity of her wording: *lam yamsasnī bashar* — no *human being* has touched me — her question itself declares both her chastity and her biology; the annunciation is impossible by *both* natural knowledge and personal history, and she says so without shame before God, teaching by example that prayers and questions of faith need never disguise the facts. In Sūrah 19:20 her similar question has the even more exact wording: "how shall I have a boy when no human being has touched me, nor have I been unchaste (baghiyyan)?" — she rules out both licit marriage and illicit act.

**The Answer: The Grammar of "Be!"**

God's reply is the most majestic sentence of creative power in all scripture, repeated across the Book: *idhā qaḍā amran fa-innamā yaqūlu lahu kun fa-yakūn* — "When He decrees a thing, He only says to it: 'Be!' — and it is." *Qaḍā* — when He decides, determines, concludes a matter — the decision occurs in His will and knowledge, instantly, beyond process. *Fa-innamā yaqūlu* — He *only says*: no exertion, no steps, no assembling; the particle *innamā* is restrictive — *nothing but* the word. *Kun* — "Be!" — two letters in Arabic, *kāf* and *nūn*, the entire creative imperative; *fa-yakūn* — "and it is" — the immediate conjugation of reality to the command. Ibn Taymiyyah drew the doctrine crisply: between God's command and the thing's existence there is no *interval*; "Our command is but one, like the glance of an eye" (54:50). Against every cosmology that needed God's labor or emanation, the Qur'an fixes sheer *address*: saying as making.

The sister formulations of this divine creative speech surround the verse: *"The Originator of the heavens and the earth — when He decrees a thing, He only says to it, 'Be!' and it is"* (2:117); *"His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be!' and it is"* (36:82; also 16:40; 19:35; 40:68). And the annunciation of Gabriel in Sūrah 19 gave Mary herself this same grammar in personal address: *"Your Lord says: It is easy for Me — and We shall make him a sign unto mankind, and a mercy from Us; and it is a matter decreed"* (19:21).
