*Fa-in tawallaw* — "so if they turn away": the conditional of the turned back is the chapter's recurring traffic-light (v. 20's preface to the same position; v. 32's; v. 64's coming) — tawallā* ever measuring the disposition of an audience rather than the truth of the message. Here its reach is political-immediate: the delegation of Najrān, eminent and argumentative, standing at the edge of the mubāhalah (mutual curse-invocation) — if they turn away from *that* test too, the next clause names what they are: *fa-inna Allāha ʿalīmun bi-l-mufsidīn* — "then truly God is Knowing of the corruptors."

**Mufsidūn: The Corruptor-Category**

*Al-mufsidūn* — corruption-worker's noun — is the Book's standing class for those whose disorder-work touches the deep structures (2:11's *do not corrupt in the earth*; 2:205's crops-and-progeny corruption; 7:56's ban; 28:77's God-loves-not-them clause). Its deployment *as a known class* — "God is Knowing of them" — rather than as a curse-addressed directly is the verse's most chilling register: the Knowledge that encounters them does so without mediation: no court is needed because no fact is hidden. The Prophet ﷺ taught the community to read such verses as personal test — *turning away* is not only a delegations' habit:

> *"Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him not sit at a table where wine is passed."* (al-Tirmidhī 2801, ḥasan) — and at its side, the warning-version the Book itself runs here: *heart that turns, reclassifies.*

For every century's readers the v. 63 question is live: having heard the true narrative (v. 62), which side of the conditional will you occupy?

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:64

> **Say, "O People of the Book! Come to a word common between us and you, that we shall worship none but God, shall not associate aught with Him, and shall not take one another as lords apart from God." And if they turn away, then say, "Bear witness that we are submitters."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Great Invitation: A Word Equal Between Us**

The mubāhalah had established the verdict; now God turns from confrontation to reconciliation, and issues through His Prophet what has been called the Magna Carta of Muslim interreligious address: *qul yā ahla al-kitābi taʿālāw ilā kalimatin sawāʾin baynanā wa baynakum* — "Say: O People of the Book! Come to a word *sawāʾ* between us and you." *Sawāʾ* is one of the Qur'an's most fertile words: same, level, equal, just, fair, and *middle* — from the tri-lateral root of leveling; al-Rāzī glosses the phrase "a word in which there is fair treatment from each of us to the other"; others, the "middle of the road (*sawāʾ al-sabīl*), the right way"; still others, "that upon which our Books do not differ." Every reading converges on the same luminous posture: the Muslims are commanded to invite the older communities not to *the Muslim distinctive*, but to the *level ground* — the common denominator — of all God's revealed religions: *allā naʿbuda illā Allāh* — "that we worship none but God"; *wa lā nushrika bihi shayʾan* — "and associate nothing with Him"; *wa lā yattakhidha baʿḍunā baʿḍan arbāban min dūni Allāh* — "and that we not take one another as lords apart from God."

**The Three Clauses Parsed**

The first clause is the worship-clause: *ʿibādah* — prayer, sacrifice, invocation — directed to God alone; the very sentence our chapter put on the Messiah's lips at verse 51: "worship Him — this is the straight path." It is, thus, *not* an Islamic imposition on Christians; it is presented as *their own prophets' creed*, reissued jointly. The second clause is the association-clause: *shirk* — pairing anything with Him — the privative of the first: no degrees, no consort, no son, no intermediary entitled to worship. And the third clause is among the subtlest in all revealed politics: *that we not take one another as lords beside God*. *Arbāb* — lords — plural of *rabb*: the verse condemns the transfer of lordship's authority — the power to command with divine weight, to legislate the forbidden as lawful and the lawful as forbidden — to any *human being*, clergy or laity. The companion diagnosis is 9:31: *"they have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords apart from God, as well as the Messiah, son of Mary — yet they were commanded only to worship one God."* And the Prophet ﷺ glossed what "taking as lords" means in an exchange with ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim (a Christian convert) recorded by al-Tirmidhī: when ʿAdī protested "we did not worship them," the Prophet asked: *"Did they not make lawful for you what was forbidden, and you held it lawful; and forbid you what was lawful, and you held it forbidden?"* — "Yes," said ʿAdī — *"that was your worship of them"* (al-Tirmidhī 3095; graded ḥasan). Lordship, in practical religion, is the *sovereignty of the command*: whoever may *declare* participation with God in that sovereignty is, in fact, being *lorded*. The clause therefore guards both monotheism and human liberty: no church, no rabbinate, no mullah-class — and by extension, in Islam's own case, the scholars guard the text that no ruler clothe his will in Heaven's command.

**"Bear Witness That We Are Submitters"**

And the close — the Book's standing exit-strategy once again (vv. 20, 63): *fa-in tawallaw fa-qūlū ish/hadū bi-annā muslimūn* — "if they turn away, then say: Bear witness that we are muslims (submitters)." The community is to say it collectively (*fa-qūlū*, plural — the whole ummah enrolled in the sentence): a public record of posture — *our practice begins at the common word you declined*. There is no violence in the verse, no bitterness: the common offer stands; the refusal is noted; the Muslim identity is defined *before the world* — submitters. The Prophet ﷺ embodied the verse in action on the largest stage: his letters of summons to Heraclius of Byzantium and the Negus of Abyssinia — preserved to this day in al-Bukhārī's Ṣaḥīḥ in the account of Abū Sufyān — opened with precisely this verse:

> *"From Muhammad, the servant of God and His Messenger, to Heraclius, the great one of Byzantium. Peace be upon whoever follows guidance. As to what follows: I invite you with the call of Islam... 'O People of the Book! Come to a word common between us and you...'"* (al-Bukhārī 7; Muslim 1773)

The verse remains the standing protocol of every Muslim address to Jews and Christians: begin at the level word — one God, no rivals, no human lordship — and end, when refused, with nothing more than an open registration of who we are. The call is perennially extended; *come* (*taʿālāw*) is present-tense, as enduring as the Book itself.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:65

> **O People of the Book! Why do you dispute concerning Abraham, as neither the Torah nor the Gospel was sent down until after him? Do you not understand?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Abraham: The Property-Claim That Precedes Its Own Deed**

The common word has been issued; now God begins the work of un-burying the shared patrimony, beginning with the father of them all: *yā ahla al-kitābi lima tuḥājjūna fī Ibrāhīm* — "O People of the Book! Why do you dispute concerning Abraham?" — *wa mā unzilati al-tawrātu wa-l-injīlu illā min baʿdih* — "when neither the Torah nor the Gospel was sent down until after him?" The argument is chronological and unanswerable in its simplicity: the contesting claims — "Abraham was a Jew," "Abraham was a Christian," in the claims the commentators record across the two communities — are definable only by texts that postdate Abraham himself by many centuries (Moses receiving Torah roughly a millennium after Abraham; the Gospel more than a millennium later again). One cannot be a member of a club that does not yet exist — the Prophets and the traditions they preside over come *later* than the man claimed for them. It was, the reports say, precisely the dispute rehearsed at verse 23 — the Jews replying to the Prophet's account of his faith "the creed of Abraham" with the claim "Abraham was a Jew" — and the Torah itself, when consulted, could decide nothing of the sort.

The concluding *a-fa-lā taʿqilūn* — "do you not understand? do you not reason?" — is among the Qur'an's standing summonses to the intellect (commentators count this address recurring dozens of times in the Book), and it places chronological reasoning within *ʿaql*, the faculty religion was designed to engage, not silence. The verse thus performs doctrinal correction *by appeal to logic* — the sūrah's verdict at verse 3 (mansions of revelation) and verse 60 (truth from your Lord) made *operational* in argument.

**The Deeper Dissolution: Property in the Sacred**

Beneath the chronological point lies the profound one the whole third chapter is driving: the great figures of sacred history are nobody's *property*. The Jews and Christians treating Abraham as *their* warrant — their exclusive title to legitimacy (cf. 2:135: "they said: be Jews or Christians, you will be guided; say: rather the creed of Abraham, the ḥanīf; and he was not of the idolaters") — were exhibiting the disease the chapter had diagnosed at verse 19: division *after* knowledge, out of mutual envy — sect-formation over the possessions of the spirit. God undoes the deed of appropriation by pre-dating the patriarch: before Torah, before Gospel, there stands the *original* religion — what verse 67 will name as *ḥanīfan musliman* — the primordial upright submission, the *fiṭrah*-religion that pre-dates denominational formations. The implication is a liberation for all three communities in every age: Abraham is not a partisan resource; he is the *common root* — and rootedness in him is not conferred by institutions but by congruence with his posture: God-friendship, pure monotheism, readiness to sacrifice. The argument therefore solves by *antiquity* what force could not solve: the last community can be nearest the first man, and the earliest institutions can be furthest, if by distance one measures fidelity of posture rather than documents.

**For Modern Ears: The Anti-Sectarian Principle**

Every age manufactures proprietary religions of lineage — our church's saint, our school's imam, our ancestry's covenant — but verse 65 insists: nobody's claim on the sacred is older than somebody's vote about it; the documents all follow the men they claim. Reason asks: who is nearest to Abraham *s* — the people who rehearse his name, or the people who repeat his act? The chapter will answer directly at verse 68: *"the people worthiest of Abraham are those who followed him."* Followership, not membership, is the only valid title of descent from prophets — and the possessors of intellect (*āl al-ʿaql* summoned at the verse's end) are called precisely to judge claims by that test.
**Anachronism as Argument: The Date-Before-Claim Logic**

The challenge's logical spine is a simple chronology the sūrah forces into consciousness: *the Torah and the Gospel were sent down only after him* — after Abraham — *do you not reason?* The argument's form is devastating because of its purity: no scripture quoted, no miracle summoned; *just a calendar*. Abraham's life predates both Moses' Book and Jesus's Gospel by centuries undisputed; *Jew* and *Christian* are labels denominated *by* those Books (and, in the narrowest usage, by later events) — so the labels cannot reach back to him. Al-Baqarah's twin passage states the syllogism as God's own courtroom: *"Or do you say that Abraham... was a Jew or a Christian? Say: do you know, or does God?"* (2:140). Ibn Kathīr files v. 65 as the climactic form of the *temporal objection*; al-Rāzī shows its general shape: *a description whose defining instance postdates the described cannot be applied to it* — a rule of reasoning the whole controversy needed anyway.

**A-lā Taʿqilūn: The Reason-Appeal as Standing Invitation**

The verse's closing appeal — *a-fa-lā taʿqilūn* — "will you not then reason?" — belongs to the Qur'an's grand summons-family (twenty-plus occurrences), and its use here is programmatic: revelation does not bypass reason but *referees* it; the reasoning faculty is invoked precisely at the points where inherited loyalties have clouded the plain chronology. The Prophet's ﷺ own deportment in dispute answered the *a-lā taʿqilūn* appeal all his life — arguing by the plainest premises, leaving boast aside — and v. 68's cap will seal the matter: the *nearest* to Abraham are neither title-holders but *those who followed him*. Date before claim; followship before label — Abraham's estate is apportioned by neither genealogy nor pride.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:66

> **Behold! You are the very same who dispute concerning that of which you have knowledge; so why do you dispute concerning that of which you have no knowledge? God knows, and you know not.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Irony of Arguing Beyond One's Authority**

The verse turns the juridical mirror, with the ringing vocative of exposure — *hā antum hāʾulāʾi* — "Behold! You are these same ones!" This construction in Arabic is heavy with rhetorical charge: it holds the addressee up in the third person to be seen — as though pointing him out to the assembly. The content of the exposure is a precise epistemic indictment: you who have disputed so confidently in matters where knowledge *was* in reach — the things of your own books and traditions that you could verify, the signs of your own time — why do you now extend the same argumentative confidence into *another* class of matters, those of which you have no knowledge? The commentators locate the first class variously: the disputes over their own doctrines and rival readings down the centuries (the councils and splits of Christology; the schools of the Law), or their knowledge of what was revealed concerning the awaited prophet in their own scriptures (7:157 states they "find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel"; cf. 2:146 — "they know him as they know their sons") — matters on which they questioned and contended *despite* access. The second class is Abraham: before whom, as verse 65 just established, they had neither text nor witness; yet on his identity they pronounced with total confidence.

**A Theory of Testimony, in One Verse**

The verse articulates nothing less than a principle of evidence, and the scholars of uṣūl have long quoted it when drawing the forms of valid knowledge: a man's right to dispute is commensurate with his *knowledge-access* to the disputed matter. Where there is access and the litem still wrangle, the malady is in will (envy, interest — v. 19); where there is no access and the litigants wrangle, the malady is compounded: to will-error is added ignorance-confident. Both species of controversy infect theological culture in every age — the polemics of the well-documented, and the mythology of the unwitnessed. The verse thereby also obliquely validates the Muslim community's epistemology of the two classes: regarding the *contents* of the scriptures and prophecies of old, the Muslims' claim is deferential — confirmed by the Qur'an honoring what it confirms; regarding the *unwitnessed* past, the Muslims' claim is anchored in the statements of the True Revealer: "the truth is from thy Lord" (v. 60), "God knows" — and nowhere does the believer found a position on tribal inheritance without warrant.

**"God Knows, and You Know Not" — The Verse's Quiet Crown**

The final phrase delivers the epistemic asymmetry in God's own economy: *wa Allāhu yaʿlamu wa antum lā taʿlamūn* — "and God knows, and you know not." The same four-word cadence closes 2:216 on the unknowability of what is good for us; its recurrence plants in the reader the *adab* of knowledge — knowing the coordinate-system of one's knowing: many things we know, many we do not; and one Thing — to speak in Qur'anic diction — knows both our objects and ourselves. The verse instructs us in the decorum of disputed questions: state where your knowing ends; argue only where you stand; and for the standings of the heart, the lineage of prophets, the destinies of peoples — receive from the Knower of the unseen. It is among the graces of this Book that after teaching us the account of Abraham, Mary, and the Messiah across sixty verses, it can still say: *God knows, and you know not* — with the tone not of suppression but of invitation into *humility*, which is the doorway of knowledge itself.
**Hā Antum Hāʾulāʾi: The Pointing-Formula of Exposure**

The verse's opening is perhaps the most pointedly colloquial of the sūrah's polemic-controls: *hāʾ antum hāʾulāʾi ḥājajtum* — "there you are — these ones — you have disputed" — a triple-demonstrative (rendered variously *lo! you! these!*) that the commentators treat as God's own pointing-finger in the courtroom. The immediate reference: they had disputed before — v. 63–65's context, above all the mubāhalah-talk — *about what they had knowledge of* (the matter of Jesus, partly documented in their books); now they reach for Abraham — *ḥājjajtum fī-mā laysa lakum bihi ʿilm* — disputing in what they have *no* knowledge of. Al-Qurṭubī reads the charge beneath the construction: a people formally equipped with scripture must be stricter, not laxer, with the limits of its license — *your books' data ends; your claims continue; God marks the breach.*

**The Epistemology of the Seal: God Knows, You Know Not**

*Wa-Allāhu yaʿlamu wa antum lā taʿlamūn* — "and God knows, and you know not": the line the community has carried as its humility-axiom — the exact words 2:216 sets above the believers' dislike of permitted and compulsory things — closes the verse, and with it the chapter's first full arbitration. The seal's function in polemic is to retire the dispute *upward*: when two sides argue prefixes (Jew? Christian?) the matter of Abraham belongs to the knower of Abraham; v. 67 will deliver the verdict in God's own speech — *Abraham was neither — but ḥanīf muslim* — and v. 68 will apportion his estate. For the reader the mechanics persist into every controversy since: *argue only to the edge of your knowledge; commit the rest to the Seal.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:67

> **Abraham was neither Jew nor Christian, but rather was a ḥanīf, a submitter, and he was not one of the idolaters.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Twelve Words That Empty the Vaults of Sectarianism**

The verse gives the Qur'an's definitive verdict on the identity of the first patriarch of the three faiths: *mā kāna Ibrāhīmu yahūdiyyan wa lā naṣrāniyyan, wa lākin kāna ḥanīfan musliman, wa mā kāna mina al-mushrikīn* — "Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; rather, he was a ḥanīf, a muslim (submitter); and he was not among the idolaters." Every term in it is a measured blade. First the negative: *neither Jew nor Christian* — the two claims neutralized by the chronological argument of verse 65; labels become property only after their own kanons exist, and Abraham precedes both. Then the positive: *ḥanīf* — one of the Qur'an's most precious words: the one who *inclines away from all deviation*, who turns his face singly toward God; al-ḥanīfiyyah is the name of the original, undistorted religion — the vertical inclination of the soul toward its Creator uncolored by institution; Abraham's own state is described with it on his lips at 6:79: *"I have turned my face to Him Who created the heavens and the earth, as a ḥanīf."* And *musliman* — a *submitter*: practicing *islām* before the word was a flag; precisely verse 19's definition of "the religion in God's sight: submission," fulfilled in one man in Ur of the Chaldees millennia before denominations. Then the second negative, which is not redundant: *he was not of the idolaters* — because in Abraham's *direct* environment idolatry was the living option (the idols of his father Āzar, of Babylon and of Harrān; the stars and moon and sun of 6:76–79), and his monotheism is expressly defined as *non-polytheism*: a singleness wrestled out of context, not inherited by location.

**The Primordial Religion and the Structure of the Three Faiths**

The theological implications are enormous, and the scholars have stacked them carefully. Abraham is the common ancestor *religiously* of Judaism (through Isaac), of Christendom (through Israel and, in Christian reading, through faith), and of Islam (through Ishmael and the Kaʿbah his hands rebuilt with Ishmael, 2:127). To declare him *ḥanīfan musliman* is to declare the *mother-current*: all three communities, at their best adequacy, flow from a monotheism that is none of them but belongs to God. The honored word *ibn Ibrāhīm* — "son of Abraham" — is thereby redefined: descent from Abraham follows from *sharing his posture*, not from inheriting his name. This the next verse will state openly. And this is why the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, challenged by claims that Abraham's legacy belonged to the People of the Book across the wall, could solidly declare: *"I am the most entitled of men to Abraham"* and, in the hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (3358) concerning the pool and the inheritance of prophethood; and in the ḥadīth regarding prayers upon the prophets: *"O God, as You sent prayers upon Abraham, surely You are Praiseworthy, Glorious"* — with Muslims making daily prayer's *salawāt* on Abraham and his house the permanent liturgical mesh with Ibrāhīm (al-Bukhārī 3370; Muslim 406).

**Ibrāhīm as the Program for Us**

Verse 67 is at last not description but *invitation*: its clauses constitute the Islamic program of self-definition in every age — refuse labels that God did not give (do not found identity on names; "do not say, we are the best of parties," without deed); *be* a ḥanīf — incline to God undividedly; *be* a muslim — surrender the face whole; and *preserve distance* from the idols of your own era, which are as periodically costumed as any era's: Babylon had statues; our ages have ideologies, appetites, states, selves. Abraham's biography in the Qur'an reads accordingly as a curriculum: he left his father's hearth rather than its idols (19:41–48); he argued a tyrant into silence about the Lord who gives life and death (2:258); he rebuilt the House with his son; he prayed for a city of security and a progeny of prayer (14:35–37) — Madinah's own arrivals are, in the Muslim reading, the *answer* to his two-thousand-year-old prayer. The ḥanīf is the overture; the rest of the sūrah is its development.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:68

> **Truly the people worthiest of Abraham are those who followed him, and this prophet and those who believe. And God is the Protector of the believers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Who Inherits the Patriarch?**

Verse 65 asked why they disputed concerning Abraham; verse 67 declared what Abraham was; verse 68 now assigns the estate: *inna awlā al-nāsi bi-Ibrāhīma la-lladhīna ittabaʿūhu wa hādhā al-nabiyyu wa-lladhīna āmanū* — "Truly the people worthiest of Abraham — with greatest claim upon him — are those who followed him, and this prophet, and those who believe." *Awlā* — the comparative of the root that gives *walī*, protector-patron — means "most entitled, nearest in bond": the key word of the sūrah's deeper grammar (which will govern verse 28's *awliyāʾ* and verse 68's own latter clause) appearing now as the criterion of sacred inheritance. Three claimants are enrolled, by deed and not by document:

**Followers of the man**: *alladhīna ittabaʿūhu* — those who followed *him* — in his own era a believing wife (Sarah), a nephew (Lot — 29:26: "Lot believed him"), and, down the ages, all who conformed in truth to his *ḥanīfiyyah* under each prophet of his line: Moses' true followers, Jesus' true apostles (vv. 52–53) — the *ittibāʿ* of Abraham, not the *intisāb* (affiliation-by-label) of Abraham.

**"This prophet"**: singular, definite, no name needed — Muhammad ﷺ — whose ministry revives Abraham's own program item for item: monotheism without mediation; the rebuilt ritual at Abraham's rebuilt House (the ḥajj retraces Hagar's running and Abraham's command to proclaim pilgrimage to mankind, 22:26–27); the creed named *millat Ibrāhīm*, with the Qur'an commanding: *"Say: my Lord has guided me to a straight path, an upright religion, the creed of Abraham, the ḥanīf"* (6:161; also 16:123: "then We revealed to you to follow the creed of Abraham, the ḥanīf — he was not among the idolaters"). The Prophet of Arabia is, in deed, the son of Abraham the Qur'an presents: not by an ethnological cord but by *covenantal identity* — the revivalist of the ḥanīf's fire across centuries of neglect.

**"Those who believe"**: his community — every reader who joins their posture. The verse rule enunciated is incalculably egalitarian in its effect: membership in the House of Abraham is conferred on *whosoever believes* — an Ethiopian slave and a Qurashī prince on one line (the Prophet's own community thus becomes the first in history enrolled under a patriarch by *franchise of faith*, not by blood). The Day of Resurrection will enforce the same principle: the ḥadīth of the pool records the Prophet addressing strangers among the gathered as his own — *"my companions"* — and the callers pulling some back, to which is said: "they changed after you" (al-Bukhārī 6576; Muslim 2290) — allegiance is current-keeping, not kept-certificate. Lineage-in-God is always *present-tense following*.

**"And God Is the Protector of the Believers"**

The verse closes with the title that anchors its own comparative: *wa Allāhu waliyyu al-muʾminīn* — "and God is the *Walī* of the believers." *Awlā* — worthiest — has led to *walī* — patron: the contest over Abraham's patronage dissolves in God's own patronage of *all* believers, regardless of tribe. God will say later in the Book: "God is the Protector of those who believe — He brings them out of darknesses into the light" (2:257). The believers' claim on Abraham is real *because* God's claim upon them is real; the inheritance of prophets flows through the patronage that encompasses every believer. And the promise is *protection*: the *walī* defends, advances, guides, and vindicates. Earlier in the sūrah the Helpers had cried "we are God's helpers" (v. 52); here is the reciprocal truth — human helpers of God are always God's *protégés*; the contract of *walāyah*, unlike any other, pays infinitely from the Stronger side.
**Awlā al-Nās: The Verb of Proximity Applied to a Patriarch**

*Inna awlā al-nāsi bi-ibrāhīma* — "indeed the nearest of people to Abraham": *awlā* — from the root *w-l-y* that gives its name to nearness, patronage, successorship — grades *nearness to a man* in God's own audit. Three classes answer to it, in the verse's chained appositions: *those who followed him* — his contemporaries of faith; *this prophet* — Muhammad ﷺ, paired at the middle like the keystone of an arch (blood-descendant through Ismāʿīl and faith-successor absolutely); *and those who believed* — the open category wherever anyone *believes as he believed*. The pedigree thereby reverts from genealogy to *followship* — the exact refutation of the prior verses' title-dispute — and the seal assigns the inheritance's stewardship: *wa-Allāhu waliyyu al-muʾminīn* — God is the believers' Patron — the *wa-lā*² bond of Abrahamic brotherhood finding its Lord at the bench.

**Paternal Brothers: The Prophets' Own Estimate**

The Prophet ﷺ sealed the doctrine inside his own family-idiom — a hadith the community has always felt as v. 68's human echo:

> *"The prophets are paternal brothers (ʿallāh): their mothers are many, but their religion is one."* (al-Bukhārī 3443; Muslim 2365, from Abū Hurayrah)

— one father of creed, many mothers of law-detail — and at his deathbed the same fraternity became his own escort-choice: *the Highest Companion*. Nearness to Abraham is thereby the household membership of all the prophets and their truest followers — not the blood of any quarter's pride. When the Najrānī and Madinan scholars argued prefixes, God's verse answered in the grammar of w-l-y: *proximity is measured in followship; the court is the Patron Himself; the door stands open to any believer in any century.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:69

> **A group among the People of the Book wishes to make you go astray; yet they make none go astray but themselves, though they are unaware.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Wishful Saboteurs and the Rebound of Schemes**

After the great invitations and verdicts, the sūrah names the party that answers grace with sabotage: *waddat ṭāʾifatun min ahli al-kitābi law yuḍillūnakum* — "a group among the People of the Book would love to lead you astray." The verb *wadda* is desiderative — *they would love, they wish* — thus locating the offense in intention before operation: here is a party whose *cherished object* is the believers' disorientation. The Qur'an does not generalize the charge to the whole People of the Book — it names a *ṭāʾifah*, a subset, a party — precision the Muslim community is duty-bound to maintain in its own judgments of others (the chapter will soon give the counter-portrait, vv. 75, 113–115, 199). And the divine commentary upon their wish contains one of the Book's repeated laws of moral physics: *wa mā yuḍillūna illā anfusahum wa mā yashʿurūn* — "yet they lead none astray but themselves, though they are unaware."

**The Law of the Returning Arrow**

The law deserves exposition, for it echoes across the Qur'an as a *axiom of God's moral governance*: deception directed at the faithful operates first and deepest upon its authors. Same wording in 2:9 — attempting to deceive God and the believers, "they deceive none but themselves, though they perceive not"; in inverted form: "they wronged Us not, but themselves they wronged" (2:57; 7:160; 16:33); and in the general maxim: *"whoever does evil, it is against himself"* (4:111). Al-Rāzī expands the psychology: the schemer pays the scheme's first costs — the constant dissimulation, the deforming watchfulness, the corrosion of capacity for sincerity; before a single victim is harmed, the schemer's own instrument has been de-calibrated. Thereafter, even when the scheme lands outwardly, the believer it strikes can be refined by the blow ("that He may test what is in your breasts," v. 154), whereas for the schemer there is no refining fire — the same blow lands on him as pure toxin, since he cannot read events as test; his compass was already false. Hence the Qur'an's closing commentary on *their* unawareness: *wa mā yashʿurūn* — the saddest clause in the matter: the strategy of misguiding generates a *clinical blindness* to its own reflux.

**Pastoral Application: Watchfulness Without Fear**

For the believers the verse is both warning and sedative. Warning: the designated threat is not open invasion but *iḍlāl* — disorientation, the subtle craft of making the straight look crooked: doubt-planting, information-shaping, selective quotation, the constant buzzing that "your tradition cannot be trusted" (the specifics appear in v. 72's scheme and v. 78's distortions). Sedative: the wish is *not* the deed; their plotting is ultimately self-referential; and God's people, kept in His protection (v. 68's *walī*), cannot be finally misled by others' wishes (2:102: "they harm no one thereby except by God's leave"). The community's standing instruction is therefore watch-and-hold: be informed about the party's schemes without being *possessed* by them — surveillance of the adversary must never become the believer's orientation; orientation is God-ward; vigilance is a perimeter, not a path. Verses 103–105 will shortly give the constructive counter-program: *hold fast together to the rope of God*. Wishers of misguidance thrive on divided attention; a community holding the rope wastes no footing on them.
**The Boomerang of Tuḍillūnakum**

*Waddat ṭāʾifatun min ahli al-kitābi law yuḍillūnakum, wa mā yuḍillūna illā anfusahum wa mā yashʿurūn* — "a party of the People of the Book would love to lead you astray; yet they lead none astray but themselves, while they perceive not." The arithmetic here is one of the Book's quiet fixed laws, repeated across its registers with almost identical grammar (6:26's *wa mā yuḍillūna illā anfusahum* in the Makkan frame): misguidance *aimed* returns misguidance *earned* — the corrupter's harvest is interior before it is ever historical. Al-Ṭabarī glosses in one line: their deception touches only their own accounts in the end; al-Rāzī strips the engine naked: he who invests thought, counsel, and reputational capital in another's ruin naturally reaps the energy's fruit *in himself*, since the target may be spared by God while the worker's heart has already worked and will not un-work.

**Wa Mā Yashʿurūn: Perception's Death as Punishment**

The last clause is the sharpest: *they perceive not* — perception (*shuʿūr*) itself listed among the losses. Obstruction's wage is not only misguidance but the very *failure to register it*, which is why the plot continues — the un-awareness functioning as both cause and continuing symptom. The early exegetes applied the verse to the specific counseling-circles of the Madinan hour (the stratagem-block, vv. 69, 72, 78); the Book's grammar opens it to every age: *the unbelieving plot against faith's people — and the ledger writes the expense in the plotters' column.* For the believer, the verse is comfort and caution in one: the enemy's plan decays on its own scaffold; the *community's* part is rather to be sure no such soil exists in its own ranks (the exact burden of the pericope closing in vv. 103–105).

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:70

> **O People of the Book! Why do you disbelieve in God's signs, while you are witness?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question of Witnessed Disbelief**

The sūrah resumes its direct address — *yā ahla al-kitāb* — with a question whose force rests on a single juxtaposition: *lima takfurūna bi-āyāti Allāhi wa antum tash/hadūn* — "Why do you disbelieve in God's signs, while you bear witness?" The clause *wa antum tashhadūn* operates in two registers, and both are active. Register one: while you are *witnesses* of the truth — custodians of scripture in which God's signs stand, and among whom the descriptions of a coming prophet circulated (2:146; 7:157). Men do not disbelieve in what is wholly alien to them as they disbelieve in what is proximate: the kind of *kufr* reproached here is not failure to *reach* the signs but failure to *answer* them — the signs are in your hands, and yet closed. Register two: while you *witness* — in the sense of God's own ongoing evidence before their eyes: Badr's arithmetic-defying victory was within their very year's news (v. 13); the Prophet's character was within their neighborhood; the light in the faces and lives of the youngest community in Arabia was before their observation. Disbelief under these conditions is not ignorance but *refusal at the window*.

**The Grammar of "Why?"**

The *lima* — "why?" — is a rhetorical tribunal the Book summons the People of the Book to repeatedly in this exact sūrah (vv. 65, 70, 71, 98, 99): not *whether* they disbelieve — that the Book has established — but *why*, since on their own terms the case should have closed. It is the question of conscience, of cross-examination: in the forum of the addressee's own witness, the Book names the contradiction, then leaves the addressee to answer — a method dignifying the listeners' reason far beyond mere verdict. The same marginal style underlies every genuine call to truth in the Qur'an: to arraign contradiction, not to eradicate the arraigned — verses 61 and 64 have already shown the chapter's invitations.

And the believer overhearing this tribunal learns the symmetrical rule: if witnessed *kufr* is scandal, witnessed *īmān* is correspondingly accountable. The Muslim who recites the Book daily while shelving its witness must expect the same *lima*: why do you *not practice* God's signs while you are witness? The question-mark God fixed over the People of the Book stands, by exact parity, over every later inheritor of revelation. The Prophet ﷺ himself made the parallel damningly concrete when he recited words the tradition treasures from the incident of the reciter who would be a lesson to others: *"They read the Qur'an but it does not pass their throats"* (al-Bukhārī 5058; Muslim 1066, concerning the Khawārij) — and in the general counsel: *"the Qur'an is a proof for you or against you"* (Muslim 223). Witnessing is both gift and ledger: the page you read will testify. Verse 70's "why" is therefore not only about them; it stands as the Qur'an's permanent invitation that every reader keep his belief and his witnessing in one column.
**Kayfa Takfurūn with the Witnesses' Clause**

The growing address-sequence — v. 65's rebuke of dispute, v. 69's exposure of the plot — now turns interrogative in the second person: *limā takfurūna bi-āyāti Allāhi wa antum tashhadūn* — "why do you disbelieve in God's signs while you yourselves bear witness?" The *kayfa/lima* family of God's questions (the verse's *limā* — why/of what cause) is never information-seeking; it is exposure-as-sentence: the double condition — denial *with witnessing* — names the exact gravity of their standing. The commentators distribute the meaning of *tashhadūn* in two complementary directions: (1) *you bear witness* to the prophecies of the Messenger's coming contained in your own scriptures — the witnessing of fulfilled expectation; (2) *you stand witnessing* the very recitation and its attendant evidences in the Prophet's own city, confirmation arriving live. Either way, denial under live witness doubles guilt: *knowledge with rejection*, the compound sin the sūrah marks irremediable at vv. 86–90 short of repentance.

**The Psychology of the Second-Person Plural**

God's own address — *wa antum tashhadūn* — stands structurally inside the youths-of-Book rebukes the chapter has been perfecting (vv. 65–98), and it is a template for reading one's self: *disbelief while perceiving* is the exact state every believer's heart is perpetually tempted to enter on a smaller scale — seeing the sign and withholding its conclusions. The Prophet's ﷺ simple reckoning stands beside the verse's door:

> *"God will not remove knowledge by snatching it from the people, but He removes knowledge by taking the scholars, until when no scholar remains the people take ignorant heads — they are asked, and they decree without knowledge; they go astray and lead astray."* (al-Bukhārī 100; Muslim 2673, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr)

— the oracles of vv. 69–70 written across the ages: denial adds nothing but darkness, and guide-loss completes it.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:71

> **O People of the Book! Why do you confound the truth with falsehood, and knowingly conceal the truth?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Mixing and Burying: Two Techniques of the Same Art**

The address immediately deepens from accusation of refusal (v. 70) to accusation of technique — the *methods* by which a knowing community resists a truth it cannot refute outright. First: *lima talbisūna al-ḥaqqa bi-l-bāṭil* — "why do you confound the truth with falsehood?" *Labs* is to dress: to robe one thing in the appearance of another, weaving truth and falsehood into a fabric where neither is any longer cleanly identifiable. It is subtler than open lying — the *content* includes genuine truth, but interlaid with what blurs its direction: history's most effective misinformation has always been selective, not invented; whole-context truth corrupted at the joints. The Book brands the same art at 2:42 ("do not confound the truth with falsehood, nor knowingly conceal the truth") — the recurring diagnosis of custodial treachery.

Second: *wa taktumūna al-ḥaqqa wa antum taʿlamūn* — "and conceal the truth, while you know." *Katama* is deliberate burial: the known held down; and the attending phrase *wa antum taʿlamūn* — while you know — makes it not error but *crime*. The commentators anchor the clause in the historical record: the recognition of the Prophet *as they knew their own sons* (2:146) categorically established in the same chapter's flow; the test of the Torah laid out at v. 23; the covered verse of stoning in al-Bukhārī's account — the palm laid over the line of Scripture so that it might not be read; the deliberate strategems of v. 72 to follow. Knowledge withheld against the arrival of its due hour is among the most solemn of all forms of theft — theft from *humanity*: knowledge denied to those for whom it was sent down as guidance.

**The Knowingly Buried Truth in Islam's Own Courts**

The gravity of the charge requires the Muslim community to hear it as regulation of itself. The Book's own legislation makes *kitmān al-ḥaqq* — concealment of the known truth — the marker of a heart at variance with God's command: "who conceals it — his heart is surely sinful" (2:283, of concealed testimony); and *"We made clear unto people, from the Book, the truth... whoever conceals what We sent down of clear proofs and guidance after We have made it clear — upon such is the curse of God and of those who curse"* (2:159–160). The Prophetic tradition furnishes the operating conditions in everyday law and diplomacy: a testimony withheld in a case of inheritance, a hadith-context trimmed to fit a fatwa desired, a translation bent to spare a verse's plain demand — all become this verse's *labs* and *katm* in current circulation. The tradition's counter-vow is salaciously direct: *"May God brighten the face of the one who hears my words, retains them, and transmits them as he heard them; for many a bearer of knowledge is not himself an understander, and many a bearer of knowledge carries it to one who understands more than he"* (al-Tirmidhī 2656; Aḥmad — multiple supports) — the chain-of-truth preserved, *unmixed and unburied*, across generations.

Verse 71 thus fixes two questions over every custodian of any scripture, including the Muslim reader: *what* are you mixing with your truth (cultures of excuse woven around plain commands), and *what* are you holding down (the demands you already know)? The chapter had already described the examiner — *"God knows what lies within breasts"* (v. 5) — and foretold the public accounting (v. 30). The verse's anticipation of that Day is this: buried truths are not deleted truths; they are seeds planted for a resurrection of questioning.
**Talbīs: Dressing Truth in the Costume of Falsehood**

The sūrah's polemic now names the subtlest instrument of all: *limā talbisūna al-ḥaqqa bi-l-bāṭili wa taktumūna al-ḥaqqa wa antum taʿlamūn* — "why do you cloak the truth with falsehood, and conceal the truth, knowing?" *Labasa* — to dress — sets the labor at its true metaphor: not open warfare on the truth but *tailoring it* — surrounding the authentic thread with imitation fabric until the buyer cannot tell the weave. The Book's own twin at 2:42 seals the prohibition in command-form: *"and do not cloak the truth with the false, nor conceal the truth while you know."* Al-Rāzī anatomizes the two sins as an industry: *talbīs* — active manipulation of presentation; *katm* — the withholding of the necessary remainder: corruption of disclosure joined to corruption of silence.

**The Concealment-Curse and Its Door of Return**

The conceal-clause (v. 71's second charge) stands in the file of the Book's gravest, for God Himself legislates the general rule barely two subject-slides later in al-Baqarah: *"Truly those who conceal what We sent down of the clarities and the guidance, after We made it clear to the people in the Book — those, God curses them, and the cursers curse them — except those who repent and amend and make clear..."* (2:159–160). The early transmitters (al-Bukhārī in the tafsīr of 2:159) hold the verses' first application to the scholars entrusted with the description of the Prophet ﷺ — with the grammar open to every concealment since. Against it the Prophet ﷺ set the scholar's charge; and the repentance-door (except those who repent and *make clear*) teaches the residue-law of every concealment-sin: its undoing requires *publication*: what was hidden must be brought out — the information owed, restored.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:72

> **And a group of the People of the Book say, "Believe in what was sent down unto those who believe at the start of the day, and disbelieve at its end, that haply they may return."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Stratagem of the Borrowed Day**

Verse 69 told of the *wish* to mislead; verse 72 exhibits a documented plot: *wa qālat ṭāʾifatun min ahli al-kitābi āminū bi-lladhī nuzzila ʿalā alladhīna āmanū wajha al-nahāri wa-kfurū ākhirah* — "a group of the People of the Book said: believe in what was sent down to the believers at the day's beginning, then disbelieve at its end — that perhaps they may return." The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr) report its concrete form: a party of the Jewish leadership of Madinah agreed among themselves to *attend the Muslims' dawn prayer, profess Islam publicly, spend the day among the believers — and then at evening renounce it*, returning to their own community. The purpose of this one-day conversion was *fissure*: to inscribe into the minds of the Muslims — especially the newest of them — the corrosive question: *these, who are masters of scripture and knowledge, looked into Muhammad's religion from inside and departed it in a day — what then did they find?* A staged exit would do what no polemic from outside could achieve: it would cast doubt by the authority of *experience*.

The plot is among history's earliest documented *false-flag* epistemological operations, and its sophistication repays attention: not assault on the message but manufacture of misleading testimony *about* the message — the modern sciences of persuasion would call it injected testimony, and every subsequent age has known its industrial versions: planted converts, paid defectors, curated apostasies arranged to run on schedule; the quality of a "who left and why" engineered as evidence stronger than argument, precisely because it steals the *form* of a witness: ḥadīth and Qur'an both implicitly mark it — how do you *receive* testimony? *"O you who believe! If an iniquitous person (fāsiq) comes to you with news, verify it"* (49:6) — and make of it no proof against the verification.

**"That Perhaps They May Return" — The Thermometer of the Plot**

The closing clause measures the design's intended yield: *laʿallahum yarjiʿūn* — "that perhaps they may return" — to their old ways: the polytheism of Makkah for the Emigrants; the jāhiliyyah-habits for the Helpers; and for all of them the relinquishing of the muḥakkam ground they stand upon. The Qur'an's awareness of the psychology is total: doubt is contagious in a new community precisely where authority is admired — and the masters of older scripture represented, to the young community, the heavy credential: *they have a book, learning, ancient cities*. The plot hopes to make confidence dislodgeable by impersonating what confidence fears most — the verdict of the learned.

**Divine Counter via the Book, and Its Echo for the Present**

The verse's reply is itself the first countermeasure: the plot is *published*. God exposes it in lasting scripture, thus inoculating every future generation of the ummah: exposed schemes lose their principal weapon — innocence. The believer is immunized not by naiveté (God has banned *that* already, v. 69's warning) but by *informedness*: knowing that engineered disbelief exists, costumed as testimony. Then the immunology continues in the immediately following verse 73 with the specific axis the plot sought to turn: authority. Their claim was: no guidance but ours. God's answer: *"say: truly guidance is God's guidance."* The chapter's full program (vv. 69–79) thus forms a coherent curriculum on religious information-warfare: the wish (69), the concealment (71), the staged defection (72), the authority-monopoly (73), defeated by the God whose bounty is in His own Hand (73–74) — a curriculum no age of believers — whether facing propaganda, funded "ex-Muslim" industries, or asynchronous doubt-manufacture — can afford to skip.
**Wajh al-Nahār: The Stratagem of the Day's Face**

The party's script is quoted as one of the most calculated sentences recorded in the tafsīr of Madinah: *āminū bi-lladhī unzila ʿalā alladhīna āmanū wajha al-nahāri wa-kfurū ākhirahu* — "believe in what was sent down upon the believers at the day's beginning, and disbelieve at its end — perhaps they will return." The term *wajh al-nahār* — "the day's face," its forenoon opening — may be read two complementary ways, and the commentators rehearse both: (1) *rotate the adoption*: publicly profess at first light, defect by dusk, so the watching community concludes the religion *could not survive inspection*; (2) gloss the *face* of the day's revelation — the parts sent earliest — as scripturally acceptable while denying *its end* — preserving the appearance of scripture-loyalty while amputating the Islamic terminus. Both readings run in the same scheme: *manage reverence as theatre; weaponize reverence's appearance.*

**Laʿallahum Yarjiʿūn: The Plot's Own Confessed Guesswork**

The plan's resolution-clause has its own subtle grammar: *laʿallahum yarjiʿūn* — "perhaps they will return" — the *laʿalla* of hope uttered within the plot itself confessing the stratagem's guesswork. Al-Ṭabarī ties the report to the named Madinan counselors (whose layer of pretended Islam the next verses will handle); al-Rāzī steps back to its generic psychology: obstruction's thinkers *measure* their strategies not by certainty but by *hope of disorientation* — seeds of doubt being the cheaper counterpart of arguments they lack. The community's own defense begins in the very next verse (v. 73's *guidance is God's guidance*) and completes in the rope-covenant of vv. 103–105: *hold together, by God's strong rope; and do not divide.* The ritual-seekers of every age still attempt some *wajh al-nahār* theatre for the credulous; the chapter's answer is unplayed stillness: religion, not appearance; rope, not rotation.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:73

> **And believe none but him who follows your religion..." Say, "Truly guidance is God's Guidance." "...lest anyone be granted the like of what you were granted or dispute with you before your Lord." Say, "Truly bounty is in God's Hand. He grants it to whomsoever He will, and God is All-Encompassing, Knowing."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Monopoly Claim and Its Two Divine Answers**

The conspiratorial speech of verse 72 continues with the second plank of the strategy: *wa lā tuʾminū illā li-man tabiʿa dīnakum* — "and believe none except one who follows your religion." It is the classic counsel of insulation: close the circle of credibility to your own adherents; treat any voice from outside the circle as inaudible — the oldest defense-mechanism of every established religious institution confronted by fresh truth. God's reply interrupts their speech mid-sentence — the verse's dramatic grammar stages it exactly so, their words broken by revelation's rebuttal — first answer: *qul inna al-hudā hudā Allāh* — "Say: truly guidance is GOD'S guidance." Guidance is not the property of any community's brand; it is a divine act, and it arrives where God sends it — with whomever He chooses. The oldest possession-dispute in religious history is thus settled in principle from above: no community, synagogue, church, or school owns the channel.

**The Envy Exposed in Their Own Words**

Their second objection is preserved verbatim, and it is reflexively self-disclosing: "...lest anyone be granted the like of what you were granted, or dispute with you before your Lord." Read their fear: if another people receives "the like of what you were granted" — revelation equal to yours — then their prophetic exclusiveness is void; and if the newcomers "dispute with you before your Lord" — out-arguing you at the Judgment with your own scriptures — then your record degrades. The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī) note the transparency of these admissions: the objection confessed that the Muslims' proof was genuinely powerful and genuinely scripture-based — otherwise, why warn against their being granted "the like" of what Israel held, and why foresee losing a debate *before the Lord*? Envy wears the mask of doctrinal caution, and underneath it speaks its true language: a property-anxiety about God's gifts.

**"Bounty Is in God's Hand"**

The second interruption answers the fear with the verse's luminous correction: *qul inna al-faḍla bi-yadi Allāhi yuʾtīhi man yashāʾ* — "Say: truly bounty is in God's Hand; He grants it unto whomsoever He wills." *Faḍl* — bounty, surplus, favor, overflowing grace — covers the whole contested estate here: prophethood, revelation, guidance, illumination. It is stored in no vault of any community's saints or archives; God's Hand dispenses it. The verse thus completes the sūrah's own recurring theology — the same Hand holds sovereignty (v. 26: "Thou givest sovereignty to whomsoever Thou wilt"), the same Hand holds provision (v. 27: "Thou providest for whomsoever Thou wilt without reckoning"); guidance is the third treasure in the same Hand. The two Names that follow install the abolition of every pessimism about God's generosity: *wa Allāhu wāsiʿun ʿalīm* — "God is All-Encompassing, Knowing." *Wāsiʿ* — He of plenitude, whose resources and grace cannot be exhausted by any number of recipients; the fear "if more are granted, less remains for us" is here canceled as arithmetic error: the fount is unbounded. *ʿAlīm* — His giving is not indiscriminate: the knowledge of where guidance belongs is His (echoed in 6:124: "God knows best where He places His message"). Who receives revelation is not a lottery; it is plenitude, governed by wisdom.

**The Standing Rule for Every Later Community**

The verse is Islam's perpetual inoculation — against others' monopolies, and equally against *our own*. The same ummah who received guidance as God's free bounty is not to re-found the monopoly in its own name a century later: the gates of ijtihād, of the hujja presented, of the stranger accepted, are guarded by this verse. A religion that begins to believe God has exhausted His generosity with its own ancestors has re-carved the idol of verse 73 in its own image. Guidance is God's guidance — yesterday, today, and at the Resurrection — and the hand of His bounty gives to whomever He wills: that sentence alone *sustains* the humility that keeps guidance alive in those who have received it.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:74

> **He selects for His Mercy whomsoever He will, and God is Possessed of Tremendous Bounty.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Mercy's Own Choice**

The rebuttal of the monopoly-claim is now completed with mercy's own prerogative: *yakhtaṣṣu bi-raḥmatihi man yashāʾ* — "He selects — singles out — for His Mercy whomsoever He will." The verb *yakhtaṣṣu*, from *khaṣṣa*, to make particular, performs God's freedom: mercy is not rationed by census of any people; God selects persons, generations, and nations for its special visitation. The consensus of the commentators identifies the immediate referent: the Prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and the acceptance of his community — God's selection, against the envy-woched claims of those who thought mercy had no further mandate to issue. The verse thereby seals verses 73's sentence: bounty is in God's Hand (the *what*), He selects whom He wills (the *how*).

**The Order of the Two Names**

The seal then repeats with exact deliberation the attribute of verse 73's ending, but in the superlative of intimacy: *wa Allāhu dhū al-faḍli al-ʿaẓīm* — "and God is Possessed of the Tremendous Bounty." Note the crescendo across the two verses: 73 ends "God is All-Encompassing, Knowing" — the attribute of capacity and knowledge of placement; 74 ends "Possessed of the Tremendous Bounty" — the attribute of *spending*. God first declares the infinitude of His store against every insider's arithmetic, and then declares Himself *the very owner of giving* — a title ('dhū al-faḍl') that treats generosity not as an occasional act but as a permanent estate: faḍl ʿaẓīm — bounty *tremendous*, an Arabic phrase of ultimate amplitude used elsewhere of salvation's highest categories (153x magnitudes?—) — "today is the tremendous triumph (4:13, abiding forever in gardens — that is the tremendous success)" and of the People of Badr's reward (3:172) — until at chapter's end "God — with Him is the best of rewards" (v. 195).

**The Selection, Received: Muhammad ﷺ and Every Chosen Vessel**

For the Prophet ﷺ personally the verse completed a thirteen-year catechesis: the orphan of Makkah, unlettered among clerics, *selected*: *"God singles out for His mercy whom He wills"* — exactly the answer to every objection of pedigree (this sūrah's verse 26 has already disposed of the crown-claim: "Thou givest sovereignty to whomsoever Thou wilt"). The Muslim community heard in it its own election: *not* as title-deed but as mercy — "that He may know the believers" (v. 141) and "you are the best community *brought forth* for mankind" (v. 110) — brought forth (*ukhrijat*) by a selective action of God, not by self-generation: nothing in our origin entitled us; everything in our election calls us.

For theology the verse guards a critical balance between the two traditional poles of the understanding of election: mercy's selectivity is *not* caprice — it is *willed* selection by the All-Knowing — and neither is it wage — it is *faḍl*, always surplus, never entitlement: the Prophet ﷺ himself taught its application to salvation: *"No one of you enters Paradise by his deeds... not even I, unless God covers me with His mercy"* (al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816). The believer who holds verse 74 rightly will carry two dispositions at once: humility (his faith was granted, not achieved) and audacity in asking (the Giver's bounty is ʿaẓīm; its ceiling is un-plumbable). And the polemical answer to the sūrah's ancient objectors remains standing: the question is never "by what right does God give the like?" but "on whom will His mercy's selection settle next?"
**Yakhtaṣṣu bi-Raḥmatihi: Purity of Selection, Breadth of Mercy**

*Yakhtaṣṣu bi-raḥmatihi man yashāʾ* — "He singles out for His mercy whom He wills": the root *kh-ṣ-ṣ* gives the Arabic world's vocabulary of exclusive specification — *khāṣṣah*, the inner circle — and here the discipline of the earlier controversy (vv. 73–74 must be read together) is single-handed: *specialization of mercy* — prophethood above all — lies inside God's own competence, not Israel's patent nor the city's elders' pride. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī see in the clause a direct reply to those who would dictate who receives revelation (Quraysh's contemporaries murmuring at 6:124: *"God best knows where He places His message"*); al-Rāzī lifts it to the general frame: *No creature budgets the Creator's mercy-allocations.* And the coupling — mercy's specialization *inside* a declared overall bounty (*wa-Allāhu dhū al-faḍli al-ʿaẓīm* — God is the possessor of tremendous bounty) — prevents the doctrine from hardening into scarcity: appointment is narrow; bounty is wide.

**Al-Faḍl al-ʿAẓīm: The Chapter's Signature Seal**

With this clause one of the sūrah's most instructive hall-marks stands in place: the seal *God is the possessor of tremendous bounty* will return at v. 174 — the chapter's two mercy-doors at either end of its argument (here against envy of the Messenger's office; there against the post-Uḥud tremors). In the pericope's application to the reader: *faḍl* is the Book's answer to spiritual economics-think — God gives beyond merit, beyond arithmetic, and His largesse is not rationed by envy of neighbors. The Prophet's own aspiration is documented as the believers' standing etiquette:

> *"Ask God of His bounty (faḍl), for God loves to be asked; and the best worship is expectation of relief."* (al-Tirmidhī 3384, ḥasan)

Bounty vast; allocation His; envy none — in three clauses coveting dies, and gratitude learns its station.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:75

> **Among the People of the Book is one who, were you to entrust to him a quintal, would render it back to you. And among them is one who, were you to entrust to him a dinar, would not render it back to you unless you kept standing over him. That is because they say, "There is nothing to stop us when it comes to the non-Jews." But they knowingly speak a lie against God.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Trust Test and the Refusal to Stereotype**

After nine verses of severely specific indictment against a *party* (ṭāʾifah) among the People of the Book, God — with the fairness that characterizes this entire sūrah — immediately legislates against generalization. The verse creates two portraits, drawn with mathematical sharpness: *wa min ahli al-kitābi man in taʾmanhu bi-qinṭārin yuʾaddihi ilayk* — "among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrusted him with a *qinṭār* (a quintal — a vast sum, the same word of the hoarded heaps of gold and silver in v. 14), would return it to you"; *wa minhum man in taʾmanhu bi-dīnārin lam yuʾaddihi ilayka illā mā dumta ʿalayhi qāʾiman* — "and among them is one who, if you entrusted him with a *single dinar*, would not return it unless you kept standing over him." The smaller trust is withheld; the larger is honored: the contrast is not of class but of *conscience*. The commentators from Ibn ʿAbbās onward (al-Qurṭubī records his own application of it) recognize the verse's teaching as possessing practical juridical force: dealing with individuals as individuals, judging by the man and not by the tribe. Indeed al-Qurṭubī relates that some Muslims once came to Ibn ʿAbbās claiming license to take property of treaty-protected non-Muslims — "there is nothing to stop us when it comes to them" — and Ibn ʿAbbās corrected them fiercely: *it is not permissible*; the trusts stand.

**"There Is Nothing to Stop Us": The Doctrine of the Second Circle**

What pathology produced the second portrait? The verse itself diagnoses: *dhālika bi-annahum qālū laysa ʿalaynā fī al-ummiyyīna sabīl* — "that is because they say: 'there is no way over us [no account against us] with regard to the ummiyyūn.'" *Ummiyyūn* — rendered "non-Jews" here — signified the Gentiles, those outside their covenant; and the doctrine alleged is one every religious claque reinvents: *in-group ethics with an out-group exemption*: the full rigor of the Law obtains toward brothers; toward outsiders, the paths of payment relax. God calls this what it is, in the verse's own closing phrase: *wa yaqūlūna ʿalā Allāhi al-kadhiba wa hum yaʿlamūn* — "while they knowingly speak the lie against God": fabricating a doctrine of exemption and attributing it to Him — taḥrīf by interpretation — the sophisticated cousin of the outright text-falsification verse 78 will name.

The moral structure of this disease is universally recognizable: the moment a community divides God's moral jurisdiction into *ours* and *theirs*, honesty finds itself taxed at the border — lying to the unbeliever is exempted, exploiting the foreigner is condoned, the *other* is computationally discounted. The Book's ruling against it, issued here in defense of the Muslims' *enemies*, carries a built-in rule for the Muslims themselves: *Islamic ethics must not have a second circle*. And the Prophet ﷺ made it personal and final, in the famous ruling on the murdered treaty man:

> *"Whoever kills a person of the covenant (muʿāhad) without right, God will forbid him the fragrance of Paradise, and indeed its fragrance is found from a journey of forty years."* (al-Bukhārī 3166; and in Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī with the forty-year distance)

**Amānah: The Whole Religion in One Word**

The incident concerns *amānah* — trust — the most load-bearing word of Islamic social ethics. Returning trusts is the Qur'anic title of the faithful: *"those who are faithful to their trusts (amānātihim) and their covenant"* (23:8; 70:32), placed in the muster-roll of the felicitous alongside prayer and chastity. And the Prophet ﷺ framed the inverse memorably in a hadith already invoked once in this series for covenants: *"the signs of the hypocrite are three... and when he is entrusted, he betrays"* (al-Bukhārī 33; Muslim 59) — betrayal of trust is *nifāq* in conduct. Adherence to it, by contrast, is so strong an evidence of religion that the Prophet's own pre-prophetic career bore it as a title: *al-Amīn*, the Trustworthy — the Makkans' unanimous name for him before they opposed him. Verse 75 thus stands among the sūrah's great equitableness-texts: it honors a believing conscience wherever it survives (among the People of the Book there is one who returns the quintal!) — and it excommunicates from the language of righteousness every ethics with a border.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:76

> **Yea! Whosoever fulfills his pact and is reverent — truly God loves the reverent.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Yea!" — The Book's Answer to Partial Justice**

Verse 75 ended on the knowing lie; verse 76 opens with *balā* — "Yea!" — the Arabic particle of emphatic affirmative reversal: on the contrary, no; not as they say; the rule is otherwise. After the exposure of the false exemption, the Book delivers the true law in one clause, universal and unbordered: *man awfā bi-ʿahdihi wa-ttaqā* — "whosoever fulfills his pact and is reverent — truly God loves the reverent." Three conditions woven in one consequence, and they repay slow reading.

First, *awfā bi-ʿahdihi* — fulfills his *pact*: *wafāʾ* is completion, discharge in full, nothing shorted (it appeared at v. 57 as God's own payment of rewards *in full*: the human virtue and the divine attribute share a root — we are called to a fidelity that images His). Second, *wa-ttaqā* — *and is reverent* — the shield-and-consciousness of God, taqwā: the pact-keeping is not stipulated as mere legalism of contract but as *the fruit of God-consciousness*: you keep promises because a Witness keeps you. The combined clause thereby defines piety's operational test: taqwā is not a private ecstasy; its recognized currency is kept commitments. And third, the consequence — one of the most consequential in religious language: *fa-inna Allāha yuḥibbu al-muttaqīn* — "truly God *loves* the reverent": the seventh of the sūrah's great love-clauses (vv. 31, 32, 57), and the first promise of divine love attaching to *behavioral* fidelity. The sūrah of love thus programs its reader: covenant-keeping is not merely social lubricant; it is a *love-language* between the servant and God.

**From a Domestic Verdict to a Universal Law**

Read in context, the "Yea!" proclaims: God's love crosses the sectarian border that the false exemption had drawn. The Jew who fulfills his pact, the Muslim, the Christian — *whosoever* (*man*, the generalizing particle) — the love of God for reverent covenant-keepers is distributed by the rule, not by the roster. The commentators accepted this universality precisely where *wafāʾ* exists — as Ibn Kathīr glosses the verse: whoever keeps covenant with God and with people, and guards himself against betrayal — the rule holds: God loves the reverent. It is the counterweight-and-complement of 2:177 ("righteousness is... [among other things] *and those who keep their covenant when they covenant*"), and the specific answer to verse 75's two portraits: the faithful quintal-returner and the evasive dinar-wrester are not adjudicated by tribe *but by covenant kept*; the verse bookends: *the faithful one is loved*.

**Covenants Great and Small**

The application sphere of *ʿahd* is vast — the jurists and teachers subdivide it into the covenant with God (tawḥīd, obedience), the covenants with people (contracts, treaties, promises, marriages, oaths, micro-commitments — "I will call you back"; "we will meet Friday"), and the covenants with oneself (resolutions taken in prayer). The Prophet's biography is the Sunnah of this verse: emissaries were safe with him; treaties were kept to the letter even when the letter cost (his honoring of Ṣuḥayl's clause at Hudaybiyyah, returning the man who came to him when the treaty had just been signed, is the sīrah's standing monument to *wafā'*: Muslim and al-Bukhārī's accounts of the Ḥudaybiyyah pact). The structure of the verse as psychology is equally precise: *keep pacts, because God watches the keeping* — and the impulse to shortcut covenants is, at root, not time-pressure but * leakage of taqwā*, the thought that small promises are unwitnessed. Verse 76 erases small promises *from existence*: a covenant is a covenant; and the God who loves the reverent is the Third Party to every undertaking, however domestic.
**Balā: The Particle That Overturns the Ledger**

The verse opens with one of Arabic's subtlest particles of correction: *balā* — "nay, rather" — the rebuttal-particle that answers a false hypothesis and installs its opposite. Against the slander implied in v. 75's final whisper — that covenant-keeping is optional with those outside one's covenant — God's *balā* overturns the whole ledger: *man awfā bi-ʿahdihi wa-ttaqā* — "whoever fulfills his covenant and reveres — truly God loves the reverent." The fulfillment-verb *awfā* (from *wafā*: completeness, the same root as the full-payment seals of vv. 25, 57, 185) ties covenant-keeping to the Book's central virtue-family; and the sequence — *fulfill covenant, revere* — compresses the entire moral law in two acts: honor given to partners outward, reverence directed upward.

**The Love-Register's Third Entry**

With this clause the sūrah's inventory of divine love receives its third name, and its counsel stands in sharper relief: first the love of God for the followers of His Messenger (v. 31), next its negation upon the disbelieving direction (v. 32), and now the positive love for the covenant-keeping reverent — structuring an ethical-ranking that no tribal math can bend. The Prophet's own summary of covenant-status stands behind every commentary on the verse:

> *"The signs of the hypocrite are three: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks; and when he is entrusted, he betrays."* (al-Bukhārī 33; Muslim 59)

— the un-fulfillment triad against which v. 76's God-loved covenant-keeper is the willing counter-evidence. Believer, write every covenant you make into the verse's ledger: *fulfill, and be loved.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:77

> **Truly those who sell God's Pact and their oaths for a paltry price, they shall have no share in the Hereafter and God will not speak to them, nor will He look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them. And theirs shall be a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Broker of the Two Committed Things**

After the luminous rule of verse 76, the sūrah stamps the antitype with terrifying particularity: *inna alladhīna yashtarūna bi-ʿahdi Allāhi wa aymānihim thamanan qalīlan* — "those who *sell* the Pact of God and their oaths at a paltry price." The commerce-metaphor is exact: *ishtarā b-* — to take in exchange — the covenant of God (with all its weight: His command, His trust, the inherited religion) and one's own sworn oaths — treated as *merchandise*, converted into *thaman qalīl*, the small price, the short gain: interest, position, exemption, comfort. The Book has applied the same verb to selling His signs (2:41), His Book (3:187), religion (9:9): *the covenant is not unsaleable; it is saleable — and that is the horror.* What could never be *worth* selling for any price is here defined to be worth infinitely more than the ritually declared paltry (qalīl) one takes for it — every price for a covenant is "paltry" because the covenant's price is infinite.

**A Fourfold Disfellowship and Its Syntax of Wrath**

The sentence pronounced unfolds in four clauses of ay-resonance, slowly, dreadfully: *ulāʾika lā khalāqa lahum fī al-ākhirah* — "they shall have no share in the Hereafter" — *khalāq*, a portion — not that they shall not exist then (they exist to be judged) but that of its *good* they have no allotment; *wa lā yukallimuhumu Allāh* — "God shall not speak to them"; *wa lā yanẓuru ilayhim yawma al-qiyāmah* — "nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection"; *wa lā yuzakkīhim* — "nor purify them"; *wa lahum ʿadhābun alīm* — "and theirs shall be a painful punishment."

In the Prophet's own preserved gloss, these very words became a named category in the hereafter's terrifying procession. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record from Abū Dharr that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Three shall God not speak to on the Day of Resurrection, nor look at them, nor purify them, and theirs shall be a painful punishment." I said: "Who are they, O Messenger of God?" He said: "The one who lets his garment trail below the ankles (al-musbil), the one who reproaches others for his own charity (al-mannān), and the one who sells his goods by means of a false oath."* (Muslim 106; cf. al-Bukhārī 2788, 5787)

Three merchants of *thaman qalīl*: the proud dresser, the proud giver, the boldly false swearer — pride in cloth, pride in alms, dishonesty in commerce — each sold, in miniature, the covenant of his dignity and his word for the day's small currency. And the ḥadīth about the false oath reaches directly to the verse's marrow. Bukhārī and Muslim transmit from Ibn Abū Awfā that a man displayed goods in the market and swore he had been offered for them such-and-such (a lie, to entice a Muslim buyer), 'and this verse descended: "Those who sell God's Pact and their oaths for a paltry price..."' (al-Bukhārī 2088, 4545; Muslim 220).

**Why No Speech, No Gaze, No Purification?**

The commentators read the three privatives as the inner form of the punishment, and their dissection is precise. *No speech*: speech from God is address of honor *or* wrath (He will speak even to the reprobate in reproach at 23:108); the silence decreed here is the deprivation of every intimate address — exclusion from the *ḥadīth* of the Divine both sweet and stern; it is the theological death of relationship while existence continues. *No look*: God's *naẓar* — His gaze of consideration and mercy *with which He regards* the servant: as the tradition says of the sinning servant: "Well done, O son of Adam — your Lord looked at you today with approval"; the removal of that gaze is the removal of every light. *No purification*: *tazkiyah* — cleansing, growth, naming-pure: their stains stand uncleaned; their works unaccepted; the soul's tax-return marked *void*. And the whole four are wrapped by the clause "painful punishment" (*ʿadhāb alīm*) — the *body* answering to the *soul's* deprivation.

Commerce is the verse's idiom of perdition: they *price* what is priceless. Faith is not an idea in this Book; it is a holding — papers of the highest value — and squandering it for the *thaman qalīl* is the universal description of every small Tuesday-afternoon betrayal: the oath inflated for a deal, the covenant trimmed for a convenience. The tragedy the verse covers is the trade's *bad arithmetic*: the "price" ages into worthlessness; the covenant, into un-buyability — and on the Day when all prices are voided, the sold pact alone stands out on the account, recited against its seller.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:78

> **And there is indeed a group among them who twist their tongues with the Book, that you may suppose it to be from the Book. But it is not from the Book. And they say, "It is from God," though it is not from God. And they knowingly speak a lie against God.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Tongues Bent Over the Scroll**

The subversive arts continue with the subtlest of all: not the concealment of the whole text (v. 71) nor the selective citation (v. 23) but *phonetic-textual bending*: *wa inna minhum la-farīqan yalwūna alsinatahum bi-l-kitāb* — "there is a group among them who twist their tongues with the Book." *Layy al-lisān* — tongue-twisting: scholars of tafsīr record the concrete senses of the phrase: mispronouncing deliberately while reading, distorting vowels and inflections so as to alter the meaning while keeping a plausible sound; wrenching words from their constructions; citing out of sequence or out of context — all in such a way that the hearer receives an impression of fidelity while the content has been bent: *li-taḥsabūhu mina al-kitāb* — "that you might *suppose* it to be of the Book; yet it is not of the Book." The target is *supposition*: engineered seeming. And then the attribution is sealed with a false imprimatur: *wa yaqūlūna huwa min ʿindi Allāh* — "and they say: it is from God — while it is not from God." The final clause repeats the fixed capital charge of this portion of the chapter: *wa yaqūlūna ʿalā Allāhi al-kadhiba wa hum yaʿlamūn* — "while they knowingly speak the lie against God."

The Book's diagnosis is surgical: the crime is *attribution* — speaking *for* God without His sponsorship — the standing opposite of the prophetic office; prophethood is defined exactly by warranted attribution ("We reveal unto thee," v. 44; "nor does he speak of his own desire," 53:3), so every self-sponsored attribution is a counterfeit of the channel itself.

**The Species Then, the Species Now**

Tongue-twisting has acquired industrial forms. In the transmitted cases of this verse the commentators describe, variously, the obfuscation of the descriptions of the coming prophet in the older scriptures (glossed, repositioned, drowned in commentary), and the cultivated dependence of the scripturally illiterate upon curated quotation. In every later age the family of methods multiplies: the traditionist-cropping (a ḥadīth with its context cut off), the translation-select (the rendering chosen to flatter the doctrine), the single-case universalized, the universal rule exceptionalized, the *taʾwīl* deployed as solvent for unwelcome commands. Modern communications have trivialized distribution of the technique: a clipped clip, a misattributed salaf-quote, a curated thread — *layy al-lisān* at scale. The verse constitutes, therefore, the standing Islamic protocol of religious speech-ethics: whatever you quote as scripture must survive *the full-file test*: full verse, full context, authentic recension. And the believer is equipped with a personal defense speech habit: *not* "it is from God" as rhetorical seasoning, but only when attendance to source has made the claim *safe for attribution* — every casual "God said" or "the Prophet said" is a signature being signed; the verse warns us of the forgery we most often commit thoughtlessly.

There is a reason the verse repeats the phrase "knowingly" (*wa hum yaʿlamūn*): the twist is not remedied by education because it is not produced by ignorance. Its producers are trained; that is what makes it twist and not error. The Book's count of the charge is accordingly among the highest in its criminal calendar: attributing lies to God — *iftirāʾ* — is ranked with shirk in the sentence of 6:21 ("who is more wrong than he who fabricates against God a lie..."), and verse 94, just after, will brand the persisters *al-ẓālimūn* — the wrongdoers. At the court of the Resurrection, verse 30 has already told us, every soul finds presented its works; the twisted tongues will find their twists, *verbatim*.
**Layy al-Lisān: Tongue-Bending as Textual Corruption**
