*Wa inna minhum la-farīqan yalwūna alsinatahum bi-l-kitābi* — "a party of them twist their tongues with the Book": *layy* — the twisting and bending verb — with *alsinah* — tongues — fixes the corruption at its organ: not (in the first instance) the manuscript itself, which God's Book elsewhere guards (15:9), but the *recitation-instrument*: slurring, misplacing accents, interpolating convenience-words until the hearer *supposes the heard to be of the Book* — *li-taḥsabūhu min al-kitābi* — whereas *wa mā huwa min al-kitāb* — it is not of the Book. The verse's anatomy is forensic: it names the tooled organ (tongue), the misrepresentation (supposing), and the conscious agency (*wa yaqūlūna huwa min ʿindi Allāhi wa mā huwa min ʿindi Allāh* — they say it is from God, while it is not), ending with the indictment in full: *wa yaqūlūna ʿalā Allāhi al-kadhiba wa hum yaʿlamūn* — "they speak the lie against God, knowing."

**The Prophet's Three-Rule Hermeneutic for the Earlier Books**

Confronted with precisely this problem — how to treat transmitters of compromised scripture — the Prophet ﷺ legislated a standing rule for the community's whole relationship with the People of the Book's information:

> *"Do not believe the People of the Book, and do not disbelieve them — but say: we believe in what was sent down to us and what was sent down to you."* (al-Bukhārī 4485, from Abū Hurayrah) — with its operational twin: *"Relate from the Children of Israel, and there is no harm."* (al-Bukhārī 3461)

Three registers — affirmed, denied, suspended — mapping exactly onto v. 78's three categories (what is of the Book; what is falsely said to be; what is knowingly lied). For every age that handles textual criticism — in its schools, its media, its seminaries — the Madinan classroom of v. 78 remains the founding discipline: *attribute nothing to God loosely; hold every transmission to the standard of the two Preserved Witnesses.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:79

> **It is not for any human being, God having given him the Book, judgment, and prophethood, to then say to the people, "Be servants of me instead of God." Rather, "Be sages, from having taught the Book and from having studied."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prophetic Self-Portrait: Never Pedestaled**

The sūrah turns from the corrupters of predecessors' scripture to the one office that could never be corrupted: prophethood itself, and its first clause is one of the most important self-definitions of religion in all scripture: *mā kāna li-basharin an yuʾtiyahu Allāhu al-kitāba wa-l-ḥukma wa-l-nubuwwata thumma yaqūla lil-nāsi: kūnū ʿibādan lī min dūni Allāh* — "It is not for any human being, God having given him the Book, judgment, and prophethood, to then say to people: Be servants of me instead of God." The grammar is categorical — *mā kāna*: it is not fitting, impossible for the office as constituted — the three gifts exhausted in a triad: the Book (revelation's content), judgment (*ḥukm* — wisdom, discernment, and governing authority), prophethood (*nubuwwah* — the office itself). The recipient of this triad *cannot* — without internal contradiction destroying the gifts themselves — turn and claim personal worship. The commentators preserve the occasion that made the point sharp: the People of the Book asked the Prophet whether he wished to be worshiped as Christians worshiped Christ (al-Ṭabarī records it); this verse answered — and Islam's bedside rule was coded into law for all time: the messenger is *highest* among men, and precisely therefore *not* God. The Prophet ﷺ himself built daily guardrails: he forbade being stood up for as kings are stood up for; he said, *"Do not exaggerate in praising me as the Christians exaggerated in praising the son of Mary. I am only His servant — so say: the servant of God and His messenger (ʿabduhu wa rasūluh)"* (al-Bukhārī 3445); and foresaw the danger-principle in his dying supplication: *"O God, not my grave as an idol worshipped after me"* (Mālik's Muwaṭṭaʾ; Aḥmad). No prophet of God ever founded his own cult — and the verse establishes this not on history but on *constitution*: the three-gift recipient's own job description.

**"Be Sages": The Right Claim a Teacher May Make**

The verse then assigns the messenger and his true scholarly heirs their actual claim, with one of the Book's most beautiful occupational titles: *wa lākin kūnū rabbāniyyīna bi-mā kuntum tuʿallimūna al-kitāba wa bi-mā kuntum tadrusūn* — "Rather, say: *be rabbāniyyūn* — godly sages — by virtue of what you taught of the Book and by virtue of what you studied." *Rabbānī* — the Qur'an's technical designation of holiness: the man *of the Lord (rabb)*: al-Ṭabarī glosses: the learned devout; al-Qurṭubī: the physicians of the lawful and forbidden; Ibn ʿAbbās is related to have defined the rabbānī as "one who instructs people in the *small wisdoms* before the great" — the spiritual pedagogue whose teaching reorders lives. The title's genius: it dignifies the *study-chain* as the true glory of religion — a faith carried by teachers and students, not by pedestals and thuribles. *Tuʿallimūn* — what you *taught* — transmission outward; *tadrusūn* — what you *studied* — assimilated inward: the two verbs together state the conditions of the rabbānī equally: unschooled teachers and un-teaching scholars both fall short.

**An Enduring Code for Every Religious Elite**

This verse is Islam's founding text against clerical absolutism, a full eleven hundred years before the West's quarrel with priesthoods: no human intermediary, however gifted, may insert himself as object of devotion between the soul and God — neither temple-priest nor politicized rev, neither saint in a niche nor celebrity scholar with an unaccountable cult of following. The dealings of the Prophet's Companions with his own *body* show the norm in action: they revered him beyond father and son — and they corrected him in mashwarah, contradicted his estimates of pollination and agriculture ("you know your worldly affairs best," Muslim 2363; Aḥmad), asked him after the Qur'an: *is this revelation or opinion?* The love taught is obedience-with-bands, never worship: at his death the community did not find itself godless, because *no man* had stood between them and God — Abū Bakr's speech answers verse 79 almost verbatim: *"Whoever worshipped Muhammad, let him know: Muhammad has died. Whoever worshipped God: God lives and does not die"* — and then he read the words of verse 144, which this sūrah will itself record.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:80

> **And he would not command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would he command you to disbelief after your having been submitters?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Structure of a Chained Impossibility**

Verse 79 declared it impossible for a prophet-bearer of the Book to say "worship me." Verse 80 chains the logic outward: *wa lā yaʾmurakum an tattakhidhū al-malāʾikata wa-l-nabiyyīna arbāban* — "and he would not command you to take the angels and prophets as lords." The particle of continuation exposes a full doctrine: prophethood does not merely exclude *self*-divinization; it excludes, in its entire function, the divinization of *any* creaturely rank, however exalted — not angels, the sinless ministers; not prior prophets, the very nobility of the human kind. Whoever has received the Book, judgment, and prophethood stands in an office-tradition whose single code is verse 64's very wording: not taking *anyone* as lords beside God. The messenger's nature thus *precedes* any possible corruption of the office: the Book's argument rides on the absurdity itself.

**The Rhetorical Tribunal: "After Your Having Been Submitters?"**

The verse then turns from description to arresting question: *a-yaʾmurukum bi-l-kufri baʿda idh antum muslimūn* — "Would he command you to disbelief after your having become submitters?" The form *a-...?* is the interrogative of astonished refutation — as though the proposition collapses under its own impossibility when merely *spoken aloud*: the teacher of submission *turn* teacher of disbelief? Commentators savor the subtlety of the wording: not "a-prophet commanding disbelief" but *any* man commanding disbelief for that post of all posts — the vocation is the negation of the very thing alleged. And the temporal phrase carries an entire anthropology: *after your having been submitters* — the disbelief he would supposedly command is not for the uninitiated but for those *already surrendered*: meaning not merely intellectual error but *reversal* — an undoing of the direction — the worst moral category (the chapter re-issues the diagnosis squarely at v. 86: "how shall God guide a people who disbelieve after having believed?").

For the sūrah's immediate audience — the communities wrestling with the *person* of Jesus — the verse's point lands home: Jesus is Book-bearer; therefore, constitutionally, he cannot command worship of himself, nor found any cult of saint or angel; and he confirmed it in the words this Book assigns him (v. 51; 5:117). Every doctrine that contradicts this must represent conference-accretion, not the Messiah's own constitution.

**Muslim Guardrails: A Permanence of Posture**

Islam read verse 80 not only as polemics but as *self-regulation*: every subsequent Muslim sanctity has been submitted to the test of this verse. Sufi hyperbole about the saints, philosophical veneration of the intellect, scholarly titles inflated into intermediary ranks — all are reined by the one sentence: would the channel itself command *you* to insert the channel as an address? The Prophet's hardest caution on the self-deification risk for his own community is the commentator's fixture: *"You shall follow the ways of those nations before you, span by span and cubit by cubit, so that had they entered a lizard's hole you would enter it." They said: the Jews and the Christians? He said: "Who else?"* (al-Bukhārī 3456; Muslim 2669) — following leading to emulation of exactly this: persons made lords. And the corrective practice is ancient: the rightly-guided disposition of veneration back toward ṣūra of the office — love the Messenger ﷺ as guide and beloved, and every saint as student of his. *Would he command disbelief after your having been submitters?* — never. And *therefore* — with love-complete and freedom-whole — the believing heart keeps worship's geometry pure: many revered faces; all facing the same Lord.
**The Agent–Principal Argument: No Prophet Preaches Prophet-Worship**

The verse's grammar runs a regression of the utmost clarity: *wa lā yaʾmurakum an tattakhidhū al-malāʾikata wa-l-nabiyyīna arbāban* — "nor would he command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords." The hypothetical *would-he* presumes the whole system of revelation: the commissioned cannot commission *against* the Commissioner — a prophet ordering worship of prophets would resile his own dispatch at the send. Al-Rāzī draws out the logic as an axiom of religion-rationality: *the sign of a true agent is that he forwards authority; the benchmark of a false one is that he absorbs it* — an axiom by which every claimant's biography may be read. The angels' own register proves the point from the heavenly side: on the Day they are arrayed for interrogation — *"did these worship you?" — glorified are You! ... rather they worshipped the jinn"* (34:40–41): heaven's ministers themselves refuse delegation of worship.

**A-Yaʾmurukum bi-l-Kufri: The Absurdity Named**

The verse's second clause sharpens the point to its edge: *a-yaʾmurukum bi-l-kufri baʿda idh antum muslimūn* — "would he command you to disbelieve after you have become muslimūn?" The inner-contradiction is total: *islam* — the submission-condition — is the very product the Messenger produces; *kufr* its inverse. Between vv. 79–80 the Madinan audience received its lasting heresy-detector: any voice — ancient or modern — diverting worship from God toward saints, angels, or the Prophet himself stands measured by the Messenger's own measure — and fails it. The women of Egypt's slip (*"this is but a noble angel!"* — 12:31, adoration hidden inside a compliment) is thereby the paradigm case: even praise that reinstalls a creature in the Lord's seat is the kufr no true prophet would ever command.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:81

> **And [remember] when God made the covenant of the prophets: "By that which I have given you of a Book and Wisdom, should a messenger then come to you confirming that which is with you, you shall surely believe in him and you shall help him." He said, "Do you agree and take on My burden on these conditions?" They said, "We agree." He said, "Bear witness, for I am with you among those who bear witness."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Primordial Synod of the Prophets**

With this verse the Qur'an draws back the curtain on the most august assembly conceivable: a convocation of *all* God's prophets, before history, bound by a single pact: *wa idh akhadha Allāhu mīthāqa al-nabiyyīna* — "when God took the covenant of the prophets." The covenant is stated as a sworn bind upon each prophet — invoked by his own endowments (*lamā ātaytukum min kitābin wa ḥikmah* — "by that which I have given you of a Book and Wisdom," in the reading that treats it as oath) — that *should a messenger come after him confirming what is with him*, he must believe in him and aid him: *la-tuʾminunna bihi wa la-tanṣurunnah* — the doubled *nūn* of the emphatic oath certifying both duties. Then God — in a moment of solemnity unmatched in revealed literature — calls for their consent: *a-aqrartum wa akhadhtum ʿalā dhālikum iṣrī* — "Do you agree and take on My *iṣr* — My binding burden — on these conditions?" The prophets answer with one voice: *aqrarnā* — "We agree." And God pronounces the proceeding enrolled: *fa-shhadū, wa anā maʿakum mina al-shāhidīn* — "Bear witness; and I am with you among the witnesses."

**What the Covenant Means for Every Messenger and Every Community**

The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr) unpack the verse's immense significances in successive layers. First: it establishes the *unity* of the prophetic office at the level of covenant: the prophets are not successive entrepreneurs but members of one chartered fraternity, each pledged to confirm the next. The chain of revelation (vv. 3–4) is thus not merely textual but *contractual*: every messenger signed, so to speak, the validity of his successor in advance. Jealousy between prophets is a contradiction of their own registered consent. Second: it binds each prophet's *people* by extension: a community's sworn adhesion to its own prophet *includes*, in the prophet's own covenant, his duty to the next confirmer — so following Moses sincerely *entails* accepting Jesus, and following Jesus sincerely *entails* accepting Muhammad ﷺ, when he arrives *confirming what is with them* (v. 3; 46:10; 61:6) — muṣaddiqan, never nullifying. "Confirming that which is with you" becomes the precise criterion of discernment: the true successor builds on the present deposit; the usurper abolishes it. Third: it explains and authentticates — against the objections of pedigree — how the People of the Book could be *obligated* by Muhammad's arrival without ever having met him: their own prophets had enrolled the obligation *for* them at the convocation; the custodians' scriptures bear the residue (cf. 7:157: the prophet "whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel... those who believe in him, honor him, help him...").

Note the final name for the enrolment: *iṣr* — the heavy, gripping tie (the same word for the yokes that burden Israel's neck, lifted, per 7:157, by the final prophet!): covenant is not ceremony but *cord*. And God Himself stands in the witness-booth — *I am with you among the witnesses* — the most exalted guarantor of any contract: a deed witnessed by the Lord of the covenanting parties.

**The Sūrah's Quiet Verdict**

Verse 81 stands as the sūrah's center-of-gravity on the interreligious question: all prophetic communities are legally pre-committed to one another's truth-fulfillments; the isolationism of each following is heresy against its own founder's sworn consent. In the Prophet Muhammad's case the application is exact: the messengers covenanted for him; Jesus proclaimed him as "Aḥmad" (61:6); and the community which reads him in its own books and withholds *īmān* and *naṣr* — belief and aid — has broken the terms held for it by its own prophets. The Muslims' own observance of the covenant takes the form declared at the chapter's next address (v. 84): "We make no distinction among any of them." Verse 81 is the source of that sentence — for who could distinguish among members of a fraternity he never founded, convened and sworn by God Himself?

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:82

> **Then whosoever turns away after that, they are the iniquitous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**After the Witness, the Turning**

The covenant convocation of verse 81 is sealed with its standing verdict: *fa-man tawallā baʿda dhālika fa-ulāʾika humu al-fāsiqūn* — "then whosoever turns away after that, it is they who are the iniquitous." *Tawallā* — turns the back — the same verb of willful aversion already twice spent in the chapter (vv. 32, 63) — and the specification *baʿda dhālika*, "after *that*," does the verdict's decisive work: the turning is *after* covenant, witness, sworn consent; not before. The word chosen for such turners is not *kāfirūn* — disbelievers — but *al-fāsiqūn* — the "iniquitous": a word that in the Qur'an's exact usage names those who *break out* (*fasaqa*: exited, burst forth, as the date-stone splits through its skin) from the binding of obedience — the *contract-breakers*, whose characteristic is not that they never saw but that, having seen and bound themselves, they *exit*. Earlier (v. 24) the Book used twin formulas against those who "turned away" from adjudication by their own Torah; here the offense is drawn at the covenantal level: to turn from the next confirmer to whom one's own prophets had pledged one is not mere disagreement — it is *fisq*, secession from the convocation one's masters signed.

The verse accomplishes, in thirteen Arabic words, the setting of the apologetic field for all subsequent revelation-claims: prophets cannot turn against a later confirmer — impossible by office (v. 79) and by oath (v. 81); communities turning against him are named — not merely unenlightened — *fāsiq*, and the charge is registered without rage: it is a classification, not an outcry.

**Iniquity as Emigration from the Covenant**

The ramifications run deep in the religious psychology of every community — the Muslims' included. *Fisq* is not the failure of the uncommitted; it is the decommitment of the committed: covenants signed and then treated as peripheral; testified truths gradually dethroned to mere information; sworn allegiances relegated to heritage. The chapter that immediately follows with its command over the Muslims — "hold fast to the rope of God, all together, and do not become divided" (v. 103) — is structurally the community's own prophylactic against becoming fāsiqūn in their turn; the failure of earlier communities stands in the Book as model *more than accusation* (the point al-Rāzī repeatedly draws). God's classic duty texts underscore it: *"the fāsiqūn" in the wider Qur'an are "those who break the covenant of God after its binding, and sever what God has commanded to be joined, and make corruption in the earth — those are the losers"* (2:27) — covenant-breach as *the* definition, and in the same register our verse speaks.

Yet the path back is part of the sūrah's map: verse 89 will open it — "except those who repent after that and make amends" — and the gate stands precisely because the verdict is classification, not annihilation. Fāsiq is the diagnosis, not the sentence executed: the iniquitous remain *addressable* — as the very act of revelation naming them demonstrates; one does not send mail to the dead. The verse therefore performs responsibly a two-fold labor: it erects, permanently, the sign over covenant-breach — *here passed the seceders* — and immediately after it builds the sūrah's characteristic bridge back toward repentance, for "truly God is Forgiving, Merciful" toward even the breakers, when they stop breaking.
**Baʿda Dhālika: The After That Condemns**

*Fa-man tawallā baʿda dhālika* — "so whoever turns away after that": the two deictics do the work — *that* being the mīthāq-scene of v. 81 (all the prophets witnessing under God's own interrogation: *believe and support the confirming Messenger*) and *after* the moment of universal ratification. Turning *after that* leaves the turned one without alibi: no ignorance, no earlier immunity-window; simply reversal. The Book's covenant-history teaches in the same direction at every repetition: the ratified covenant creates *responsibility of the highest order* — 2:27's clause classing covenant-breakers after ratification among the *khāsirīn*; 5:13's consequence for Israel's own break; the hypocrite-class of Madinah's portrait (63:1–3) sourced to exact ruptures *after belief*.

**Ulāʾika Hum al-Fāsiqūn: The Date That Leaves Its Skin**

*Fa-ulāʾika hum al-fāsiqūn* — "those — they are the transgressors": *fāsiq*, from the root the lexicons define by the image of a *fresh date pressing out of its skin* — the thing exiting its appointed bounds — installs the taxonomy of v. 82: turning post-covenant is *exit*, unnatural rupture of the sealed arrangement. Al-Ṭabarī's gloss is terse and total: *the fāsiqūn are the exiters from obedience of their Lord*; al-Qurṭubī reads the definite-article construction as class-making — *they are the fāsiqūn*, the very file-name of the category. For the Muslim every generation-motion of faith faces this verse's question at its heart: covenants are easy at festivals and heavy at winters; *the turning is measured in the after* — the believer's own conduct months and years after his blessed moments is the only comb by which his *fāsiq* or *faqīh* status can be drawn.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:83

> **Do they seek other than God's religion, while whosoever is in the heavens and on the earth submits to Him, willingly or unwillingly, and unto Him they will be returned?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Absurdity of an Alternative to What Everything Obeys**

The verse poses its question over the whole creation: *a-fa-ghayra dīni Allāhi yabghūna, wa lahu aslama man fī al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi ṭawʿan wa karhan, wa ilayhi yurjaʿūn* — "Do they, then, seek other than God's religion, while to Him submits whosoever is in the heavens and the earth — willingly or unwillingly — and to Him they shall be returned?" The rhetorical form *a-fa-* is the Book's rebuke-by-astonishment: to opt out of God's religion (*dīn Allāh*) is to seek lodging outside the only inhabited house. Since verse 19 the chapter has defined the content: *al-dīn* in God's sight is *islām* — submission; verse 83 now extends the definition across ontology: submission is not merely the creed of the faithful; it is the *condition of all things*: *man fī al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍ* — everyone in the heavens (angels, per Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī, and every heavenly reality) and everyone on earth (people, and every earthly reality) — *has submitted* (*aslama*, the very verbal form of *islām*) *willingly or unwillingly*.

**Two Kinds of Surrender: The Volunteer's and the Conscript's**

The doubled qualification *ṭawʿan wa karhan* — willingly or unwillingly — is the verse's deep watermark, and the commentators sound out several complementary depths. In the *cosmic* register: everything that exists serves God involuntarily, by sheer constitution — stones fall by God's gravity in them, fire burns by God's chemistry in them, seasons run by God's astronomy in them; the "religion" of nature is *aslama* without the option of refusal — Sūrah 41:11 pictures primordial heaven and earth answering God's call "Come, willingly or unwillingly," saying, "we come willingly." In the *human* register: freedom introduces the scission. Some — the faithful — submit *willingly*: they convert cosmic necessity into chosen worship; they *volunteer* before the compulsory moment arrives. Others submit only *unwillingly*: every human being without exception will finally bend — in death's seizure (6:61; 32:11), in the Resurrection's return ("to Him they shall be returned"), in the judgment's sentence — as al-Rāzī frames it: the disbeliever's submission comes at the moment of death (40:85: "their faith availed them not when they saw Our might"), when belief can no longer be chosen and therefore can no longer be credited. And the book's parallel — 13:15: "to God prostrates whosoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly — *and their shadows, in the morning and the evening*" — seals the imagery: even your shadow, a black nonvoting body of yours, already prostrates twice a day before God; only your *heart* is free to withhold joining it.

**"And unto Him They Will Be Returned": The Sūrah's Inescapable Third Term**

The verse's ceiling-line — *wa ilayhi yurjaʿūn* — swings the argument from the present universe to its termination. Return (*rujūʿ*) is this sūrah's own constant theme (v. 55: "unto Me is your return"; v. 109: "unto God are all matters returned") — and function: seeking is licensed in time; but seeking terminates in returning; and returning has a single destination. To "seek another religion" is then a logistical absurdity precisely because there is no *elsewhere* in which to practice it: the road out circles back; *yurjaʿūn* is the arc of every existence drawn back to its issuer.

The believer reading this verse discovers within it both a magnificent scope of tawḥīd — submission as the *physics* of being — and a precise *spiritual reformation*: the matter with religion is not whether to submit, but *whether to convert the submission from compulsion to love while there is still time to convert it.* The wise are those who willingly, *now*, live out in choice what they shall one day live out in decree; the prayer of the deeply rooted ("make not our hearts swerve," v. 8) and the covenant of the prophets (v. 81) are the same act in different dress: volunteering. The remaining verses of the sūrah — pledge of pilgrimage, of spending, of patience — are all, in the deepest sense, summonses to deliver one's submission freely while it can still be called worship rather than eclipse.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:84

> **Say, "We believe in God and what has been sent down upon us, and in what was sent down upon Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, and in what Moses, Jesus, and the prophets were given from their Lord. We make no distinction among any of them, and unto Him we submit."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Creed of Total Reception**

After the prophets' primordial covenant (v. 81) and the cosmic submission (v. 83), the believing community receives its own sentence to speak — and what a sentence it is, the fullest creedal formula in the Qur'an after the Fātiḥah: *qul: āmannā bi-Allāhi wa mā unzila ʿalaynā wa mā unzila ʿalā Ibrāhīma wa Ismāʿīla wa Isḥāqa wa Yaʿqūba wa-l-asbāṭ, wa mā ūtiya Mūsā wa ʿĪsā wa-l-nabiyyūna min rabbihim; lā nufarriqu bayna aḥadin minhum, wa naḥnu lahu muslimūn.* Its structure is so exact that it deserves to be mapped clause by clause:

**"We believe in God"** — the foundation and the content of contents: faith's first object is the Speaker before any word.

**"And in what was sent down upon us"** — the community's own revelation: the mercies of the Qur'an and the entire deposit of the Prophet's ﷺ ministry; belief begins where one lives, not as nostalgia for other ages.

**"And in what was sent down upon Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes"** — the patriarchal canon of the monotheist house: four generations named, then *al-asbāṭ* — the Tribes, Israel's twelve prophetic lines — sweeping in the whole Israelite deposit from the household of prophecy down through its national channel. The enrollment of *Ishmael* immediately after Abraham, *before* Isaac — in v. 84's own order — is significant: the Arab branch of Abraham is honored equally; the line of the Kaʿbah's builders is prophet-bearing too.

**"And in what Moses, Jesus, and the prophets were given from their Lord"** — the two great names of the two communities surrounding Madinah — *Moses and Jesus* — followed by the general: *the prophets* — the whole convocation of verse 81, exhaustively affirmed.

**"We make no distinction (*nufarriq*) among any of them"** — the verse's theological spine, and the direct practice of the convocation-covenant: between the Book-bearers, no partisans. Distinctions of *rank* God makes among messengers (2:253: "those messengers — We favored some over others"); distinctions of *validity* men must not make ("we believe in some and disbelieve in some" — the very formula of 2:85, which the People of the Book themselves once practiced: "do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?") — the believer refuses the sectarian picking.

**"And unto Him we submit"** — *muslimūn*: the whole string of beliefs resolves into the single act the sūrah has defined as religion itself (vv. 19, 83): *islam*.

**A Creed Built for Conversation**

The verse's instruction — *Say!* — commands its public recitation: this is the Muslims' own published charter of religious universality, designed to be said *to the People of the Book*: we are not a sect rejecting your prophets; we are the people who believe in *all* of yours and more. It is, in effect, the community's answer-creed to verse 64's invitation to a common word — the common word, now confessed *from our side*: one God, all His messengers, all His books, one submission. The chapter thereby completes the apologetic circle: *they* may have claimed Abraham (v. 65 answered); *they* may have stipulated borders around guidance (v. 73 answered); but *our* creed contains no borders; our religion carries inside it everything true that anyone else has ever received.

The same formula reappears verbatim at 2:136, and at 2:285 as the community's nightly creed ("the Messenger believes in what was sent down to him from his Lord, and the believers... 'We make no distinction among any of His messengers'"), and at 4:150–152 as the very line between real and nominal faith. Learn it, Muslim tradition says, as a *practice*, not a boast: the one who truly "makes no distinction" honors Moses' Torah in its truth and Jesus' Gospel in its truth, and — the cost of consistency — stands free of every chauvinism. A faith that holds *all* prophets is inherently incapable of pride of proprietorship; and the God who gave *each* portion is the God all the portions confess.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:85

> **Whosoever seeks a religion other than submission, it shall not be accepted of him, and in the Hereafter he shall be among the losers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Standing Rule of Acceptance**

Having defined religion (v. 19), cosmic submission (v. 83), and the creed of total reception (v. 84), the Book now states the rule of acceptance itself: *wa man yabtaghi ghayra al-islāmi dīnan fa-lan yuqbala minhu, wa huwa fī al-ākhirati mina al-khāsirīn* — "whoever seeks other than *al-islām* as religion, it shall *never be accepted* of him; and he, in the Hereafter, shall be among the losers." The severity of the sentence is held, by all schools, in a tension with the breadth of *islām* that the Qur'an itself has built into the word — and the key to the verse lies exactly in this sūrah's own definition of *islām* at verse 19: *submission to God*, not a later denominational label but the eternal posture. The commentators unfold it along two axes that are finally one. Axis one — the universal: he who seeks a *dīn* constructed otherwise than as *submission to God* — be it the worship of another, or the retention of worship-with-conditions after truth has come — has sought something that does not exist in God's register: no path to Him runs through non-submission. Al-Zamakhsharī glosses *islām* here precisely as "tawḥīd and surrendering the face to God" — broader than a flag, narrower than anything. Axis two — the historical: after the arrival of the confirming messenger — the one covenanted at verse 81, whose truth the communities recognize (2:146: "as they know their own sons") — *submission to God takes, for whoever recognizes it, the form of following His confirmed messenger.* Ibn Kathīr's formulation: "whosoever seeks a path other than what God has legislated" — the verse is then read against the backdrop of those who *received the Book and knew*, and nonetheless fashioned for themselves a private path.

**The Occasion and the Gate It Leaves Open**

The classical asbāb (al-Qurṭubī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Māturīdī) record the verse's first incidence concerning a companion — al-Ḥārith ibn Suwayd per some reports — who left the faith and emigrated back to Makkah with others of his kind: the word "seeks" (*yabtaghi*) lands, in that incident, on one who had *held* submission and *abandoned* it — the apostate — and its sternness is accordingly moderated by verses 86–91 which describe his kind fully, and verse 89 which opens the way back to him ("except those who repent after that and make amends").

The jurists of meanings have also preserved the pasturing balance between this verse and 2:62 ("those who believe, and the Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabeans — whoever believes in God and the Last Day and works righteousness..."). The mainstream settlement — al-Rāzī's articulation being classic — differs from crude supersessionism one way and from indifferentism the other: virtues and faith where they truly exist are never refused by God (2:62; and this sūrah's own v. 115: "whatever good they do shall not be denied them"), while *religion as an offered system* — the dīn one *seeks* and offers God as one's road — is accepted only as *islam*: submission on God's terms, through His confirmed channels. The first guarantees God's fairness to every soul; the second guarantees God's sovereignty over His own religion. Both are folded into this chapter, four verses apart: verse 85 guarding the gate, verse 89 holding it open, and verse 115 promising that no atom of good — of *anyone* — is ever shredded at the border.

**"Among the Losers": The Verse's Inventory**

The final phrase — *fī al-ākhirati mina al-khāsirīn* — names the final state by the Book's heavy economic term: *khusr*, loss — the ruined trade: not dethroned merely, but negative-balance; life spent and nothing carried; the tally of 18:103–104 ("shall We inform you of the greatest losers in works — whose striving goes astray in the life of this world while they think they do well") is their portrait. The verse's severity is therefore not theatrical but ledgerial: acceptance is the currency of the Hereafter, and only the truly-submitted road arrives with *valid tender*. And standing, as it does, four verses before the chapter turns at 89 to repentance's door, it functions as all Qur'anic severity functions — as a floodlight over the one road that *does* run uphill to God: "Truly the religion in the sight of God is submission" (v. 19).

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:86

> **How shall God guide a people who have disbelieved after having believed, having borne witness that the Messenger is true, and the clear proofs having come to them? And God guides not wrongdoing people.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Inversion of Guidance**

After the gate-rule of verse 85, the Book puts the case in its sharpest interrogative form: *kayfa yahdī Allāhu qawman kafarū baʿda īmānihim* — "how shall God guide a people who disbelieved *after* having believed?" — *wa shahidū anna al-rasūla ḥaqq* — "after they bore witness that the Messenger is true" — *wa jāʾahumu al-bayyināt* — "and after the clear proofs had come to them?" The *kayfa* — "how?" — is not a search for method but an astonishment at possibility: what *can* guidance mean for those who have already held it, signed for it, and then handed it back? The sequence of clauses builds the culpability to its peak: they *believed* (īmān arrived, was experienced from inside); they *bore witness* (publicly testified — no mere private leaning — that the Messenger was true); they *saw the proofs* (*bayyināt* — the clarified demonstratives, the same class of evidences that converted their questioners) — and the apostasy follows *all three*. The classical case is before the commentators: the man who left the community for Makkah (v. 85's occasion); and parallel cases among the People of the Book who believed in the coming prophet on their own scriptures' description and then, seeing him arrive *and* his community flourish, balked at the cost — the pattern of not ignorance but *renunciation of recognized truth* — precisely what the third chapter keeps indicting (vv. 70–72, 75, 78).

**"God Guides Not Wrongdoing People": The Meaning of the Withheld Lamp**

The verse's final clause names the deeper mechanism: *wa Allāhu lā yahdī al-qawma al-ẓālimīn* — "and God does not guide the wrongdoing people." Divine guidance (*hidāyah*) in the Qur'an operates on laws, and the Book has disclosed them earlier in this very series: the God who said "He misleads thereby only the iniquitous (fāsiqīn)" (2:26) and "God does not guide the disbelieving people" (refrain across the Book) is describing not divine stinginess but the *function of guidance itself*: it is light — and light helps only eyes that open. When the commentators say "God does not guide X," they mean (al-Rāzī's classic phrasing) that guidance is *tawfīq* — the actual leading of the heart to acceptance — and that God withdraws this from those who *use* their light otherwise: the knowledge-wielders who turn it into property, envy, and stratagem (vv. 72–78). A people that has seen and reversed must be left, justly, to the momentum of its reversal; to guide them forcibly would falsify the distinction between willing and unwilling that verse 83 built into creation. It is not that truth changes; it is that *eyes* choose cataracts, and God is under no covenant to pour sight into deliberately shut lids.

**The Standing Hope Inside "How Shall?"**

And yet — the verse is a *question*, not a closed door: "how *shall* God guide...?" anticipates its own divine answer in the immediately following passage: if ordinary law holds no path, mercy shall make one. The classical case ends in verse 89 — the apostate writes home asking *is there repentance for me?* — and God answers there *is*. Verse 86's amazement that such people could ever be re-guided becomes, in this chapter's very next verses, God's announcement that even *their* return is purchasable — with repentance and amendment — for "truly God is Forgiving, Merciful" (v. 89). The warning is therefore complete in mercy: the state is dreadful not because God's mercy is short, but because the distance covered in the wrong direction is long, and no one chooses the moment at which his life-cord is cut. Verse 91 seals the point: die in the wrongness, and an earthful of gold buys nothing back. Until then — the Book's underlying posture resounds — *the door is at 89.*
**How Shall God Guide? The Three Clauses of Compound Guilt**

*Kayfa yahdī Allāhu qawman kafarū baʿda īmānihim* — "how shall God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief?" — with the third, heaviest middle-clause: *wa shahidū anna al-rasūla ḥaqqun wa jāʾahumu al-bayyināt* — "and witnessed that the Messenger is true, and the clear proofs came to them." It is the Book's anatomy of *apostasy of the informed kind*, and its three clauses descend in charge: belief was present (īmān first); reversal followed (kufr after); and the transition was made under full illumination (witnessing the Messenger's truth with proofs arrived). The *kayfa* — how — is no real question; it is the Book's rhetorical astonishment — *what guidance-mechanism remains for one who arrives at the destination and turns back deliberately?* Al-Rāzī's comment names the psychology: guidance is out of countenance not because God is unable but because *the instruments of guidance have themselves been repudiated* — the proofs handled, weighed, refused.

**Guidance's Two Kinds and the Lock of Wilful Reversal**

The commentators distinguish here with their usual care the Book's two senses of *hudā*: *guidance of indication* (irshād, showing the road — rendered to all, even disbelievers, by the signs and the messengers) and *guidance of success* (tawfīq, the grant of following it — God's own donation). Verse 86 speaks of the second: the wilful reverser *has consumed his irshād in unbelief* — the proofs came — and the sealing verse (v. 88's permanence) awaits unless the v. 89 door is used: *except those repent after* — after which everything re-opens. The Prophet's description of the heart's turning clarifies the mechanics:

> *"The hearts are between two fingers of the Merciful's fingers — He turns them as He wills."* (Muslim 2654, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr; al-Tirmidhī 3522)

The fingers turn — to those who turn themselves back, first.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:87

> **They are those whose recompense is that upon them shall be the curse of God, the angels, and mankind all together,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Recompense Named in Three Choirs**

The verse assigns the recompense of the renouncers of verses 86, and there is a terrible stateliness about its composition: *ulāʾika jazāʾuhum anna ʿalayhim laʿnata Allāhi wa-l-malāʾikati wa-l-nāsi ajmaʿīn* — "they are those whose recompense is that upon them is the curse of God, and of the angels, and of mankind — all together." Three choirs of *laʿnah* — curse — recited over them: God's own, the angels', and humanity's entire assembly. The word *jazāʾ* — recompense — must not slip by: this is stated not as an arbitrary sentence but as *recompense*: the exact fitting counter to their act. What did they do? After having possessed and witnessed, they traded the covenant for whatever pale *thaman* moved them (v. 77's paltry price); that is, they voted to be *outside* the community of truth. The recompense is the simple universal *execution of their vote*: three realms extolled with truth — heaven's King, heaven's hosts, earth's assembled races — jointly pronounce *expulsion* upon them. *Laʿnah* itself, in its Qur'anic-precise meaning, is *buʿd* — expulsion, driving-far — from mercy: to be cursed is not to be insulted but to be *distanced*: the opposite of qurb — being brought nigh — which the whole chapter has been offering (the muqarrabūn of v. 45, the muslimūn of v. 84).

**Why Three Voices?**

The triple form is found twice in the Qur'an — here, and at 2:161, also concerning those who disbelieve after the state of faith and die in it — and the commentators (al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr among them) unfold its fittingness. God's curse: the Judge's own decree of remoteness from His mercy — the substance. The angels' curse: the execution-register: they are the ministers of ordering — they brought the revelation down; they will meet the disbelievers with another descent (6:93; 8:50 — "the angels take them, striking their faces and backs"). Mankind's curse: the community's own judgment across generations — the renouncer's name worn as a byword; posterity's verdict. The pattern has a living illustration in this very chapter's history: the mubāhalah the Prophet offered Najrān involved precisely *laʿnata Allāh ʿalā al-kādhibīn* — God's curse on the liars (v. 61) — a miniature, targeted form of this universal sentence, invoked only at the summit of proof.

The verse also yields, by exact contraposition, the high meaning of blessing: if curse is remoteness-in-three-realms, then *salāh/salām* — the blessed state — is nearness-in-three-realms: God speaking peace over the servant, the angels seeking forgiveness for "those upon the earth" (42:5), and men joining in prayer upon him — which is precisely what the Book assigns the Prophet ﷺ (33:56: "Truly God and His angels bless the Prophet — O you who believe! Bless him and greet him with abundant peace"). The two verses together thus calibrate the whole moral atmosphere of the cosmos: it re-echoes what we *are*: blessing and cursing are social facts of heaven and earth following persons according to truth.

**Dignity of Warning, Exit at the Next Verse**

The tradition has never read this verse as a text of revenge-gleefulness — the sūrah's own Prophet wept over enemies — but as *assessment*: so costly is the spurning of witnessed truth that the architecture of all being resounds with its expulsion. And precisely because the verse names price, not persons, its purpose is deterrent-gracious: *see your road's end before you reach it* — return traffic remains live — verse 89's exception opens, as if deliberately, on the very heel of mankind's assembled "laʿnah": "...except those who repent." The believer's practical hearing of verse 87 is thus reduced to one resolution: *never* treat covenants, testimony, and known truth as disposable; the universe itself keeps record of the keeping and the selling — and respond, for those caught in the verse's shadow, as the sūrah itself will: with the summons of verse 89, not with fire.
**Laʿnah: The Sentence of Expulsion**

*Ulāʾika jazāʾuhum anna ʿalayhim laʿnata Allāhi wa-l-malāʾikati wa-l-nāsi ajmaʿīn* — "those — their requital is that upon them is the curse of God, and of the angels, and of mankind — all together." *Laʿnah* — from the root the lexicographers tie to *buʿd*: distance, expulsion — is in God's court the sentence of *removal from mercy's reach*, and the triple-agents of the clause assemble its execution in full: God's curse (the source), the angels' (heaven's service of it — the very armies of blessing now ranged), and *mankind's — all together* (the created world's total constituency, on the Day when all past generations assemble and every mouth speaks to its moment). Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr both mark how the curse becomes *atmospheric*: as the community of the righteous live in ṣalawāt (God and His angels bless the Prophet, 33:56), so the reversers live in the reverse environment — repudiation, all agencies concurring.

**All Together: The No-Exception Mass**

The phrase *al-nāsi ajmaʿīn* — mankind *entirely* — is the grammar of total unanimity: no cluster reserved, no advocate left out of the sentencing choir. It stands across the Book's registers of unity (the army-unanimity of 4:71's praise; the all-of-them calls of the Day) as the exact negative-image of salvation consensus. For the believer the verse is preventive before descriptive: *the community of God's creation, with God at its head, values apostasy of the informed as expulsion-worthy.* The door against it stays open in v. 89 — repentance and amendment — the only clause in the Qur'an's judgment-catalog that reverses the laʿnah sentence *universally*: *there is no curse-file that repentance cannot empty* before death.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:88

> **Abiding therein; the punishment shall not be lightened for them, nor shall they be granted respite,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Grammar of No Exit**

Verse 87's triple curse is now given its temporal dimensions, and they are stated through three clauses whose cumulative architecture is the closest the language comes to the experience of finality. First: *khālidīna fīhā* — "abiding therein" — *khuld*, the Qur'an's word of permanence: residence without end-date. Not days numbered (v. 24's delusion is hereby voided at last), not a term of purification followed by release, but an abode whose lease does not expire. The verse's decisiveness against the ancient numbered-days doctrine of verse 24 is total: after faith, divine witness, clear proofs — and then renunciation — the "forty nights" of hoped-for punishment is replaced by *khulūd*.

Second: *lā yukhaffafu ʿanhumu al-ʿadhāb* — "the punishment shall not be lightened for them." *Takhfīf* — lightening, mitigation, commutation: the clause eternally forecloses parole; no day of relief breaks the sentence; not by degrees, not by intermissions. The parallel texts multiply the other occasions where the same language is spent: 2:86 ("the punishment shall not be lightened for them, nor shall they be helped"), 2:162, 35:36 ("that neither it pass away from them nor that it be lightened"), 40:49, 43:75. The horror is not only intensity but *constancy* — the certainty that tomorrow is, exactly, today again.

Third: *wa lā hum yunẓarūn* — "nor shall they be granted respite." *Inẓār* — deferral, reprieve, look-of-wait: even *delay-in-hope* is excluded: there is nothing to wait *for*; the future has been evacuated of alternatives. The same pair returns at 2:162 and 16:85 — and the Qur'an's contrast is instructive: *reprieve is among the graces of the living world* (every sinner in time is in inẓār state — punishment has not yet landed, and the delay is the space into which repentance is invited — 35:45: "if God were to take mankind to task... He would not leave upon its back a creature; but He grants them respite till a stated term") — while in the final state, deferral itself is withdrawn. All that is left of time is *duration*.

**The Value of This Severity**

The tradition has never deployed these verses as an excuse to terrorize consciences already tender — the same Book that pronounces *khālidīn* now will say, four chapters later, "God desires to lighten for you" (4:28), and our next verse holds the largest possible exception — but to install, in the hearer, finality's *weight*: choices about God are not played out in a world without ends. The psychologically precise benefit of reading verse 88 as a believer is *profound seriousness*: the knowledge that some exits close converts relativist looseness into moral ownership. Everything in the sūrah thereafter — the golden exceptions of verse 89, the call to repentance and raced forgiveness at 133 — is graced by this verse's gravity: *because* one knows what unlightened persistence means, one also knows what the word "except" costs when God utters it. And the soul that arches back to Him, sooner than late, discovers it was never this verse He wanted for her — never one soul of His did He create *for* the curse; the cursed are those who, possessing the map, burned it.
**Khālidūn Fīhā: Permanence Addressed to Sentences**

*Khālidūna fīhā* — "abiding in it" — the abiding-verbs of the Book are always attached to destinies rather than comforts: permanence inside the sentence, with *hā* referring back to the curse-environment of v. 87. The two additional negations that follow build the doctrine of irrevocability in three distinct registers: (1) *lā yukhaffafu ʿanhum al-ʿadhāb* — the punishment is not lightened for them: no commutation, no good-behavior remission, no seasonal relieving (contrast the lightened-gradation granted in other files: 35:36's "neither decreed to die nor lightened"); (2) *wa lā hum yunẓarūn* — nor are they granted respite: no stays of execution, no deferment of the next stage; (3) implicitly, no term: *khālidūn*. The three together overturn the very hope-structure apostates usually rely on — that endings soften with time.

**The Counter-Scene of the Pleaders**

The Book paints the failure of *tanāẓur* — seeking deferment — in its permanent gallery for standing instruction: "our Lord, remove us from it — if we return, then we are wrongdoers" (35:37); "send us back, we shall work righteousness" (32:12) — answered by the tasting-sentence. These futile requests are the v. 88 negations staged as drama: no lightening, no respite, no *send-back*. The believer reads the three clauses as motivation rather than horror: *every softening a soul might wish belongs to the Day's other side*; this side holds only one negotiation-office — repentance (v. 89) — and it opens only before the end arrives.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:89

> **Except those who repent after that, and make amends, for truly God is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Door in the Wall of the Cur­se**

Into the sealed corridor of verses 87–88 — triple curse, abiding, no lightening, no respite — God sets the word *illā* — "except." The entire architecture of finality opens on a single hinge: *illā alladhīna tābū min baʿdi dhālika wa aṣlaḥū* — "except those who repent after that, and make amends — for truly God is Forgiving, Merciful (*ghafūrun raḥīm*)." The tradition reports the exception's historical occasion with moving concreteness (al-Ṭabarī; al-Qurṭubī): the man who had left Islam for Makkah — his name is given in the reports as al-Ḥārith ibn Suwayd (some narrate the incident of others like him) — wrote back to his family in Madinah, his heart having turned: *"Is there repentance for me?"* — and God answered his question in lasting scripture: *tābū*, yes — repent; *aṣlaḥū*, and repair what you marred. Then the promise is not merely that the curse lifts but that God's two favourite names in this sūrah replace it — names whose conjunction in Arabic is an almost technical term for the hope of returning sinners: *ghafūr* — covering forgiveness for what *was*; *raḥīm* — cherishing mercy for what is *coming*.

**Repentance's Two Verbs: Turn, Then Repair**

The twin requirements are exact: *tābū* — *tawbah*, the turning: the trajectory reversed, the dividing return to the Owner abandoned — the heart's verb; *wa aṣlaḥū* — *iṣlāḥ*, amendment: the *works effected by the wrong* now mended: the hand's verb. The Qur'an's formula for release never stops at sentiment: faith alone unworked (v. 57's formula) is not sufficient; contrition alone un-*repaired* is not sufficient; the *doing* of repair is the second wing of return — one of the commentators' constant pairs: *an-nadam* (remorse) plus *al-iqlaʿ wa-l-ʿazm* (abandonment and resolve) plus *qadaʾ* (making good what can be made good): the scholars of repentance — Ibn al-Qayyīm above all — built the entire science of *tawbah* on this pattern. Note also *min baʿdi dhālika* — "after *that*": repentance remains possible at *any* point after the apostasy, however far the decline — the verse contains no statute of limitations; the only conditions are turn and repair, not duration.

**The Exception's Supremacy Over Copy-Book Justice**

Theologically, the verse asserts God's sovereignty *over* His own sentences: after describing a law of consequence whose three clauses are literally endless, God reserves, not as contradiction but as **majesty**, the power to lift it for the returning — and in the ḥadīth that the tradition loves above nearly all others on the subject, God declares the policy Himself, as it were, as the very index of His nature:

> *"God is more joyous at the repentance of His servant than one of you who comes upon his lost camel in the desert — the rope slipped from him while he slept, bearing his food and drink; he despairs of it, lies down despondent, and wakes to find it at his head."* (Muslim 2747, from Anas)

And in the ḥadīth qudsī of Abū Dharr (Muslim 2577): *"O My servants! Even if your sins reached the clouds of the sky and you then asked My forgiveness, I should forgive you."*

For the sūrah's pastoral design, this is the pivotal clause of the second movement: after the whole grim series (v. 82's *fāsiqūn*; v. 85's refused religion; vv. 86–88's curse-abiding), God *interrupts the architecture of judgment* to say: the map is never closed while breath remains. The believing reader is invited into two habits at once: the *fear* of verses 86–88 (finality is real) and the *hope* of verse 89 (return is realer — it has width; God is *ghafūr*). And the practical rule for counselors of others is unwritten but plain: in *our* speech to the fallen, verse 89 precedes verse 87, always — for God positions the doorway before the warning completes its sounding, and those who announce His Book should keep to His ordering.
**Except: The Exception-Particle and the Mercy-Structure of God's Sentences**

*Illā alladhīna tābū min baʿdi dhālika wa aṣlaḥū* — "except those who repent after that and amend": the *illā* of exception enters the bleakest stretch of the sūrah (vv. 86–88's curse-architecture) like a door let into a prison-wall — and the Book intends the drama: no sooner does any sentence in God's speech reach its maximum severity than the exception-clause appears (2:160 — the same except; 24:5; and the spectacle of 4:145–146). The scholars of the sūrah — al-Qurṭubī above all — treat v. 89 as programmatic for the whole structure of Islamic legal-theology: *no individual is born under the laʿnah of vv. 87–88; only conduct writes the sentence; repentance erases.* The paired verbs set the repentance-protocol: *tābū* — the inward turn (regret, resolution, cessation) — and *aṣlaḥū* — the outward repair (restitution and amendment), together the whole of tawbah.

**The Lost Camel of the Merciful**

The verse seals with the Name-pair *inna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm* — Forgiving, Merciful — and the Prophet ﷺ gave the ummah its most human measure of what that seal means on the ground:

> *"God is more joyful at the repentance of His servant than one of you who, upon his riding-beast in a waterless desert, loses it, upon it his food and drink; he lies down in the shadow of a tree, despairing of it — then, while he is in that state, there it is standing at his side; he takes its reins and says in the excess of his joy: O God, You are my servant and I am Your Lord — erring from the extremity of joy."* (Muslim 2747)

The camel found in the desert is v. 89 in a single parable: lost, despaired, restored — and the joy runs in heaven's direction. Whoever reads vv. 86–88 over his own file is being walked to v. 89 deliberately: *the door is in the wall; go through.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:90

> **Truly those who disbelieve after having believed, then increase in disbelief, their repentance shall not be accepted, and they are the ones who are astray.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**When Increase in Disbelief Seals the Ledger**

The exception of verse 89 is now bounded by its counter-case, and the analysis is of high diagnostic precision: *inna alladhīna kafarū baʿda īmānihim thumma izdādū kufran* — "those who disbelieve after believing, *then increase in disbelief*" — *lan tuqbala tawbatuhum* — "their repentance shall not be accepted" — *wa ulāʾika humu al-ḍāllūn* — "and it is they who are the astray." The fatal symptom is in the verb *izdādū* — *increased*: not a fall but a *progression*: disbelief with accruals, disbelief gone into investment, asset of error compounded. The commentators have read the clause through four classical lenses, all compatible:

First — *the temporal*: those who persist on increase until the final crossing, so that repentance arrives, if at all, at the sight of the waning — and the Book's standing rule about deathbed repentance applies (4:18: "repentance is not for those who do evil works until, when death presents itself to one of them, he says: now I repent"). Second — *the repeated*: those who disbelieve, repent, disbelieve again, and increase — the earlier repentance consumed, as it were, by the later career — each new insobriety converts the former turn into a strategem, until the whole exercise of repentance has been treated as a revolving door; repentance offered under that arithmetic is not accepted because it is not *present* — the thing called by its name is no longer the turning of the heart but the management of outcomes. Third — *the deliberate*: those whose *increase* is a policy: each year more entrenched, more camouflaged, more invested in the refutation of what they know. Fourth — *the simply factual*: such people's "repentance," in the rare cases it is uttered, is found on examination to be no repentance at all (al-Rāzī's point): *lan tuqbala* states the verdict over the *counterfeit*.

**"And They Are the Astray": Ḍalāl as a Final Address**

The final designation is *al-ḍāllūn* — *the astray, those who have lost the road* — the starkest of the Qur'an's topographies of ruin, from the Fātiḥah's daily petition ("not of those who go astray"). To be *ḍāll* is not to be in a low condition while still headed somewhere; it is the absence of heading altogether: effort without orientation — horizonless labor. Those disqualified by verse 90 are thereby described finally as those without a trajectory toward God at all: the curse-state (v. 87) becomes a *condition*, not a journey.

**The Distinction That Keeps Hope Honest**

Verse 90's severity must be kept in exact subordination to verse 89 — the two form one law: the man who *turns and mends* — however far gone — passes through; the man whose biography is "then increased in disbelief" until there remains in him no repenting subject — for repentance is possible only to the living soul in business of return — does not. The tradition's great exempla are invoked: Abū Sufyān, the arch-enemy of Badr and Uḥud, came late but came truly; his is the case of verse 89. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy died *inside* his increase; his is the case of verse 90. And the principle was set in prophetic speech with characteristic brightness: *"God accepts the repentance of His servant so long as he has not reached the gurgle (the death-rattle — al-ghargharah)"* (al-Tirmidhī 3537; Ibn Mājah — graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ). Until the gargle — the living soul, whatever its interim career, is under verse 89's door; after it, verse 91's golden planet buys nothing.

The pastoral counsel the verse teaches is unmistakable: never confuse "repentance" with *the indefinite deferral of mending* — the soul that plays with its return plays against time's closed account; and never, in speaking to one who has *turned*, deny the door of verse 89 — our judgment of the sincerity of others' repentance is too small a vessel for the ocean of God's; we are bid to treat the returning as returned, and leave the heart-weights to God.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:91

> **Truly those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, an earth full of gold would not be accepted from any one of them, were he to offer it in ransom. For them there shall be a painful punishment, and they shall have no helpers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Bankruptcy of Postponed Currency**

The case is completed with its final scenario: *inna alladhīna kafarū wa mātū wa hum kuffār* — "truly those who disbelieve and *die* while disbelievers" — *fa-lan yuqbala min aḥadihim milʾu al-arḍi dhahaban wa-law iftadā bih* — "an earth full of gold would not be accepted from any one of them, even were he to offer it as ransom." The image concentrates the chapter's long economic idiom of salvation (selling covenants for paltry prices — v. 77; availing wealth and children — v. 10) into one hypothetical transaction: the disbeliever, confronted at last with the balance, makes the offer of staggering prodigality — *an earth's fullness of gold* — because to him wealth was the universal solvent, the thing by which all his life's debts had been managed; and it is refused — *lan yuqbala* — not because the offer is small but because the *exchange no longer trades*. Two clauses decipher the refusal:

**Time is the first.** "Were he to offer it" — the counterfactual mood rules: this offer never in fact happens; death has foreclosed the possibility of the transaction. It is the completion of verse 90's terminality and 4:18's no-repentance-at-the-rattle. The world's currencies — gold, gold-heaped qanāṭīr (v. 14), pedigree, excuses — were redeemable only within the market day; the evening changes the nature of wealth from negotiable to inert.

**Value is the second.** And even if offered it would fail: a finite sum cannot ransom an infinite charge; the debt owed to the Almighty by the obstinate rejecter is not quantum-priced — only God can *remit* such a charge, and remission He offers freely but only in life — "say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, despair not of God's mercy; God forgives all sins" (39:53 — addressed to the living). The Taghmah? The parallel passages confirm the formula across the Book: 5:36 ("if they possessed all that is in the earth, and as much besides, to ransom themselves with it from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted of them"); 10:54; 13:18; 39:47. The principle is not that gold is small, but that salvation was *never* priced in gold — the dishonor was in the species of the attempt: trying to buy what was offered free, at a time when the market is closed.

**"No Helpers": The Third Refrain**

And the ending revisits the sūrah's loneliest clause for the third time (vv. 22, 56, 91): *wa mā lahum min nāṣirīn* — "and they shall have no helpers." Against every ḥabīl of rescue — every advocate that wealth recruits, every intercessor that family deploys, every scheme of *days numbered* (v. 24) — the verse sets the one permanent fact: *there is no helper after death's passage* within God's own policies: the intercession that will exist is by God's permission and for whom God accepts (2:255; 53:26), and the false sponsor-structures in which humans invest so much of their religion-inheritance collapse at the counter where the *iftadā* — the ransom-offer — is read.

**The Mercy in the Merchant's Warning**

But the verse should be read in its function: it is not information for the dead — who are beyond benefit — but *warning-spice* for the living. Every clause is written in the conditional of present possibility: kafarū wa mātū — *die not in that state* — and the door re-opens to verse 92, which will tell us by what *small*-seeming currencies the account *is* settled: not an earth of gold, but a true submission (v. 19), covenant-keeping (v. 76), spending from what we love (v. 92), reverence and patience (vv. 15–17). God is not expensive to be right with; He is only *exclusive*: the price is *īmān* and the life that accompanies it — not the vaults of the earth. The sting of verse 91 is therefore the sting of the wise salesman: *buy with the currency the market was founded on, while the market is open — an earth of gold will not pass tomorrow what a believing heart passes today.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:92

> **You will never attain piety till you spend from that which you love. And whatever you spend, truly God knows it.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The True Definition of Treasure: What You Release**

Verse 91 ruled out salvation by gold *after* death; verse 92 names the gold's true purpose *before* it: *lan tanālū al-birra ḥattā tunfiqū mimmā tuḥibbūn* — "You shall never attain *birr* until you spend from that which you love." *Birr* — piety, goodness, the full benign weight of righteousness (whose muster is read at 2:177: birr is belief fulfilled in conduct: wealth given despite love, captives freed, prayer established, covenants kept, patience held) — is placed behind a gate whose lock is *love*. Not "spend" simply — spending is easy from surplus and from the uncherished — but *spend from that which you love*: the beloved object departing the beloved owner. The verse thereby discloses the deepest law of charity: its value is measured not by the ledger of the recipient but by the *closeness* of the thing to the giver. Alms of the unwanted are disposal; alms of the beloved are sacrifice, and sacrifice is the coin in which God honors purchase.

**The Date-Palm Proofs of Madinah**

The Companions understood the verse's meter at once. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record of Abū Ṭalḥa al-Anṣārī — the wealthiest of the Anṣār in date-palms — what the verse occasioned: his dearest property was the garden of *Bayruḥāʾ*, facing the mosque; and when this verse descended he came to the Prophet ﷺ:

> *He said: "O Messenger of God! God says: 'You will never attain piety till you spend from that which you love' — and the most beloved of my wealth to me is Bayruḥāʾ, so I give it as charity to God, hoping for its piety and its store with God. Place it, O Messenger of God, wherever God shows you." The Prophet said: "Blessed property that is! I have heard what you said, and my judgment is: distribute it among your kin."* (al-Bukhārī 1461, 2769; Muslim — with Abū Ṭalḥa's cry "it is sold!" more than once, as the Prophet ruled each time)

Observe the full pattern of sanctified spending: identification of *the most beloved* thing (not the least!); the promptness — "when the verse was revealed," without delay; the consultation that kept the gift lawful and wise (distributed to kin — the finest of alms being to one's own); and the Prophet's approval measured in the word *bākh, bākh* — "blessed is that wealth!" A republic of such givers built Islam; the ḥadīth supplies dozens — — of Abū Bakr bringing all he had (*"what have you kept for your family? — God and His Messenger,"* Abū Dāwūd 1678; al-Tirmidhī 3675) and ʿUmar fearing to be outdone with half. The principle scales downward duly: *mā tuḥibbūn* — "what you love" — in your own measure: the beloved book, the beloved watch, the beloved hour of sleep; God's market accepts all denominations of dear.

**"And Whatever You Spend, God Knows It": The Auditor of Sacred Giving**

The second clause settles the anxiety every generous heart feels in the shadows — *wa mā tunfiqū min shayʾin fa-inna Allāha bihi ʿalīm* — "and whatever you spend — *of a thing* — truly God is of it Knowing." The indefinite *min shayʾ* — of anything — reduces the scale from qinṭār to date-stone (2:265's garden on a height; the ḥadīth: *"protect yourselves from the Fire even with half a date"* — al-Bukhārī 6023; Muslim 1016); and the *ʿalīm* — God *knows it* — covers the three registers of a gift's value: its *amount* (He counts), its *source* (halal or otherwise), and its *intention* (why it moved). Security of the charity — this is the believer's deepest reassurance: *no act of giving is lost in transit*. The verse thereby closes the anxiety of both directions: the giver is justified not by the size but by the love; and the gift is archived not by recipient-accounting but by the Knower of breasts (v. 29). Generosity, in God's ledger, is *the most carefully kept of all accounts* — "the likeness of those who spend their wealth in God's way is as a grain that grows seven ears; in every ear a hundred grains — and God multiplies for whom He wills" (2:261) — seven hundredfold *minimum*, "and God is Vast, Knowing."

**The Verse as a Standing Therapy**

In a century whose signature disease is attachment — the therapy of release — verse 92 prescribes a regimen no asceticism improves on: regular, purposive *detachment by donation*: periodically locate the *mā tuḥibbūn* of your current age — whatever has begun to own *you* — and discharge it for God. This is taqwā (v. 15) practiced in property, the "spending" badge of verse 17 personal-fied, and the exact schooling for the chapter's later demands — spending in ease and hardship (v. 134) — and the culminating promise of verse 195: *"I will not let the work of any worker among you be lost."* What leaves the hand for God, arrives. What an earth of gold could not buy after death (v. 91), a beloved garden buys *now* — and it buys *birr*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:93

> **All food was lawful unto the Children of Israel, save what Israel had forbidden for himself, before the Torah was sent down. Say, "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**An Actual Evidence Dispute: Bring the Scroll**

The debate of the chapter descends from theology into a very concrete test-case: food-law. The polemical background, supplied by the commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Thaʿlabī), concerns the claim pressed against the Prophet ﷺ: Abraham's religion (which the Muslims claimed as theirs — vv. 65–68) must have borne the dietary prohibitions Israel knows; if you are Abraham's heirs, why is your law different? God's answer is juridical history in one sentence: *kullu al-ṭaʿāmi kāna ḥillan li-banī Isrāʾīla illā mā ḥarrama Isrāʾīlu ʿalā nafsihi min qabli an tunazzala al-tawrāh* — "all food was lawful to the Children of Israel except what Israel [Jacob] forbade upon himself, before the Torah was sent down." Before the Torah, then, the *blanket rule* was permissibility: no corpus of dietary law held the Children of Israel; the sole exception was a *personal discipline* of Jacob himself (Israel) — the commentators report the traditional accounts: he was afflicted by an ailment (the sciatica of Genesis 32's wrestle is a scriptural cognate of the story), and forbade to himself some foods in a vow or on medical counsel — and his children followed his custom. When the Torah finally descended, it *codified* restrictions that had developed — some imposed by God as penalty on a rebellious generation (4:160: "for the wrongdoing of those who are Jews, We forbade them good things that were lawful to them"; 6:146 catalogs them), some built on Israel's own self-denials.

**The Challenge: Verifiable, Public, Textual**

Then the Book does something that distinguishes revelation's argument from rhetoric — it demands the *receipt*: *qul: ʾtū bi-l-tawrāti fa-tlūhā in kuntum ṣādiqīn* — "Say: bring the Torah and recite it — if you are truthful." As with the book-adjudication of verse 23 and the mubāhalah of verse 61, the Prophet's method with disputed questions is *documentary*: return to the evidence; lay the scroll open. The scholars esteem this as one of Islam's founding precedents in argumentation ethics: religious disagreement must be conducted against checkable sources, and the Muslim is commanded to invite the checkers. And the verdict on the whole debate is one the rabbis' own scholarship would later confirm: Genesis knows no Torah-given food-law, and the genealogical claim of Abrahamic *kosher* collapses — Abraham pre-dates the corpus by an ocean of centuries.

**A Principle About Law Buried in the Detail**

The verse contributes a principle of religious law that would become central in uṣūl al-fiqh: *al-aṣl fī al-ashyāʾi al-ibāḥah* — in matters of the world, the default ruling is permission: "all food was lawful" — until a divine text confines it. The religious instinct of generational accumulation is toward *embargo*: holy people tend to sacralize austerity and then sanctify the accumulated austerity as *law*; the Qur'an keeps restoring the baseline: nature's provision is innocent until God — not custom, not clergy — indicts. This principle protects religion from becoming, in the long run, an ever-heavier rigorism (which v. 50 told us Jesus himself was sent to relieve!): every community must audit its lawful-and-forbidden ledger against revelation, or it re-becomes Israel forbidding itself — third-generation austerity wearing Moses' signature. The liberation is mandate-level: *do not be shamed by installed scaffolding that God never commanded*; and its counterweight is equally divine: what He *did* command is non-negotiable. The entire structure is suspended on one credentialed phrase: *if you are truthful.* Where a community's restriction is of God, it will survive the Torah-test; where it is of the ancestors, it should be released back to the ancestors.
**The Default of Permissibility: uṣūl Before Lists**

The verse's verdict — *kullu al-ṭaʿāmi kāna ḥillan li-banī isrāʾīl* — "all food was lawful for the Children of Israel" — establishes in passing one of the foundational rules of Islamic jurisprudence: the *original state of edibles is permissibility* (*al-aṣlu fī al-ashyāʾi al-ibāḥah*): prohibition must be *legislated*, permission needs no proof. The exception the verse records — *illā mā ḥarrama isrāʾīlu ʿalā nafsihi min qabli an tunazzala al-tawrāh* — "except what Israel forbade upon himself before the Torah was sent down" — is thus the first prohibition-by-vow in scriptural history: Jacob's self-denial (universally identified in the tafsīr with the camel-meat and milk of his vow — and cognate in the nations' memory with the Genesis 32 abstention) binding himself, and consequently his house, until revelation re-ordered the diet.

**Why the Jews Raised It, and How the Book Answered**

The occasion in the Madinan debate — per al-Ṭabarī's custody of the reports — ran thus: the Jewish scholars put to the Prophet ﷺ the dietary puzzle designed to corner him: *if you claim the creed of Abraham, how do you eat camel and drink its milk?* God's answer unpacks the history they themselves owned: the ban pre-dates the Torah, was self-imposed upon a vow, then taken up legislatively *as discipline* (4:160's *because of wrongdoing from those who became Jews, We forbade them good things that had been lawful*; 6:146's claw-and-fat list) — then relieved in the community of Jesus's confirmation and re-set in Muhammad's. The verse's closing directive — *fa-ʾtū bi-l-tawrāti fa-tlūhā in kuntum ṣādiqīn* — "then bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful" — is the Book's standard evidence-challenge (2:111's *bring your proof*): scripture against scripture, openly read, in the Prophet's own city. The reader carries away the courtroom habit: *traditional food-restrictions carry histories; check when they started and Whom they bind.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:94

> **So whosoever fabricates a lie against God after that, it is they who are the wrongdoers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"After That": Fabrication in the Face of Table­d Evidence**

The verdict following the Torah-challenge is compact and absolute: *fa-maniftarā ʿalā Allāhi al-kadhiba min baʿdi dhālika* — "whosoever fabricates a lie against God *after that*" — *fa-ulāʾika humu al-ẓālimūn* — "it is they who are the wrongdoers." The time-marker *min baʿdi dhālika* — *after that* — is the operative word: after the text has been challenged for and laid out; after the chronology of Jacob and the Torah has settled the question; after every excuse of genuine uncertainty has evaporated — persisting then in ascribing one's own prohibitions, doctrines, or exemptions to God is no longer *error* but *forgery* — *iftirāʾ* — the active manufacture of false revelation: not a misreading but a knowing construction. The charge is this section's third and sternest: "knowingly speaking the lie against God" (vv. 75, 78) — and fabrication after demonstration is its maximum degree.

**"They Are the Wrongdoers": Ẓulm as Religious Forgery**

The noun chosen — *al-ẓālimūn* — repeats the sūrah's own verdict of v. 57 ("God loves not the wrongdoers") and v. 86 ("God guides not wrongdoing people"), and its root meaning must lie at the center of comprehension: *ẓulm* is *misplacement* — putting a thing out of its place. Forgery against God is designated *wrongdoing* rather than mere lying because it does something worse than distort a fact: it *displaces God's voice* in the world: it seats another speaker at His desk. Every subsequent soul misdirected by the forgery's attendant rules walks a path with a forged signature; God's religion is thereby *usurped* — and the community that learns its disciplines from warehouses of accumulated *attribution* is, in the deepest sense, governed by the wrong sovereign. Ibn Taymiyyah and his school fixed the infernal twin at exact parity: *shirk* — assigning God's *authority* to others — arrives in two vessels, false worship and false legislation; the forger is worshipper of the self in the robe of the Deity.

**The Verse Against Every Later Atelier of the Holy**

Fabrication does not die with its first practitioners; it industrializes.
