The traditions concerning *religious forgery in Islam's own house* have their own book-sized warnings: the Prophet ﷺ himself authorized an unheard-of exception to his normal ban on attributing things to him carelessly: *"Whoever lies against me *intentionally*, let him take his seat in the Fire"* (al-Bukhārī 110; Muslim 3 — in the very opening of Muslim's Ṣaḥīḥ, transmitted by over seventy Companions, a mutawātir warning). The guardians of the ḥadīth-science — the chain-critics, the text-critics — are the living outworking of verse 94's severity: fourteen centuries of isnād-verification exist because the early community took "whosoever fabricates a lie... after that" so seriously that it *built an entire science* to arrest attributions before they hardened into law. The etiquette the verse teaches every later religious conversation is total: never let convenience decorate doctrine; *label* your analogies as analogies, your reasonings as reasonings, your school-preferences as school-preferences — and keep the title "thus says God" for the narrow ground where it belongs. Verses like this are why Islam's ordinary Muslims are trained to ask, in the middle of any moving sermon: *where is that?* The question is not impoliteness; it is the direct legacy of 3:94 — and the protection of the faith's posterity from the wrongdoers.
**Iftirāʾ: Forgery as the Summit of Ẓulm**

*Fa-man iftarā ʿalā Allāhi al-kadhiba min baʿdi dhālika fa-ulāʾika hum al-ẓālimūn* — "whoever fabricates against God the lie after that — those, they are the wrongdoers." The sūrah's polemic-sequence has now run its full course: the anachronisms exposed (vv. 65–67), the plots rehearsed (vv. 69–73), the dietary-history corrected (v. 93) — and the *post-correction* forger is named with the Book's most common noun of moral catastrophe: *ẓulm*, the displacement of things from their rightful places. The root *f-r-y* paints the crime itself: *farā* is the leather-worker's *cutting* — and by extension the smithing of speech — a lie *manufactured*, shaped, and dressed as revelation. The class-exclusive formula *ulāʾika hum al-ẓālimūn* (*those — the very ones — are the wrongdoers*) reserves the category: attribute-forgery against God is not error's province; it is injustice's.

**The Prophet's Warning at His Own Pulpit**

No hadith is more potently sited for this verse than the Prophet's own:

> *"Whoever tells a lie upon me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire."* (al-Bukhārī 110; Muslim 3&ndash;4 — the opening tradition of Muslim's *Muqaddimah*, related through dozens of companions)

— the preacher foreseeing, in his very lifetime, the industry of attribution that would grow over his words and his Lord's. The scholars of isnād built an entire science under this verse's shadow: *jarḥ and taʿdīl*, the wounding and accrediting of transmitters — the ummah's professional answer to *iftirāʾ*. And the modern reader is no spectator: every forwarded "verse," every captioned quotation, every unattributed "the Prophet said" circulating without check is weighed at this bar: *cutting speech and clothing it in God's robe is the crime of v. 78 repeated in the age of the share-button.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:95

> **Say, "God has spoken true. So follow the creed of Abraham, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the idolaters."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"God Has Spoken True": The Liturgy of the Settled Argument**

The Torah-challenge concludes with a formula Muslims have made liturgy: *qul: ṣadaqa Allāh* — "Say: God has spoken true." On its first occasion the phrase functioned forensically: the case about Israel's food-law and Abraham's freedom therefrom, just dispensed, is hereby counter-signed by God; not the Prophet's essay but *God's true account* (cf. v. 62). The community embraced the phrase until it became a reflex: on completing a recitation of the Qur'an outside the prayers, the tongue seals it with *ṣadaqa Allāhu al-ʿAẓīm* — "God the Magnificent has spoken true" — a salutation of the Book's verdicts before moving on. There is pedagogy folded into the habit: the believer is trained to end every engagement with the Book not in commentary about the text but in *testimony directed at the Speaker*: You have spoken true. Reading becomes relationship; study becomes address.

**The Command Restates the Inheritance: Followown, Not Labels**

Then the positive injunction completes the whole argument from verses 65–95: *fa-ttabiʿū millata Ibrāhīma ḥanīfan, wa mā kāna mina al-mushrikīn* — "so follow the creed of Abraham, a ḥanīf; and he was not of the idolaters." Since the custodians' claims on Abraham have been foreclosed (vv. 65–68), and the terrified of legal accretion have been answered (vv. 93–94), the way is clear for the actual summons: *follow Abraham's religion* — *millah*, his way, his trodden track — whose entire content has been compressed into the one word of his posture: *ḥanīf* — the one inclining singly to God — and the one denial: never of the *mushrikūn*. The command *ittabiʿū* — *follow* — returns us to the sūrah's master-term (vv. 31, 53: following as the nature of love and discipleship): one inherits by *tracking*, not by banner.

**Qibla and Millah: The Verse's Setting Within the Whole Book**

Al-Qurṭubī and the commentators connect this command's position in the chapter with the pending settlement of the great ritual question of the Muslim community's direction — for the next two verses (96–97) will immediately declare the primacy of Abraham's House at Bakkah and institute the pilgrimage: the *following of Abraham's creed* issues straight into *facing Abraham's sanctuary* and *completing Abraham's circuit*: identity, posture, and ritual choreographed as one inheritance. And in 16:120–123 the attribution is crowned by God Himself: "Truly Abraham was an *ummah* — a community of one — devoutly obedient to God, a ḥanīf, not among the idolaters, grateful for His blessings; He chose him and guided him to a straight path... then We revealed to you [O Muhammad] to follow the creed of Abraham, the ḥanīf; and he was not of the idolaters." The pattern settles: *the Prophet the Muslims follow is God's final ḥanīf-standard, himself following the first ḥanīf-standard.*

For the believer's modern life among competing labels and claimants, verse 95 is the standing exit from all the stale claim-wars: *God has spoken true* — the question is never whose ancestors owned the patriarch but who *follows the creed* — single inclination, zero associating. Follow that, and the whole wealth of Abraham is yours; leave that, and no document of descent anywhere helps. The verse thus converts polemics into program: *ṣadaqa Allāh; therefore walk.*
**Ṣadaqa Allāhu: Truth-Witness as a Standing Formula**

*Qul ṣadaqa Allāh* — "say: God has spoken truth": the imperative makes the rebuttal-liturgy permanent — not a one-time retort to the Madinan debaters but a *standing formula* for every controversy over Abraham's estate ever since. The Book itself models the same seal in the voice of its Speakable Persons — Joseph's *"this is what my Lord made true; He has spoken truth"* (the sense of 6:151 and 18:98's *promise of my Lord is true*) — and the Prophet ﷺ adopted it in his addresses, the believers after him in theirs: *God has spoken truth* as the preface whenever His revealed ruling displaces inherited assumption. Ibn Kathīr notes the clause's positioning exactly: after the Torah-challenge of v. 93 and the forgery-warning of v. 94, the formula confirms *God's narrative* as the court's final exhibit.

**Ḥanīfan Musliman: The Two-Word Portrait of the Patriarch**

*Fa-ttabiʿū millata ibrāhīma ḥanīfan* — "then follow the creed of Abraham, ḥanīf" — pairs the sūrah's restored title with v. 67's full portrait (*ḥanīfan musliman*), here codified as imperative *to the whole audience*: follow — the verb *ittibāʿ*, practical adherence — the millah, the way-made-beaten, inclining (*ḥanīf*, from the root of inclination: turning in from every false orbit toward the One) and surrendering (*muslim*). The Lord's own summary of that creed stands at 16:120–123, where Abraham is called an *ummah* — a nation in one man — and concluded: *"then We revealed to you to follow the creed of Abraham ḥanīf; he was not of the polytheists."* Between v. 95 and 16:123 the whole inheritance-dispute of vv. 65–68 is finally settled: the patriarch's *estate* is this creed, and the will is probated in favor of *whoever follows.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:96

> **Truly the first house established for mankind was that at Bakkah, full of blessing and a guidance for the worlds.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First House: Geography as Theology**

"Follow the creed of Abraham" (v. 95) leads directly to Abraham's stones: *inna awwala baytin wuḍiʿa lil-nāsi la-lladhī bi-bakkata mubārakan wa hudan lil-ʿālamīn* — "Truly the first House established for mankind was that at Bakkah, full of blessing, and a guidance for the worlds." *Awwal* — first — has been expounded by the commentators in three reinforcing senses: first *in time* — the tradition that the Kaʿbah's foundations reach back to Adam's age, rebuilt later by Abraham and Ishmael (2:127: "when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House"); first *in function* — the first sanctuary established *for all mankind* (not for a tribe or a dynasty but *lil-nās*, for people as such); and first *in rank* — foremost, as *awwal* carries priority of status (Ibn Kathīr notes the usage of "I am the first of those who submit," 6:163, as priority not chronology). All three are finally one: the sanctuary that humanity's own father laid, rededicated by the father of the three faiths, is the worship-address of the species.

*Bakkah* — the philologists teach — is Makkah named by an ancient dialectical exchange of *mīm* and *bāʾ*, with a savor of special meaning from the root *bakka* — "to crowd, to press upon one another" — the city where humanity *crowds* around its center; al-Rāzī and others note the usage distinguishes the immediate sanctuary-ground (*Bakkah*) from the town around it (*Makkah*).

**"Full of Blessing" — Barakah and Its Measure**

The House's first epithet is *mubārak* — filled with *barakah*: blessing — a word whose root image, the philologists note, is the kneeling of a camel that *settles* and the welling of water that *endures* — increase and permanence. God's toast to a place: multiplication that lasts. The tradition gives *barakah* this House's most staggering concrete measures. Abū Dharr asked the Prophet ﷺ, as al-Bukhārī and Muslim record:

> *"I said: O Messenger of God, which mosque was founded first? He said: 'The Sacred Mosque.' I said: Then which? He said: 'The Farthest Mosque (al-Aqṣā).' I said: How much between them? He said: 'Forty years. Then — wherever the prayer time finds you, pray: for there is virtue (faḍl) in it.'"* (al-Bukhārī 3366; Muslim 520)

— the two poles of worship fixed by God Himself, forty years apart in sacred time, with all earth between as *second*-choice virtue. And its multiplicity: *"a prayer in this my mosque is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere, save the Sacred Mosque"* (al-Bukhārī 1190; Muslim 1394) — regarding Madinah — while the Sacred House is assigned its own vast multiplication (a hundred thousand, in the reports of Aḥmad and Ibn Mājah). The "blessing" of the verse is thus not a decorative epithet but a functioning economy: one act at the House outweighs lifetimes elsewhere.

Al-Rāzī pauses here in his commentary for one of his rare lyrical passages: consider, he says, the *aggregate* — thousands of years of worshippers facing this single point, five times daily, without one day's interruption — luminaries and laborers, saints and schoolchildren, all orbiting one axis; whatever the buildings of men have meant in history, no other spot on earth has *received* this much directed devotion; the "blessing" is palpably visible in the congregation itself.

**"A Guidance for the Worlds"**

The second epithet — *hudan lil-ʿālamīn* — a guidance for the worlds — places the House in the register of the revealed books themselves: the same phrase described Torah and Gospel (v. 4). The guidance of the House is *orienting*: it unifies direction — every compass of prayer on the planet converges (2:144: "turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; wherever you are, turn your faces toward it") — and unifies *narrative*: Abraham, Hagar's running, Ishmael's submission, the well of Zamzam, the footprints of the Station: the House is a *library in stone*, and pilgrimage is the re-reading of the whole monotheist story with the feet. And it guides in a third way, as the next verse will declare: into it men and women learn security — security as a *practiced* experience of the species, rehearsed annually so the species does not forget how to be one flock around one Lord.
**Bakkah: The House Before the Town**

The verse's honor-roll has three grades of supremacy: *awwala baytin wuḍiʿa li-l-nāsi* — "the first House placed for the people" — firstness in the very file of sacred architecture; *la-lladhī bi-bakkah* — "that which is at Bakkah" — the naming of the site in its older name (the philologists offer the familiar readings: *Bakkah* from *bakka* — crowding and pressing of the multitude in the pilgrimage-season — or from another *bakka* — tears, weeping — and the letters *b* and *m* interchanging in the dialects of the Arabs, as al-Qurṭubī registers at length); *mubārakan wa hudan li-l-ʿālamīn* — "blessed, and a guidance for the worlds" — the House's export-status: blessing localized, guidance globalized. The Prophet ﷺ himself supplied the firstness-clause its precise sense to Abū Dharr's direct question:

> *"I said: Messenger of God, which mosque was founded first? He said: al-Masjid al-Ḥarām. I said: then which? He said: al-Masjid al-Aqṣā. I said: how long between them? He said: forty years."* (al-Bukhārī 3366; Muslim 520)

— forty years between the two sanctuaries of the prophets: firstness measured in created-time, yet both planted by the prophets' own hands (Ibrāhīm raising the House's foundations, 2:127).

**Multiplication at the Centre**

From the same blessing-promise the Prophet drew the community's standing incentive, the comparative prayer-measure:

> *"A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers in any other — except al-Masjid al-Ḥarām"* (al-Bukhārī 1190; Muslim 1394) — and al-Masjid al-Ḥarām's own measure: *a hundred thousand prayers* (Ibn Mājah 1406, ṣaḥīḥ, from Jābir).

Firstness, blessing, guidance, multiplication — the world's map of worship has its North in Bakkah; every prayer-direction since is a spoke back to the first House placed for the people.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:97

> **Therein are clear signs: the station of Abraham, and whosoever enters it shall be secure. Pilgrimage to the House is a duty upon mankind before God for those who can find a way. For whosoever disbelieves, truly God is beyond need of the worlds.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Signs in Stone: The Station of Abraham**

The House now discloses its credential, its sanctuary-status, and its summons, in one of the most concentrated verses of the Book. Its credential: *fīhi āyātun bayyināt, maqāmu Ibrāhīm* — "in it are clear signs: the Station of Abraham." *Maqām Ibrāhīm* — the stone on which Abraham stood while building the upper courses of the Kaʿbah, preserved near the sanctuary, in whose face, by transmitted report, his footprints remained (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr record the early Muslims' veneration of it; 2:125 commands the believers to "take the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer") — a sign because, in the midst of a desert valley, an ancient builder's work-print endures as God's own notarization of the House's builder: the signature of the patriarch set in masonry. The signs (*bayyināt*) include, by extension (Ibn Kathīr's wider list), the whole visible evidence of divine election of that valley: Hagar's spring that still pours (Zamzam), the peace that descends on circling crowds, the geometry that draws the prayers of a planet.

**"Whosoever Enters It Shall Be Secure"**

Then the status: *wa man dakhalahu kāna āminan* — "whoever enters it shall be secure." The commentators describe the ancient reality: the ḥaram made the most dangerous peninsula of the age a sanctuary where the hunted could not be taken, where men laid down feuds at the boundary stones; the Prophet ﷺ consecrated its perpetuity on the day of the conquest in words al-Bukhārī preserves:

> *"This town God made inviolable on the day He created the heavens and the earth; it is inviolable by the inviolability of God until the Day of Resurrection. It was not lawful for anyone before me [to fight in it], and will not be lawful for anyone after me; it was made lawful for me only for an hour of a day."* (al-Bukhārī 1834; Muslim 1353)

Some commentators constrain the meaning to the ancient status or to exemption from worldly seizure; al-Qurṭubī and others transmit the spiritual extension: *whoever enters it for God's rites emerges with the sinner's security* — amnesty from the Fire itself (the ḥadīth of the performed ḥajj: "whoever performs ḥajj for God's sake and does not approach obscenity or sin returns as on the day his mother bore him," al-Bukhārī 1521). The two meanings interlock beautifully: the body is safe at the walls; the soul, beyond them.

**The Summons: "A Duty upon Mankind unto God"**

Then the verse institutes one of the five pillars: *wa lillāhi ʿalā al-nāsi ḥijju al-bayti man istaṭāʿa ilayhi sabīlā* — "and unto God, upon mankind, is the pilgrimage of the House — for whoever can make his way thereto." The accusatives matter: *lillāhi* — the duty is owed *to God*, whatever men may organize; *ʿalā al-nās* — its address is the *species*: humanity is invited to the House its first father founded, at least once in an able lifetime; *man istaṭāʿa ilayhi sabīlā* — "who can find a way" — the jurists ground here the exemption of the unable: provision, transport, safety, health, and (by near-consensus of conditions) accompanying security; Islam's fifth pillar is duty constrained by mercy from its first day. The Prophet ﷺ defined the rite's rank in the hadith of Gabriel (al-Bukhārī 8; Muslim 16: "Islam is built upon five... the pilgrimage..."), and explained its mean: *"al-ḥajj is ʿArafah"* (al-Tirmidhī 889 — the standing on the plain), and assigned its reward: *"the accepted ḥajj has no reward but Paradise"* (al-Bukhārī 1773; Muslim 1349: *"from one ʿUmrah to another is expiation for what is between them; and the ḥajj that is mabrūr has no reward but the Garden"*).

And the closing edge — *wa man kafara fa-inna Allāha ghaniyyun ʿani al-ʿālamīn* — "whosoever disbelieves — truly God is beyond need of the worlds": refusal of the summons — whether by denial of its obligation (al-Qurṭubī names this *kufr* in the juridical sense) or by negligence's disdain — harms only the refuser. The world's richest assembly is God's feast; the Host is *ghanī* — free of need for guests, for worshippers, for attendees; the invitation is itself the entire generosity. The believer who cannot yet afford the road memorizes the verse with longing; the one who can hears in it the mercy of a command that is, strictly speaking, *an appointment with the first House of his species* — an appointment to which, once in his life, he owes the body as well as the soul.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:98

> **Say, "O People of the Book! Why do you disbelieve in God's signs, while God is Witness over what you do?"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question Renewed, With a New Auditor Named**

Verse 70 asked the People of the Book why they disbelieved God's signs "while you are witnesses"; the challenge now returns with a sharpened addressee in the witness-box: *qul yā ahla al-kitābi lima takfurūna bi-āyāti Allāhi wa Allāhu shahīdun ʿalā mā taʿmalūn* — "Say: O People of the Book! Why do you disbelieve in God's signs, *while God is Witness over what you do*?" The loop is not redundant but developmental: verse 70 arraigned their *own* witness — the signs within their custody — while verse 98 adds the *sovereign* witness: every maneuver catalogued in the intervening twenty-eight verses (the wish to mislead, the burying of knowledge, the staged conversions of v. 72, the attribution-forgeries of v. 78, the resistance to the Torah-test of v. 93) has occurred not in a privacy they owned but under the continuous Observation of *shahīd*: God-as-Witness — seer, knower, recorder-in-court.

*Shahīd* in Qur'anic theology is among the most juridical of God's names: it names not only perception but *testimony-keeping* — the attribute by which no act is merely *known* but *held ready to be borne witness of*: "He is *shahīd* over His servants" (41:46: "your Lord wrongs not His servants"); *"does he not know that God sees?"* (96:14). The verse, then, quietly moves the controversy into God's courtroom: the question "why do you disbelieve?" is not only reproach; it is advance notice that all has been *entered into evidence*. The sūrah's own earlier sentence (v. 30: every soul will *find presented* the good and the evil) receives its application: the strategies of verses 69–78 are not only *readable* in Madinah; they are *readings* in heaven.

**The Productive Fear, and the Two Judiciaries**

Why does this verse stand exactly here — after the gifts of Bakkah, the security, and the pilgrimage summons (vv. 96–97)? The juxtaposition is eloquent: God has just done *mankind* a historic kindness — the House re-centering monotheism's geography and inviting the species — and the immediate head-turn is back to those resisting the kindness: the contrast shows *with what God is busy* (opening a House, making security, inviting to pilgrimage) and *with what they are busy* (resisting signs). The verse thereby also functions as the chapter's standing principle of conscience for every community of scripture, including ours: faith-conversations debased into stratagem war are not played under cover of religious complexity; the Witness writes continuously; and the sheer presence of His *shuhūd* is the plurality of decency in every speech-act.

The Prophet ﷺ taught the operating form of this fear as *iḥsān*, in the Gabriel hadith which closes every manual of the religion's core:

> *"Iḥsān is that you worship God as though you see Him; and if you do not see Him — He sees you."* (Muslim 8; al-Bukhārī 4777)

Verse 98 is that hadith's negative form: the people addressed did *not* act as though seen; they acted as though unseen — and that, at bottom, is what "disbelief in God's signs" always reduces to: conduct that makes sense only in an unwatched universe. The believing reader draws the practice: read every temptation to conceal, spin, or bias the truth under this light — *wa Allāhu shahīdun* — and let the Witness be enough of a court; the society built by such souls needs fewer watchers, because its members have One.
**Shahīd ʿalā Mā Taʿmalūn: The Standing Witness**

The Mekka-Madina question-form returns once more — *limā takfurūna bi-āyāti Allāh* — "why do you disbelieve in God's signs?" — now capped by the divine attribute deliberately chosen for every disputation in the chapter: *wa-Allāhu shahīdun ʿalā mā taʿmalūn* — "while God is Witness over all you do." The Shahīd-attribute closes the argument as it opened it (v. 70's *wa antum tashhadūn*): their own witnessing was already entered as evidence; now the Witness above all witnesses stands over the proceedings — the disputations of the parents-of-the-Book are tried in a court where no testimony can be sequestered, since the Judge was *present* at every transaction between text and conscience. Al-Ṭabarī's gloss: *a watcher and keeper over your works, requiting you upon them*; al-Rāzī: the verse's terror is intellectual before judicial — *the entire debate took place before the One Witnessed in it.*

**Iḥsān: The Practical Algebra of a Live Witness**

The Prophet ﷺ, asked by Gabriel in the celebrated interview, defined the religion's highest station with this very attribute as its casuistry:

> *"al-Iḥsān — that you worship God as though you see Him; and though you do not see Him, He sees you."* (Muslim 8, from ʿUmar)

— the shahīd-doctrine translated into the believer's daily operating system: not surveillance-worn but *witness-perfumed*, every act presented to the best of attendance. Read so, v. 98's question converts from polemic to personal piety — the *Why do you... while God is Witness?* addressed to every denial-deed small or great, every concealment-move, every slowed response to a clear sign. The court is in session wherever a servant considers a work: *the Witness files, and the file never sleeps.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:99

> **Say, "O People of the Book! Why do you turn those who believe from the way of God, seeking to make it crooked, while you are witnesses? And God is not heedless of what you do."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Obstruction: The Gravest of the Seven Counts**

The questions of verses 98 and 99 climb from personal rejection to *organized obstruction* — the gravest charge in the series: *lima taṣuddūna ʿan sabīli Allāhi man āmana, tabghūnahā ʿiwajan, wa antum shuhadāʾ* — "why do you turn aside from God's way those who believe, seeking to make it crooked — while you are witnesses?" The verb *ṣadda* — to block, barricade, divert from — followed by *ʿan sabīl Allāh* — *from God's way* — belongs to the Qur'an's own criminal lexicon of the very worst order of offense: not rejection of the way but *engineering the rejection of others*. The Book sentences this class in the harshest comparative it knows: *"who is more wrong than he who bars from God's path and seeks it crooked?"* — cf. 7:45; 11:19, which pronounce: such are far astray; "those are the ones in the Fire" — and 14:3. The sought operation is then named with geometrical precision: *tabghūnahā ʿiwajan* — *seeking it crooked*: not to erase the path but to *skew* it — "crookedness" (*ʿiwaj*) being that subtler sabotage in which the road remains nominally present while its perceieved alignment is distorted, so that travelers following it conscientiously still miss the destination. The moderns know the operation well: truth not denied but *slanted* — presented in its least convincing portrayal, taught through its worst adherents, discussed only in its hardest cases — the craft this chapter has just anatomized in vv. 71–78.

**"While You Are Witnesses": Knowledge Buried Under Strategy**

The closing phrase of the accusation brings back the witness-clause, yet differently weighted: *wa antum shuhadāʾ* — "while you are witnesses": the obstructers are not innocent of what they obstruct; they stand as *shuhadāʾ* — having seen the Messenger in their own city, having watched his unlettered integrity, having read their own books' descriptions — the obstruction is thus *knowing* obstruction, strategy upon recognition — precisely the state verse 86 arraigned as godforsaken ground: how shall such be guided? And the closing verse-seal answers the conspirators' premise of invisibility: *wa mā Allāhu bi-ghāfilin ʿammā taʿmalūn* — "and God is not heedless of what you do": the double negation planted against every scheme, the counter-note to every whispered council: *no session was secret.* The chapter thereby installs God's wakefulness alongside God's witness (v. 98) as the twin guarantee that the road cannot finally be vandalized: watchmen may sleep on earthly walls; the Builder of the road is *ghāfil* — never.

**The Rule for the Ummah of the Road**

The believer who reads verse 99 watches, in consequence, three things in his own religious life. First, *his own straightness*: the *ṣirāṭ* is one and God's; crookedness of our own (*ʿiwaj*) is not only their sabotage but our own ornamented compromises — and the chapter has already taught the prayer against it (v. 8: "make not our hearts swerve"). Second, *his own non-obstruction*: never to stand, by tongue or example, between others and the road — the smallest ṣadd is the Muslim whose manner repels the seeker; the gravest ṣadd is the scholar whose bending turns the road unseen. "Invite to your Lord's way with wisdom and beautiful exhortation" (16:125) presumes one is not *impeding* it in behavior. Third, *his own trust*: the way's defense is not finally his anxiety: "God is not heedless" — roads of God are maintained by God; the believer guards *his* post upon them (v. 200's *rābiṭū*) and leaves the anti-sabotage to the Wakeful. Verses 96–99 thus complete one architectural unit: God offered *a House* and *a Way*; the obstruction parties answered with skews; and God answered the skews with testimony and wakefulness — until, in verse 100, the address turns home to us: "O you who believe..."
**Ṣadd and ʿIwaj: The Obstruction Industry Named Twice**

The locus of the verse's offense is *double*: *taṣuddūna ʿan sabīli Allāhi man āman* — "you divert from God's way the one who believes" — obstruction-by-interception (*ṣadada* — to bar the road, to stand across the thoroughfare) — and *tabghūnahā ʿiwajan* — "seeking for it crookedness" — misrepresentation-by-distortion (*ʿiwaj* — the twist in timber or road: not blocking a path the traveler might orbit, but *bending* it so the follower himself turns). Two trades of one shop: keep believers from the Way and, where keeping fails, *crook the Way itself* in the public's eyes. The Book ranks the shop furiously — 7:45's description of its workers as those who *"bar from God's path and seek to crook it, being disbelievers in the Hereafter"* sets them at the bottom order of the punishment-scales — and al-Ṭabarī places the verse's Madinan referent with the pericope's whole stratagem-file (vv. 69–73): the counseling-circles working on the Prophet's people from behind the minbar of their own scriptures.

**Mā Allāhu bi-Ghāfilin: The Un-sleeping of the Court**

The seal — *wa mā Allāhu bi-ghāfilin ʿammā taʿmalūn* — "and God is not unmindful of what you do" — appoints the divine attribute precisely opposite the shopkeepers' hope: obstruction requires *distraction above* to succeed, and it is announced unavailable. The believers of every age, reading the verse, take the inverse comfort immediately: the plots they cannot see past are not past the Plot-witness; and the plotters themselves receive the only mercy such adoption ever gets — plain warning while the matter is theirs to reverse. The extended pericope will close at vv. 103–105 with the community's own prescribed immune-regimen — *hold fast, all together, by God's rope* — and v. 99 supplies the reason for the prescription: obstruction is an industry; concentration is its antidote.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:100

> **O you who believe! If you obey a group among those who were given the Book, they will render you disbelievers after your having believed.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn Homeward: "O You Who Believe"**

The addressee changes — and the chapter pivots. After three-sevenths of the sūrah addressed to disputants and delegations, God's direct speech now turns to His own: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* — "O you who believe!" — the vocation-vocative of the covenant-community. Every Muslim knows the weight of this summons: in the Book's diction it marks command-shifts of the most solemn register, ninety times across the text. And the first command to the faithful, after the long exposure of obstructions, is a warning *not about the enemies' strength* but about *the believers' susceptibility*: *in tuṭīʿū farīqan mina alladhīna ūtū al-kitāba yaruddūkum baʿda īmānikum kāfirīn* — "if you obey a group of those given the Book, they will send you back, after your having believed, into disbelief." *Obeying* (*tuṭīʿū*) with them as its object is the operative danger: not co-existence but *obedience* — the transfer of directive authority (the taking-as-lords the chapter banned at v. 64): once a community cedes the channel of its norms, its faith is tractable by those who hold the channel.

**The Sentinel Event at the Gathering of Shās**

The commentators (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Wāḥidī in the asbāb) report the occasion that let the general law descend in blood and feathers: a man of the Jews of Madinah — the reports name him Shās ibn Qays — found himself incensed at the sight of the Aws and Khazraj, the two tribes whose histories before Islam were written in each other's blood, sitting together in one conferring harmony. He commissioned a youth to sit among them and recite, with feeling, the old war-poems — the taunts and boasts of the battle of Buʿāth, the verses that each tribe treasured against the other — and watched as the gathering kindled: memories, then boasting, then fury, until arms were lifted among men who an hour before had been as one soul. Word reached the Prophet ﷺ, and he came with his close companions in haste, crying, in the force of shock:

> *"Would you return to the ways of ignorance while I am among you?! — after God has guided you to Islam and honored you with it, and severed you from the matter of ignorance, and rescued you from disbelief, and joined your hearts?!* (narrated in the reports of the asbāb; preserved in the tafsīr literature and the Musnad of Aḥmad; cf. al-Qurṭubī on this verse)

And the men threw down their weapons, wept, and embraced one another. The verses immediately following — 101 through 103 — descend upon this exact bruise and its medicine.

**The Law in the Event**

Observe the machine God intended the community to see: the saboteur spent *nothing* — no army, no treasury, no argument; he recited *old poetry*. The vulnerability he found was not Islam's logic but the believers' *unhealed inner geography*: memory-war structured deeper than creed-peace; the new bond overlaid the old strata without dissolving them. The warning of 3:100 thus governs all the later incarnations of the method: sectarian and tribal summonses dressed as scholarship or brotherhood; old identities weaponized inside the new *jamāʿah*; the managed nostalgia by which small cadres have "obeyed" their way back out of the common *islam* into the parties of death — *yaruddūkum* is a *gradual* verb. The antidote the Book will immediately prescribe is exactly the counter-consciousness the Prophet invoked in the gathering: *you were enemies... He joined your hearts* (v. 103): memory not of *what the tribes were to each other* but of *what God did between them*. Verse 100 teaches the consolidating rule of the chapter's whole second movement: the community's own integration is the primary theater of its preservation, and those who would re-royalize the pre-conversion selves — *the old regicides of Aws and Khazraj, the modern regicides of every faction the ummah has since manufactured* — are answered not with their own weapons but with the shared, still-wet gratitude of a joined heart.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:101

> **How can you disbelieve, while God's signs are recited unto you and His Messenger is among you? And whosoever holds fast to God is indeed guided unto a straight path.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Presences That Make Disbelief Inexplicable**

The rebuke rises one degree, and its form — as with verse 86, the question of astonishment — is *how can it be?*: *wa kayfa takfurūna wa antum tutlā ʿalaykum āyātu Allāhi wa fīkum rasūluh* — "And how can you disbelieve — while God's signs are recited upon you, and His Messenger is *in your midst*?" The two dative circumstances are the chapter's two greatest gifts, and the argument is laid out in plain logistics: disbelief presupposes the absence of access to the truth; for the community addressed, access is *total* and *bilateral* — (1) the *āyāt*: God's signs recited alive into their ears — the Qur'an descending among their own gatherings, answering their own events, teaching them every day's ethics; and (2) *the Messenger* himself: *fīkum* — "among you" — present-tense embodiment: the walking, boarding, forgiving, judging, weeping proof — the man they knew as *al-Amīn*, whose physical nearness — the tradition's whole literature of *shamāʾil* records it — was itself an argument: the light on his face, the veracity of his manner, the transformation of everyone who kept his company (his enemies mocked that magic changed men who sat long with him; the sīrah's answer is the dozens of delegations that entered hostile and exited in tears of faith). *How* — with the text in your ear and the prophet in your city — does kufr even *occur* to a mind? The question is designed to make disbelief *feel* strange again, in a society that had begun treating the question as abstract.

The implied answer for every later century is deliberately open: the Messenger's physical among-ness lasted one generation; the *recited signs* — *tutlā ʿalaykum* — have never left; and the Prophet's *fīkum* persists in the Sunnah's vividness (the tradition's report: "I have left among you two things; you shall not go astray so long as you hold fast to them: the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Prophet — *kitāb Allāh wa sunnat rasūlih*" — Mālik's Muwaṭṭaʾ 1661; al-Ḥākim; and in the farewell-sermon recension of Muslim 1218 from Jābir: "the Book of God" and his guidance). Each generation reads its own verse with due adjustment — *how can YOU disbelieve, with the Recitation among you?* — and the strangeness of unbelief is meant to return with each reading.

**"Whoever Holds Fast to God..."**

Then the verse pronounces the active counter-motion — one of the chapter's signature clauses and among the most quoted sentences of the Book: *wa man yaʿtaṣim bi-Allāhi fa-qad hudiya ilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm* — "and whosoever holds fast to God is indeed guided to a straight path." *Iʿtiṣām* — from the root of *ʿiṣmah*, protection — is gripping the lifeline of the Protector Himself: the verb of a man above an abyss seizing the rope; the *ʿiṣmah*-root passes on to the direct demand of verse 103 — *wa-ʿtaṣimū bi-ḥabli Allāh* — with the rope named. The commentators distribute its sense (al-Ṭabarī: holding fast to God's rope and covenant; al-Qurṭubī: to the Qur'an itself — God said of it: *'this is My straight path — follow it'*; al-Rāzī: to reliance upon God entirely) — and no gloss contradicts another: *to hold to God is to hold to everything He extended His hand through: His Book, His Messenger, His religion*. And the existential law stands as contrast to the saboteurs' physics: those who let the *ṭāʾifah* recite them a way *back* were pulled by arms they could see; those who take hold of God are led by One they cannot — to a *ṣirāṭ mustaqīm*, the very straightness whose name Jesus taught (v. 51), whose petition the daily prayer makes, whose road the covenant of prophets walked. The believer who reads the verse is thus removed from the question of *whether* guidance exists (ridiculous: the two presences), to the question of *his grip* — and the grip is designed for the weak: a rope requires only a hand.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:102

> **O you who believe! Reverence God as He should be reverenced, and die not except in submission.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Due of Taqwā, and the Grammar of Its Due**

The second "O you who believe" brings the chapter's charge to its highest spiritual register: *ittaqū Allāha ḥaqqa tuqātih* — "reverence God with the reverence that is *due* to Him" — *wa lā tamūtunna illā wa antum muslimūn* — "and do not die except while you are submitters." The first clause has drawn commentary because of the grammatical boldness of ḥaqq: *al-taqwā* is commanded *by its own ḥaqq* — its right, its due measure: God deserves a *certain quality* of fear-and-shield consciousness, and the verse names the deserving exactly. Al-Ṭabarī preserves the earliest and most luminous gloss, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd:

> *"That He be obeyed and not disobeyed, remembered and not forgotten, thanked and not denied."* (al-Ṭabarī; and in this chain the Companion-commentators added: desired and not bored with)

Each pair inscribes the due: an obedience whose opposite is not hesitation but defiance; a remembering whose opposite is not distraction but oblivion; a thanking whose opposite is not silence but denial. And the tradition recounts that this high command sobered the Companions — some narratives say the elders among them grieved: *who can reverence God as He should be reverenced?* — and the commentators record the reconciliation in God's own voice at 64:16: *"so reverence God as much as you are able (mā istaṭaʿtum)"* — not as abrogation, for matters of creed and Godly right are not abrogated, but as *specification*: the due-measure, for each soul framed by God Himself, is *true-total capacity* — a full-emptying of what one actually can. Al-Rāzī's synthesis crystallizes the two verses into one occupation: offer everything; be judged by the offering's completeness, not its bulk. God's ḥaqq and God's mercy inscribe, in two texts, one and the same demand: *nothing left over*.

**"Die Not Except as Submitters": Planning the End of Your Sentence**

The second clause is one of the most arresting imperatives in the Book — since no man commands the *when* of his death, the command is understood by all commentators as clothing, not scheduling: *take such care of your islam now, every now, that whenever death arrives it finds you inside it* — for the manner of the end mirrors the condition of the life (the ḥadīth: *"a man is raised according to the manner of his death, and he dies according to the manner of his life"* — transmitted by Aḥmad and others from Ibn ʿUmar; and the positive: *"whomever God wills good for, He employs him: it is said, how does He employ him? — He opens for him righteous deed before his death"* — Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī, from Abū Hurayrah and Anas — graded sound). The same charge was the deathbed curriculum of the first Muslims' own patriarchs: *"Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and Jacob: 'O my sons! God has chosen the religion for you — so do not die except as submitters (muslimūn)'"* (2:132) — the family-counsel of the house of Ibrāhīm across three thousand years: the last state is the sum of the kept ones; make dying-muslim a *project* by living muslim today.

**The Two Clauses as One Verse**

Together the two halves print the whole anthropology of the religious life: (1) the effort-dimension — reverence due — *your maximum*, God's minimum demand (per capacity); and (2) the end-dimension — death in submission — *your continuity*, the state in which God promises to land you if the flight was aimed at Him. The believer internalizing 3:102 does not measure himself by the distance he remains from *perfection* — a measure that breeds despair — but by the completeness of his *given-ness*: is today emptied for God? Is the trajectory of the week islam-ward? Then the end is entrusted to the One who says elsewhere: *"those who believe and do righteousness — their Lord guides them by their faith"* (10:9), and *"those who strive in Us — We shall surely guide them to Our ways"* (29:69). Taqwā *ḥaqqa tuqātih*: everything; and the ending: safely His.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:103

> **And hold fast to the rope of God, all together, and be not divided. Remember the Blessing of God upon you, when you were enemies and He joined your hearts, such that you became brothers by His Blessing. You were on the brink of a pit of fire and He delivered you from it. Thus does God make clear unto you His signs, that haply you may be rightly guided.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rope: One Hand-Hold for a Whole Community**

The deliverance of the Aws–Khazraj event now receives its eternally-binding formula — arguably the most quoted verse of the Qur'an in every century that Islam has suffered its divisions: *wa-ʿtaṣimū bi-ḥabli Allāhi jamīʿan wa lā tafarraqū* — "and hold fast to the rope of God, all together, and do not be divided." The image is drawn from rescue-architecture: many people hanging over one fall must take the *same* rope — gripping different ropes is plurality; *jamīʿan* — all together, in one gathering, on one strand — is survival. The commentators distribute the rope's identifications with perfect unanimity of spirit though not of word: the Qur'an itself (al-Ṭabarī's first gloss, as in the ḥadīth in which the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse and said of the Qur'an: *"it is God's firm rope — ḥabl Allāh al-matīn"* — al-Tirmidhī 2906, and in Aḥmad and al-Ḥākim: "a rope extended from the heaven to the earth"); the covenant and religion of God (Ibn Kathīr); the community's holding of God's command (al-jamāʿah sense); — and all converge on the meaning that matters: *the one thing God actually extended between Himself and the believers*, the revealed order. To "hold fast" to it *jamīʿan* adds the sociological clause that changes everything: Islam's bond is not only *vertical* — each soul holding God — but *horizontal*: the holding is *shared*; and its very sharing is the barricade against the *tafarraqū* — the splintering — that killed the earlier communities (v. 105 makes precisely this historical lesson against the People of the Book).

**"Remember": The Therapy of Shared Gratitude**

Then the verse performs the healing itself, and its means are remarkable for their psychology: it does not simply command unity; it *re-narrates memory* — *wa-dhkurū niʿmata Allāhi ʿalaykum idh kuntum aʿdāʾan fa-allafa bayna qulūbikum* — "remember God's blessing upon you when you were enemies, and He joined your hearts — *fa-aṣbaḥtum bi-niʿmatihi ikhwānan* — so that you became, by His blessing, brothers." Three steps: *idh kuntum aʿdāʾan* — you *were* enemies: the honest naming of the old condition (Aws and Khazraj's Buʿāth; the peninsula's decades of vendetta — and, in every century, the ummah's own buried angers); *fa-allafa bayna qulūbikum* — and *He* joined your hearts: the verb *allafa* is the craft of joining unlike things into one working whole — used again at 8:63: *"if you had spent all that is in the earth, you could not have joined their hearts — but God joined them"* — the commentators savor it: *hearts* are joined, not contracts; the work is divine, not a treaty of convenience; *fa-aṣbaḥtum... ikhwānan* — you *became* brothers — by *His blessing*, with the same word of sheer gift (niʿmah) that verse 74 gave to mercy's selection: unity is *grace*, not achievement — a fact which kills pride in it and makes gratitude for it the only sane posture.

**"The Brink of a Pit of Fire": The Memory That Guards**

And the verse closes its curative sequence with the image that seals gratitude into vigilance: *wa kuntum ʿalā shafā ḥufratin mina al-nāri fa-anqadhakum minhā* — "and you were on the brink of a pit of fire — and He delivered you from it." *Shafā* — the lip, the edge: one stumble from the fall; the state of the pre-Islamic Arabian in God's assessment: near-edge, near-hell, delivered not by their own braking. The commentator-veterans read *ḥufrat al-nār* in both registers: the brink of *fitan* (civil fire — the war-machine of tribal hatred ready to consume them in this world) and of the Fire itself. *Thus does God make clear to you His signs* — the same reader-training the Book always stamps at the end of beats like this (*kadhalika yubayyinu Allāhu lakum āyātih*): the signs were *made clear* for you *laʿallakum tahtadūn* — that you may thereby *be kept guided* — history recited as covenant-education.

**The Verse's Immortal Labor in Muslim Memory**

No verse has been more invoked in the ummah's reconciliations, and none is more maligned in its neglect: every secession, every takfīr-war within the house, every bitter fence inside the *millah* has been addressed by the *ḥabl Allāh jamīʿan* — and there is hardly a century in which Muslims did not need it anew. Its rules, as the believers' jurists of society distilled them, are few and crystal: (1) the rope is objective — no unity is sound around a banner other than God's own; man-made coalitions against the revealed order are *also* departures from the rope; (2) its grip is plural — *jamīʿan*: met in congregation, in consultation, in shared meals, in mutual *ʿatto* — circles that pray together and forgive together are the rope's visible knots; (3) its force-therapy is *remembrance* — the Prophet ﷺ at Buʿāth-reminder did not reach for *fiqh*-arguments but for *memory*: would you return to ignorance *while I am among you*? (v. 100) — the sūrah says again with His voice: remember. And its promise is concealed in its syntax: the verse is a command whose obedience has always produced exactly what it predicts — *hearts joined despite the past*. The rope has never failed hands that held it; hands are what fail ropes.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:104

> **Let there be among you a community calling to the good, enjoining right, and forbidding wrong. It is they who shall prosper.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Maintenance Crew of the Rope**

The rope-verse is followed immediately by its institutional elaboration: existence is one thing; *maintenance* is another: *wa-l-takun minkum ummatun yadʿūna ilā al-khayri wa yaʾmurūna bi-l-maʿrūfi wa yanhawna ʿani al-munkar, wa ulāʾika humu al-mufliḥūn* — "and let there be of you a community that calls to the good, enjoins what is right, forbids what is wrong — and those are the prosperous." The command is one of the structuring sentences of Muslim civilization. Where verse 103 legislated *negative* unity (do not split), this legislates *positive* ministry: an ummah's coherence is preserved not by walls but by *callers* — a working party within it whose everyday labor is invitation and repair. The commentators and jurists divide its consignment beautifully: some take the *minkum* ("of you") to mark the *fard kifāyah* — a collective obligation discharged when a segment of the ummah performs it (teachers, scholars, officers of conscience), while falling upon none when adequately performed (al-Qurṭubī); others read it as the command to the *whole* community, so that every believer is commissioned in his own reach — *"and may you be a community that calls to good"* (al-Rāzī's reading) — and the Prophet's own hadith of the three hands implies the universal:

> *"Whosoever among you sees a wrong (munkar), let him change it with his hand; if he cannot, then with his tongue; if he cannot, then with his heart — and that is the weakest of faith."* (Muslim 49, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī)

Whatever its juristic assignment, its social thesis is invariant: the religion without consciences *at work within it* decays.

**What Is Maʿrūf? What Is Munkar?**

The two terms themselves contain an anthropology. *Maʿrūf* — "what is recognized": the good that sound conscience and revealed norm *both* know — custom at one with the command of God, like the English word *moral* preserving *mores*; *munkar* — "what is denied": what both scripture and the uncorrupted intuitive judgment turn from. Islam teaches that the God-given fitrah within a healthy human being overlaps in its register with the revealed code: the caller invites people back to what, in some deep precinct, they already know — the Prophet ﷺ teaching this anthropology of moral knowledge in the famous reply to Wābiṣah: *"ask your heart: piety is that with which the soul is at rest"* (Aḥmad 18006; al-Dārimī — graded ḥasan) — and complete the conquest with the word of knowledge: *to call, one must first know* — hence the jurists' insistence that the caller be reliably instructed (one does not wrench what one cannot name), gentle (the hadith of Usāmah: *"the most beloved people to God are those who lead people to Him"* in the bearing of gentleness *rifq*), and consistent (2:44's prohibition on exacting from others what one neglects oneself).

**The Ministry's Fruits**

*Wa ulāʾika humu al-mufliḥūn* — "and those are the prosperous": the verdict's placement is a rebuke to everyone who has spoken of commanding-right as a hard, thankless cause: it is, God says, *falāḥ* itself — plowed, opened earth come to harvest; the verb of the farmer's success — the same word the call to prayer repeats five times daily (*ḥayya ʿalā al-falāḥ* — *come to prospering*) — attached not now to private salvation but to communal repair-work. History vindicated the economics: the Islamic cities that took the verse seriously produced an indigenous mechanism of moral upkeep — muhtasibs, teaching-circles, the standing *daʿwah* — capable of civilizing rulers and reproducing piety across generations without a theocratic clergy, exactly because the duty was *fard kifāyah* upon all and not a caste's prerogative.

And the individual reader receives the verse at his own scale: in every family, workplace, and friend-circle, God's question is, in a sense, the verse's: *who is the ummah-crew here?* Not the nag, not the inquisitor — the caller: the person whose presence gently selects for the good, whose disapproval is credible because his affection has already been proven, whose voice is the one friends ask before doing something foolish. Those, God declares, are *al-mufliḥūn*: the world's quiet winners — the people whose accounts at the Resurrection show, among their own deeds, the harvests of *consciences they kept alive in others*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:105

> **And be not like those who became divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them. And it is they who shall have a great punishment,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Historical Warning Made Personal**

Having commissioned the maintenance crew, the verse immediately shows what a religion looks like *without* one: *wa lā takūnū ka-lladhīna tafarraqū wa-khtalafū min baʿdi mā jāʾahumu al-bayyināt* — "and be not like those who split and differed after the clear proofs came to them." The referents, per all commentators, are the People of the Book — the same couplets the chapter diagnosed at verse 19 ("they differed only after knowledge came to them, out of envy") and the Book records at 42:13–14 ("He ordained for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah and what We revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: *establish the religion and do not become divided in it*... yet they became divided only after knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves"). The tragic structure repeats with documentary regularity: proof → division; bayyinah → tafarraqu; light → schism — never because the light flickered but because *baghy* — envy and appetite — found in the light new materials for empire-building. The law of history stands: religions rarely fracture over mysteries; they fracture over *power using mysteries*; the historian of religions can forgive mistakes of mind; what he keeps finding is strategies of party.

**"A Great Punishment."**

The verse's final clause — *wa ulāʾika lahum ʿadhābun ʿaẓīm* — "and for them shall be a great punishment" — detonates the assumption that theological division is an innocent academic matter. The Book counts schism — engineered in the face of evidence, for envy — among the capital offenses. And the commentators (al-Rāzī's eye is acute here) extend the plain meaning beyond the People of the Book: the Muslims, commanded "be not like them," are told that *the same rule applies in their own house*: there is no "Muslim exception" in the mathematics of schism; if proof comes and party-building follows, the name on the licensure does not commute the sentence. The Prophet's standing prophecy then hangs over every century: *"the Children of Israel split into seventy-two sects; and my community shall split into seventy-three — all in the Fire save one." They said: which, O Messenger of God? "What I am upon and my Companions."* (al-Tirmidhī 2640; Aḥmad — graded ṣaḥīḥ) — the "saved faction" defined not by a proper noun but by a *position-fidelity*: what the Prophet was upon, and his Companions — the community of the *rope* before the weaving of sects.

**How Does a Community Escape This Verdict?**

The whole third chapter has been building the answer: by keeping knowledge bonded to worship (vv. 79's *rabbāniyyūn*, teachers who study), by refusing the monopoly of guidance (v. 73), by not fabricating after proof (v. 94), by holding one rope (v. 103), by maintaining the repair-crew (v. 104): in short, by *never letting religious intelligence become a business of dominance.* Schism in the Qur'an's diagnosis is not a theological accident; it is a *moral* condition — envy (v. 19), concealment (v. 71), fabrication (v. 78, 94), arrogance — dressed in the clothing of doctrine. Therefore its true prophylaxis is not doctrinal policing alone but the state of the *heart of the community's learned*: gentle, studious, repentant. And for each believer personally the verse prescribes its immediate regulative behaviors: love the ummah's synthesis more than your own laptop; distrust the excitement of schism (the Prophet said of the ḥawāʾ — desires: "the truth is heavy and bitter" in the reports of ʿAlī); refuse to let difference in branches become severance at the trunk; and grieve, Godward, for every fissure — as the Prophet was grieved at the rising of the first sects, never gleeful: *"my community — my community"* (Muslim 202, in the intercession narratives): the great punishment is for those who split — and the great mercy of those who hold the rope is for those whose eyes *weep at the splits*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:106

> **On the Day when faces whiten and faces blacken. As for those whose faces blacken, "Did you disbelieve after having believed? Then taste the punishment for having disbelieved."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Day of the Two Complexions**

The schism-makers' "great punishment" is now unveiled across the register of the final morning: *yawma tabyaḍḍu wujūhun wa taswaddu wujūn* — "on the Day when faces whiten and faces blacken." The image is drawn from the universal language of the face: in Arabic as elsewhere, blackness of face stands for distress, gloom, dishonor (43:17's man whose face darkens at bad news; 39:60: "on the Day of Resurrection you shall see those who lied against God with faces blackened"), whiteness for joy, relief, honor (10:26: the sincere have "no darkness upon their faces nor abasement"; 80:38–41: "faces that day shall be radiant, laughing, joyful — and faces that day with dust upon them, veiled in gloom"). On that morning, deeds of a lifetime issue their *complexion-reports* without need of dossiers: faith, kept covenant, and the unbended truth appear as *light*; renunciations, distortions, and party-betrayals, as *darkness*. The Book's eschatology thereby completes the symbolism it has been using since 3:103 (faces of brothers rejoined) and 3:98 (the Witness over all things done): the Face-test — the heart's history — gets printed at last upon the front of every man.

**"Did You Disbelieve After Having Believed?"**

The address to the darkened is itself a torture of clarity: *a-kafartum baʿda īmānikum, fa-dhūqū al-ʿadhāba bi-mā kuntum takfurūn* — "Did you disbelieve *after* having believed? Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve." The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī) collect the readings of who is meant: the apostates of this chapter's narrative world (vv. 85–91); the hypocrites (faith attested outwardly, betrayal internalized; cf. 2:19, 63:1); those of the People of the Book who bore witness and swerved; and — in the wider-bearing reading — every soul that tasted belief and then sold it at any price (v. 77) — among whom al-Rāzī explicitly places sectarians who broke the roll of the saved one into banners. What all share is the *temporal order*: disbelief *after* belief — the usage is one the Book restricts to the most culpable category of all renunciations — and the Resurrection's manner of charge is not abstract lecture but Article-of-Address read back: *did you? — taste.* In the ḥadīth that al-Bukhārī and Muslim keep at the pool (al-ḥawḍ), the theme receives its most heart-rending form:

> *"I shall arrive at the Pool before you... and men will be taken away to the left, and I shall cry: 'My companions! My companions!' And it will be said: 'You do not know what they innovated after you.' And I shall say: 'Away, away — perish those who changed after me.'"* (al-Bukhārī 6576; Muslim 2290–2292, from Anas and others)

The Prophet's *my companions!* is the pain of 3:106 in advance: faces loved once, gone dark by change.

**A Verse Made for the Reader's Mirror**

And so the chapter intends this text not finally for others but for *us*: the reciter is to read the Day of Complexions as his own appointment: *my* face has a color it is *currently manufacturing*; every action today is pigment; every concealment, every bent text, every kept covenant, every prayer before dawn is mixing in that color as we speak. The remembrance of the Two Faces should settle the believer's habits quickly: he cannot *see* the paint, but he can *trust the formula*: revelation-purity produces light; falsity-darkness. Hence the wisdom of the Prophet's oft-repeated supplication: *"O Light of the heavens and the earth... make me light"* (al-Bukhārī 6316; Muslim 763-ff: *"O God, place light in my heart, light upon my tongue... make me light"*) — the prayer of those who understood that faces ride, finally, upon what hearts have stored. And for the community, the Day of Whitening and Blackening remains the final audit of all *tafarraq* (v. 105) — since whiteness will not be awarded to banners, only to hearts.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:107

> **And as for those whose faces whiten, they will be in the Mercy of God, abiding therein.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Bright-Morning People**

The verse completes the double portrait with its gracious half — deliberately shorter, because felicity pays in one installment: *wa ammā alladhīna ibyaḍḍat wujūhuhum fa-fī raḥmati Allāhi hum fīhā khālidūn* — "and as for those whose faces whiten — they are in God's Mercy; therein abiding." The reprieve of grammar is itself luminous: the darkened were addressed with a question and a lineage of indictment; the brightened receive *location*: *fī raḥmati Allāh* — *inside* God's mercy — as though mercy were a land and they have already crossed into its borders. And the endowment is matched with the chapter's own term of finality: *khālidūn fīhā* — therein *abiding*: the bitter khuld of verse 88's curse mirrored here (the same word) — durational forever — but turned on its axis: permanence is agony only when the state is wrong; permanence in mercy is the content of hope itself.

**"In Mercy," Not "In Earnings": The Sūrah's Doctrine of Salvation Summarized**

The commentators note the freight of the location: the verse does not say "in *payment* for their works" (though works are truly paid in full — v. 57), but places the whitened *inside raḥmah* — and the tradition has always unfolded the difference as the final law of Islam's soteriology. Salvation is wages *only* in respect of faithfulness; in respect of *worth* it is pure grace:

> *The Prophet ﷺ said: "None of you shall be saved by his deeds." They said: Not even you, O Messenger of God? He said: "Not even I — unless God covers me with His mercy (raḥmah). Do right and seek nearness (saddidū, qāribū), and give glad tidings: none shall enter the Garden by his deeds. They said: Not even you? He said: Not even I — unless God envelops me in His forgiveness and mercy."* (al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816, from Abū Hurayrah)

The whitened *did works* — patiently, truthfully, spendingly, taqwā-fully (vv. 15–17), covenantedly (v. 76), with hands on the rope (v. 103) — and their deeds *purchased* them nothing in the strict ledger; what they did was *place them in the category upon which mercy descends*. The two registers are wedded: effort is the door of the category; mercy is the land itself. Verse 107 thus stands among the sūrah's great balancing sentences: against despair — effort does not *earn* heaven by worth, so no humble sinner is priced out of it; against presumption — mercy lands only on the *whitened*, so no one enters who would not whiten.

**"Abiding": The Word That Fixes All the Rest**

*Khālidūn* is the verse's keystone of consolation. The chapter has taught us to hear in eternity the test of every offer: the six banners of verse 14 all carry expiry; hell's khuld is the negation of every strategy (v. 88); and the blessing-klud of verse 107 bestows on the believers' toils what they could never bestow on themselves — *stability with no term*. The joy of the Garden — as the prophet-narratives unfold it — is doubled by this clause: nothing will leave; nothing dims; the face whitened at dawn whitenines on shade of evening never falls again. The sīrah's report of the tradition's beloved image of the saved hearing finally: *"O people of the Garden: for you is health for ever, life for ever, youth for ever, bliss for ever — you shall never die"* (Muslim 2837, in the description of the *call* of eternity made over the dwellers of the Garden after the final entry) — and the Book's own formula at 43:71: *"they shall not taste death therein after the first death; and He will shield them from the punishment of the Blaze"* — with the prayer of 3:16 directly annexed as answered.

Later sages of Islam wrote the whole spiritual life as a war between two pigments: the ṣalāt, the taṣdīq, the ikhlāṣ of the day painting light; the riyāʾ, the kitmān, the makr painting dark. Verse 107 is their benediction: *paint on — there is a morning, and a mercy, and an abiding.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:108

> **These are God's signs which We recite unto thee in truth, and God desires no wrong for the worlds.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Seal Stamped on One Hundred and Eight Signs**

The verse is one of the sūrah's periodic sutras — like verses 58 and 101-103 — in which God halts the current to certify the channel: *tilka āyātu Allāhi natlūhā ʿalayka bi-l-ḥaqq* — "these are the signs of God, which We recite to you in truth." The *tilka* — "those" — points back over a hundred verses of comported discourse: the letters of v. 1; the testimony of Mary and Zachariah; the mubāhalah; the invitation to the common word; the law of the rope; the two complexions of the final morning. All of it is gathered into one descriptor: *āyāt Allāh* — God's signs — recited not in narrative felicity but *bi-l-ḥaqq*: with truth, by truth, for truth; every word warranted. The seal is a merciful reminder mid-course: the believer is not consuming sacred history for entertainment but *receiving recitation (natlūhā — We recite) from God* — the speaker of the entire sūrah is its Creator addressing His Messenger and, through him, us.

**"God Desires No Wrong for the Worlds": Justice Set Above Every Charge**

The verse's second clause — *wa mā Allāhu yurīdu ẓulman lil-ʿālamīn* — "and God wills no wrong for the worlds" — is simultaneously statement of fact, refutation, and comfort. Statement of fact: injustice (*ẓulm*) is un-willed by God at the level of His being: the entire *architecture* of sign giving and judging just shown runs on truth's rails; Refutation: against any suspicion — among the People of the Book's polemics, among the doubters the mubāhalah silenced, among later philosophical skeptics — that God's rule could carry arbitrariness: the verses of curse and punishment just pronounced (vv. 87, 106) are recommended by *ḥaqq*, not by appetite; Comfort: for every soul trembling before its own Day: God does not *want* you to be wronged; your case before Him will be decided in justice square. The theologians of Islam carried heavy arguments under this verse — the Ashʿarī explanation that God's willing-no-wrong is, in part, definitional (injustice being trespass upon another's property, and all property being His) and the Muʿtazilī explanation that justice is objective and God is eternally conformed to it — and both houses agreed upon the practical creed the verse plants: *the Judge of the worlds will not wrong you*; your terror should be of *your ledger*, not of His heart.

**"For the Worlds" — Not for a Tribe**

The universal dative — *lil-ʿālamīn*, all the worlds, all the worlds' peoples — is a quiet rebuff to every theology of selected peoples and hereditary rights: God's justice is not tribal property; *ẓulm* is off-limits for everyone, *raḥmah* on offer for whosoever turns (v. 89) — the same universalism the chapter had staked out right in its court-phrase: God "upholding justice" (v. 18, *qāʾiman bi-l-qisṭ*). The third chapter, in one hundred and eight signs, has described God's conduct with texts, prophets, scoffers, hypocrites, believers — and now stands still a moment to state the common engine: *no wrong intended, by the Maker, against any world.*
**Tilāwah in Truth: The Repeated Signature**

*Tilka āyātu Allāhi natlūhā ʿalayka bi-l-ḥaqq* — "those are God's signs which We recite to you in truth": the sūrah now re-signs its own origin at the closure of the People-of-the-Book pericope exactly as it signed the Christology-pericope before it (v. 58's *dhālika natlūhu ʿalayka*). The refrain gives the Book's readers its own reading-instruction: these polemic-histories and verdict-sentences are not the Prophet's advocacy but *God's signs, recited* — and *bi-l-ḥaqq* — *in truth*: the narration's every clause corresponds to what was and what will be, no advocacy-tax deducted. Al-Ṭabarī's plain gloss holds: *as established and true, no falsehood in it*; al-Rāzī remarks on the pairing-pattern: the recitation-in-truth seal accompanies precisely those sections where the adversary's voice was strongest — as if to say, *above all these disputes the written stands, truth-marked.*

**No Wrong Willed for the Worlds**

The verse's second half is theology complete in nine words: *wa mā Allāhu yurīdu ẓulman li-l-ʿālamīn* — "and God wills no wrong for the worlds." Seated here, at the end of the longest succession of indictments (vv. 98–107 — concealment, obstruction, mockery, requital), the clause acquits the verdicts themselves: the sentences spoken against the obstructers are *no injustice upon them* — their own works authored every line. The Book rings the identical bell wherever the punishments are enumerated (3:182's *God is never unjust to His servants*; 4:40's not-an-atom-weight; 18:49's not-a-wrong; 41:46's *your Lord wrongs no one*) until the doctrine is complete: judgment-day's arithmetic is a closed system; nothing enters but earned figures. And the reader is left at v. 109's door to meet the ledger's Owner: *to God returns the matter entire — no appeal outside the court that wrote the file.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:109

> **Unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth, and unto God are all matters returned.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Ownership and Return: The Two Pillars of Absolute Peace**

Verse 108 grounded justice in the will; verse 109 grounds it in *title*: *wa lillāhi mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ* — "unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth" — *wa ilā Allāhi turjaʿu al-umūr* — "and unto God are all matters returned." Two clauses, and the entire metaphysical order of Islam is gathered in them.

**Clause one: *mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ*.** Everything — every thing — is *His*: ownership in the fullest sense (creation, possession, disposal). God's claim of ownership is reiterated across the Book like a royal seal (2:284; 3:189; 5:17–18, 120; 7:158; 20:6; 34:1; 42:53; 48:14; 57:2, 5, 10; 63:7; 64:1, 4) and its operational force in *this* chapter arrives immediately at verse 180 ("unto God belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth): the world is not *running loose*; men are administrators under titles, not freeholds — the theory which will make miserliness (v. 180) and false lordship (v. 64) what they are: squatters forgetting the Landlord. And ownership here is the ground of verse 108's unwilled-ẓulm: is injustice conceivable toward what is entirely His? The classical Ashʿarite formulation stands: wrongdoing is misallocation of *another's* property; God misallocates nothing of His own: to exist at all is gift; to be judged by truth is gift's accountability — never wrong.

**Clause two: *wa ilā Allāhi turjaʿu al-umūr*.** And all matters — every case, every affair, every destiny, every dispute — *return* (*turjaʿu*) to Him. *Rujūʿ* — return — has been the chapter's deep current all along (v. 55: "then unto Me is your return"; v. 83: "and to Him they will be returned"), and now the current is named in its full generality: *al-umūr* — *the matters*: Najrān's departures and the believers' fears; the buried secrets of breasts; the market-price of covenants; the affairs of the House and the pilgrimage; the fates of tribes and scriptures: everything unfinished is *in post*, everything decided provisionally in time awaits *final certifié* at the Address.

**The Verse's Spiritual Technology**

The believer who truly installs verse 109 finds it doing the work of whole treatises on trust (*tawakkul*): if everything is already His, nothing can be *lost* — only relocated; and if all matters return to Him, nothing is *concluded* until the Return validates it. Anxiety about outcomes is thus revealed as an invalid bookkeeping — we keep accounts of property that never left its Owner and forecasts of cases still in His post. The two clauses, recited together slowly, were enough for the Prophet's ﷺ own bed-side constitution of serenity: from the *simān* of duʿāʾ in al-Bukhārī: *"bismika Allāhumma amūtu wa aḥyā"* — "in Your name, O God, I die and live" — and the formula taught to Barāʾ for sleeping: the last words being *amantu bi-kitābika alladhī anzalta, wa bi-nabiyyika alladhī arsalt* — "and he said: if you die that night you die upon the fitrah" (al-Bukhārī 247, 6320) — sleep practiced as miniature return; death as its full form. And for the community, verse 109 is the necessary ballast before the chapter turns to its heaviest announcement — verse 110's "you are the best community" — lest that commendation be received as vanity: it belongs to the Owner and to the Return… the ummah's nobility is entirely a *deposit from the One to whom everything belongs and returns*.
**The Rujūʿ-Chain: Return as the Chapter's Geography**

*Wa li-Allāhi mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍi wa ilā Allāhi turjaʿu al-umūr* — "and to God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and in the earth; and to God the matters are returned." The sūrah's pericope-seal builds on a chain the attentive reader has been walking since v. 55's *then to Me your return* and v. 83's *to Him they return*: the *rujūʿ*-motions — matters returning upward — form the chapter's geography of finality. Al-Rāzī marks the order's didactic care: possession (God's) is named first — the universe as estate; the return is named second — the estate's administration never lapses from its Proprietor; v. 109 thereby seals the whole People-of-the-Book argument in property-law: *the books and the disputants and the plots all belong to One Owner, and all files are posted back to Him.*

**The Return-Accounting as Daily Practice**

The same pairing concludes 42:53 verbatim, and its pastoral use is among the oldest in the community's preaching: when outcomes discomfit — when truth's side is out-voted, out-plotted, out-chronicled — the believer performs the return-inventory in prayer: *these matters were never finally handed to their interceptors; they are in transit to Him.* The Prophet's own resignation-idiom taught by his own house: ʿĀʾishah's report of his nightly words, and the ummah's standing death-announcement liturgy — *innā li-Allāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn* (from 2:156, the verse the Book itself assigns to the afflicted: *"who say, when calamity strikes them..."*) — is v. 109 personalized: possession acknowledged, return awaited. Everything the chapter has disputed — Abraham's estate, the Book's custodies, the covenant's terms, the plots and their foils — is thereby filed *en route*: to God the matters are returned.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:110

> **You are the best community brought forth unto mankind, enjoining right, forbidding wrong, and believing in God. And were the People of the Book to believe, that would be better for them. Among them are believers, but most of them are iniquitous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"The Best Community": A Function, Not a Banner**

This verse has been inscribed on the hearts of Muslims for fourteen centuries as the charter of their collective worth — and its careful reading protects both its honor and its health: *kuntum khayra ummatin ukhrijat lil-nāsi* — "you are the best community *brought forth* for mankind." Three attendancies immediately temper the commendation. First, *kuntum* — "you are/were" — has been read by the commentators in registers that all keep the verb's force covenantal rather than racial-decisive: in God's foreknowledge written (you *were* the best, in the Preserved Tablet); as factual address to the first generation on condition of conduct (you *are*, insofar as you enact); and as an address-summons (you *are* — *so act worthy of it*) — and whatever the reading, the verse itself immediately appends the functional specifications: best *not* in bloodline, not in history-writ pride, but *in what you do for mankind*: *lil-nāsi* — *for people*, for-their-sakes: the ummah's worth is measured in service-of-others. Second, *ukhrijat* — "brought forth" — passive-voice: brought by God; election is *issuance*, not self-manufacture (v. 74's mercy-selection returned at communal scale). Third, the qualifications follow immediately, hanging the whole commendation on the three working tasks: (1) *taʾmurūna bi-l-maʿrūf* — enjoining the right — the positive ministry of v. 104; (2) *wa tanhawna ʿani al-munkar* — forbidding the wrong — its necessary complement; (3) *wa tuʾminūna bi-Allāh* — and believing in God — the root-faith in the Source, placed deliberately *after* the two social verbs by a sequence the commentators have debated and Ibn Kathīr explained: the ummah-as-community is *known in action* for its public ministry, while the engine of that ministry is *īmān* — ministry without faith is mere sociology; faith without ministry is incomplete religion (cf. 9:71: "the believing men and women, protectors one of another — they enjoin right and forbid wrong, establish prayer, give alms").

**A Rank Fulfilled in History — and Audited by Each Age**

The first generation enacted the verse to such masterpiece extent that the tradition itself canonized their rank in the Prophet's ﷺ own grading of history:

> *"The best of people is my generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them..."* (al-Bukhārī 2652, 3650; Muslim 2533 — from ʿImrān ibn al-Ḥuṣayn and Ibn Masʿūd)

—a testimony that commends while it *expires gradually*: the blessing thins outward from the source against every nostalgia of later ages. The "best community" is thus always the community that in *its* century lives the three verbs: calling, restraining, believing. The failure-terms of the commendation — uncommanded maʿrūf, unforbidden munkar, belief-lamp gone out under party-dust — are the very exact biography of the "worse" communities of verse 105. The honor of verse 110 is permanent; its *appropriation* is reviewed every day.

**"And Were the People of the Book to Believe...": The Open Invitation Within the Correction**

The verse's second half administers one of the most misunderstood balances in interfaith scripture: *wa law āmana ahlu al-kitābi la-kāna khayran lahum; minhumu al-muʾminūna wa aktharuhumu al-fāsiqūn* — "and were the People of the Book to believe, it would be better *for them*; among them are believers, yet most of them are iniquitous."
