Three precise clauses: (1) belief is offered as *khayr lahum* — good *for them* — not as bonus to us: conversion is prescription for their savedness, and thus the invitation remains framed in mercy; (2) *minhumu al-muʾminūna* — among them are believers: the named examples in the commentators — ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and the learned righteous of the Jews who embraced the Prophet; the Negus of Abyssinia and the pious of the Christians who wept at the Qur'an (5:83) — the door never stereotyped shut; (3) *wa aktharuhumu al-fāsiqūn* — yet most are *fāsiqūn* — a word the commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī) bind to its exact meaning: not "disbelievers" as pure category but *fisq*: the exit from their *own* covenant's obligations — falling short of the truth they possess and know: most of them are *lapsed*, in the theological exactitude; and it is *their* religions whose strict custodianship would have brought them to the conclusion this sūrah keeps presenting. The non-vindictive structure is amazing: immediately after declaring them mostly *fāsiq*, God calls them in the very next verses (113–115) not all alike, honors their upright remnant, guarantees their good is not denied them. The theology of the sūrah is consistent: *judgment uttered always with the remnant left standing* — as al-Rāzī and the commentators insist: the categories are moral descriptions, never ethnic erasures.

Verse 110 ends up, therefore, a mirror and a mandate: to the ummah it says — you are *only* the best insofar as the three verbs are alive this morning; to the People of the Book it says — your believing would be *your* good; and to every reader: the final curve is the distinction, not the nation: *al-jāmiʿ* — the tie is īmān-living — inside or outside the fold of Madinah.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:111

> **They will not harm you save a [trifling] hurt. And if they fight you, they will turn their backs upon you; then they will not be helped.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Tween Hurt and Ruin: God's Boundary Over Hostility**

Immediately after the hard balances of verse 110, God issues to the believers a statement of security, and its precision has served the ummah as armor in every besieged age since: *lan yaḍurrūkum illā adhā* — "they shall not harm you, save a hurt" — *wa in yuqātilūkum yuwallūkumu al-adbār, thumma lā yunṣarūn* — "and if they fight you, they shall turn their backs to you — then they shall not be helped." The distinction coded between the two clauses is the whole verse: *adhā* — hurt — versus *ḍarar* — harm. *Adhā* is the irritating wound: the insult, the taunt, the abrasion, the schemed annoyance, the provocation, the slander of the tongue; *ḍarar* is the substantial structural damage: a wound that reaches the body of the community itself. God's promise is absolute in *scope*: the *party* of the People of the Book addressed — combined with the machinery of their alliances (in the commentators' reading: with their confederates and their grander sponsors) — may *hurt*, often and bitterly (v. 186 already forecasts "you shall hear much hurt"); they are denied *harm*: the faith's integrity, the community's survival, the religion's destiny is sealed from their reach. The verse's second clause then commits the battle-outcome in the same asymmetry: *yuwallūkumu al-adbār* — backs turned in rout — closed again with the chapter's precise suffix of helplessness: *thumma lā yunṣarūn* — "then they shall not be helped"; for help abandoned heaven when their positions became *fisq* and obstruction (vv. 81–82, 99). The same verdict was issued as history's own commission: five years later the allies of the apostasy-front of Khaybar and the planned conspiracies after Uḥud found themselves, precisely, either turned back in the field or dismantled from inside by their own fractures (the sīrah of Banū Naḍīr is the classical exhibit, and its own chapter unfolds the same clauses at 59:2–14, including the verbatim recurrence: *"if they are expelled, they will not go with them; and if they are fought, they will not help them"* — 59:12).

**The Theology of Managed Suffering**

The verse reveals a whole Islamic doctrine that the believing generations leaned on in the harshest tests: the qualitative difference between *the allowed hurt* and *the denied harm*. Between them lies the whole theater of faith's proving: hurt is *permitted* (because it refines, it tempers resolve, it separates the sound from the swollen — 2:214's "do you think you will enter the Garden without such as came to those before you?"); harm — in the deeper sense — is *denied* (because God's covenant does not deliver His religion into the hands of its enemies, though He delivers the *pages* of every age inside it into trials — "if a wound has touched you, a like wound has touched the people," v. 140 — the hurt-event is *not evidence* of the harm-permission). Contextual balance: the promise is framed upon the community's *ṣiḥḥah* — its own wholeness — rope-holding, ministry, faith; the tragic pages of Muslim history in which one people of Islam has "harmed" another are governed by other verses — God can and does execute trials of humiliation at the hands of *factions within* (24:55: succession is conditioned: *if they believe and work righteousness*, He shall surely grant them succession as He granted those before). Verse 111, therefore, is promise *with a title-deed*: the collective wholeness.

**Consolation for the Believer Under Annoyance**

And in personal scale the two-word medicine is immediate: *adhā* and *ḍarar*. In every life the *unavoidable hurt* — gossip, slight, provocation, the procedural friction of obstructions — is sized up into *catastrophe* by anxiety; verse 111 re-sizes it: it is the *adhā*-class: expected, permitted, survivable, *small in the ledger of destinies*; the *ḍarar*-class — your Islam itself, your certainty, your *ṣirāṭ* — is held under God's own clause: they shall not be helped. Two rules of conduct follow from the two clauses: do not amplify *adhā* into war (the chapter's own patience-command at v. 186 will exactly counsel: "if you are patient and reverent — that is a course worthy of resolve"); and do not fear *ḍarar* into compromise (the chapter's own courage-command at vv. 102 and 200 covers it: die only as muslim; stay posted). The tongue of the Prophet at Ḥunayn — *"I am the Prophet, no lie / I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib"* — was this verse embodied: hurt abundant, harm impossible; then backs turned; then He helped.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:112

> **They shall be struck with abasement wherever they are come upon, save by means of a rope from God and a rope from mankind. And they shall earn a burden of wrath from God, and they shall be struck with indigence. That is because they used to disbelieve in God's signs and kill the prophets without right. That is for their having disobeyed and transgressed.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Strikes: Abasement and Indigence**

The verdict over the obstructers is now pronounced in space and in estate, and its first clause is among the Qur'an's most pondered: *ḍuribat ʿalayhimu al-dhillatu ayna mā thuqifū* — "abasement is struck upon them wherever they are come upon." *Ḍuriba ʿalā* — struck upon, imposed like a stamp — gives the verdict the force of a mark: *al-dhillah* — lowness, subjugation, the impossibility of sovereign stature — laid upon the party (the commentators direct it primarily at the obstinate of Ahl al-Kitāb who, in covenant-breach, had made war on God's messengers and Truth). Then the clause that runs through every reading of the text: *illā bi-ḥablin mina Allāhi wa ḥablin mina al-nās* — "save by a rope from God and a rope from mankind." The classical gloss of this exception is a theme of stature in law and history (al-Ṭabarī mounts the principal explanations): *rope from God* — His over-arching covenant-mercies, by which they may earn His forgiveness in repentance at any hour; and *rope from mankind* — the *dhimmah* treaty-relationship granted by the believing polity, by the terms of which they may live securely as protected communities under Muslim rule. Between the two ropes the verse maps the exact outlines of their possible dignity: *not* as sovereigns over God's road, but as either repentants before God or covenant-holders under shelter — whose persons, property, and churches the Islamic law thenceforth protected by some of history's most developed minority-protections (the Prophet's formal covenants of Najrān — with the guarantee from God and His Messenger over their persons, religion, lands, and goods — stand as the model; and history's verdict on the dhimmi order of Madinah, Syria, Egypt, and Spain is better than any polemic: a millennium of survival and flourishing in the house of their strongest rival).

**Wrath Earned, Indigence Struck**

The interior sentence follows: *wa bāʾū bi-ghaḍabin mina Allāh* — "and they incurred wrath from God" — *bāʾa bi-*: to return home carrying, to *earn-and-lodge*: a verb of dreadful precision: *they went back with* wrath as purchased commodity — the same semantic field as 2:90's "they incurred wrath upon wrath" — and then the second strike: *wa ḍuribat ʿalayhimu al-maskanah* — "indigence is struck upon them" — *maskanah*: poverty laced with humbling: the double yoke: *dhillah* in standing; *maskanah* in substance. The commentators read it historically (the abasement and the tribute of the class as sentence), some read its fulfillment in the longer exilic poverty of the communities that had made war on prophecy, some read its widest scope as a *spiritual* sentence: wealth accumulated while knowledge is held hostage purchases *no* felt sufficiency — indigence of the soul in the midst of possessions.

Then the rationale, closed twice — the Qur'an's own docket-signature — *dhālika bi-annahum kānū yakfurūna bi-āyāti Allāhi wa yaqtulūna al-anbiyāʾa bi-ghayri ḥaqq; dhālika bi-mā ʿaṣaw wa kānū yaʿtadūn* — "that, because they used to disbelieve in God's signs and kill the prophets without right; that, for their disobedience and transgression." Two *dhālikas*: the remoter cause — the persistent *kufr* of signs and the centuries-long disgrace at the top of the chapter's indictment (v. 21: killing the prophets without right, killing the enjoiners of justice) — and the proximate cause — *ʿaṣiy* — rejection of the rule after it reached them, and *iʿtidāʾ* — aggression beyond bounds: ringed twice, as on an indictment sealed in duplicate: no single verdict in the Book isolates more plainly the fact that community-downfall is never imposed ethnic fate but *consequence*: because (bi-anna) ... for (bi-mā).

**The Verse's Sobering Universality**

The Muslim commentators were never tempted to turn this text into triumphalism: its structure is too plainly causal to allow it. Al-Rāzī's eye upon the principle: the sentence of *ḍarb* falls upon *behaviors*, not upon genealogies — "and had the Muslims behaved so, the same would strike them" — how could it not, with one Lawgiver who wills no wrong for the worlds (v. 108)? The verse offers the ummah its own spectator-warning: flags do not immunize; the ropes that suspend the fate of peoples are behavior and covenant; God struck abasement *only* after the indices were full — and could strike them into repentants the moment any man of them turned (v. 89), as numbers of their righteous did and do. The believing community must therefore hear in verse 112 two things: the due gravity of remaining within the two ropes ourselves (rope of God — His text, rope of mankind — covenants honored among men), and the due hope in the restoration of others: verse 115 remains undisobeyed — whatever good they do is never denied. The One who stamps *dhillah* on covenant-breakers is the same who stamps honor on the *awliyā* who keep the covenant: *"and to God belongs honor, and to His Messenger, and to the believers"* (63:8) — and the choosing is done every day, by everyone, in private and public conduct.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:113

> **They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite God's signs in the watches of the night, while prostrating themselves.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"They Are Not All Alike": The Great Correction**

The very verse after the double-thunder of 112 inserts a clause that has governed Islamic interfaith ethics ever since: *laysū sawāʾ* — "they are not all alike." After the indictment — obstruction, concealment, fabrication, hostility — the Book stops itself and declines the slander of a single lump: those People of the Book through whom the allegations of verses 71–112 ran are a class; and *against* the class stands another — the un-swallowed: *min ahli al-kitābi ummatun qāʾimatun* — "among the People of the Book is an upright community." The phrase *ummatun qāʾimah* is dense: an ummah (community-character) marked by *qiyām* — standing posture — upright in conduct and, as the very next words unfold, upright in the night before God. The commentators identify its members with the luminous individual names the sīrah and tafsīr treasures: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his learned companions among the Madinan Jews who came to faith; the Negus of Abyssinia and the circle of righteous Christian priests and monks who wept at the recitation (5:83–85 — "when they hear what was sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of what they recognized of the truth; they say: Our Lord! We believe — so write us among the witnesses"); Jābir's accounts and others. And the great expositors (al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr) then generalize: verses 113–115 are a standing rule for *every age* — among the communities of prior revelation, any soul or company that *did not* bend the text, *did not* build on obstruction, came upright to God — these are covered by this clause of honor: *laysū sawāʾ*.

**The Portrait of the Upright: Recitation in the Night, in Sujūd**

Their portrait is painted with two strokes only, and the two suffice for a whole qism of piety: *yatlūna āyāti Allāhi ānāʾa al-layli wa hum yasjudūn* — "reciting God's signs through the watches of the night, while they prostrate themselves." (1) Reciting the *āyāt*: a life organized around the text: not as academic inventory (as their corrupters had, who knew the book "as they knew their sons" — 2:146 — and *did not* walk it); but as *tilāwah* — received reading, followed stream — the sign of the qāʾim: the text is *kept in view*. (2) *Ānāʾ al-layl* — through the hours and watches of night — with *wa hum yasjudūn* — while in prostration (the scholars differ whether it means literally awakening in prayer in the night's precincts or reciting through the positions of the night prayer; both amount to a known center of gravity): the dark hours reserved for God — the sunnah-medicine of the elect through all ages (the Book's own register of the elect through all ages: 32:16: "their sides forsake beds, calling upon their Lord in fear and hope"; 51:17–18: "they took but little sleep at night, and at dawn would seek forgiveness"; 17:79; 25:64; 73:1–7, where God tells His Messenger precisely why night-watch is central: *"indeed, the hours of night are mightier in impression and more upright in discourse"*).

The scene of their uprightness is thus God meeting them where obstruction meets no one: in the last watches, in private, on the forehead. It is the verse's double answer to pessimism about human religious integrity: the establishment may be corrupt to its marrow (v. 112) while lit lamps remain alive in its midst — upright souls recognizable not by their party-charts but by their *night-watch* and their *recitation*. Islam's own mystics and masters of the heart knew these two verses (113–115) as a *map of the saved remnant anywhere*: any person or community ever found under heaven with these exact marks — no bending of their received light; standing-worship in the evening depths; prostration's frequency — those, the verse sweeps under its rubric *ummah qāʾimah*, regardless of the sundering of the institutions over them.

**The Immediate Ethical Mandate: Fairness as Creed**

And for the Muslim reader the verse legislates a creedal *ʿadl* (fairness) with binding force: it is unbelief in practice to pronounce upon human groups what God has explicitly withheld; the healthy Islamic heart hates the *behavior* — kufr, obstruction, slander, fabrication — and refuses the ethnic shortcut. The Prophet ﷺ lived the rule: his sweetness to the decent among the People of the Book (his standing with the Negus — the man prayed over in absentia at his death: narrated by Jābir and others in al-Bukhārī 1333; Muslim 951 — the funeral prayer for the Negus), his denunciation of their wrongs; his marriage to Mariah; his trade with the Christian Waraqah's in-law's; his treaties with the Jews of Madinah until they broke them — all receives its scriptural footings right here: *laysū sawāʾ* — they are not all alike; and their qāʾimah is honored out loud in the Recitation, in God's own register, as the last best hope of every elder community in the world, and of ours.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:114

> **Who believe in God and the Last Day and enjoin right and forbid wrong and hasten unto good deeds. They are among the righteous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Working Charter of the Upright Remnant**

Verse 113 sketched their worship; verse 114 logs the rest of their business — and the inventory turns out to be precisely the charter the Book holds up for all believers: *yuʾminūna bi-Allāhi wa-l-yawmi al-ākhiri* — "they believe in God and the Last Day": the two anchoring certainties (God as Lord, the end as real) placed first. Then: *wa yaʾmurūna bi-l-maʿrūfi wa yanhawna ʿani al-munkar* — "and they enjoin right and forbid wrong": the very two public verbs by which verse 110 had defined the best community — the remnant's classification *inside* the saved few is by the same ministry: they are not pious recluses (though their night-watch is prayer-in-silence); in their own communities they were the callers — kings' and priests' prophets-without-offices — the believers under the Roman persecutions in Abyssinia; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām announcing from the minbar of the old synagogue the coming of the Prophet whose description he carried; the monks who, upon their first hearing of the Qur'an's delegations, "recognized it" (5:83). And then the verse adds the conjugation that separates sincerity from structure: *wa yusāriʿūna fī al-khayrāt* — "and they hasten unto good deeds" — *musāraʿah* from *surʿah* (speed): a positive *race* — the same verb-cluster and the same racing-energy the Book uses for aspirants of forgiveness at 3:133 (only verses ahead: "and hasten unto forgiveness from your Lord") and at 57:21 ("race toward forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden whose breadth is as the breadth of heaven and earth"): religion for them is not inertia but pursuit; the opportunities of goodness are *sought*, contested, *outrun toward* — a phrase that indicts every languorous piety: if good is approaching you and you never move, something has died.

**"They Are Among the Righteous": The Placement Clause**

And the verse completes its register of them with the inclusion that has settled forever the question of their rank before God: *wa ulāʾika mina al-ṣāliḥīn* — "and those are among the righteous." *Min* in the commentators' decisive reading here: *partitive* — among the righteous — meaning they are enrolled *within* the file of the ṣāliḥīn, not stepping outside a great one: upright souls of any prior community who believed uprightly and labored so — counted inside the same registry. The phrase partakes of all the chapter's stated doctrine about salvation through God's merciful classification (v. 15-17's muttaqīn, muḥsinīn; v. 107's whitened): righteousness is the title-file. And thus on the level of interfaith grammar the verse is remarkable for its simplicity: for the remnant, *no conversion of label was demanded* in this clause as a pre-condition (they *believed in God* — found, in the road of their intact prior light and night vigil, the final meeting with the Truth; and whenever the Prophet was placed before them, great numbers of the qāʾimah indeed followed into the visible umma — the Negus, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, Salmān's teachers along the road of his seeking). The two ethics the chapter repeats without fatigue: (1) God recognizes righteous souls wherever they stand; (2) light recognized calls to light: the qāʾimah is not a final resting category in history but an *expectant* one — leaping forth obediently whenever God's full presentation arrives, per v. 19's and v. 19-22's diagnoses of its opposite.

**The Verse as a Manifesto for Late Ages**

The final believer-readers of all ages find in 3:114 a triple comfort and a triple discipline: it declares that the world's visible religious establishments *do not exhaust* holiness: God keeps lights in obscure quarters, and He knows them *by very specific marks*: recitation-organized life, night-standing, prostration-frequency, God-and-Last-Day anchorage, *amr* and *nahy* ministry, and the racing stride toward any good that appears. The lists, note, contain *nothing* ecclesiastical: no ordination, no land, no numbers, no endorsements — only the marks a believer can himself pursue and verify tomorrow morning. That the chapter situates this *in its interfaith block* is itself the final lesson in Islamic diversity-economics: the ummah of Islam is the chapter's final home (v. 110); the qāʾimah — wherever it subsists — are *min al-ṣāliḥīn*; and the two files greet each other at the Return (v. 109) — one Lord receiving *all* His upright from every corner where they kept vigil in the dark, bent text or no.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:115

> **And whatever good they do, it shall not be denied them; and God knows the reverent.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Shall Not Be Denied": God's Guarantee Over Small Goodness**

After the detailed portrait of the upright remnant, the verse affixes the security-clause that protects every honor just bestowed: *wa mā yafʿalū min khayrin fa-lan yukfarūh* — "and whatever good they do, it shall not be denied them." The verb *kafara* appears here in its older, pre-theological sense — *denial by covering*, the denying of a thing's due (the Arabic idiom *kufr* of a favor = ingratitude, blotting out): *lan yukfarūhu* — God will not *cover over* what they did; no work gets swallowed; no overlooked kindness, no unseen prayer, no anonymous decency is *erased by awkward category*. The commentators loved the scope placed under *wa mā ... min khayrin*: the phrase is infinitely open — *whatever, of good, they do* — any deed qualifying as good under the measure of God's law: small or great; public or lonely; while among disbelieving neighbors (v. 113's remnant) or among believers.

**The Verse's Syntactic Theology**

Two structural assets of the sentence deserve notice. First, the *indefinite*: *mā yafʿalū* — whatever they do — God's books are not closed-scrolls of select merit-cities; they are comprehensive ledgers where nothing of the good is disqualified by *small size* (34:3 — "not the weight of an atom escapes Him in the heavens and on the earth"; 99:7–8 — "whosoever does an atom's weight of good shall see it; whosoever does an atom's weight of evil shall see it"). Second, the *passive-then-impersonal* guarantee: *fa-lan yukfarūhu* — it shall *not be denied them* — the divine commissioning: God names no intermediary: He is Himself the guarantor of the non-erasure. Then His closing identification: *wa Allāhu ʿalīmun bi-l-muttaqīn* — "and God knows the reverent" — addresses the anxiety that always follows guarantees of receipt: how does the counter know *whose* deeds counted? The answer stops the question: God *knows* — no clerical registry need file; class of counted deeds is *taqwā* — reverence — known fully only to Him. The verse thus seals verses 113–115's whole decompression with the two clauses of assurance: good is not denied; the doers are fully known: no remnant-member anywhere in history obscured by a fallen establishment has labored in a black hole: the Receiver accepts, identifies, stores, and returns (v. 109).

**The Hadith's Proof-Text at the Well**

The tradition has one of its sweetest anecdotes built precisely upon this verse's guarantee, recorded in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections: the Prophet ﷺ narrating of the earlier peoples the man journeying in burning thirst, who found a well, descended, drank, climbed out — and found a dog panting at the verge of death from thirst, eating moist earth for its dampness: he descended again, filled his shoe with water, clenched it in his teeth to climb, and gave the dog to drink:

> *"So God thanked him for it and forgave him." They said: O Messenger of God — is there reward for us in animals? He said: "In every moist liver (kulli kabidin raṭbah) there is a reward."* (al-Bukhārī 2466, 3321, 3467; Muslim 2244 — from Abū Hurayrah; in parallel versions the man is a sinner of the Children of Israel — and yet by one ghayr of good that "God thanked him for it" — *shakara Allāhu lahu* — and remitted his whole account)

The anecdote sums up verse 115's whole sociology: *one* good work of authentic size — weighed not by donor-title but by its truth before a Creator with whom all parties are *creatures* — can overturn an entire biography in God's audit. *God thanked him*: the language holds the final kindest inversion of all — the All-High thanking a thirsting man for shoe-water: the raḥmah of Raḥmān in a hadith's eight words.

For every reader, the rules of living this verse are straightforward and large: (1) do good *now*, where you are, with whatever offers: no field is too small for the Guarantee; (2) never allow the corruption of establishments *around* you to induce the calming of your own goodness — the remnant's honor is that while the market grows old they remained productive; (3) when you see good from unexpected quarters — outsiders, outsiders of outsiders — praise it, and learn it, for God credits it unerringly; and (4) fear *kufr* in its residual sense: deny no one his kindness, belittle no deed, hide no generosity — the sin of the obstructer-class was, at its root, exactly this: denying a good when it appeared (vv. 70–71); the salvation of the remnant was exactly this: refusing to deny theirs.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:116

> **Truly neither the wealth nor the children of those who disbelieve will avail them aught against God. They it is who are inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Pillows of False Security**

The chapter now turns its face from the remnant's hope to the security-systems of those who refused every call — and it names the two foundations upon which unbelief habitually rests its confidence: *inna alladhīna kafarū lan tughniya ʿanhum amwāluhum wa lā awlāduhum mina Allāhi shayʾan* — "as for those who disbelieve — never shall their wealth nor their children avail them aught against God." The two categories are exactly, and famously, the two front-banners of the ornament-selection of verse 14 — *min thumari al-dhahab wa-l-fiḍḍah... wa-l-mawāshī fī al-banīn* — property and sons: the things men relied upon in every age that God would be stayed, argued with, or compensated by them. The verse's verdict is comprehensive of *both*: the deepest commercial inventory (wealth) and the most primal dynastic instinct (children: one's living continuation, one's name-posterity — "wealth and children are the ornament of the life of this world" — 18:46) — and the availing-verb is set in the absolute: *lan tughniya... shayʾan* — "shall avail *nothing*," with *min Allāh* — against God: both words work the same refuting-grounds as verse 91 (an earthful of gold not accepted): *the "against" is settled already — against God there is no offsetting market*.

In the immediate polemical frame the verse closes the chapter's long assessment of the obstructionist class among the People of the Book who had, among their other boasts, assumed that their lineages from the prophets (v. 65's claims, 5:18's "we are the children of God and His beloved"), their treasuries, their properties, and their sons-continuities somehow constituted a collateral with heaven; the verse pronounces the whole ledger worthless outside the one compound account of faith. In the reflective universal frame it is one of the Book's reiteration-centers, ringing with 58:17 — *"their wealth and their children shall avail them nothing against God; those are the inhabitants of the Fire"* — and with the testimony of Noah's son (11:42–46) — the one prophet-child cited by the Book as *unrescued* by kinship itself ("he is not of your family; he is an unrighteous work") — and with that of Abū Lahab, the Prophet's own uncle, for whom all the wealth of Quraysh's seigneurs availed nothing (Sūrah 111) — and with the universal principle the Prophet ﷺ preached to his own family at the beginning — the hadith preserved from ʿĀʾishah and others:

> *"Save yourselves from the Fire! O people of Quraysh... I cannot avail you aught against God... O Fāṭimah daughter of Muḥammad, ask me of my property what you wish — I cannot avail you aught against God."* (al-Bukhārī 2753, 4771; Muslim 205–206)

— spoken at the advent of "and warn your nearest kin" (26:214), and repeated as the clinic of Islam's entire kinship-economics: *no one is availed by anyone else's anything — each soul's briefcase is its own faith-works*.

**"Inhabitants of the Fire" After Availment Fails**

The consequence-clause is stated in the chapter's exacted register: *wa ulāʾika aṣḥābu al-nāri hum fīhā khālidūn* — "and those are inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein" — *aṣḥāb*: claimants, owners-in-residence: the possessive after everything else has been dispossessed — the only thing they *own* at the end is residence in the Fire. The juxtaposition of the two classes in vv. 115–116 is intended as the Book's own mirror-construction: to the remnant — *whatever good they do is not denied*; to the disbelievers — *whatever masses they mass avails nothing*; to the remnant — *God knows the muttaqīn*; to the disbelievers — *they are the owners of the Fire, abiding*: two opposed laws of escrow, both simultaneous, both perfectly just.

**Why the Two Pillows Fail: A Meditation on Availment**

The meditation the commentators exercise here anchors the whole of Islamic ethics. Availing-quintessence (*tighnī*) is worth: nothing *avails* anyone between him and God except what *meets God's own currency*: that is īmān (v. 19: God's religion is *islām*), its twin-certainties (God and the Last Day — v. 114), and their fruit of right-living (v. 115). The wealth and children are, by contrast, *loans from Him* (v. 180 will claim the heavens-and-earth *inheritance* as God's) — a loan cannot be tendered as payment to the lender! The lender's own property in escrow cannot purchase exception from Him — the simple absurdity that makes ransom-culture ridiculous in God's sight. The believer therefore does not despise wealth or children; the chapter's heroes had both (Zachariah prayed for a son; the muttaqīn *spend* of their wealth); what he refuses is resting them between himself and his Lord as *shields*: hence the daily recital the sūrah recommends in its very next verses: hasten to the Garden wide as heavens and earth — by *spending* (v. 133–134) — the blessed opposite of hoarding-shield: the things of verse 14 and verse 116 *released*, not clung to, become ladders rather than pillows. The wisdom of every beatitude-narrative in the sīrah stands on this: souls at the end found their wealth and children worthless when they had kept them *as defenses*; found them multiplied when they had spent them *as paths*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:117

> **The parable of what they spend in this life of the world is that of a frigid wind that strikes the tillage of a people who have wronged themselves, destroying it. God wrongs them not, but themselves do they wrong.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Wind That Has Winter in It**

Having sealed the account of wealth that avails nothing (v. 116), the chapter displays *why* it avails nothing, in one of the Qur'an's far-reaching agricultural parables: *mathalu mā yunfiqūna fī hādhihi al-ḥayāti al-dunyā ka-mathali rīḥin fīhā ṣirrun aṣābat ḥartha qawmin ẓalamū anfusahum fa-ahlakath* — "the likeness of what they spend in this worldly life is the likeness of a wind in which there is biting frost; it strikes the tillage of a people who wronged themselves and destroys it." Every image-member carries weight. The spenders are assumed to be *spending* — this is not a parable of those who hoard but of those who give, outwardly munificent — yet their crop is destroyed. Why? The nature of the wind: a *rīḥ fīhā ṣirr* — wind carrying *ṣirr*: piercing, shriveling cold, the blast that reaches the field at the worst hour and converts green to withered black in one night. And the field's own description closes the circuit: *ḥartha qawmin ẓalamū anfusahum* — the tillage *of a people who wronged themselves*: destruction comes as *sentence*, not accident: the crop was vulnerable to exactly the frost it met because the owners had corrupted the ground itself. As the commentators note (the source commentary's synoptic exercise), the Qur'an deploys the wind in two opposite registers: destructive for unrooted works — here *cold*, at 2:266 *burning* (the garden struck by a fiery whirlwind after the owner mocks his poorer neighbor), at 14:18 deeds like *ashes blown by wind* on a stormy day (already ashes before the wind arrives — the outer force only reveals the inner condition); nourishing for rooted life — 7:57, 25:48, 30:46, 35:9: winds of mercy bearing clouds that revive dead earth. One element, two outcomes: what the wind *does* depends on what the field *is*. The disbeliever's charity is destroyed not by an external misfortune but by the impossibility of an act surviving when it was never planted in the soil of face-for-God: *no cold is kind to a crop that rotten-planted.*

**Why Give Without Faith? — The Disbeliever's Paradoxical Charity**

A psychological depth opens here that the verse quietly explores. Unbelievers *do* spend: the unbelieving philanthropists of history, the Quraysh who fed pilgrims and ransomed captives at costs that strained (their boasting poems tally the water and the bread), modern benefactors planting faculties, hospitals, fountains. If wealth avails nothing (v. 116), what was the spending? The Book's diagnosis, repeatedly: its end is *ḥayāt al-dunyā* — "in this worldly life," the very words of the verse (*fī hādhihi al-ḥayāti al-dunyā*): spent *for* world-life currency: reputation, gratitude-bonds, rank, memory after death, the internal glow of being one's own benefactor; and therefore *repaid in the same currency* — world-life pays its debts scrupulously: the towers stand, the monuments bear names. The ḥadīth of the three admitted first to the Fire takes the parable and drives it through every pious reader's chest:

> *A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and cast into the Fire... another who was killed in the cause of God... another a scholar... another to whom God gave wealth: it will be said: "Did I not make you wealthy?" He will say: "I spent on Your paths." It will be said: "You lie! you spent so that it would be said, 'He is generous' — and so it was said." Then he will be ordered carried to the Fire.* (Muslim 1905, at length, from Abū Hurayrah)

The frost on the crop is the very sentence "so it was said": every return already collected at the newspaper stand and the banquet; nothing left to forward to the one place where forwarding counts.

**"God Wrongs Them Not" — The Verdict's Jurisprudence of Mercy**

*Wa mā ẓalamahumu Allāhu wa lākin anfusahum yaẓlimūn* — "God wrongs them not, but themselves they wrong." The closing clause is one of the great recurring restatements of God's juridical innocence across the Qur'an (3:135's "wrong themselves"; 4:97; 9:70; 16:33; 29:40 — the same fairness)."Wrong" (*ẓulm*) is, in the exact sense, doing less than the claim requires; God gives these souls the thing itself — *not one act wipes less than what it is*: a dunyā-seeking act receives a dunyā-payment, complete and exact. Where the ẓulm lies is there, in their own hands: they sold the seed for less than they could have had for it: the same wealth spent at the same hour, *turned by one intention*, would have warranted the garden-wide-as-the-heavens (v. 133, seven verses ahead!). The two opposed ledgers of this very section then stand in perfect stillness before every reader: verse 115 — whatever good the remnant does is *never denied*; verse 117 — whatever the self-wronging spender spends is *never credited*: and the operational difference between "not denied" and "not credited" is *which God the coin was minted in the name of*. All that separates the believer's at-last *ibyaḍḍat wujūhuhum* (v. 107) from the spenders' frost-bitten field is a line of intention at the moment of spending — cheap to fix this morning; impossible to repair when the wind has already passed.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:118

> **O you who believe! Take not intimates apart from yourselves; they will not stint you in corruption. They wish you to suffer. Hatred has appeared from their mouths; yet what their breasts conceal is greater. We have indeed made clear the signs for you, were you to understand.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Inner Lining of the Garment: What Is a Biṭānah?**

The third movement's address opens (as all its conferral charges do) with "O you who believe" — but the object this time is not bond but *boundary*: *lā tattakhidhū biṭānatan min dūnikum* — "do not take as intimates those apart from yourselves." *Biṭānah* is the old sartorial word an Arabic listener could feel in his fingers: the *inner lining* of a garment — the layer that lies directly against the skin, that gathers the body's oils and its unbroadcast scents, that is worn *inside*, where no eye measures it. By extension the biṭānah of a person is the staff-of-confidence: the privy counselors to whom one opens the ledgers of the soul — al-Ṭabarī glosses directly: those to whom one tells one's *secrets* (asrār). God is thus mapping a leadership-discipline: the believer is commanded to *reserve the layer next to his skin* — the inner-court position — for those who share his inner commitment. The wisdom is self-demonstrating in the very clauses that follow: *lā ya'lūnakum khabālā* — "they do not stint you in corruption": with you in corruption-*khabāl* (harm, ruin) they are *not miserly* — they pour; *waddū mā ʿanittum* — "they wish you suffer": the inward *wish* (*wadd* — they would love it) is named outright: affliction you is their delight; and the final diagnostic pair: *qad badati al-baghḍāʾu min afwāhihim wa mā tukhfī ṣudūruhum akbar* — "hatred has appeared *from their mouths* — and what their breasts conceal is *greater*." Note the forensic grammar: God's specification of evidence runs *mouth-first* — visible speech — because speech can at least be audited; and then closes with the dimension you can *not* audit, and with its size-comparison: *greater*. The breast-concealed is thus not presented as a murmuration but as the main mass — the visible words of coldness are icebergs' tips.

**The Ruling's Real Reach: Confidence-Estate, Not Friendship**

The commentators (Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī) fix the prohibition's center of gravity: the verse does not forbid friendship, trade, hospitality, kindness, neighborliness — the sīrah is furnished with all of these between the Prophet ﷺ and decent people of every community — it is forbidding the *insertion of adversarial outsiders into the state's trust functions*. In the concrete reading: in matters of weight — writing contracts, carrying significant dispatches, holding the confidences of the community's strategy — one should not rely on those whose subterranean wishes run against you. Al-Qurṭubī writing in Córdoba centuries later bemoans the state of his own day — Muslims employing Jews and Christians as scribes and secretaries — and his grief is instructive precisely as an application log: the verse was never dead text; every age of Muslim civilization audited its inner lining. The prohibition-class is, of course, not about ethnicity: *min dūnikum* — "apart from yourselves" — the antonym is fidelity, not blood; the same Book forbids taking the treacherous *Muslim* as confidant (60:1 commands against taking God's enemies as friends even by affection; 58:22 describes those who do not support enemies "even though they be their fathers or their sons"), and the righteous non-Muslim ally was modeled in the Prophet's own career: he trusted ʿAbd Allāh ibn Urayqiṭ, a pagan of known reliability, as guide on the Hijrah — the most secret-and-dangerous dispatch of all, yet measured case by case: the rule is *wise caution*, not blanket suspicion.

**"Made Clear for You, Were You to Understand": The Intellect as Watchman**

The seal — *qad bayyanā lakumu al-āyāti in kuntum taʿqilūn* — "We have made the signs clear for you if only you would understand" — locates the safeguard at exactly the right altitude: God does not promise to *remove* disguised haters; He discloses enough signs to make their detection *an exercise of intellect* — *ʿaql*. The believer's safeguard is intelligence grown discerning by scripture: watch words (mouths leak), watch wishes (suffering-measured delight shows at calamity — v. 120), watch pattern-congregations (who gathers behind whom in crisis). And the tradition couches the matter at its deepest, most existential floor — from the reported hadith preserved in the commentary lore:

> *"No prophet has God sent, nor any vicegerent appointed, save that he had two intimates: one enjoining and encouraging the good, and one enjoining and encouraging evil. And the protected is the one whom God protects."* (transmitted as explanation of the verse in the tafsīr literature; cf. al-Ṭabarī on 3:118, and in substance the report of two companions al-Bukhārī preserves from Abū Saʿīd and Abū Hurayrah: *"God has not sent any prophet who did not have two classes of companions..."* — narrated in various wordings)

The final clause is the ummah's every working prayer: protection is *willed gift*: *al-maʿṣūm man ʿaṣamahu Allāh* — and the chapter's own rope already lies ready in the reading: the rope of God jamīʿan (v. 103), the refusal of any *biṭānah* woven from fibers other than His: the inner lining must be *muslim* — for everything at its contact will be tasted, in time, by your skin.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:119

> **Lo! You are the ones who love them, while they love you not, though you believe in the Book entire. And when they meet you they say, "We believe," but when they are alone they bite their fingers at you from rage. Say, "Die in your rage!" Truly God knows what lies within breasts.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The One-Way Love: A Diagram of Asymmetry**

The boundary set in verse 118 is explicated now by describing the *painful asymmetry* it protects against: *hā antum ulāʾi tuḥibbūnahum wa lā yuḥibbūnakum* — "lo — you are the ones! You love them, and they do not love you." The opening *hā antum ulāʾ* is the Qur'an's dramatic pointing-finger: *there — that's you*: the look in the mirror that names the phenomenon: the open-faced believer's native benevolence runs head-first into the concealed adversary's reserve. The commentators (al-Rāzī's listings are exact) unbind the three readings of the asymmetry, and each is a present observation in any mixed society: (1) *you love them in Islam* — treat them with the believing heart's native good-will, wish them no harm — while they do not reciprocate even the wish-of-good; (2) *you love that they become Muslim* — your desire for them is the best thing that could happen to a soul — while theirs for you is your ruin: unbelief; (3) *you wish they be spared distress* — harm-repelled — while they wish you fall into affliction — harm-wished. The asymmetry is *total*: not even the object of the love is the same object; you love *them*; they love *your absence*.

And God names the unfathomable charity of the believer's own constitution: *wa tuʾminūna bi-l-kitābi kullih* — "while you believe in the Book, all of it": Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī gloss the beautiful ownness of the phrase: the Muslims believe in *the whole Book* — the scriptures sent before their own *included* — affirming — not requiring the prior communities' written members to be frauds, not needing the prior prophets to be false, not erecting their Islam upon the nullity of every antecedent light — while the obstructing classes of Ahl al-Kitāb believed only selectively (v. 72's concession; 2:85's "do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?"). Belief in the Book entire pours into the believer's chest the largeness that runs ahead of cases: the believer's heart is structured as *impossible to make narrow*: he loves by religion's own protocol. But love's traffic is slit by the unfair other side: professing and concealing.

**The Meeting and the Solitude — and the Finger-Biting**

*Wa idhā laqūkum qālū āmannā wa idhā khalaw ʿaḍḍū ʿalaykumu al-anāmila mina al-ghayẓ* — "when they meet you, they say, 'We believe'; when they are apart, they bite the fingers at you from rage." The double register has twins throughout (2:14: "when they meet those who believe they say, 'We believe,' and when they are apart with their satans they say, 'We are with you'"; 2:76; 5:41). The detail of *ʿaḍḍ al-anāmil* — biting the literal tips of their fingers — is the verse's unforgettable image of impotent rage: fury with no discharge channel: anger that cannot even *work* in the open any more, reduced to self-mutilation; the physical contract of rage with helplessness across the history of every man whose hatred outgrew his power. The commentators note: it is the rage of the recognition-failed: they bite not from strength but because *your very flourishing* — which begins to confirm a faith they refuse — drives their frustration off the chart: malady well described by the older Book's own proverb ("he that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" — Prov 16:32) — they rule nothing, and bite what is within reach: their own hands.

**"Say: Die in Your Rage" — The Mandate to Flourish**

The commanded riposte — *qul mūtū bi-ghayẓikum* — "say: die in your rage" — is among the chapter's most quoted turns, and al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī pre-empt its misreading: not a curse-wish of death but a *formula of unchangeability*: your rage is incurable; your hatred shall reach no terminus of satisfaction — *therefore die with it*, then, for we shall not stop the flourishing that feeds it: the Prophet's ﷺ answer to hatred was never de-escalation into disappearance but *continued visible thriving* — the best of all replies: Islam's health itself. The final clause stamps the case before the Judge that knows: *inna Allāha ʿalīmun bi-dhāti al-ṣudūr* — "truly God has knowledge of what lies within the breasts": the last instance of the chapter's running signature (vv. 29, 119, and later 154's "God knows what is in the breasts"): concealment is of zero probative value in the true court; the one decrees judgment on files the tongue has never written. The believer who internalizes 3:119 is treated for two chronic pains at once: (1) the grief of non-reciprocity — his love, God's own requirement, spent on pockets that hold nothing: answered: God knows the pockets within and credits the love at its Sender; (2) the temptation toward symmetry — the withdrawing of benevolence once love is unreturned: answered: the one-sided love is itself his covenant: he loves them *before* God — the asymmetry is his credential: "even though ye have been deceived in your trust," as the Prophet's code runs, your conduct remains yours. Love without reciprocity is, to God, the most valuable love on His books.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:120

> **If good befalls you, it vexes them, and if evil befalls you, they rejoice in it. But if you are patient and reverent, their plot will not harm you in the least. Truly God encompasses what they do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Emotional Ledger of the Adversary**

The chapter closes its exposure-triptych (vv. 118–119–120) with the final clinical finding: the enemy's *feelings at your fortunes*: *in tamsaskum ḥasanatun tasuʾhum, wa in tuṣibkum sayyiʾatun yafraḥū bihā* — "if good touches you, it vexes them; and if evil befalls you, they rejoice in it." The two verbs are as opposite as the fortunes: *tasuʾhum* (it vexes them) — *suʾ*: your good arrives at their chest as pain; and *yafraḥū* (they rejoice) — your harm arrives as celebration. Ibn Kathīr's comment cuts to the diagnosis: joy at another's suffering — *schadenfreude* in the one word the modern languages have needed to borrow — is among the severest indices of enmity, severer than competition or even resisted interest; it signifies that the adversary's own welfare is now *indexed* to your collapse: the loss-adjacent joy of those for whom your calamity *is* their gain. Nothing is left in their ledger that could honor you: you can neither do well (it wounds them) nor amiss (it delights them). The commentaries cross-refer the litany's canonical twin — Moses' prayer at his terrible hour: *"My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for you are the most merciful of the merciful... and do not set the enemies as those who gloat over us"* (*wa lā tushmit binā al-aʿdāʾ* — 7:150, in the reading): the admitted saints of God's road all asked to be spared the spotlight of adversarial glee. The moral the chapter means to leave on the believers' table is ripening: you cannot *earn* the adversaries' affection by either excellence or distress; your diplomacy with their envy is a closed door; hence — pivot — the verse supplies the only responsive field that remains.

**"If You Are Patient and Reverent": The Two-Pillar Immunity Clause**

*Wa in taṣbirū wa tattaqū lā yaḍurrukum kayduhum shayʾā* — "and if you are patient and reverent, their plot shall not harm you in the least." Two conditions are annexed to the immunity warranty, and the order is surgical:

**First: *ṣabr* — patience.** The word carries here its full classical range: not passive waiting but *steadfastness under fire* — constancy in doing right while wrong is done; the refusal to be dislodged from one's own program by the adversary's emotions. The vexer and the rejoicer are most powerless before *unmovedness*: their strategy requires your psychological reaction, and patience is precisely the refusal to give it: patience cancels their only product. The Prophet ﷺ summed the stance in his general constitution of the believer: *"Amazing is the affair of the believer! all of his affair is good — and that is for no one but the believer: if prosperity reaches him he is grateful, and it is good for him; and if adversity strikes him he is patient, and it is good for him."* (Muslim 2999 — the total inversion of the adversary's ledger: *every* fortune, good or ill, *yields good* to the person so related to God.)

**Second: *taqwā* — reverence.** The shield-of-God-consciousness that has been the chapter's principal refrain (v. 15; v. 76; v. 102): the discipline of remaining within God's bounds *even when wronged* — not answering slander with slander, conspiracy with conspiracy, hatred with hatred: taqwā fences the believer inside the territory in which God's warranties run. Al-Ṭabarī's canonical gloss — keeping God's command, avoiding His prohibition — becomes operational: the plot-dueling temptation is the trap; escape it and the warranty pays out: *lā yaḍurrukum kayduhum shayʾan* — no harm *in the least*: the same clause-scale as verse 111's *adhā*: annoyance reachable; ruin unreachable. Plot (*kayd*) admits the foe's scheming is real and *architectural* — planned, engineered, budgeted; and the answer to architecture is not better architecture but a life *beyond the jurisdiction of architecture*: domiciled in God.

**"Truly God Encompasses What They Do"**

The sealer — *inna Allāha bi-mā yaʿmalūna muḥīṭ* — "truly God encompasses all they do" — is the last word of the whole triptych. *Muḥīṭ* — encompassing, surrounding on all sides — the same word the Book uses of the *muster* of hell (2:126's-inclusive family) turned here to God's super-encirclement of the plotters: their machinations are conducted *inside* His comprehensive grasp: every plot is transmitted as it is born; every sealed room they gather in has God's hearing as the fourth wall. The believers' security thus rests not on intelligence-gathering — the verse nowhere instructs them to infiltrate or obsessively diagnose — but on *God's environments*: the believer suffices with two disciplines (patience, reverence); the surveillance is assigned upwards. The triptych's complete teaching can now be summarized in the three lines every Muslim community memorized over the centuries: (1) line your intimacy with your own kind (v. 118); (2) expect no love in return, yet love anyway; refuse symmetry (v. 119); (3) under vexation and glee, be patient and reverent — their plots are bounded, and their bounded world sits inside the All-Encompassing's (v. 120). The next movement begins, fittingly, with the one historical theater where all three disciplines were tested in the same morning: Uḥud.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:121

> **And remember when thou didst leave thy household at daybreak to assign the believers their positions for the battle. And God is Hearing, Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Counsel-Tent to Battle-Line: The Morning the Chapter Turns Military**

The sūrah now enters its celebrated narrative heart — the literature of Uḥud, the greatest single sustained historical sequence in the Qur'an outside the Baṭū of Mary — and its first scene is deliberately small and human: the Prophet ﷺ *leaving his house at dawn*: *wa idh ghadawta min ahlika tubawwiʾu al-muʾminīna maqāʿida lil-qitāl* — "and when you left your household at daybreak to seat the believers at their posts for the battle." Every word is chosen with narrative tenderness: *ghadawta* — you set out early, in the ghuduw — the cool first hour; *min ahlika* — from *your household*, from family-peace, the world of warm thresholds; *tubawwiʾu* — you *assign seats* — the verb of installing each man at his station; *maqāʿida lil-qitāl* — sitting-places for fight: battle-order conceived as a liturgy: stations assigned like prayer-rows. The gentle dawn-scene is the Book's way of saying: the epic begins in the quotidian — a rising, a parting from family, a walk through the sleeping city.

The occasion's frame is famous history. Uḥud was fought in Shawwāl of year 3 (March 625), almost exactly a year after Badr: Quraysh, smarting from the most humiliating defeat in their memory — seventy of their nobles dead and seventy captured, at the hands of a fraction of their number — assembled a three-thousand-strong army, with their women riding to spur vengeance (Hind bint ʿUtbah at their head), and set out against Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ consulted the community — the full *shūrā* the sīrah reports — and two counsels divided them: the elders and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy preferred defense from within the city's fortress-like quarter-network; the young men, whose blood Badr had made bold, pleaded to go out and meet the enemy in the field, lest Quraysh write of their hiding. The Prophet inclined at first toward the city's plan; the enthusiasm of the youth tipped the consultation; and he went into his house and came out armored — the narrative's famous beat — whereupon, when the second thoughts of some began ("we pressed him against his wish"), he answered with the compound maxim that became a fixture of Muslim civic ethics:

> *"It is not right for a prophet, once he has put on his armor, to take it off until God has judged between him and his enemies."* (from the Uḥud narratives in al-Bukhārī 2906–2922 and the sīrah literature)

Decisiveness after consultation; then firmness after decision — a whole theory of communal leadership in three moves of one morning.

**The Withdrawal of Ibn Ubayy**

Between house and field the great stress-fracture of the army occurred: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl — the man who had been on the verge of Madinah's kingship before the Prophet came, whom the sīrah ever after names the leader of the hypocrite party — withdrew with roughly a third of the force, about three hundred of the thousand, ostensibly out of anger that his council to remain in the city had not prevailed. The verses ahead will treat him in detail (v. 154's interior monologue, vv. 166–168's excuses); here the narrative passes over him in silence — as though to say: the army that marched was already *purified* by the withdrawal, the commentators observe: the numerically reduced seven hundred were a truer army than the thousand had been. God's method of readiness often runs through shrinkage first — the same arithmetic as Badr's three hundred against the thousand, the same as Gideon's lapping waters (in the older scripture, Judges 7, whose story the Qur'an's own Saul-tale re-tells at 2:249): *the winnowing before the trial is mercy, not loss*.

**"To Assign Their Positions": The Archers' Hill**

The jurisdiction of *maqāʿid* was, in the battle's topography, the celebrated mount of the archers — the little hill of ʿAynayn (later called, grimly, the hill of the archers): the Prophet stationed fifty bowmen there with their commander ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jubayr and bound them with the order whose middle hours would echo across every reading of the sūrah for fourteen centuries:

> *"Keep the cavalry off us with your arrows; let them not come upon us from our rear. Whether we are victorious or defeated — do not leave your posts, even if you see birds carrying men away."* (al-Bukhārī 3039, 4043; Muslim 2415 — from the Uḥud reports of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib and others)

No-slip orders — *no matter what transpires* — because the hill was the army's exposure-silicone: as long as it held, the Muslim rear was closed. The verse's quiet word *maqāʿid* — sitting-places — thus compresses the entire military tragedy to come: the failure-to-hold of assigned sitting-places will be, within hours, the hinge of the battle (vv. 152-155 will narrate it sternly and then forgive it). And the verse seals with the two names that already audit every stationed heart: *wa Allāhu samīʿun ʿalīm* — "and God is Hearing, Knowing": the consultation heard, the motives weighed, the whisperings of morning — all already in the two registers before a single station was taken. The reader thus walks into the Uḥud sequence with both lessons preloaded: God's battle preparations are run through *shūrā* (community) and *tawakkul* (God-heardness); and the map of the field is mostly the map of the *heart* — a theme the whole sequence will prove at terrible cost and at greater mercy.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:122

> **Remember when two companies among you were on the verge of losing heart, though God was their Protector. And in God let the believers trust.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Clans at the Edge of Turning Back**

Before the battle's blows begin, the Book opens its first trial-report — and it chooses, with pastoral care, not to begin with the cowardice of enemies or the betrayal of hypocrites, but with the near-faltering of *godly clans within the faithful army itself*: *idh hammat ṭāʾifatāni minkum an tafshalā* — "when two companies among you were on the verge of losing heart" — *wa Allāhu waliyyuhumā* — "though God was their Protector." The two parties are named by the whole tafsīr tradition (Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī): Banū Salimah of the Khazraj and Banū Ḥārithah of the Aws — the two mother-tribes of Madinah, the joined hearts of verse 103. Ibn Ubayy's withdrawal with a third of the army had just passed in front of them; a desertion that size, in the hour before engagement, was a psychic event of the first magnitude: the mind's arithmetic — seven hundred against three thousand — reasserted its terror, and the reports say the two clans discussed turning back after him. *Ḥamma* ("was on the verge," "entertained the intent") is itself carefully weighed: the commentators dwell on it — the Qur'an records not a deed but a *wavering*, and it records the wavering not to shame but to comfort: faltering in the heart, unconsummated, is real, is human, was felt by men of undoubted faith — and is immediately cheered by the next five words.

**"Though God Was Their Protector": Grammar's Mercy**

The syntax has been lovingly parsed by al-Rāzī and others: *wa Allāhu waliyyuhumā* — the wavering clause interrupted by the protective clause — and the whole point is the *order*: God mentions His protection *before* He mentions any act of theirs: whether read "though God was their Protector" (walāyah as ground upon which the faltering was ultimately reversed), or "and God is their Protector" (walāyah as sheer gift *over* their faltering — mercy shown despite the inner equivocation, al-Rāzī's reading), the structure is identical in tenor: the two clans' standing does not derive from the perfection of their nerves; it derives from God's being *their wali*. And the wavering itself was thus treated by God the way the sūrah has just taught us to treat the emotional waverings of contested friendship (v. 119's asymmetry): by *covering* it — the story is recorded in revelation, yes, but with noteworthy gentleness: the verse says "on the verge," never "they faltered"; it names them by *collective* (two companies), never by finger-pointing roll; and it seals the account not with rebuke but with prescription for the whole community of believers in all later days:

*Wa ʿalā Allāhi fa-l-yatawakkali al-muʾminūn* — "and in God let the believers trust."

**Tawakkul at the Edge of Panic: The Prescription for All Future Vacillators**

The closing clause is the general law appended to the particular history: since the brave men of Khazraj and Aws wavered, every believer since — every council before an undertaking, every soul at the margin of an entrance into danger or sacrifice — will feel the *hamma*: the almost-decision to retire. The sūrah's own therapy is engraved right here: (1) *the near-fall is not the fall*: God's coverage of the two clans proves that fear-visited hearts are *not yet* charged to account — 2:286's foundational pardon: "our Lord, take us not to task if we forget or err," and the Prophet's report: *"God has pardoned my community the errors, the forgettings — and what their souls prompt them with, as long as they do not act"*: in the reading of the hadith of the inner conversation: *"God has forgiven my community what their souls whisper to themselves, so long as they do not speak or act" —* *"inna Allāha tajāwaza ʿan ummatī mā ḥaddathat bihi anfusahā"* (al-Bukhārī 6664; Muslim 127, from Abū Hurayrah and Ibn ʿAbbās); (2) *the tonic for the hamma is the walāyah*: remembering *you have a Wali* — the first lesson named at Uḥud's very threshold, in the battle's own liturgy of fear-management: "say to them" — the sūrah's other missile of courage comes at v. 173: *"those to whom men said: 'the people have gathered against you — fear them!' — yet it increased them in faith, and they said: 'God is sufficient for us, and excellent is the Trustee!'"* — the alchemy that turns gathering-enemies into gathered-courage; and (3) the final two clauses actually *instruct the exact casting of the verse's own grammar*: look again — "two companies were on the verge of losing heart, *though God was their Protector*; *and in God let the believers trust.*" The believing community is told to *map the sentence forwards*: my wavering-frame stands exactly where theirs stood; my Wali is the same Wali; so my trust is appointed the same as theirs — *in God let the believers trust*: the one Great Trust that, under the walls of any Uḥud, holds.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:123

> **God certainly helped you at Badr, when you were lowly. So reverence God, that haply you may give thanks.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Before Uḥud's Verdict, Badr's Memory**

The narrative strategy is transparent pastoral care: on the eve of analyzing Uḥud's wounds and waverings, God first sets before the army the memory of the victory they could not humanly have earned: *wa la-qad naṣarakumu Allāhu bi-Badrin wa antum adhillah* — "and God indeed helped you at Badr, while you were lowly." *Adhillah* — lowly, small, humbled in resource — is the condition-word that turns the memory into a precedent: on the 17th of Ramaḍān, year 2, three hundred and thirteen men, mostly on foot, two horses among them, seventy-odd camels ridden in turns, swords short and leather harness scarce, met the armored thousand of Quraysh by the water-wells of Badr — *and the help of God fell*; the leaders of unbelief who had spent a decade tormenting the believers by the Kaʾba were within three hours dead in the dry pit of the battlefield. *Lowly* — you were precisely *adhillah* and you won: the completion of the verse's implied logic is immediate: Uḥud's odds (seven hundred against three thousand) are *less* lopsided than Badr's; the One who helped then is unchanged. The remembrance thus functions as God's own fear-medication — issued before the combat begins rather than after its failure: memorize the *pattern* while calm, to retrieve it under fire.

**Badr in the Book's Own Register**

The fuller treatment of Badr lives at Sūrah al-Anfāl (8:5–19), whose own verses the commentators recall here — the night rain that firmed sand, the smallness made *in the eyes* of each army of the other ("He showed them to you in your eyes as few, and made you few in their eyes" — 8:44), the thousand angels descending rank after rank (8:9), the Prophet's ﷺ supplication under the tree — *"O God, accomplish for me what You promised me! O God, if this small band is destroyed, You will never be worshiped on this earth!"* — with Abū Bakr holding his shoulders, saying, *Enough, O Messenger of God, He shall surely fulfill what He promised you* (Muslim 1763, from ʿUmar); and the verdict-sentence, which deserves to be set directly beside 3:123 as its twin exposition:

> *"And God already helped you at Badr, when you were lowly (adhillah); so reverence God, that haply you may give thanks."* — the parallel runs, saw-Keen, through 3:123's own wording; with 8:26's twin: *"And remember when you were few, deemed weak on the earth, fearing that men would snatch you away — and He lodged you, and helped you with His victory, and provided you with good things, that haply you may give thanks."*

**"Reverence... Thanks": The Two Installments Owed on Past Victories**

The verse's own prescription is two verbs in series: *fa-ttaqū Allāha laʿallakum tashkurūn* — "so reverence God, that haply you may thank." Taqwā shield-consciousness comes first, gratitude as its hope-*laʿalla* — the assembly is fixed: thankfulness is not sentiment-generated but *conduct-generated*: the man who keeps the limits after God's help becomes, daily, the "thanker." The chapter's economy of memory is thereby full: at verse 103 gratitude for joined hearts; here gratitude for joined victory — and in every age the ummah's deepest tactical reserve is neither manpower nor matériel but *exactly what the verse models*: the verified record of God's past interventions, kept stocked in liturgy and chronicle. The Prophet ﷺ himself visited the field of Badr on later journeys and marked where each man fell — men by name; the memory site became the mental armory. So with every believer's own ledger: anyone who has lived a decade with God owns a *private Badr* — some hour when help arrived from outside every calculation; sūrah 3's instruction is: keep it in the refer of your thought, *before* the tables turn, and at the new test take station on its precedent — *the God of Badr is in the field again*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:124

> **Remember when thou saidst unto the believers, "Is it not enough for you that your Lord should support you with three thousand angels sent down?"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reassurance Spoken Aloud**

The remembrance now quotes the Prophet's own words of encouragement on the field: *idh taqūlu lil-muʾminīna a-lan yakfiyakum an yumiddakum rabbukum bi-thalāthati ālāfin mina al-malāʾikati munzalīn* — "when you said to the believers: will it not suffice you that your Lord should reinforce you with three thousand angels, sent down?" The commentators (al-Rāzī catalogues the debate) divide over whether the words belong to Badr or to Uḥud: if to Badr, the verse continues the memory of verse 123 ("when you were lowly... *when* you said to the believers"); if to Uḥud, it continues verse 121 ("when you left your household... *when* you said"). The two readings are not rivals but twins, and the tradition received both: angelic reinforcement is the Qur'an's settled doctrine for Badr (8:9 — "when you sought succor from your Lord, and He answered you: I am reinforcing you with a thousand angels, rank upon rank"), while the Uḥud-frame of the verse's own *promise-rise* in 3:125 belongs most naturally to the Uḥud dawn, where the words were timely against the new odds. The chiasmus of the two campaigns — Badr's delivered help; Uḥud's offered help — is itself the centerpiece of the sequence's teaching, as verse 125 will unlock.

**"Is It Not Enough for You?" — The Question That Makes Heaven's Cavalry Visible**

The Prophet's syntax is the pedagogy of rhetorical question: *a-lan yakfiyakum* — "is it *not sufficient* for you?" — *sufficiency* floating between heaven and earth in a single ask: believers' panic is recalibrated by being made to *rank* their assets: do you have — here he counts it — three *thousand* angels, *munzalīn*: sent down, descending, heaven's reserves committed to your file? In the economies of God's help, arithmetic reverses: man-counts lose their causal place; *angel*-counts are introduced precisely to dissolve the tyranny of human surveillance: the visible balance sheet is a lie; the invisible ledger is the truth. Badr had already demonstrated the literal dimension — a thousand angels (or three thousand per these narratives of remembrance) — and our hadith-literature keeps the marks of their presence: heads of enemy champions falling before swords visibly struck (in the narrative of 8:17: "you did not slay them, but God slew them; and thou threwest not when thou threwest, but God threw"); mysterious horsemen, white-turbaned, seen where no men had stood; 8:12's angelic mandate: *"I am with you — so make firm those who believe; I shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve"*. Whether the angels fought at Uḥud or "only" steadied hearts (the majority classical view: at Uḥud their presence was moral reinforcement, per Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī), the doctrine of a cosmos in which God's *munazzal* ranks accompany His believing servants is integral: *"He it is Who sends down serenity (sakīnah) into the hearts of the believers"* (48:4); *"then God sent down His serenity upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down hosts you did not see"* (9:26 — of Ḥunayn): the hosts are always available; what varies is the *condition* that summons them.

**"Sent Down" and the Believer's Gaze**

The word *munzalīn* holds a final sweetness: heaven *de-scends* to help: the vertical is the direction of assistance — every Muslim's tree-chart of hope is oriented upward: from the earth, cool discretion; from heaven, columns. The verse trains the community's eyes: look up, not around. In every community-struggle since, the register remains open to the same "is it not enough": sufficiency-claim placed on God's own commitment — *yumiddakum rabbukum* — *your Lord will reinforce you*: the continuous future-tense: reinforcement is *habit* of the Lordship. The Prophet's ﷺ own teaching on remembering God's hosts under distress was corned into his most famous dua-shaped missile at Uḥud itself — and, after the battle, heaven's voice returned the compliment in the chapter's own records: *"God has helped you at Badr...'* (v. 123); *"is it not enough...three thousand?"* (v. 124); and *next* the prophecy-clause forward into the future — verse 125's *balā* — "yea — verily": if you are patient and reverent... five thousand marked ones — which the next verse unveils.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:125

> **Yea, if you are patient and reverent, and they come at you immediately, your Lord will support you with five thousand angels bearing marks.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Balā" — The Particle That Upgrades the Offer**

The verse opens on a tiny word of great transactions: *balā* — "yea — verily": Arabic's particle of *affirmative escalation*, the utterance by which a proposition is not merely granted but advanced. Three thousand sufficed — "is it not enough for you?" (v. 124); now comes *balā*: indeed — *more*: *in taṣbirū wa tattaqū wa yaʾtūkum min fawrihim hādhā yumdidkum rabbukum bi-khamsati ālāfin mina al-malāʾikati musawwimīn* — "if you are patient and reverent, and they come upon you instantly [in this fury of theirs], your Lord shall reinforce you with five thousand angels, bearing marks." The escalation of the number — three to five thousand — is matched to the escalation of the trial: *min fawrihim hādhā* — "immediately, on the boil of this very charge of theirs*": the *fawr* is the boil-over, the eruption of the attacked opponent's instant rage — and the promise scales the reinforcements to exactly the speed of the threat: your enemies' swiftness is *multiplied back* by reinforcement more than proportionate. And the angels' descriptor — *musawwimīn* — "bearing marks" (the commentators explore the semantic field: *taswīm* as marking — emblazoned, badged, distinguishable — or deploying mounts sometimes: the angels come *insignia'd*, identifiable by banners and mounts: heaven's hosts not sent anonymously but *marked as sent* — the classical accounts preserve the white turbans of Badr's angelic cavalry, and the signal-lines of the years' sightings) — a signature-line upon which the community's conviction rests: God's help is never anonymous mercy; when He sends, the help is *declared*.

**The Two Conditions: Ṣabr and Taqwā as Summons-Protocol**

The miracle-offer is locked to two keys, and the lock is the verse's deepest law: *in taṣbirū wa tattaqū* — "if you are patient and reverent." The two terms we have been tracking through the chapter (v. 120's exact pairing, already the immunity-clause) return in battle-dress: (1) *patience* — the holding of assigned stations and of battle-order; the refusal to bolt or break in panic and *the refusal to break discipline for spoils* — both forms of "standing" that Uḥud's morning was about to test, one held (the seven hundred in their files) and one, for one hour, compromised (a portion of the archers); (2) *taqwā* — God-consciousness under fire: obedience of command, integrity of purpose, no-transgression limits even in war. The majority of the commentators (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī) reckon, on the terms of the condition itself, the battle's *outcome*: when the key slipped from the lock — when positions were left before orders released them — the flow of promise was suspended: the five-thousand offer was real; the trigger was *real*; the whole trial-ledger of vv. 152–154 records precisely the dialectic of unlocked-document: offer-annexed-to-discipline, discipline broken, offer pulled — and then *God's greater mercy unveiled over the breach* — v. 152's "He forgave you," delivered in its place. The discipleship-lesson is immortal: heaven's offers are conditional, and conditions are *mercies*: the conditions alone, absorbed by a community, are already victory — *patience and reverence constitute the interior five thousand*: had every man of the seven hundred merely stood and feared God, the angels' count would have been redundancy.

**The Verse's Perpetual Tender**

Read without the battlefield, 3:125 remains among the great open-door promises of Scripture: whenever a band of God's servants meets a *fawr* — any instant-boiling onrushing — and answers with the two keys, the Lord's *yumdidkum* runs: reinforcement proportional out of all visible counting, *marked* to their case. Chapter 33 will say it again word-for-word at the Trench — *"O you who believe! remember God's blessing upon you when hosts came against you, and We sent against them a wind and hosts you did not see"* (33:9) — because the offer is standing. The two keys cost nothing, are open to the poorest believer as to princes — and cost everything, for ṣabr and taqwā are the whole practical religion in two words. That is why the chapter, whose final v. 200 will later close the whole sūrah with the congregation-call of *ṣbirū* (hold fast in patience!), allows no one to mistake the sequence: God's hosts *follow* His conditions; the believer does not sit waiting for hosts to exempt him from effort; he stands at the keys, and the doors of the unseen unlock behind him.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:126

> **God made it not save as a glad tiding for you, and that your hearts may repose thereby—and there is no victory save from God, the Mighty, the Wise—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Angels as Envelope — Not Engine**

The verse's theology is the great middle-way correction to all the excited arithmetic just offered: *wa mā jaʿalahu Allāhu illā bushrā lakum* — "God did not make it [the reinforcement and its promise]" — *illā bushrā* — "anything except *glad tidings* for you" — *wa li-taṭmaʾinna qulūbukum bih* — "and that your hearts might repose thereby." The angels, the numbers, the banners — God identifies the entire apparatus as *bushrā*: good-news-mail: its primary value is not that three-thousand-no-five-thousand horsemen independently win battles; its value is that the *believers receive the message*: the unseen is committed; you are not abandoned; your standing is witnessed from above; and thereby — *the design aim is named outright* — *li-taṭmaʾinna qulūbukum*: so that your *hearts settle*, roots down in calm (ṭ-m-n: stillness of the agitated chest). The inner settlement, not the outer cavalry, is the battle's real weapon. The soul at repose fights without tremor, plans without panic, holds its post without watching the odds-board; every general on earth knows that the army whose morale holds is already half-victorious; the verse reveals that God administers His own morale-operations: no later recruiter's drum-slogan, but *angels assigned to chests*.

The classical commentators (al-Rāzī articulates the hermeneutic spelling-out of this) note a further dimension: even at Badr, where the majority holds angels actually *engaged*, their engagement was the visible drapery of God's decree — for God needs no creatures to kill or scatter, as al-Ṭabarī anticipated the scholastic point: the help descends *for the believers' chests*, through the *window of the senses*. God's angels fight "as signs that God is involved"; He could have wrought Badr's outcome with or without visible forms.
