The point is sealed in the very installment-structure: the promise had two registers (v. 125): the steadfast get the *marked visitation*; the falterers get — v. 126's abiding gift — *the news itself*, unrescinded: the *bushrā* is not clawed back; what changes when conditions slip is the full deployment, never the Good News's *linguistic truth*: the glad message remains in revelation, readable by every later steadfast roster, and thereby the object of 3:126 is achieved across history — hearts reposing on the *memory* of the promise, even on battlefields where no turbans gleam.

**"No Victory Save From God" — The Axiom the Whole Sūrah Rests Upon**

And then comes the clause that governs all the rest — indeed one of the most militarily wise sentences ever revealed: *wa mā al-naṣru illā min ʿindi Allāhi al-ʿazīzi al-ḥakīm* — "and victory is from none but God, the Mighty, the Wise." *Naṣr* — victory/help — is *titled* to God absolutely: numbers do not win; plans do not win; even God's own angels do not win, on their own account: all are instruments of the *ʿAzīz* — the All-Mighty whose cause cannot be frustrated — acting in *Ḥikmah* — Wisdom that distributes outcomes in patterns men's myopic mornings cannot measure. Two complementary names close the list: *Mighty* guarantees can; *Wise* governs whether-and-when. The victories He gives are victories *strategically assigned*: sometimes Badr's clean granting (to launch the new community on the world-stage), sometimes Uḥud's interrupted loss (to train that community in the deeper mechanics of covenant — v. 152's purpose-thread runs right through it) — both are *naṣr from God* when read at the correct altitude: Uḥud's day ended, withal, not in Muslim ruin but in the enemy's failed object — they did not enter Madinah, did not kill the Prophet, did not break the faith — and with Quraysh going home nursing the memory that they had *not* won.

The believer's practical synthesis is required total: work at causality like a professional (the Prophet set archers, chose ground, organized ranks — no passivity), and consider the *outcome* like a theologian: all of it, His. Muslim-civilization's old warrior-ethic codified it in the two-word motto: *ṣiddiq wa tawakkul* — be truthful and rely: *victory is from God alone —* therefore never despair in weakness (He can give it) — and never strut in triumph: *"if God helps you, none can overcome you; if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him?"* (3:160 — the same axiom re-ringed, nine verses later in the exact Uḥud cure): *the Mighty, the Wise*: One holds the ledger; all others hold spears.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:127

> **that He may cut off a faction of those who disbelieve or abase them, so that they be turned back disappointed.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Object-Clause of Help: What the Naṣr Is *For***

The grammar pins 3:127 as the *object* of the sentence just completed (the whole arc vv. 124–127 reads: your Lord reinforces you with thousands... which He made only as glad tidings for you and to settle your hearts... and victory is only from God, *so that He may cut off a faction of the disbelievers or abase them, turning them back disappointed*). God's design in the help runs thus shown concentrically: the envelope to *your chests* (v. 126), and the outward assignment on the enemy's case-file: *li-yaqṭaʿa ṭarafan mina alladhīna kafarū* — "to *cut off a flank* of those who disbelieve": *qaṭʿ al-ṭaraf*: the pruning-off of a section from a hostile whole: losses that cripple, positions carved away, leadership lopped: at Badr this clause was fulfilled verbatim — the heads of the lie — seventy of Quraysh's titled elite (their Abū Jahl, their ʿUtbah, their Shaybah, their Umayyah) — were cut off in one morning, an amputation from which Makkan polytheism's command-structure never recovered; at Uḥud (per the alternative situating, al-Ṭabarī) it operates in the second mode the verse sets as variation — *aw yakbitahum* — "or abase them": *kabt*: frustation-humbled thwarting: to be rolled back with objective unmet: and disappointed: *fa-yanqalibū khāʾibīn*.

**The Two Verb-Options: Cut Off or Abase — Wisdom's Distribution**

The disjunction (*or*) carries God's whole doctrine of strategic variety: not all engagements with falsehood are assigned the same outcome. Some venues are fated for *cutting off*: the enemy visibly loses flesh, ground, and face; others for *kabt*: no amputation, but the offensive deflated, the momentum snapped, the plans soured, the enemy withdrawing in road-wearied frustration — *yanqalibū khāʾibīn*: *turned back disappointed*: *khāʾib*: the precise word of a traveler who arrived and found the prize moved: they came to exterminate, achieved a maiming, and *went home un-upgraded* — which in war-science is *defeat*, since offense without objective is loss. Quraysh at Uḥud went home precisely *khāʾib*: they had killed seventy-two of the best Muslims, had bloodied the Prophet himself, had reached within an hour of Madinah — and standing there, did not walk in; their expedition dissolved in mutual blame and the mountains watched them turn; Abū Sufyān's parting cry ("Badr for your Uḥud — war is a rotation; another day will come!" in the sīrah) is the sound of *kabt*: unmatched boast heard as confession — they must come *again*; the objective they launched for remains unachieved; and the Prophet's stand-to posture reached them in the rear-guard of their withdrawal: *"they curl back unfulfilled, disappointed."*

**The Spiritual Reader's Clause**

Read at the angle of the believing community's millennia, the verse is a God's-eye rule about religions in contention: God's help of His servants aims at two calibrated outcomes for irreconcilable falsehood: *disjunction* (a piece lopped off: the bold front broken: *qaṭʿ al-ṭaraf*) or *containment-rollback* (*kabt*): both forms preserve the community of believers. What is *not* on offer is premise-three: the faith's ownership of every day's optics. *Khāʾib* is a splendid word for falsehood's evening: disappointment is built into the *position*, not merely the campaign: hoping against God, one invests in a stock whose ceiling is God Himself. Verse 127 closes the battle-promises: the tension it leaves deliberately unresolved — whether the next verses will bring cutting-off or abasement — is answered in the event's own historiography: Uḥud is, in the Book's own chronology, followed by verse 128's cautioning of the Prophet against imprecation: *naught is thine in the matter*: within the two permitted outcomes, *the choosing is God's*: armies returned home disappointed under both verbs; the wisdom assigns which. And the next verse (128) — among the most fervently-pasted-on-the-heart verses of the Prophet — is unlocked from precisely this: outcomes are God's; and the Prophet's task is what it has always been: stand, station, promise, and (as v. 128) *release the case-file upward*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:128

> **Naught is thine in the matter, whether He relent unto them or punish them, for truly they are wrongdoers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verse Born of a Bleeding Face**

The occasion of this verse is among the most famous in all tafsīr — al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, and the sound sīrah books record it, in slightly branching reports, and the picture is unforgettable: Uḥud's worst hour, the Prophet ﷺ struck — his helmet's chain-links driven into his blessed cheek, his lateral incisor broken, blood running down his face, his noble mouth the target of the battle's fury — and in that hour, wounded among his dead and his wounded, the Prophet of mercy cried out, in the anguish of office: *"How can a people prosper who have bloodied the face of their prophet while he calls them to their Lord?"* (al-Bukhārī 4077 and Muslim 1792 report in the reading of the battle-wound; the wording of his cry *kayfa yufliḥu qawmun faʿalū hādhā bi-nabiyyihim* is widely transmitted in the Companion-reports — e.g., from Ibn Masʿūd, reported with its verse-link in the tafsīr of 3:128). And heaven answered its Messenger in the downline that became the verse you now read: *laysa laka mina al-amri shayʾ* — "you have nothing of the matter at all."

**What "Nothing of the Matter" Relieves**

The rebuke-correction — tender, majestic — relieves the Prophet of a jurisdiction-prophet never held: *the amr* — the whole case-matter: outcomes, fates, turnings of hearts — is *not his dossier*. His register was to *call*; the disposition belongs to the Caller. The verse then maps the two possible dispositions in God's hand: *aw yatūba ʿalayhim* — "whether He relents toward them" (tawbah here used of God: *turns back toward them in acceptance* — repentance's divine mirror-face; before v. 89 this same word covered the door of the repentant murderers of prophets themselves) — *aw yuʿadhdhibahum* — "or punishes them": and the judgment-nail that closes both branches: *fa-innahum ẓālimūn* — "for truly they are wrongdoers": worthy of chastisement *as a matter of fact*, though fact does not decide fate: God's mercy may reach what their ẓulm does not deserve. Two clauses that thus open for the Prophet a horizon even over his bloodied hour's persecutors: *they are ẓālimūn — and they may yet be His*. How literal the fulfillment: within a handful of years many of that day's assailants themselves stood in the Muslim prayer-lines — Khālid ibn al-Walīd, the architect of the wheel that had overrun the archers' hill, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ in the raiding lines, Hind herself by the conquest — men and women for whom the bloodied face of Uḥud had been, by God's *tawbah-turning*, the door of prophecy finally come home. The Prophet who cried *how can they prosper* lived to *see them prosper* — in the only prospering that counts (v. 104's *mufliḥūn*): the sūrah's operative word carrying its own answer across eight years.

**The Qunūt and the End of Private Cursing**

The second line of occasions (Ibn Kathīr, al-Wāḥidī) completes the administrative lesson: the Prophet ﷺ, during the grievous season after the massacre at Biʾr Maʿūnah and al-Rajīʿ (when dozens of the Qur'an-memorizing missionary-reciters were betrayed and murdered), prayed *qunūt* — aloud in the dawn prayer — imprecating named tribes and individuals: *"O God, curse so-and-so, and so-and-so..."* — and the verse descended; and the reports state: thereafter he ceased fixing curses upon named parties. The correction is lifted into the permanent code of the religion: the believer may *present grievance to God* — the prophets were granted the full grammar of lament (Moses's prayer at 7:150; Jesus's at 5:118 — "if You punish them they are Your servants, and if You forgive them — You are the Mighty, the Wise") — but the *verdict-issuance* — this one damned, this one lost — is not a human file. God's own law over the whole species is printed next door in the same sūrah: *He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills* (v. 129), and the *door of return* is open to the very worst (v. 89). The believers' duty toward the ẓālimūn is therefore triple: (1) truthfully name the wrongdoing — the verse itself stamps them as ẓālimūn; (2) release the sentencing to God's custody — not ours; (3) never rule out God's *tawbah* reaching them — for are surely more souls won by the prisoner's silence-and-decent-endurance than by the imprecatory tongue. History measured it exactly: the Uḥud-commanders whom the wounded Prophet was anguished over became, by the conquest and after, the commanders of Islam's outer marches — *and the matter that was not his was managed, in twenty years, into a wonder no curse could have purchased*. Whether He relents or punishes: both paths are pure wisdom (al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm, v. 126 — the very name-pair framing this whole Uḥud block); and the Prophet's relief from the case-file is passed on as every believer's relief from their own: *laysa laka mina al-amri shayʾ* — the most restful sentence in the entire theology of agency.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:129

> **Unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth. He forgives whomsoever He will and punishes whomsoever He will, and God is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Ownership That Legitimates the Unsearchable Will**

Verse 128 stripped outcomes from the Prophet's hand; verse 129 explains *whose* hand lawfully holds them, and why no one may subpoena that hand: *wa lillāhi mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ* — "unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth" — the exact clause the chapter had already lodged as verse 109's opening half (the reader registers the near-verbatim: the Book re-teaches by ring). Ownership is the ground-axiom: *because* everything is His — every creature-property, every soul-file, every consequence — *therefore*: *yaghfiru li-man yashāʾu wa yuʿadhdhibu man yashāʾ* — "He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills." The clause-order matters theologically: forgiveness is placed first; punishment second — the Book's grammatical register here being mercy-precedent (cf. 39:53's prohibition of despair before the same dual), though the decisive element in doctrine is the *will*: *mashīʾah*: God's counsels are not answerable to custom, precedent, tribal pressure, or prophetic sentiment — *not even the Prophet's*, as v. 128 just ruled. The verses the commentators marshal alongside are the full jurisprudence of agency: *"Thou art not tasked with their guidance — but God guides whom He wills"* (2:272); *"thine is only to convey"* (3:20); *"surely thou guidest not whom thou lovest — but God guides whom He wills, and He knows best who are the guided"* (28:56). Prophets are witnesses, warner-physicians, urgency-embodied — not spiritual registrars.

**Where the Will Must Not Become Fatalism**

The two immediate dangers the verse's careless reading breeds are both pre-empted by the Book's own system. First, fatalism toward *self*: "if forgiveness hinges simply on will, repentance is pointless" — answered at 13:11 ("God does not change a people's state until they change what is in themselves"), at v. 89's door ("except those who repent and amend"), and at the chapter's own ring-verse coming five seats ahead (vv. 133–135): the "hasteners to forgiveness," by the plain mechanics of cause-and-mercy, are *those toward whom the will has already turned*: the will of God is not a competitor with the sinner's repentance but its *divine hour*. Second, casual etiquette toward *God*: "so the punishing-is-just by definition, anything goes" — answered at the chapter's own permanent seal: "God wills no wrong for the worlds" (v. 108) and "God wrongs them not" (v. 117): the Punisher never wrongs; the Forgiver never *fails a promise*. Between these two guardrails the verse stands monumental: absolutely free, absolutely wise, absolutely just — sovereignty without caprice, freedom without chaos.

**"God Is Forgiving, Merciful": The Names That Frame Every Case**

The seal, *wa Allāhu ghafūrun raḥīm*, is the Book's own signet: *Ghafūr* — the intensely-covering Forgiver — and *Raḥīm* — the intense,dedicated-Merciful. For the final teaching of verses 128–129 to rest on this pair is the chapter's mercy-architecture again: the passage that began with the Prophet's wounded cry over *ẓālimūn* closes not with the wrath-register but with the double name of *mercy directed at creatures*. The believer reading the sequence with knowledge receives the complete medicine of the administration of outcomes: (1) do not grab the gavel (v. 128); (2) do not interrogate the Owner (v. 129's first halves); (3) do not despair of the disposition: *Ghafūr, Raḥīm* is the final line of the docket. And the Prophet's ﷺ own spiritual practice showed what becomes of a heart trained by this: he who was corrected never turned bitter; he who was wounded by enemies continued, at the conquest-bound vista of Taʾif's stoning, to hear the angel of the mountains offer their crushing and answer:

> *"No — rather I hope that God will bring forth from their loins those who will worship God alone, associating nothing with Him."* (al-Bukhārī 3231; Muslim 1795, from ʿĀʾishah — on the Day of Taʾif, the Prophet's answer to the Angel of the Mountains)

Verse 129 practiced is, in that answer, visible at full height: ownership known, the will released, and the hope — mercy's own grammar — fixed on the future of the very stoners.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:130

> **O you who believe! Devour not usury, doubling and multiplying. And reverence God, that haply you may prosper.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Battle-Verses to the Market: Why Ribā Follows Uḥud**

The address-signal returns — "O you who believe" — and the sūrah steps, with narrative suddenness, from casualty-lists to *cash*: *lā taʾkulū al-ribā aḍʿāfan muḍāʿafah* — "do not devour usury, doubled and multiplied." The juxtaposition is not accidental in the Book's own order: Uḥud taught that true security lies in God's reinforcement, not in visible accumulation; the next verses forbid precisely that form of accumulation which *eats* communities — the compounding of debt upon the weak — and then offer their alternative super-asset (vv. 131–135: the Garden-wide-as-the-heavens, raced for by *spenders*): the sequence is a short course in divine economics: the false growth engine (ribā) versus the true growth engine (charity and forgiveness). The full juristic anatomy of *ribā* belongs to the al-Baqarah block (2:275–281), whose principal sentences the commentators recall here: *"God has made lawful trade and forbidden ribā"* (2:275); *"God blights ribā and causes charity to grow"* (2:276); the last-revealed verse in the Prophet's ministry per several reports being in the ribā-block (2:281); culminating in the declaration of *war from God and His Messenger* upon those who persist (2:279) — the only sin in the Qur'an so indicted: a war-declaration, upon ledger-writers. The word *aḍʿāfan muḍāʿafah* — *doubled, adoubled*: interest raised upon interest with each default — transmits the pre-Islamic practice in its perfected cruelty: the term fell due; the debtor could not pay; the principal was *doubled for extension*, and doubled again — careers, families, and clans consumed in ten-year cycles: *devour* (*taʾkulūn*) is the eating-verb: consumption by feeding: the usurer's economy as digestion of the debtor-class: exactly the moral of 4:161 — the practice charged also against a faction of the People of the Book: *"and for their taking ribā, though they were forbidden it, and their devouring people's wealth in falsehood"*: one eating-dish served across very different religious tables, and banned in all.

**Taqwā and Falāḥ: The Two-Word Alternative Portfolio**

The verse's own counsel is the complete opposite asset-allocation in two verbs: *wa-ttaqū Allāha laʿallakum tufliḥūn* — "and reverence God, that haply you may prosper." Note: the normal commercial promise-map is *inverted*: in the street-arithmetic of ribā, taqwā costs you the double-multiples (the refusal of interest "loses" the growth); in God's ledger, taqwā *is* the prosperity: *tufliḥūn* — the chapter's own prosperity-word (v. 104). God's anti-usury counter-offers are abundantly documented in the Book's own trade-columns: (1) alms-parity: *"if you give to God a goodly loan, He will multiply it for you manyfold"* (2:245 — *ḍiʿfan kathīran*: the very vocabulary of ribā transplanted to generosity — *ribā without a victim*; and 2:261's seven-hundred seed-ear parable, which v. 92 of this sūrah already retold); (2) deferral over compound: *"if [the debtor] is in hardship, then delay until ease"* (2:280) — profit measured as *time gifted*, not as time charged; (3) the nullity of the usurer's apparent victory: 2:276 — *yamḥaqu Allāhu al-ribā*: God *blights* ribā — its cruel result: what ribā accumulates lacks *barakah*: it draws from the world and rents, and cannot generate what matters: peace, trust, or abiding wealth.

**Ribā in the Ummah's Conscience: A Standing Word**

The prohibition installed at 3:130 — one of the earliest anti-interest verses of the Madinan period per several chronologies — made *interest-refusal* a core mark of Muslim identity, across fourteen centuries of enormously varied economies: the jurists opened its categories (*ribā al-faḍl* — excess; *ribā al-nasīʾah* — deferral — in the Prophet's six-commodity hadith: *"gold for gold, silver for silver... equal for equal, hand to hand"* — Muslim 1584–1587), enforced its cancellation at the Farewell Pilgrimage with a personal beginning (the Prophet declaring, in the farewell encyclical, *"every ribā of the Jāhiliyyah is abolished — and the first ribā I abolish is the ribā of al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib"* — Muslim 1598), and opened the social imagination to its alternatives (the zakāh system, the waqf foundations, the ḥasan-loan discipline — *qarḍ ḥasan*: lending with God's multiplication as the yield). Its interior teaching is truly simple: *in God's market, the categories of "asset" are redefined*: the creditor's peace is an asset; the debtor's survival is an asset; the distance from God's war (2:279) is an asset; and the taqwā-shaped, ṣadaqah-fueled prosperity is — per this verse — what *falāḥ* means. All that doubling-and-multiplying, and the final bankers of Jāhiliyyah died no richer for eternity; while the seven-hundredfold returns still pay out, every day, on the smallest coin given in God's name.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:131

> **And be mindful of the Fire that has been prepared for the disbelievers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**One Line, Whole Territories of Weight**

The verse is eight Arabic words and closes a thousand words of economics with a single furnace-door: *wa-ttaqū al-nāra allatī uʿiddat lil-kāfirīn* — "and be mindful of the Fire that has been prepared for the disbelievers." Its brevity is itself rhetorical design: after the accounting of verse 130 no elaboration is needed — the anti-ribā law rests on an *ultimate* stake: God's penalties reach infinitely beyond forfeited profits. The commentators (the source recalling 2:2's glosses) note the root-freight of *wa-ttaqū* — the *taqwā-verb* again, the chapter's governing ethic: not "fear" as shiver alone, but a full *discipline of mindful shielding*: to fence yourself, by conduct, from the place named: to practice a kind of spiritual fire-prevention in advance of the fire.

**"Prepared for the Disbelievers" — A Destination Already Built**

Two details of the phrase press for notice. First, the tense: *uʿiddat* — *has been prepared* — perfect tense: the Fire is not a contingency to be commissioned at some future tribunal but an existing, ready installation: the Qur'an returns to the fact with sober consistency (25:11: "We have prepared a Blaze for the one who denies the Hour"; 25:37; 67:5; 76:4: "We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a Blaze"): accountability operates on a completed infrastructure. The final army of God's universe is not improvising; the believer is therefore not asked to *believe in a future penalty* so much as to reckon with an already-standing one. Second, the addressee-class: *lil-kāfirīn* — "for the disbelievers" — deliberately chosen in a verse addressed to *believers*: God does not tell them "prepared for you"; He tells them "prepared for *disbelievers*": the law of warning by classification: the Fire is not the believers' *destination*: it is their *frontier*: identify on which side of it your choices are lining up — ribā's consumption (v. 130) is listed among the trade-routes *to* that side: usury-armies marched Jāhiliyyah straight there, per the verse's implied cartography; and the bridge from the frontier is the chapter's own immediate next command (v. 133): *hasten to forgiveness*: "prepared for you" — a Garden-wide-as-the-heavens: the verses' alternation (Fire prepared — Garden prepared — Fire prepared at 133/136: "forgiveness... and Gardens, rivers below" — and the same architecture at vv. 131 vs. 133) rehearses the Qur'an's own rhetorical balance (targhīb–tarhīb): the soul is prodded from behind and beckoned from ahead — and the two preparations sit, side by side, awaiting the conclusions of life-spans.

**Mindfulness as a Daily Firewall**

The verse's enduring practical life is in the summoning it performs of taqwā's smallest muscles: mindfulness of the Fire — as al-Ghazālī and the sages of the heart taught for a thousand years — is not morbidity but *prevention-habit*, exercised three times daily without strain: at the moment of temptation ("this Fire is ready" — would I buy a minute of gain by standing near it?); at the moment of hardship ("any hardship-eye in this world compares to what?"); and at the moment of prayer (the Prophet ﷺ taught to seek refuge from it in precise words, *Allāhumma ajirnī mina al-nār* — "O God, rescue me from the Fire" — kept among the daily adhkār counts; and its twin lens: 2:201's "and shield us from the punishment of the Fire" — the mosque-going ummah's most-repeated single entreaty). Verse 131 thus holds, in nine words of English translation, a whole fire-chapel where the believing heart rehearses its safety-protocols: prepared — for disbelievers — be mindful.
**Ittaqū al-Nār: Taqwā Addressed as Fire-Prevention**

*Wa-ttaqū al-nār allatī uʿiddat li-l-kāfirīn* — "and be wary of the Fire prepared for the disbelievers": the verse lands the chapter's longest instructive run (vv. 130–136's ribā-ban and forgiveness-race) on taqwā's most concrete object. The verb *ittaqā* — taking a shield — with the Fire for its accusative creates the Book's standard prevention-idiom: taqwā is *conduct-as-fireproofing*, undertaken now, in the world where precautions still work. Al-Qurṭubī dwells on the past-tense of the preparation — *uʿiddat*: prepared *already* (as its twin 67:11's confessed-blaze and 25:11's seen-from-distance fury) — the Fire is not contingency but *finished facility*, awaiting its designated residents; and its designation — *li-l-kāfirīn* — assigns the property-title to disbelief, while its warming-shadow falls across every believer's own heedlessness as the next verses (132–136's race into forgiveness) make plain.

**The Hope-Fear Engine: Winged Parable of the Salaf**

The community's earliest teachers fixed the sūrah's paired pedagogy (fear v. 131; hope v. 132's *that you may be shown mercy*) in an image al-Ghazālī would canonize: the bird of the believer's heart flies on *two wings — fear and hope* — and its head is love of God. Strip the fear-wing and the bird folds into presumption; strip the hope-wing and it folds into despair — the two folded states the Book itself maps at 15:56's *none despairs of God's mercy but the astray* and 70:28's *the punishment of their Lord is not to feel secure from*. The Fire-verse's daily practice, in the pious generations, ran exactly between the wings: Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's companions would weep reading vv. 130–134, then work as though v. 133's race-bell had just rung — *the prevention-fear of v. 131 always emitted into the race of v. 133*; and the Prophet's own assembly left them the operational rule in the briefest of counsels: *"the clever is he who audits himself and works for what is after death"* (al-Tirmidhī 2459, ḥasan).

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:132

> **And obey God and the Messenger, that haply you may receive mercy.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Shortest Complete Prescription in the Chapter**

Between the Fire's door (v. 131) and the Garden-race (v. 133) — between the two preparations — stands this tiny hinge sentence: *wa aṭīʿū Allāha wa-l-rasūla laʿallakum turḥamūn* — "and obey God and the Messenger, that haply you may receive mercy." It is, in effect, the sūrah's whole ethics compressed to its operational minimum: *āṭīʿū* — obey — *Allāha wa-l-rasūla* — God and the Messenger — *laʿallakum turḥamūn* — that you may be shown mercy. The commentators note the pairing's placement alongside the book's wider theology of obedience (4:80: "whosoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God"; 8:1; 24:54: "say: obey God and obey the Messenger... if you obey him, you will be rightly guided"; 48:17) — and the particular twinning here, as the source observes: at verse 31 *following* the Messenger was linked to *God's love* (*yuḥbibkumu Allāh* — He will love you); at verse 132 *obeying* the Messenger is linked to *God's mercy* (*laʿallakum turḥamūn* — you may be shown mercy): two currencies of grace annexed to the same act: love attaches to *following*; mercy attaches to *obedience*: the whole-hearted Muslim gets both: the amiably-loved, the pardon-enveloped.

**Why "Obey" Is the Whole Reform of the Heart**

The verb in its Arabic instruction — *aṭīʿū* — carries the specific sense of directed compliance: obedience is the religion's litmus verb because it is the only posture that directly contradicts the autonomous self: faith can be held in the mind by a rebel, charity can be performed for show by an egoist, even prayer can be done for display (4:142 warns of those "who remember God but little") — but *obedience in the direction that crosses your desire* is the command that translates every verse of the Book from content into life. The commanding *couple* — God and the Messenger — seals the obedience-channel: God's historical communication with our species is *sourced* and *clarified*: the source is God's word; the clarified is His Messenger's living explanation (16:44: "that you may make clear to mankind what was sent down to them); hence obeying both names is *one* act of surrender: the Prophet ﷺ himself taught the correspondence in its sharpest form: *"whosoever obeys me has obeyed God; and whosoever disobeys me has disobeyed God."* (al-Bukhārī 7137; Muslim 1835, from Abū Hurayrah).

**"That Haply You May Receive Mercy": The Desired Outcome of an Entire Sūrah**

The terminal *laʿallakum turḥamūn* — *that you may be granted mercy* — is, as the section's own structure shows, the chapter's third petition-*laʿalla*: (1) verse 102-103's "that you may be guided"; (2) verse 123's "that you may give thanks"; and here "that you may receive mercy": guidance, gratitude, and mercy — the complete triptych of what the Book wanted for this ummah from God: and the three keys appointed to them were also exactly three: *ittaqū* — reverence (v. 102), *iʿtaṣimū* — hold fast (v. 103), and *aṭīʿū* — obey (v. 132). The three imperatives are one thing in three weights of speech: to hold God fast is to shield for God-is-Him; to obey is to hold *in acts*; all of it is named *taqwā* when quiet. The immediacy of mercy to obedience is confirmed across the Book: 7:204 — "when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent, that haply you may receive mercy (*laʿallakum turḥamūn*)" — the same formula: listening-there, obeying-here; 24:56; 49:10. For the reader at the chapter's own hinge (vv. 131–133), the line is also the exact crossing-instruction *from* the Fire-door *to* the Garden-door: the bridge between the prepared-for-disbelievers and the prepared-for-reverent is a plank of obedience, crossed by racing feet — as the next verse commands the stride: *and hasten*.
**Mercy as the Terminal Framing of Command**

*Wa aṭīʿū Allāha wa-l-rasūla laʿallakum turḥamūn* — "and obey God and the Messenger, that you may obtain mercy": the sūrah's third full *aṭīʿū*-pair (vv. 32, 100, 132) is sealed here — uniquely — by the *laʿalla* of hoped-mercy. The commentators' points run in three: (1) obedience is not barter — the hope-particle preserves God's freedom to give; (2) yet obedience is *channel* — mercy is never promised to the disobedient direction (4:175's twin-manner leading: guidance and mercy *for those who believe in God and hold fast to Him*); (3) the position of the clause — after the fear-command of v. 131 — restores the machine of taqwā to its two-winged balance: *fear the Fire — then obey, hoping mercy:* prevention and progress in the same breath.

**The Mercy of 7:156 and the Written Heritage**

The Book's own commentary on the seal comes at 7:156, in God's answer-register after Moses' plea — *"My mercy embraces all things — so I shall write it for those who revere, give the zakāh, and believe in Our signs"* — the mercy *written in advance for the obeying*; and the believers' own ritelanguage holds the pairing still at the end of every prayer's tashahhud-sequence: *ibārak ʿalā muḥammad* beside the plea that rang Ibrahim's house — mercy asked *in severalty*, as if each soul expected to be written in the 7:156 register separately. The Prophet's ﷺ own estimate of the mercy-mechanism remains the school-text:

> *"God wrote, above His Throne upon His Book: My mercy overcomes My wrath."* (al-Bukhārī 7404; Muslim 2751, from Abū Hurayrah)

Obeying, then, is walking into the written side of the ledger — v. 132's *laʿalla* as set forth by God Himself.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:133

> **And hasten unto forgiveness from your Lord, and for a garden whose breadth is the heavens and the earth—prepared for the reverent,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Sāriʿū": The Command to Run Toward Pardon**

The verse is the whole architecture of the religious life in two destinations and one verb: *wa sāriʿū ilā maghfiratin min rabbikum wa jannatin ʿarḍuhā al-samāwātu wa-l-arḍ* — "and hasten unto forgiveness from your Lord, and unto a Garden whose breadth is the heavens and the earth." *Sāriʿū* — *race!* — the speeding imperative has appeared twice already in the chapter's register (v. 114's "hasten unto good deeds" — *yusāriʿūna fī al-khayrāt*: the remnant's racing stride, now made the reader's own command). The choice of *race*-verb over all possible verbs of piety ("seek," "strive," "pray for") is the Qur'an's own psychology of salvation: forgiveness and the Garden are not to be *approached timidly*, negotiated toward, or waited upon: they are to be *run for* — with the runner's whole stake of urgency, competition's joy, and the fixedness of the finish. The hadith of the Prophet two cities deep in the tradition gives the runner's daily starting-gun:

> *"Hasten to deeds before seven things... And vie one with another in forgiveness from your Lord"* — and for urgency-particulars: *"the Prophet ﷺ commanded: 'race to good deeds before trials come like patches of dark night'"* (cf. Muslim 118, 2947 on racing before fitan; and 57:21 the verse-twin of this racing-verse: *"race unto forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden whose breadth is as the breadth of heaven and earth, prepared for those who believe in God and His messengers — that is the bounty of God, which He gives to whom He wills"*)

**"A Garden Whose Breadth Is the Heavens and the Earth": Infinity, Measured Sideways**

The description is one of the most famous in Scripture — and its dimension-term is chosen with calculated audacity: not the *length* (nor simply the "vastness") of the Garden but its *breadth* — *ʿarḍ* — the measurement of spread: a breadth of *the heavens and the earth*: the whole sky and the whole planet, laid out as the *width* of the Garden — its length, by communal silence of the verse, beyond word. The commentators dwell on the image's scale-meaning: existence itself — the widest imaginable banner within all creation — marks merely the *transverse* of this Garden. The famous story the commentary retains — the letter from Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium, to the Prophet ﷺ: *you speak of a garden whose breadth is the heavens and the earth — where is the Fire, then?* and the Prophet's answering riddle:

> *"Glory be to God! — and where is the night when the day comes?"* (preserved in the tafsīr-reports on this verse and in early sīrah literature)

—the answer's compactness matching the question's cleverness: infinity admits more dimensions than the inquirer's own map supplies; the unrolled vastness of God's mercy does not exhaust God's justice; the two are not rivals for scarce room.

**"Prepared for the Reverent" — The Directory Is Ready and Addressed**

And then the clause that completes the chess-mirror of verse 131: *uʿiddat lil-muttaqīn* — "prepared for the reverent": the same ready-perfection as the fire (*uʿiddat* — same verb, passive) — but the address reversed: *for the muttaqīn*, the very word-class of the chapter, whose portraits the next two verses proceed to paint (vv. 134–135). The verse's rhetorical architecture is thereby whole: two prepared realms, one Garden addressed-to-*taqwā*, one Fire addressed-to-*kufr* — and the *only membership-transfer form ever issued between them is taqwā itself*: which the next verse defines not by visions nor seniority but by four daily behaviors (spending, anger-control, pardoning, returning) — the sūrah's own answer to the perennial question "which of the two preparations is mine?": the answer: whichever your conduct is presently aiming you toward; and as long as the legs run (sāriʿū — the present command is a standing imperative: continuance of running), the address on your deeds can be re-addressed tonight — the finish-line of pardon sits, after all, at arm's length of every repentant stride.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:134

> **who spend in ease and hardship, and curb their rage, and pardon others—and God loves the virtuous—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Mark: Spending in Both Weathers**

The muttaqīn — the addressees of the broad Garden — receive their working portrait in the next two verses, and the first stroke lands on the property of the pocket: *alladhīna yunfiqūna fī al-sarrāʾi wa-l-ḍarrāʾ* — "who spend in ease and in hardship." *Al-sarrāʾ* and *al-ḍarrāʾ* — the paired states of comfort and distress: plenty and famine; wealth and want; joy and wound. Al-Ṭabarī anchors the plain reading (they give whether flush or straitened), and al-Rāzī unfolds its psychological range (happy or sad, whether giving delights them that day or costs them, they persist). A *philanthropy that weathers* is, precisely, the test of its source: giving in ease costs surplus; giving in hardship costs *substance* — and hence only trust in God sustains the second: hence its enormity in heaven's register. The Prophet's ﷺ most urgent investment counsel in times of famine — and the tradition's own testimonies that he was "more generous than the free-blowing wind," al-Bukhārī and Muslim's report from Ibn ʿAbbās — were flowerings of this exact clause; and its living instances in the sīrah include ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, ʿUthmān's provisioning the army of ʿUsrah, and above all Abū Bakr's gift of *all* his property to the Tabūk campaign (v. 92's scene), and ʿAlī's prostration of soul — remembered in the reports about Laylat al-Mabīt — and the book's own charter of the spending-class at 63:10's "spend of what We have provided you, before death comes to any of you." The ornament-selection of verse 14 is here exactly reversed: the *same* objects, seen as lending-row material to God rather than as self-adornment.

**The Second Mark: "Kāẓimūna al-Ghayẓ" — Swallowing the Rage**

Then comes the mark the sages of the ummah have always treated among the highest interior achievements: *wa-l-kāẓimīna al-ghayẓ* — "and the curbers of rage." *Kaẓm* is the closing of a vessel — the language is the language of *bottling*: not absence of anger from the human breast (the tradition does not teach the impossibility, nor praise the apath) but its *containment at the instant of force*: the fire exists; the valve holds. Al-Qurṭubī's differentiation of the two anger-words is precise: *ghaḍab* is anger manifesting outward in words and deeds; *ghayẓ* is the inner *boil* — the verse's choice thus legislates at the deepest interior register: mastery before manifestation. The Messenger's own instruction delivered it with the simplicity of a complete psychotherapy:

> *A man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Give me a command, and make it short." He said: "Do not become angry." The man repeated several times; he said: "Do not become angry."* (al-Bukhārī 6116, from Abū Hurayrah)

And the strength-redefinition hadith that the source commentary retains:

> *"He is not powerful who throws men down [in wrestling]; the strong is the one who controls himself when angry."* (al-Bukhārī 6114; Muslim 2609, from Abū Hurayrah)

The metaphysical complement arrives in the Qur'an's own complete anger-regulation at 42:37 ("when angry, they forgive") and in the hadith the source records: whoever curbs his anger while able to act upon it shall be filled by God with security and faith (preserved in the books of the sunnah, from Anas; transmitted with varying wordings in al-Ṭabarānī and others). The *science* of the constraint Muslims practiced for a millennium: the Prophet's ritual of *istiʿādhah* ("I seek refuge in God from the accursed satan" — al-Bukhārī 6115: "I know a word which, if said, removes what he feels: aʿūdhu billāh..."), the posture-change ("if one of you becomes angry while standing, let him sit" — Abū Dāwūd 4782), wuḍūʾ (anger is from fire; extinguish it with water — Abū Dāwūd 4784), silence — the full bottling-craft: *kaẓm* engineered daily, until the bottled becomes genuinely the outside-at-peace.

**The Third Mark: "ʿĀfīna ʿani al-Nās" — Pardoning People**

The trajectory continues outward: from the interior-valve to the public-memory: *wa-l-ʿāfīna ʿani al-nās* — "and the pardoners of mankind": *ʿafw*: the letting-go, the erasure even of the *claim*: al-Qurṭubī's eye notes the exaltation packed into *ʿani al-nās* — pardoning *people* — those *over whom one has power*: pardon is real only when denial was available; slaves cannot pardon masters. The for-giving of men thus becomes, in God's register, the highest form of Lordship's own quality descending into servants: God is *al-ʿAfuww*, the Eraser; the muttaqī practice His own name. And the tradition's measure of the office is the exact structure of a deal-offered:

> *"Shall I not tell you what is better than the degree of fasting, prayer, and almsgiving? The making of peace between people."* (Abū Dāwūd 4919; al-Tirmidhī 2509)

And at the end the whole verse is capped with the love-clause: *wa Allāhu yuḥibbu al-muḥsinīn* — "and God loves the virtuous" — the iḥsān-class: spenders-in-both-weathers, anger-bottlers, pardon-issuers — the collective names of this verse assemble, under a single predicate — *yuḥibbu* — the one audience that ultimately matters, returned to the register of verse 31 (love and its seven foods): the God who loves *His muḥsinīn* has just published their physical description.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:135

> **and who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember God and then seek forgiveness for their sins—and who forgives sins but God?—and who do not knowingly persist in what they have done.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Fourth Mark — The Sin-Recovery Sequence of the Muttaqīn**

The verse extends the portrait to the point every sinner has prayed for: *wa alladhīna idhā faʿalū fāḥishatan aw ẓalamū anfusahum dhakarū Allāha fa-staghfarū li-dhunūbihim* — "and who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember God — and seek forgiveness for their sins." The reverent are here declared *not sinless* — an honesty that rescues millions: the muttaq wobbles; the difference lies in *what activates when the fall happens*: the sequence God praises has three precise moves.

**Move one: *dhakarū Allāh* — they remember God.** The moment the indecency (*fāḥishah*: the ugly act, the trespass of limits) is done, *remembrance fires*: some commentators (the Sufi canon the source cites, Abū ʿAlī al-Rūdhbārī and Junayd's circles — "Aj" in the Study Quran apparatus) list the contents of the memory: God's gaze (He is watching — the iḥsān-reality of v. 99's sealer), His anger's just gravity, the scene of the Resurrection's reckoning, the name of God itself pronounced over the heart — any or all: the fall is met by *theophany-memory*, and the memory burns the fall's anesthetic instantly. This is the decisive moment of the religion of the heart: sin's greatest lethality is its *forgetting-mask* — the drug of rationalization; taqwā is precisely the nervous system that *cannot* forget: its first reflex after fault is the Face of God.

**Move two: *fa-staghfarū* — they seek forgiveness.** The *fa-* prefix marks immediacy: instantly after remembering, the petition issues: pardon-plea, tailored to the fault (*li-dhunūbihim* — *for their sins*, specified and owned, not vague air-sighing): no brokerage, no middle-court — and the verse interrupts itself to certify the directness: *wa man yaghfiru al-dhunūba illā Allāh* — "and who forgives sins but God?" — the rhetorical clause that Islam's entire devotional architecture hangs upon: forgiveness's monopoly is God's: no priesthood absolves; the muttaq is sent to no booth but the throne. The famous occasions (al-Qurṭubī reports: the verse was sent down concerning a man of the believers who had bought dates from a beautiful woman seller, embraced and kissed her impulsively, and came to the Prophet devastated) — whatever the details, the pastoral architecture is the same: return before despair hardens.

**Move three: the negative: *wa lam yuṣirrū ʿalā mā faʿalū wa hum yaʿlamūn* — they do not knowingly persist.** *Iṣrār* — persistent sticking, knowing-insistence: al-Ṭabarī's gloss fixes the clause: they do not, *in awareness* that the thing is forbidden, settle into the act as practice. Not *they never re-err*: the prophetic hadith and the consensus read the clause exactly as the safety-valve of the entire law: recommission after renewed repentance is not iṣrār; *programmatic continuance while knowing* is — the difference between the falling walker and the determined encamper. The Sufi maxim the source preserves encodes it as law of gravity: *"there is no great sin with istighfār — and no small sin with iṣrār"*: guilt's size is determined not by the deed but by the stubbornness above it. The whole of God's agile anthropology in three moves: fall-remember-return: and the promise already floats in the next verse.

**The Tradition's Own Confirmation**

God ratified this verse in the Prophet's standing teaching: *"by Him in Whose hand is my soul, if you did not sin, God would remove you and bring a people who sin and seek forgiveness — and He would forgive them"* (Muslim 2749, from Abū Hurayrah): *sin-then-return* is designed human weather — *taʾs*, not death: designed to grow the seeking-tenderness in the creature, and the answering expansion in God's own display of Ghafūr-titles. And behind it all the final solvent assurance: *"O son of Adam, so long as you call upon Me and hope in Me, I forgive you what came from you, and I do not mind... though your sins reached the clouds of the sky and then you sought forgiveness of Me, I would forgive you"* (al-Tirmidhī 3540, qudsī, from Anas). The fourth mark of the muttaq is thus comfortably located in every believer's reach: *sincerity after sin* — a forgivable sin, not an impossible innocence.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:136

> **For these, their reward is forgiveness from their Lord, and Gardens with rivers running below, abiding therein. Blessed indeed is the reward of the workers [of righteousness]!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Twenty-Fold Answer: What the Sin-Recovery Sequence Purchases**

The wages-clause arrives — *ulāʾika jazāʾuhum* — "those — their reward" — and the verse spends the sūrah's treasure on the behavior-list it just enumerated (spending in both weathers, bottling rage, pardoning people, the remembering-and-seeking after fault): *maghfiratun min rabbihim* — "forgiveness from their Lord": pardon named *first*, before Paradise — for upon pardon *everything else depends*: the entering of the Garden is the motion after the gate of forgiveness opens; and the naming of it as coming *min rabbihim* — from *their* Lord, possessor-guardian of beloveds — gives it the personal signature. Then *wa jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār, khālidīna fīhā* — "and Gardens with rivers running below, abiding therein": the river-phrase — the Qur'an's most repeated vision-fragment (over forty occurrences, from 2:25 onward) — with its sensory full-assembly: shaded orchards, water visible *beneath* pavilions, movement and murmur: paradise as living environment, not static hall; and *khālidīna fīhā*: the settling of the *Khuld* that every earlier verse hammered: permanence.

But the verse's own crown is its concluding line — the evaluative seal that God Himself stamps upon the religion-labor of the portrait: *wa niʿma ajru al-ʿāmilīn* — "and blessed is the reward of the workers" — *niʿm*: how good, how excellent — with *ʿāmilīn*: the *doers*. Al-Rāzī and the long line of scholars after him noted the plain theological beacon of this final word: God's Book closes the entire profile with the term *workers* — Paradise's pay-attributed-to *action*. For Islam the two doctrines co-exist without quarrel: (1) no one enters the Garden by merit alone — it remains mercy (Muslim 2816, cited at v. 107); (2) no one arrives without *work* — the entire portrait of vv. 134–135 is nothing but verbs of effort. The doctrine's joint articulation is the hadith's own exact pairing: *"do right and seek nearness, and give glad tidings"* — labor ordered, nearness hoped, hope enjoined: *niʿma ajru al-ʿāmilīn* is God's own amen over that compound.

**The Verse in the Life of the Believer**

The finishing thought of the whole passage, from ribā-fire through the Garden-race, is thus one sentence whose structure is the believer's daily life: *act beautifully; fall; rise; remember; return; be paid double — pardon now, Garden at end — and known, lastly, by the class of the doers*. The muttaq is not a monk beyond work, nor an activist beyond heart: the portrait, read whole, is a human being of pockets, tempers, and memory, aimed at God and maintained there by remembrance — *niʿma ajru al-ʿāmilīn* — blessed indeed is the pay of workers such as these: the most summarizing commendation God bestows anywhere upon ordinary religious conduct.
**Niʿma Ajru al-ʿĀmilīn: The Doer's Wage-Praise**

The reward-side of the race closes with a clause the worker never outgrows: *niʿma ajru al-ʿāmilīn* — "blessed is the reward of the workers": *niʿma* — the particle of praise — from the root *n-ʿ-m* — sets God's own adjective upon a payroll: the forgiveness (first item) and the Garden of rivers (second) together constitute *the beautiful wage*. The clause's grammar deserves its pause: the reward is enfolded in a *job-title* — *al-ʿāmilīn*, the doers — not in an ethnic or tribal register: the wages of v. 136 attach to the action-file, never to the badge-file. Al-Qurṭubī cites in its direction the long-standing wisdom-tradition of the early community: *work is the community's universal application* — the ṣabr (v. 134), the standard (v. 15), the fast-clause of forgiveness (v. 135) — all *works*; and God's seal on them is personal praise: *blessed is the workers' wage.*

**Rivers Flowing Below: The Refrain of the Gardens**

*Jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār khālidīna fīhā* — the Garden-image of the rivers flowing beneath, abiding therein — recurs through the Book's registers not as refrain-fatigue but as *estimate-promise*: the same picture issued again and again *because its likeness is unachievable any other way* (2:25's *provision resembling* — the fruits of Paradise resembling yet surpassed). The believer counting occurrences finds the image planted everywhere a people are invited upward: after the patient (13:24), after the believers in their Lord (18:31), after the race-winners here — the garden's geography always expressed in its river and its permanence. The sūrah's own final reward-clause will return the composition in personal address at v. 198: *Gardens with rivers flowing below, abiding therein — a welcome (*nuzul*) from God* — the wage of v. 136, by chapter's end, shown issued *by His own hospitality.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:137

> **Wonts have passed before you; so journey upon the earth and behold how the deniers fared in the end!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Sunan" Before "Sunnah": The Word's Larger Biology**

The chapter now turns from the Garden's portrait back to the field of history — the two panels of hope and warning alternating as the Book always alternates them: *qad khalat sunanun min qablikum* — "wonts have passed away before you" — *fa-sīrū fī al-arḍi fa-nẓurū kayfa kāna ʿāqibatu al-mukadhdhibīn* — "so journey in the earth and behold how was the end of the deniers." The word rendered *wonts* — *sunan*, plural of *sunnah* — holds, as the commentators and the source note, the full lineage of what Arabic hears here: an established way of conduct; a norm of practice set and followed; a culture in its habitual bearings. Its most famous usage in Islam is of course *the Sunnah* — the Prophet's normative path — but the Qur'an itself uses the word at three altitudes (and the source catalogs them): the wonts of preceding *peoples* (4:26; 8:38: "unless they forego what has already passed as wont of the ancients"; 15:13; 17:77; 18:55; 35:43) — denial, patron-pride, hoarding, obstruction; the *wont of God* in His handling of nations (33:38, 62; 35:43; 40:85; 48:23: "you will find no change in God's wont") — divine action's unvarying patterns: punishment of the obstinate, rescue of the steadfast, respite of the continued-sinner; and the Prophet's own *sunnah*, which sits inside the earlier two as his pattern extracted from all peoples' prompted histories. Verse 137 trades on all three beacons at once: people's wonts passed before you — and God's wont with them — and the Prophet's wont now stands before you. The pronoun-less admonition can even — as al-Qurṭubī indicates — be read elliptically: *[the communities of the] wonts have passed before you*: the bearers themselves, gone.

**"Journey in the Earth and Behold": Islam's Educational Mandate of Ruins**

Then comes the command that made Muslims, across the centuries, the first systematic travelers in pursuit of religious evidence: *fa-sīrū fī al-arḍ* — *journey in the land* — *fa-nẓurū kayfa kāna ʿāqibatu al-mukadhdhibīn* — *and behold how was the end of the deniers*. The *ʿāqibah* — as the source commentary specifies — is not merely "end" as termination but *result*: the upshot, consequence, the final state of a whole mode of life. The verses network is dense (10:39: *behold the end of the wrongdoers*; 10:73: *the end of those warned*; 16:36: *the end of the deniers*; 27:14; 30:9–10; 30:42; 40:21, 82: "have they not journeyed in the land and beheld the end of those before them? They were greater in strength and left greater marks — but God seized them in their sins; they had no defender against God") — and the named ruins were physically accessible to the Qur'an's first audience: the Arabian journeys passed the dwellings of ʿĀd (46:21–26) and Thamūd (27:45–52) — sandstone façades and rock-cities of al-Ḥijr on the trade-roads; the Greeks' Sinai and the Nabataean towns; the caravan-dwellers saw the crumbling tombs of Sodom along the Dead Sea road (37:137–38: "you pass by them in the morning and by night"): the Book is directing curriculum: *theolology made of scenery*. Al-Rāzī's pastoral note distinguishes the grades of the education: seeing *by report* is also gain (the Qur'an itself narrates the ends), but *seeing by eye* — as travel — is the stronger teacher; hence the lasting Muslim custom of visiting relic-fields with the prescribed posture of *iʿtibār* (lesson-taking, not romance) — the Prophet ﷺ at the wells of Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ warning his army: *"do not enter upon those who were punished except weeping; if you do not weep, then do not enter upon them, lest what befell them befall you"* (al-Bukhārī 433; Muslim 2980, from Ibn ʿUmar — on the expedition to Tabūk passing al-Ḥijr).

**The Uḥud Connection — And the Reader's**

Al-Qurṭubī directly fastens the verse into the Uḥud flow: having lost seventy-two martyrs and endured a tactical reversal, the believers are told to measure outcomes at the correct altitude: deniers have *always* ended the same way; the enemies who gloated yesterday are walking a documented road — whose terminus is visible in every cliff-city and drowned plain. And for the later reader the command converts to a standing travel-ethic: history-journeys (museums of dead empires, ruins of the self-glorious, chronicles of the arrogant) as devotional exercise; seeing *ʿāqibah* in every picture of fallen greatness; and sealing every such excursion with the verse's implicit prayer — 16:35's-conjoined plea: do not let my feet share this road. The wonts have passed; the Wont is continuing: *"you will find no change in the wont of God"* (35:43).

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:138

> **This is an exposition for mankind, and a guidance and exhortation for the reverent.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Hādhā Bayānun Lil-Nās": It's Already Explained**

The pause between movements (the deep Uḥud narrative resumes at v. 139) is filled with a signet-verse of the Book upon itself: *hādhā bayānun lil-nāsi wa hudan wa mawʿiẓatun lil-muttaqīn* — "this is an exposition for mankind, and a guidance and exhortation for the reverent." *Bayān* — ex-plaining, laying-bare, clear speech: the full demonstrative *hādhā* ("this") points in the commentators' two directions: to *the sūrah so far* — its hundred and thirty-eight verses: the creed-chapters, the family of ʿImrān, the delegations, the warnings, the trials announced, the ethics charted — *all of it already a bayān*: nothing crucial left obscure; to *the Qur'an entire* — whose self-descriptions this verse joins (2:185's "in it guidance for mankind and clear signs"; 10:57's exact twin: "there has come to you an exhortation (mawʿiẓah) from your Lord, and a healing for what is in breasts, and guidance and mercy for believers"; 16:89: "We sent down to you the Book as a clarification of everything"). The self-certifying of Scripture is not arrogance but *inventory*: after having watched Mary's vigil, Jesus's miracles, the mubāhalah-lifted face of the Prophet, the delegation of Najrān's priests, the analysis of Uḥud's first tremors — the reader is asked to *register* what a book this is: a *demonstration-engine*, not a hymn-book.

**Two Addressees, Three Gifts — And Their Distribution**

The verse's three nouns divide precisely across mankind's two classes: *bayān* — exposition — goes to *al-nās*, all people: clarity is owed to everyone, believer and denier; the demonstration that Mary was real, that Jesus was God's word, that the covenant binds, that Uḥud had meaning — addressed to the species entire: *the Book itself refuses to be the property of an eleé class*: its explication is public. The other two gifts have addressees slotted: *hudan wa mawʿiẓah lil-muttaqīn* — "guidance and exhortation-for-the-reverent": guidance (*hudā*) is the deeper *internal* leading — He who's muttaq gets not just the argument but the road itself under his feet; exhortation (*mawʿiẓah*) — heart-address, the counsel that pierces — again *to the muttaqīn*: not because God withholds them from others, but because only taqwā's receptors can receive them: the ear must be unsealed to hear exhortation; the foot must be willing to receive guidance: 17:41's doctrine — "We have dispensed in this Qur'an every kind of reminder, and it increases none save in aversion" — and 17:82's — "We send down of the Qur'an what is healing and mercy for the believers; and it increases the wrongdoers only in loss": the very same text, two biologies.

**The Verse's Standing Ministry**

Every recitation since has certified the three promises: the bayān continues to work on the unschooled multitudes — every year millions of non-Muslims read the Qur'an and find its demonstration-engine intact — and hudā and mawʿiẓah continue their specific commerce with hearts that form the two disciplines (fear of God, outpouring sincerity): the Book's own inner guild of listeners. The unassuming position of verse 138 — at the chapter's exact cusp before Uḥud's full flood — gives it the force of a title-page placed halfway through: *what you have read so far has been the demonstration; *what follows will test it in blood;* all of it, classed by God Himself, is addressed: to the species — explanation; to the reverent: guidance and warning, both.*
**Bayān: Demonstration as the First Name**

The verse assigns the whole communication three titles distributed across three audiences: *hādhā bayānun li-l-nās* — "this is a demonstration for mankind" — *wa hudan wa mawʿiẓatun li-l-muttaqīn* — "and guidance and exhortation for the reverent." *Bayān* — from the root of opening and clarifying — names the Book's own speech-mode: not information dropped but *demonstration*, things *shown forth* — and the chapter has been performing the title ever since: Adam and Jesus demonstrated in parallel (v. 59); Abraham's estate demonstrated by chronology (vv. 65–68); Uḥud demonstrated by its morning (vv. 121–155). The Raḥmān-sūrah's opening bayān — *"the Merciful taught the Qur'an; created man; taught him the bayān"* (55:1–4) — ranks the capacity itself among the primal gifts; al-Rāzī accordingly reads our clause as genre-naming: *this, the thing you are hearing, is the demonstration-figure itself* — a claim no rival composition has answered in thirteen centuries of attempts.

**Hudā and Mawʿiẓah: The Two Registers for the Reverent**

The distribution's second beam is heavier because its audience is committed: *guidance* — the road-showing in perpetuity, renewed at every re-reading — and *mawʿiẓah* — exhortation of the specific heart-softening kind the Arabic reserves for admonition that *reaches and warns together* (its root *w-ʿ-ẓ* producing the schoolroom-word of rebuke tempered by mercy). Yūnus's parallel unfolds the same two beams as the prophet's ministry-statement: *"there has come to you a mawʿiẓah from your Lord, and healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers"* (10:57) — mawʿiẓah arriving *from the Lord* to the chest's diseases, with guidance and mercy escorting. The verse thereby closes the Uḥud-file with the sūrah's own classification-labels: *demonstration to all listeners; guidance and softening-warning to those who shield themselves with God.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:139

> **Do not falter and do not grieve, for you will be ascendant if you are believers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Words After the Wound**

The full Uḥud narrative proper opens not with casualty lists but with first aid — two prohibitions and a promise shaken into one vial: *wa lā tahinū wa lā taḥzanū, wa antumu al-aʿlawna in kuntum muʾminīn* — "do not falter, and do not grieve; you are the ascendant, if you are believers." The first verb — *lā tahinū* — is from *wahn*: enervation, the softening of a structure's resolve; al-Qurṭubī glosses its total range: do not deem yourselves weak — the interior sag that precedes the outer collapse (47:35 wields the same word at the hour of peacemaking: *"so do not falter and call for peace, when you are the ascendant"* — the exact coupling again). The second — *lā taḥzanū* — do not *grieve*: al-Ṭabarī's concrete referent: grieve not over what befell you of loss and wound: the dead are named martyrs elsewhere; the here-spoken *ḥuzn* is the morale-fluid that bleeds away from an army — and a faith — after a setback. The two prohibitions together attend to the two time-directions of a broken heart: *wahn* is forward-looking (loss of force for what is coming); *ḥuzn* is backward-looking (loss of peace over what happened): God's field-medicine treats both limbs in one breath.

**"You Are the Ascendant" — Grammar as Prophecy**

The promise then arrives in a construction of unusual boldness: *wa antumu al-aʿlawn* — "and you are the uppermost" — pronominal *hum* of emphasis and the definite *al-*: *the* ascendant-party, by definition. What does ascendancy mean when seventy-two of your finest lie buried on the battlefield's edge? The commentators (Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī answering al-Qurṭubī's) unfold its layers: eventual triumph over the enemies (the commission that history delivered: Quraysh never again mustered the confidence of that expedition; within eight years the Muslim army stood at the walls of Makkah); the superior *end* and issue even when a hand-to-hand day goes sour (*ʿāqibah* — the chapter's own end-word of v. 137); moral and doctrinal height — the truth's side is, by position, the side occupied on high ground, no matter who charges when: the ascendant *if you are believers*. And al-Qurṭubī's grammatical note turns the phrase *in kuntum muʾminīn* ("if you are believers") into the conditional *idhan* of many readers — *"since you are believers"*: the ascent already belongs to you insofar as the īmān is intact: the one non-negotiable claim-ticket: let belief fall and the altitude reverts to altitude-unearned — ascent as *function of faith*, as at v. 110: not birthright, but operating condition.

**The Verse's Standing Service in Muslim History**

No battlefield-verse has seen longer service: recited by commanders before outnumbered encounters, whispered in prison cells, printed on refugee-camp walls — 3:139 courses through fourteen centuries of beaten-but-unbroken Islam. The tradition's internalization is worded by God's own parallel at 4:104 — *"do not flag in pursuit of the enemy: if you suffer pain, they suffer pain as you do, while you hope from God what they hope not"* — the full morale-equation of every conflict of principle. The believer personally translates the two prohibitions into daily commission: setbacks in work, reputation, provision are all *Uḥud-days in miniature*: if you are believers, none of those can rob you of the ascendant-position — because ascendancy is not the ledger of days; it is the Ledger of ends.
**The Double Negation as Prescription**

*Wa lā tahinū wa lā taḥzanū* — "and do not falter, and do not grieve": two prohibition-verbs addressing the two failure-modes of a wounded army-religion — *wahn*, faltering, the slowing and weakening of the limbs of resolve (a word for both body-flagging and morale-flagging), and *ḥuzn*, grieving, the heart's backward-facing distress. The commentators fix the order's exactness for the post-Uḥud moment: faltering is *about what remains to be done*; grieving is *about what has already happened* — and prohibition covers both time-directions, so that no quadrant of the defeated psychology is left unregulated. The twin at 4:104, revealed against the same event, shows the prescription already operational: *"do not falter in pursuing the people — if you are suffering, they are suffering as you suffer; and you hope from God what they do not hope."*

**Antum al-Aʿlawn: Ascendancy Declared, Condition Applied**

*Wa antum al-aʿlawn in kuntum muʾminīn* — "while you are the ascendant, if you are believers": the declaration is the verse's audacious center — spoken *to the wounded, the day after the wound* — and its little conditional is the sūrah's most-quoted clause in every pulpit since: *in kuntum muʾminīn* — *if you are believers* — faith itself nominated as ascendancy's only ingredient. Al-Ṭabarī: the upper hand is God's promise to the truthful, unconditioned by the morning's casualty-list; al-Qurṭubī: the conditional makes morale a *creed-department* — discouragement, after such a promise, becomes a question about one's īmān rather than about one's fortunes. Badr's seventy prisoners and Uḥud's seventy graves close one another's accounts under this verse: the community ascends by what it *is*, and what it is is verified in its response to mornings like these.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:140

> **If a wound afflicts you, a like wound has already afflicted that people. And such days We hand out in turns to mankind. And [this is] so that God may know those who believe, and take witnesses from among you—and God loves not the wrongdoers—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wound for Wound: The Parity That Precedes the Alternation**

The field-medicine continues, now with a *differential diagnosis*: *in yamsaskum qarḥun fa-qad massa al-qawma qarḥun mithluh* — "if a wound has touched you, indeed a like wound has touched that people." *Qarḥ* — wound, gash — is chosen with its parity-twin right in the verse: *your* gash has a match on *their* side: at Badr one year before, the same Quraysh who today erect their boast carried seventy dead and seventy captive out of a morning's three hours — whose tribal aristocracy was, in the words of history, decapitated in an afternoon. The exactness of the correspondence is itself pedagogic (Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī): your loss is not anomaly; it is a *repeat* — the same inventory of hurt, distributed one year to them, this year to you: wounds went even rounds. And the universal law follows immediately: *wa tilka al-ayyāmu nudāwiluhā bayna al-nās* — "and such days We cause to alternate among mankind": *mudāwalah* — rotation, the taking of turns: days do not settle on one party; they revolve: the old Arabic proverb al-Ṭabarī quotes — *yawmun laka wa yawmun ʿalayk* — a day for you, a day against you — receives its full theological perfecting: the alternation is *not mechanics* — not blind Fate's wheel, in the pagan sense — but *God is rotating them*: *nudāwiluhā*: We *hand them out* in turns: an administration, deliberate and wise (al-Rāzī: the point is ephemerality — the world, by construction, refuses to be any party's steady possession).

**Why the Rotation? — Two Purposes Named**

Then the verse names the two curriculum-aims for which God rotates the day-beams: *wa li-yaʿlama Allāhu alladhīna āmanū* — "and so that God may know those who believe": the expression — *so that God may know* — has generated the Book's most careful doctrinal commentary (see the discussion at 2:143 and al-Zamakhsharī's own grammatical frame): not that the All-Knowing learns anything — verse 139's own *if you are believers* already stands upon complete knowledge — but that God makes *visible, existent, operative in the world of testimony* what He knows eternally: Arabic idiom permits "I know no good in him" to mean "he had none to show" (al-Zamakhsharī's analogy, cited in the source): the trials bring into being *witnessable reality*: faith on display — not for God's information but for the creation's evidence and the soul's own harvest (29:2–3 states the doctrine in naked form: "do people think they will be left to say 'we believe' and not be tried? We tried those before them, and God knows-in-deed the truthful and knows the liars").

And the second aim, in words of extraordinary dignity: *wa yattakhidha minkum shuhadāʾ* — "and to take from among you witnesses": *shuhadāʾ* in this station means — as the whole tafsiric majority (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī) reads it — *martyrs*: those who testify with their blood: God *takes* them — the verb is elevating, not confiscating: He selects for His own alcove, out of the battlefield's apparent wreckage, the men whose deaths are crowned as testimony: Uḥud's seventy-two, including Ḥamzah the Prophet's uncle and Muṣʿab the standard-bearer, were not casualties of mismanagement but *appointments*: the rotation of the days was, in their case, the mechanism of promotion: the Prophet ﷺ himself was reported to have said later, pointing at Uḥud's mountain: *"this is a mountain that loves us and we love it"* (al-Bukhārī 2889); and standing over the martyrs' graves he addressed them: *"I bear witness over these..."* with the blessing he gave at their graves — the tradition preserves his periodic visits of salām upon them as upon living guests (from Ibn ʿUmar — the Prophet visited them and greeted them, and Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthmān after him continued the practice).

**"God Loves Not the Wrongdoers" — The Clause That Closes**

The dual-purpose recital is closed with the clause that prevents every misreading: *wa Allāhu lā yuḥibbu al-ẓālimīn* — "and God loves not the wrongdoers": the rotation of days is not God's love exchanged for hatred: those wound-delivering idolaters were still ẓālimūn, and still love-barred in God's register — His using their swords as His instruments changes nothing of their classification: the instrument is not loved; the outcome is just; and the martyrs are taken. Readers of temperament vulnerable to the doubt "did God's friendship fail at Uḥud?" are answered with one line: *the love-classes (muḥsinūn, muttaqūn, ṣābirūn, shākirūn) are not the same as the win-classes of every given afternoon* — the chapter has already distinguished them at length (vv. 76, 134, 146, 148, 159's coming cadences of love). Wound-parity today, witnesses taken, and love never transferred: the whole theodicy of the Uḥud morning in one verse.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:141

> **and so that God may assay those who believe and blight the disbelievers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Yumaḥḥiṣ": The Refining Fire Has a Name**

Verse 141 extends the ledger of aims with two more purpose-clauses — completing a curriculum of four (know the believers; take witnesses; assay the believers; blight the disbelievers) — and its first verb is technical: *wa li-yumaḥḥiṣa Allāhu alladhīna āmanū* — "and so that God may assay those who believe." *Tamḥīṣ* is the metallurgist's word: the clearing-off of dross from metal in the fire — the removal of impurity from the genuine article. What does a believer's dross consist of? The age of religious scholarship specified it: sins clinging to the heart (the chapter's whole iṣrār-lesson of vv. 135–136); the concealed allegiances to worldliness that come up in the moment of sacrifice (the *dunyā*-desire v. 152 will name in the archers' own instance); the unrecognized reliance upon numbers and plans rather than upon the Lord who hands out the days (v. 140's lesson). Al-Ṭabarī's gloss centers *tamḥīṣ* at *patience under trials*: refined by testing. The most eloquent image the tradition gave the clause is the hadith of Musaylimah's opposite — in Abū Hurayrah's report:

> *"Trials descend upon hearts as the reed-woven mat is woven, stick by stick: any heart that soaks them in is marked with a black spot; any heart that rejects them, with a white spot — till hearts are of two kinds: a white one like smooth stone — no trial harms it as long as heavens and earth endure — and a black, dust-colored one like an up-turned vessel..."* (Muslim 144, at length)

Assaying is thus mercy's anvil — the refiner does not hate the ore he heats; the heat is precisely his regard.

**"Wa Yamḥaqa al-Kāfirīn": The Fade of the Other Side**

The companion verb matches it metalinguistically: *wa yamḥaqa al-kāfirīn* — "and blight the disbelievers": *maḥq* is the opposite motion of blessing: the quiet draining-away of substance from what looks full — the same word as 2:276's "God blights ribā," here deployed upon the disbelieving war-party itself: diminishment until, as al-Rāzī's gloss says, *there is no sight left of it*: the decrease of a thing by degrees until it disappears. Not instant annihilation — God does not promise to vanish the opposition in one flash — but *blight*: the structural fade: their number hollows out; their energy exhausts; their causes fail of recurrence. History bore it out in the case Uḥud belonged to: the Quraysh that came yearly to Madīnah progressively *thinned*: the Naḍīr exiled, the Qurayẓah gone, the Khaybar garrison defeated, the Aḥzāb confederacy dissolved in wind and trench — each successive "day" they rotated toward was weaker than the one before, until the eleventh-year conquest day found no army to muster at all: maḥq at documentary scale.

**Assay and Blight — The Double Track Under Every Setback**

For readers in every later age of testing, the verse thus maps what is *actually happening* during a season of loss: two concurrent processes, one in each camp: the believers under the refiner's assay (their dross burning off, their sincerities sharpened) and the adversaries under blight (their totality thinning, though their daily gloating carries on). The rotation of days (v. 140) is thus not the doctrine of equal fortunes; it is the doctrine of counter-directed processes visible only to faith: the assayed climb as the blighted sink, even while the interim scoreboard says the opposite. The believers' one duty in the process is to remain metal worth refining: the Refiner wastes no fire on mere dust.
**Yamīz: The Separation-Verb and Its Badr Precedent**

*Wa li-yamīza Allāhu lladhīna kafarū* — "and that God might separate the disbelievers": the second purpose-clause of the Uḥud morning stands the same verb the Book applied to Badr's own outcome — *"that God might distinguish the foul from the fair"* (8:37, *li-yamīza Allāhu al-khabītha min al-ṭayyib*) — and the two deployments assemble the separation-doctrine complete: battle as *sorting* — at Badr, foul from fair; at Uḥud, committed from pretending (v. 140's first purpose-clause, the believers' assaying) and here, *the disbelieving from every proximity to triumph*. Al-Qurṭubī notices the reciprocity patiently: the sūrah's two battles ended in opposite parades — Badr's victory-parade and Uḥud's wound-parade — yet the *yamīz* ran in both: the war's own arithmetic is not the verdict; the *sorting* is.

**Foul and Fair as Heart-Inventory**

The separation-direction reaches the individual interior in the Prophet's own cardiology:

> *"Truly the believer is like an ear of wheat: the wind bends it and straightens it... and the hypocrite is like the pine-conifer: standing fixed until it is snapped."* (paraphrased register of the famous Muslim 2809/2811 series)

— and its register-prime: *"When a servant sins, a black dot is dotted on his heart; if he abandons and seeks forgiveness, his heart is polished; and if he returns, it is increased until it overtops his heart — that is the *rān* which God mentioned: *nay, what they were earning has rusted over their hearts*."* (al-Tirmidhī 3334, ṣaḥīḥ, from Abū Hurayrah; citing 83:14)

The Uḥud-clause thereby instructs every later morning: outcomes are sorters, not grades; and the believer reads defeat exactly as v. 134 trained him — *the foul separated from the fair, then the fair paid the wage of the workers.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:142

> **Or did you suppose that you would enter the Garden without God knowing those among you who strived, and without knowing those who were patient?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rhetorical Awakening**

Then God addresses, in one long question, the assumption the wounded bears unknowingly: that Paradise is administered by self-declaration: *am ḥasibtum an tadkhulū al-jannata wa lammā yaʿlami Allāhu alladhīna jāhadū minkum wa yaʿlama al-ṣābirīn* — "or did you suppose you would enter the Garden without God knowing those of you who strived, and knowing the patient?" The *am ḥasibtum* formula — "or did you *reckon*?" — is the Book's classic device for asserting against human expectation (its twin at 29:2 runs the same argument in the Book's own parallel: "do people think they will be left saying 'we believe' without being tried?"), and *lammā* compounds it — "not yet": entry is on hold pending an identification, and the identification happens only in *event*: strive, and God *knows* you as striver; be patient, and He *knows* you as patient — while yet you stand theory-idle, you are *not yet* either.

**What "Knowing" Means at the Gate**
