Al-Rāzī's commentary unpacks the theology exactly: the verse does not impute a deficit in omniscience; it tells you that the gate of the Garden opens *on the record of deeds*, not on the record of identities: God knows eternally; but the created rank *jāhid/ṣābir* exists only by enactment: between heaven's intended list and manifest reality stands your *performance*: al-Rāzī paraphrases the sense rightly: as if to say, I know no striving in this one — by which we mean: there is none: epistemic language describing moral facts. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī also note the alternate syntactic bridge some read ("that He might know *thereby* the patient"), but the senses coincide: both striver and patient are identified through trial, together — and Uḥud was, in point of fact, the identifying event: every man of that morning was *made manifest* by it: the archers' wavering, the hypocrites' retreat and taunting (vv. 154, 166-168), the steadfast around the Prophet's wounded person, the women who took up waterskins and swords — all were *known* by noon in the created sense; the earth now contains their story as permanent witness; the Garden's gates now hold their names.

**Al-Rāzī's Homily on Love — The Commentary Tradition at Its Height**

Al-Rāzī's own extended meditation on this verse has remained across the centuries among the most quoted expository passages in tafsīr — it deserves to be heard here in full:

> *"Know that love of this world cannot coexist with happiness in the Hereafter: to the degree that one of them increases, the other diminishes. For the happiness of this world is only achieved by the heart's occupation with worldliness, and the happiness of the Hereafter is only achieved by emptying the heart of all that is other than God and filling it with the love of God. And not everyone who affirms the religion of God is truthful in it. The difference lies in the sway of things hated and things loved. True love is that which does not diminish at the onset of hardship and does not increase at the time of fulfillment: if your love survives the arrival of suffering, it has been shown true."* (al-Rāzī on 3:142)

The instrumentation of the human heart is here calibrated as finely as in any analytic write-up of the spiritual life: love's *authenticity-conditions* are constancy under hardship, not ardor at gratification; the trial verses are, accordingly, *authenticators*: without God knowing — *evincing in His moral world* — the striver and the patient, no Garden-entry: not because God withholds gift, but because gift's very shape fits *wrought* souls: the unassayed would not fit the pasture prepared for the muttaqīn.

For the personal believer the verse remains the first mirror of fasting, crisis, loss, temptation: every hardship whispers the same *am ḥasibtum*: did you think the Garden would be cheaper than the résumé? And every endurance converts the whisper into receipt: the knowing is accumulating; the gate is reading your file.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:143

> **You did indeed long for death before you met it. Now you have seen it, looking on.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Longing Confessed, the Sight Attained**

The verse addresses the believers who had missed Badr and had spent the whole intervening year saying, in many registers of sincerity, *would that we had another day like it — we would show God what He loves*: *wa la-qad kuntum tamannawna al-mawta min qabli an talqawh* — "and indeed you used to long for death before meeting it" — *la-qad raʾaytumūhu wa antum tanẓurūn* — "now you have seen it, while you look on." The structure of the address is divine tenderness: it does not mock; it states: you *used* to wish — the wish has been *fulfilled*: death passed in your full view this morning: *tanẓurūn* — while you watch: no longer a rumor, no longer a poem. Al-Ṭabarī explains the *tamannī* exactly: the longing was for the *fighting-that-might-lead-to-death* — the martyrdom-seat the Badr martyrs were visibly occupying across the year, envied by those at home — the same longing that made the young men press the Prophet out of Madinah to battle (v. 121's context): God granted the wish contents: a day at Uḥud came; death came upon some; the rest *saw* it — truly.

**The Rhetoric of Fulfillment — A Test in Reverse**

The commentators (al-Qurṭubī especially) unpack what follows the *fulfilled longing*: several heard in *wa antum tanẓurūn* an implied question — you have seen it looking on *— so why then did some flee?* (v. 144's context at Uḥud's rout-hour) — al-Qurṭubī's own reading: the verse divides the men by their reactions to the very thing they wished for: the longing was real; its object arrived; some stood upon the meeting with honor — and God took from them the martyrs He wished (v. 140); and some *turned away at the sight* — and found in the failure of the flesh the great humbling that teaches all future longing to be schooled: do not wish for what you cannot carry; and do carry it when it comes. The Prophet's ﷺ standing instruction seals the pastoral balancing that 3:143 establishes: *"None of you should wish for death because of harm that has befallen him; if he must do something, let him say: O God, keep me alive so long as life is better for me, and take me when death is better for me."* (al-Bukhārī 6351, 5671; Muslim 2680, from Anas): longing for the conditions of true service — yes; longing for *escape* — no: the two are separated at this very verse's line.

**The Verse's Surgical Service**

At Uḥud itself the test served its diagnostic ends: the heroism of the steadfast who *did* receive the martyrdom they had asked for is among the death-scenes the tradition holds most dear — Ḥamzah's last defiance at center-field ("O God, I seek refuge" in his mouth); Ṣaʿd ibn al-Rabīʿ found with seventy wounds still breathing: *"tell my people: if the Prophet is safe, my excuse is safe in God"*: the wished-for death arriving and being *met with consent* — the sight of a true tamannī. And the lesson for every believer who has ever said *I wish God would test me, that He might see my faith* — the verse teaches: longings are promises God may cash. Treasure them accordingly: desire courage, then; and when the longed-for hour comes — whether on a battlefield, or in a hospital corridor at 3 a.m., or in a moment where truth-telling costs a career — recognize the sight you asked for: *you have seen it, looking on — now show what the wish meant*.
**Tamannī al-Mawt: The Pre-Theatre Longing of the Brave**

*Wa laqad kuntum tamannawna al-mawta min qabli an talqawhu* — "and you had longed for death before you met it": God's reminder is gentle in grammar and unsparing in content — addressed to the men of verified courage who had *longed* for the martyr's death while it was distant literature, it records the Book's standing lesson about *aspiration tested*: praising death at a distance is one of the species of piety; meeting it is another. The verse's two complements — *fa-qad raʾaytumūhu wa antum tanẓurūn* — "now you have seen it, looking on" — deliver the lesson's sight: the longed-for thing has been *passed before the eyes* at spear-length, and the longing is hereby examined. Al-Rāzī's pastoral note deserves its room: longing for the martyr's death is no sin — the prohibition-hadith (al-Bukhārī 6351: *"let none of you wish for death ... either a doer of good who may increase, or a doer of ill who may apologize"*) guards the *servant's* patience; the thirty-year-old of Uḥud's standard is thereby not rebuked for the longing but *schooled* by the meeting.

**2:94–96: The Longing Test Elsewhere**

The Book levels the identical trial at other pulpits: *"say: if the Last Abode with God is yours alone, apart from mankind, then long for death, if you are truthful"* (2:94), with its sequel's camera-proof — *"they will never long for it, for what their hands have forwarded"* (2:95) — and its psychology-verdict in 62:6–8 retorted against the claimants: *"say: you who became Jews — if you claim you are God's patrons apart from mankind, then long for death, if you are truthful; and they long for it never, because of what their hands have sent before — and God is Knowing of the wrongdoers. Say: indeed the death you flee from — it will meet you."* Longing for death is thus the Book's load-bearing claim-test: the confident ask for it; the guilty refuse it; the believing are taught neither to demand it nor to flee it — only to be ready when its morning arrives.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:144

> **Muhammad is naught but a messenger; messengers have passed before him. So if he dies or is slain, will you turn back on your heels? Whosoever turns back on his heels will not harm God in the least, and God will reward the thankful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verse the Rumor Provoked**

This is among the twenty most consequential verses of the Qur'an — revealed in relation to Uḥud's darkest fog, and publicly recited again at the moment of the Prophet's actual death — and its every phrase is load-bearing. At Uḥud, when the Prophet ﷺ lost consciousness among the wounded and word raced the field that he had been killed, the army buckled — some dropped their weapons in the open field; the hypocrite-party took the moment to sneer its thesis: *had he been a prophet, death would not have reached him*; and the rumor nearly inverted the nature of the mission itself — as though Islam had been a *personality-cult in God's name* — which is precisely the doctrinal confusion the verse descends to cut off forever: *wa mā Muḥammadun illā rasūl* — "and Muḥammad is nothing except a messenger": a function, an office, a vessel: *qad khalat min qablihi al-rusul* — "messengers have passed away before him": Moses died on the edge of Moab; Jesus was raised; John was slain; Abraham my friend was buried at Hebron: prophecy's mechanism is not the immortality of the messenger — proof of prophecy is the message; and the message is from above the death that reaches all flesh. *A-fa-in māta aw qutila-nqalabtum ʿalā aʿqābikum* — "if he dies or is slain, will you then turn back on your heels?" — the turnback-*ʿalā al-ʿaqib*: the exact phrase the Book assigns to apostasy (v. 149 adjoins)): your islam was *in God* — or was it in the visible comfort of Muḥammad's breathing presence? — the diagnostic question of every faith after every death.

**Abū Bakr's Recital: The Verse in History**

The verse's full force detonated ten years later, in the debate-chambered confusion of the Prophet's actual death-day. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, sword half-drawn in denial, strode among the stunned Muslims declaring the Messenger had only gone as Moses went to the mountain, and would return — until Abū Bakr, after entering, uncovering the noble face, kissing it, and whispering *"you are sweet in life and sweet in death"*, came out and delivered the address that became the ummah's constitutional precedent:

> *"O people! Whoever worshiped Muḥammad — know that Muḥammad has died. And whoever worshiped God — know that God is Living and does not die." Then he recited: "Muḥammad is naught but a messenger; messengers have passed before him..." — and, in the narration, "it was as though the people had never heard the verse before that day" — and ʿUmar said: "By God, it is as if I had never recited it *until that day*; I fell to the ground and my legs could not carry me."* (al-Bukhārī 3667, 1241; and the fuller scene in the sīrah-reports; the ʿUmar-attestation is preserved in the tafsīr and in al-Bukhārī's own recension of the day)

A building held together had Abū Bakr not carried this verse into that courtyard: the community-on-the-step's whole post-prophetic existence was pivoted upon it: no defenders emerged demanding a living imam in his body's continuation; islam of the worshipers-of-God began at the threshold of the worshipers-of-God. And the verse's own companion-at-Uḥud words are preserved in the sīrah as the earlier modeling of the same act: the Companion's cry on the field, carried in the source commentary, "O people — if Muḥammad has died, then the Lord of Muḥammad does not die! How shall you live after the Messenger of God? Fight as he fought, and die as he died" — the answer born instantly to one steadfast man, long before the verse's second test.

**"He Will Not Harm God in the Least" — And the Thankful Will Be Rewarded**

The theological clauses close the case with the two positions: *wa man yanqalib ʿalā ʿaqibayhi fa-lan yaḍurra Allāha shayʾan* — "who turns back on his heels harms God not at all": the same doctrine ribā's verse wraps at 2:164 family, and the chapter's 3:97 closed with (*God is free of need of the worlds*): defections damage defectors; God's road rolls on with or without. And the counter-clause plants the verse's own sufficient reason to stand: *wa sa-yajzi Allāhu al-shākirīn* — "and God shall reward the thankful": *al-shākirīn*: those who thank — gratitude under bereavement, gratitude as the form loyalty takes after death removes the beloved object: the Prophet's whole ummah is divided by this verse, on any day a tower falls, into *turnbackers* and *thankers*. May God make us of the shākirīn.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:145

> **It is not for any soul to die save by God's Leave—an enjoined term. Yet whosoever desires the reward of this world, We shall give him of it; and whosoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We shall give him of it. And We shall reward the thankful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Death's Registry Is Closed: The Verse of Terrified Relief**

The previous verse asked the dark question (if the messenger dies — will you turn back?); the present verse answers the panic behind every fear of every death that has ever been: *wa mā kāna li-nafsin an tamūta illā bi-idhni Allāhi kitāban muʾajjalā* — "it is not for any soul to die except by God's leave — a written, appointed term." Three nested facts: (1) death requires *permission* — no arrow, no plague, no ten-thousand odds can kill outside the license: the projectile's path is a line in a ledger first; (2) the permission is *written* — *kitāb*: a document, set down, existing: not improvised; (3) the document has an *appointed term* — *muʾajjal*: scheduled: what is scheduled cannot be early by an hour nor late by a breath (63:11: "God never delays a soul when its term has come"). The commentators immediately read the verse's two directions (al-Rāzī among the most exact): against the coward: flight cannot postpone death, so want not flight; and against the fatalist-in-reverse: courage cannot advance it, so want not recklessness — the door of mortality opens on one appointment; your *character* in the corridor before it is yours. The verse also barricades forever the hypocrites' mockery at Uḥud ("had they stayed with us, they would not have died" — lodged, as v. 168 will record, in their own words): response: *the scheduled would have gone forth out of their houses to their lying-places* (v. 154's own sealer), since the ledger lies above geography. The practical ethics the scholars distilled is the Muslim doctrine of courage: *fear not any death whose time has not come; want not any life whose time has*: heroism and calm in one herbal.

**The Two Desires and the Two Payouts**

Then the verse pivots to the ledger of *intentions* — and in this pivot the whole previous doctrine of risk is joined to the doctrine of reward: *wa man yurid thawāba al-dunyā nuʾtihi minhā; wa man yurid thawāba al-ākhirati nuʾtihi minhā* — "whosoever desires the reward of this world — We give him of it; and whosoever desires the reward of the Hereafter — We give him of it." The two *thawābs* (rewards) and the two *givings*, set in parallel — with an asymmetry the commentators (al-Rāzī; al-Qurṭubī's own extension) mark as decisive: *minhā* ("of it") — the partitive *of* — recurs in *both* clauses, yet only the Hereafter-clause closes with... *wa sa-najzī al-shākirīn* — "and We shall reward the thankful": the dunyā-desire receives its of-it — spoils, glory, songs — *exhaustively*: what it sought is what it gets, and nothing more arrives with it (the long hadith the source invokes — the three first thrown into the Fire: the warrior, the philantropist, the scholar, each told *you acted to be called brave/generous/learned — and so it was said*: Muslim 1905, quoted already at v. 117); the ākhirah-desire is not subtracted but *showered*: its of-it arrives with worship, hidden accounts, and the endowment of the thanked — *the thankful* named once more (v. 144's own ending, repeated in echo): God pays the Godward hearts twice — the gift asked, and the gift of gratitude's reward.

**The Dual Aim That Is Not Split**

The verse's wellness-code for balanced wanting — which the source rightly marks by reference to 2:201 ("our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter") — is the reader's needed complement: Islam does not preach contempt of dunyā-good: it *reorders* it: recognition-wealth, contest-victory, livelihood — these are lawfully welcomed *as provision*; they fail only when constituting the *desire*: the pivot-word of the verse is *yurīd* — wants, intends, desires: the same battle-spoils that made the archers slip (v. 152) would make other men among the same army of God blessed increases: the differentiator is never the *object* taken but the *orientation* of the wisher at the taking: *We shall give him of it* — both ways: the despisers of the Hereafter receive their full wage here, and leave the Field with it: the askers of the outworld find it — and find, behind it, the thankers' reward that outpaces all asking.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:146

> **How many a prophet had many devoted men fight alongside him! They did not then falter in the face of what befell them in the way of God, nor did they weaken, nor did they demean themselves. And God loves the patient.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Precedent-Lineage: This Has Happened Before, and They Stood**

The comfort of Uḥud's aftermath is now sought in the annals of prophecy itself: *wa ka-ayyin min nabiyyin qātala maʿahu ribbiyyūna kathīr* — "how many a prophet fought, with whom fought many devoted men!" *Ka-ayyin* — how many a — the particle of large-number wonder (wa kam min nabi': Arabic's way of exclaiming at multitude): the Uḥud morning is not the first morning a godly company took wounds: prophet-led bands have been beaten before, and the line of them runs through history — Moses and the tribes at the edge of the promise (v. 146's own fourteenth parallel family at 5:21–29: the faithless *stayed home*; the steadfast prophets called, nevertheless); David and Saul's remnant at the torrent (2:249–251, tested by the river and coming out, the few, saying: "how often has a small party overcome a numerous host, by God's leave"); the friars of the captivity; the resistants of every persecuted prophet. The reading of *ribbiyyūn* — devoted men — has two folds the commentators both retain (al-Zamakhsharī inside the source among them): derived of *rabb* — God-tied men, *rabbāniyyūn* (v. 79's sages, the studious-worshipers) — the fighting companions of prophets as men-of-learning-and-piety; and (al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī) derived of *ribb*: large congregated numbers — *multitudes*: stalwart masses: prophethood surrounded by ranks.

**The Three Negations — A Creed of Bearing**

And then the verse's charter — the moral portrait the whole Uḥud address is ultimately painting: *fa-mā wahanū li-mā aṣābahum fī sabīli Allāhi wa mā ḍaʿufū wa mā istakānū* — "they did not falter at what befell them in the way of God, nor did they weaken, nor did they demean themselves": three escalating negatives: (1) *mā wahanū* — did not *soften* at the wound: the *wahn* word of verse 139 enclosing anew — resolve kept its hardness; (2) *mā ḍaʿufū* — did not *lose capacity*: not only nerve but *resource* held — they continued planning, standing, working; (3) *mā istakānū* — did not *demean themselves*; *istakāna*: bending low before the stronger: the base-creep of self-abasement: asking pardon of pride's victors, taking the lowered station an oppressor offers to his beaten: *they did not abase* — the hardest discipline of all, for pain defeats the body in minutes but humiliation is contracted only by *consent*: they stood at perfect height before taller men. The three negations together total the whole spirit-manner of the prophets' companions: endurance of the *pain*, preservation of the *power*, refusal of the *bowed head*: for the Book's law is that God tests the first two and never licenses the third.

**"And God Loves the Patient" — The Predicate That Crowns the Ancestry**

The verse seals again with the love-predicate: *wa Allāhu yuḥibbu al-ṣābirīn* — "and God loves the patient" — re-ringing in the sūrah's running chime (God loves the reverent, the trusters, the relied, the beneficent, now the *patient*): the predicate is chosen after the three negations because endurance is the positive content of them all: *wahn, ḍuʿf, istikānah* are precisely the three *failures of ṣabr* — the soul's softening, the body's falling, the spirit's bowing; where the ṣābir endures all three tests at once. The tradition's own commentary on the practice of ṣabr is the Prophet's: the entire month of fasting named in his telling as "the month of patience" and the famous exchange: *ʿĀsim? No — the sure report: "ṣabr is illumination"* (Muslim 223 — *al-ṣabru ḍiyāʾ*) — patience as light-granting: it reveals what panic conceals. And at Uḥud the lineage-verse came true in men by name: al-Zubayr refusing withdrawal; ʿAlī binding the Prophet's wounds between ventures; Umm ʿAmārah Nasībah bint Kaʿb standing in front of the Prophet shielding with her body till the Prophet said of her (al-Bukhārī 4076, in the Uḥud reports): "the stand of so-and-so was better than the stand of so-and-so" — men and women now entered in the Book's permanent roll of the *ribbiyyūn* — with the whole ummah invited, by this verse, to take its own station at the same roll.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:147

> **Their words were but to say, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our prodigality in our affairs, and make firm our steps, and help us against the disbelieving people."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Whole Speech of History's Steadfast, in One Prayer**

The portrait of the *ribbiyyūn* is completed with the verse God reports as *the entirety of their discourse*: *wa mā kāna qawlahum illā an qālū* — "and their speech was nothing but that they said": the saints' *total* public oratory, summed up by God Himself, is this appeal — *rabbanā ighfir lanā dhunūbanā wa isrāfanā fī amrinā, wa thabbit aqdāmanā, wa-nṣurnā ʿalā al-qawmi al-kāfirīn* — "our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excess in our affair; make firm our feet; and help us against the disbelieving people." Three petitions, exactly ordered, and the ordering is a theology.

**First: forgiveness, before everything.** Before asking for victory they ask for pardon — *dhunūbanā* — our sins — *wa isrāfanā fī amrinā* — and our *israf* in our affair: *isrāf*: going beyond bounds: waste, excess, prodigality — as al-Qurṭubī notes, some took the pair as listing small and great transgressions; others read it as the whole clause inventory: whatever fault and whatever overshoot there has been in our *amr* — our mission-management: our own conduct of this business: the expectation-warriors of God begin by leasing their claim *upward*, not outward: they audit themselves first, since — the whole chapter has established — the only thing that can turn God's help aside against His believing party is their own unforgiven state. David's raw honesty after victory at the gate of the valleymen (2:250) ran the same course: "our Lord, pour patience upon us": the looking-in before the looking-up is the standing ritual of prophets' companies at their low points: *what thieves our reinforcements is our own file; so clear it first*.

**Second: firm feet.** *Thabbit aqdāmanā* — make firm our *aqdām*: feet: battlefield language: slipping feet lose battles; sound hearts on unsound footing still fall: firmness requested at the *interface* of body and ground — the prayer covers biology and spirit in one word: *all that keeps us from sliding*: no romantic heroism is claimed: they know feet slip (v. 152 had just recorded feet that slid); they ask the Slipper-proofing from above.

**Third: the victory request — *nṣurnā ʿalā al-qawmi al-kāfirīn* — help us against the disbelieving people.** Named last, on the prepared base: self-purified, stance-firmed — *then* the outward contest. God's own answer arrives in the next verse (v. 148): He gave them the reward of this world *and* the better reward of the Hereafter — two payments on the one prayer — because the prayer itself was the proof of its own worthiness.

**The Standing Duʿāʾ of the Ummah**

The verse immediately became one of Islam's living prayers — whispered by armies, schools, sickrooms, and by ordinary believers at any doorstep of risk. Its three joints compose a *complete* model of how the Book wants requests constructed: (1) discharge the guilt-account first — all duʿāʾs in the scripture of prophets (Adam — 7:23; Moses — 28:16; Jonah — 21:87; Joseph — 12:101) begin at confession; (2) ask for *firmness*, not exemption — the saints' regular currency is not rescue-out-of but standing-power-through; (3) only then ask for the outward object, and in its generic form — *against the disbelieving party*: a formula that fit every prophet's band and fits every believer's contest-filled life: *three clauses: clear my file, plant my feet, and God: the rest*: the most economical war-prayer ever revealed, and the most heard.
**The Priests of Battle: The Duʿāʾ's Three Requests**

The verse records the whole of their speech under fire — *wa mā kāna qawlahum illā an qālū* — "and their speech was only that they said" — then the prayer: *rabbanā-ghfir lanā dhunūbanā wa isrāfanā fī amrinā* — "our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excess in our affair" — *wa thabbit aqdāmanā* — "and make firm our feet" — *wa-nṣurnā ʿalā al-qawmi al-kāfirīn* — "and help us against the disbelieving people." The anatomy is a complete field-liturgy: confession first (sins, and the *isrāf* — wasteful overshoot — in *our affair*, the campaign itself); grounding second (feet made firm); the request for victory *third and last* — and the commentators mark the order as the community's everlasting protocol: no help demanded before forgiveness sought; no standing asked before footing secured.

**2:250: Where the Prayer Was First Standard-Issue**

The three requests are nearly verbatim the army-prayer passed down the prophetic line, for Ṭālūt's exhausted few said it at the valley of Goliath: *"our Lord — pour out patience upon us, and make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people"* (2:250) — the same *thabbit aqdāmanā* at the center, the same closing-clause against the kāfirs — and the Book stages the repetition deliberately: Muhammad's companions, praying the patriarchs' battlefield words, are hereby shown *in the same army*: the forces of God have one prayer-book. The *sabab al-khāṣṣ* of the verse fixes its station-world the more: David's three hundred praying as Muhammad's three hundred would — God's doors open to the small army that begins with its own sins rather than the enemy's numbers.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:148

> **And God gave them the reward of this world and the most beautiful reward of the Hereafter, and God loves the virtuous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Payout on the Prayer: Two Currencies**

The answer to the three-petition prayer arrives at once, in God's own tense of swift fulfillment: *fa-ātāhumu Allāhu thawāba al-dunyā wa ḥusna thawābi al-ākhirah* — "so God gave them the reward of the world, and the most beautiful reward of the Hereafter." The pairing is among the Book's consistent doctrinal settlements: the two worlds are not rivals to be either-ored; the righteous *ribbiyyūn* were paid in *both*: (1) *thawāb al-dunyā* — the world's reward: al-Ṭabarī and the commentators name its ordinary wages — *victory, spoils, consolidation, alive to witness the sealing of their cause*: history kept the receipts: the small remnant of each prophet's party that stood through the worst hour ended up, within the plan of God, seated upon inheritances — the Israelites after Pharaoh, David's remnant entering Jerusalem, the Muslims of Uḥud within five years looting the Khaybar estates, within eight walking into Makkah without a battle; (2) *wa ḥusna thawābi al-ākhirah* — and the *most beautiful* of the Hereafter's reward — note the comparative *ḥusnā*: the world's wage is *a* reward; the outworld's is *the beautiful*: the grading is done by God Himself — the daily harvest of the steadfast dwarfed by the everlasting one: same labor, two payscales (the prayer of 2:201 honored — "give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter"} — the Book's own proof that balance, not fleeing, is the intended discipline).

**The Third Clause: The Love That Outranks Both Payments**

And the verse closes with its repeated chime: *wa Allāhu yuḥibbu al-muḥsinīn* — "and God loves the virtuous." After two payables, the gift of gifts is spoken last: God's *love* — the predicate-band that has now crowned the chapter's three classes-patient (v. 146), reverent (v. 76), and here — as in v. 134 — the *muḥsinīn*: those of *iḥsān* — the doing-of-beauty. Why is love named *after* both rewards? Because rewards, by their nature, remain *payables* — contracted, registered, finished at receipt; love is *relation* — ongoing, infinite, the final end of every lawful pursuit. The sage tradition reduced the entire theology of commerce-with-God to this exact order: work for the Hereafter — you will also get the world (as David's kingdom outlived Saul's); work for the *world* only — you will get that, *and that alone* (v. 145's *minhā*); but work for *God's love* — and the two rewards arrive as *annexes* of the relationship: *iḥsān* is defined by the Prophet as worshiping God "as though you see Him" (Muslim 8) — and its pay is, precisely, that you are seen *with love* in return.

**Reading the Verse Upon Uḥud Itself**

For the Uḥud-bereaved who first heard it, the verse redrew the battle's ledger: the dead-in-the-field were paid their *ḥusnā* at the moment of falling (v. 157 will announce their accounts precisely); the living were paid in the *thawāb al-dunyā* within the decade — spoils, security, and above all the standing-wage of the purified faith the battle had assayed out (v. 141); and the *sum* was God's love over the whole camp: *Uḥud was not a defeat-account; it was a three-line credit memo*: for the reader at any later setback, the verse's instruction stands: after every loss honestly weathered (the three petition-vocabulary of v. 147 recited *during*, the three negations of v. 146 held *under*), open this verse and wait: the payouts follow the prayer by design — world, world's beautiful successor, and the Beloved's love on top.
**Two World-Rewards: The Door Opened Both Directions**

*Fa-ātāhumu Allāhu thawāba al-dunyā wa ḥusna thawābi al-ākhirah* — "so God gave them the reward of the world and the fair reward of the Hereafter": the verse completes the prayer of v. 147 with a two-column payout, and its first column is the one the materialist does not expect in the prophets' ledger: *thawāb al-dunyā* — a world-reward — given *to the praying army*. The commentators specify it historically: Badr's outcome, the spoils, the standing, Madinah's consolidation — grant-in-aid for the campaign still unfinished. The second column — *ḥusna thawābi al-ākhirah* — the beautiful Hereafter-payment — is the payroll's un-defeatable entry (4:134's doctrine: *whoever wants the world's reward — with God is the reward of the world and the Hereafter — God is ever Hearing, Seeing*).

**Love of the Muḥsinīn: The Register Completed**

*Wa-Allāhu yuḥibbu al-muḥsinīn* — "and God loves the muḥsinīn": the chapter's love-register receives its sixth name, with iḥsān crowned — that highest station of worship the Gabriel-hadith defines (*worshipping God as though you see Him*, Muslim 8). Placement is the doctrine: the battlefield-prayer answered by double-reward terminates in God's *love* — as if the Lord of the ledger, paying two wages to the prayerful, were yet unwilling that payment be mistaken for the top of the scale: above both wages sits love. And 9:52's triptych for the embattled — *"say: do you await for us but one of the two fair outcomes? — and we await for you..."* — shows the same ledger applied prospectively to every later campaign of the religion: martyrdom counted as fair outcome *one*, victory as fair outcome *two* — the believer's war-economy containing no column of loss.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:149

> **O you who believe! If you obey those who disbelieve, they will turn you back on your heels; then you will be overturned as losers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Vocative Returns — And With It the Gate-Theory of Eternal Loss**

The "O you who believe" address returns — and the sūrah's greatest gentleness now frames the sternest articulation so far: *in tuṭīʿū alladhīna kafarū yaruddūkum ʿalā aʿqābikum fa-tanqalibū khāsirīn* — "if you obey those who disbelieve, they will return you upon your heels — and you will turn about as losers." *Al-ʿaqib* — the heel — reappears two verses after 3:144's "turning back on your heels": the Book is intent on the imagery: heel-turning is the exact geometry of a man about-face on the road — the 180° reversal of conversion — and its vehicle, spelled out once more, is not violence but *ṭāʿah*: *obedience*: the slow transplantation of counsel-and-command authority into hostile hands (the lesson first taught at v. 100 in the Aws–Khazraj gathering; now taught again at the battlefield's mouth). Al-Ṭabarī names all the addressees whose counsel the believers are thus forbidden to *obey* — the idolaters' advisers, the hypocrites' whispers, the obstructing wings of the People of the Book — since each had its post-Uḥud opinion to offer ("come back; this mission is over; blood is proof of error"), and every dynasty since has supplied its own variant ("your religion is the obstacle; hand the keys of your doctrine to our committees, and you will prosper").

**"You Will Turn About as Losers": Total-Loss Declared**

*Fa-tanqalibū khāsirīn:* the Book's loss-register is final-domed: *tanqalibū*: you will rotate back, you will come round — after all landings — *khāsirīn*: losers: as the commentators (with the source's precision) note, the word covers both senses — *lost* and *having lost everything*: the translation's "overturned as losers" catches the totality: this is not an accounting of some losses within general gain: this is the *khusr* of the very journey: the exchange of 3:85's fate-word (*khāsirūn*: those who lose all) re-rung — the end-scene of the man who gave his islam for tactical counsel: he has not lost a skirmish; the whole convoy has gone over the ledge with him. The psychological acuity of the verse lies in its insistence upon *obey* as the lethal verb: kufr's re-entry into a believer rarely begins with denial-propositions; it begins with *advisor-appointments*: whom you *take counsel of* in your life's pivot-moments — marriages, resignations, compromises of principle, the setting of true worth — becomes, within years, your theology. The prophet's own standing teaching on companionship translates verse 149 into a house-rule:

> *"A person is upon the religion of his intimate companion — so let one of you look to whom he takes as an intimate."* (al-Tirmidhī 2378; Abū Dāwūd 4833 — from Abū Hurayrah; graded sound)

Obedience is measured not only in commands received but in norms absorbed: the counsel-channel is the conversion-channel — in both directions.

**The Verse's Function Within the Uḥud Cure**

Its placement is, again, exact pastoral timing: verse 144 has just completed re-anchoring the army's loyalty in God (death of the messenger changes nothing); verse 149 pre-empts the *ongoing* counseling-campaign the enemies and their mouthpieces will now conduct across Madinah (v. 151 records their regret; vv. 166–168 record the hypocrite-line in detail: "had we any decision, we would not have been slain"; v. 154 has already recorded the whisper: "do we have any decision?"): the believers are told in advance: *their advice is a gradient-back*: heedless reception of it rotates your whole orientation, slowly, until one day you find yourself at the exact heel-turn. The one asset that blocks the rotation is named in the very next verse — 3:150's *bal Allāhu mawlākum* — "nisay, God is your Master": the alternative lordship: *masters are obeyed; and you already have One* — as the following commentary unfolds.
**The Heel-Turn in Sentence-Form**

*Yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū in tuṭīʿū alladhīna kafarū yaruddūkum ʿalā aʿqābikum fa-tanqalibū khāsirīn* — "O you who believe — if you obey those who disbelieve, they will turn you back upon your heels, and you will overturn as losers." The heel-idiom (*aʿqāb*, heels) drew its permanence from Uḥud's fuller shadow — v. 144's *whoever turns on his heels* — and here it binds the turning to a *causal chain*: obedience to counsel from outside the lamp is presented as the *mechanism* of regression, not its accompaniment. Al-Qurṭubī states the jurisprudence flatly: the believer's counsel-accessories must be of the house of faith — the hypocrite-class and the delayers being expressly portraitured in v. 167–168's strategy (sedentary men counseling others to sit) — for the chain that drags by the heel begins with the advisor's voice, not the enemy's spear.

**Fanqalibtum Khāsirīn: The Overturn as Total-Loss**

The verse's final verb — *tanqalibū*, overturn — returns with its accusative *khāsirīn* (losers) in the mode of state (*ḥāl*): *returning as losers* — the loss compounded: world's campaign forfeited, Hereafter's standing compromised, and the rollback itself finished — *heel-ward*, the salvation-direction reversed. The Book's own diagnosis of the greatest such file runs at 18:103–104: *"shall We inform you of the greatest losers in works — those whose striving goes astray in the world-life while they reckon they do well in workmanship"* — loss measured by misdirected labor — and the believer's audit under v. 149 is daily and deliberate: *whose counsel* — internal and external — *is scheduling my steps?* For the chain-drag backward rarely announces itself as counsel; it arrives as reasonableness — the v. 175 Satan-friend fear-voices included — and its tell is invariable: *it always proposes the heel-direction.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:150

> **Rather, God is your Master, and He is the best of helpers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Bal": The Particle of Substitution**

The verse is nine Arabic words, and they function as the complete alternative constitution to the verse before them: *bali Allāhu mawlākum wa huwa khayru al-nāṣirīn* — "nay — God is your Master, and He is the best of helpers." *Bal* is Arabic's particle of abnegation-and-substitution: cancel the premise just offered and install this one: *their* counsel-channel, *their* patronage, *their* slow shepherding of your heels — cancelled; and installed: God's mawlāship. *Mawlā* — master, patron, protector-guardian, ally-by-right: the word whose density the tradition keeps unpacking: your *mawlā* is the One who holds your case-file, to whom your ultimate referral runs, whose counsel *is* counsel, whose party you belong to by covenant (2:257: "God is the friend/mawlā of those who believe — He brings them out of darknesses into the light; and those who disbelieve, their patrons are the ṭāghūt — they bring them out of light into darknesses": the exact total antonym). Al-Ṭabarī's gloss centers refuge and help-seeking: *God is your Mawlā — so from Him alone seek succor*: the counseling function and the helping function unified in a single patron: the man who obeys the disbelievers has *outsourced his referral-chain*: the believer's chain terminates at One desk only.

**"The Best of Helpers": The Superlative Species**

*Wa huwa khayru al-nāṣirīn* — "and He is the best of helpers": the superlative is total: among all *nāṣirīn* — all helpers ever sought — His help is *best*: best in reach (His help cannot be out-flanked: *"if God helps you, none can overcome you"* — v. 160's direct outworking, ten verses ahead); best in purity (help without secondary motive, without bill); best in efficacy (His help succeeds — nothing that is genuinely helped by Him can be made to fail: *"if God helps you..."*); best in persistence (human helpers age, tire, counsel you into their own interest, and die — He does not: 3:144's whole doctrine). The phrase — *khayr al-nāṣirīn* — became a fighter's call of the Prophet: in the hadith of the march to Badr and at the terrible moments of expeditions, he (ﷺ) and the Companions are recorded crying, among their station-words: *ḥasbunā Allāhu wa niʿma al-wakīl* — "God is sufficient for us, and the best of Trustees" — from 3:173's own formula, adjacent in this sūrah — and *Allāhu mawlānā... wa niʿma al-mawlā wa niʿma al-naṣīr* — "God is our Patron... excellent the Patron, excellent the Helper!" — the very words of 8:40 ("if they turn away, know that God is your Patron — excellent the Patron and excellent the Helper"), which the early Muslims are narrated to have taken up as their combat-and-crisis *waṣīyah* (the Companions' saying in the reports: when this verse came down, *the Prophet's loved sentence*, taught to them at times of testing: *niʿma al-mawlā wa niʿma al-naṣīr* — carried at Badr by the prophetic men) — a liturgy in four nouns.

**The Replacement Made Personal**

The contrast of verses 149–150 as a pair now stands complete as the chapter's full constitution on counsel-loyalty: (1) obeyers of the disbelievers rotate heel-ward into total loss; (2) God's mawlāship replaces every alternative patronage with the best help available in existence. The believer thus runs the daily diagnostic of 3:150 quietly: *whose counsel am I currently obeying?* — the advisors one takes without thinking are one's actual mawālī; and the answer, if the answer be God, settles every fear the adversaries cultivate: *the patron who owns the heavens and the earth has already the best help; your enemies have grievances*.
**Bal: The Turn to the Patron**

*Bal Allāhu mawlākum* — "Nay — God is your Mawlā": the sūrah's answer-particle *bal* (nay — rather) overturns the whole premise of v. 149's frightened arithmetic: you do not need their counsel to survive; your Patron is God. *Mawlā* — the word of nearness-with-protection that runs from the freeing-patron of the jurists through the client-ally of the Arabs to the supreme Patron of creed — concentrates three relations in one: He is owner-like *near*, patron-like *responsible*, friend-like *present*. The Book contrasts the patronage exactly by class: "God is the Wall of those who believe — He brings them out of the darknesses into the light; and those who disbelieve — their patrons are the ṭāghūt, who bring them out of the light into the darknesses" (2:257): every soul walks out under some patronage, and v. 150 declares the exchange-rate: *theirs is darkness-end; yours is the Best Nāṣir.*

**Niʿma al-Mawlā: The Crisis-Cry of the Companions**

The title's life in the ummah's mouth is documented at its hardest hours: at the Ḥunayn morning when ambush folded round the Prophet ﷺ and his thousands, the remnant heard him calling; and through the whole war-history of the call the believers' settling-refuge is God's own instruction recorded at 8:40: *"if they turn away, know that God is your Mawlā — excellent the Mawlā, and excellent the Nāṣir"* — *niʿma al-mawlā wa niʿma al-naṣīr* — the cry the salaf made into their standard remedy in every overwhelmed hour. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's school repeated it through fitnah-decades; travelers and the buried-alive in collapsing fortunes repeat it still. Verse 150 thereby delivers post-Uḥud its personal liturgy: *the advisor-quilts fold; Niʿma al-Mawlā stands.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:151

> **We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve for having ascribed partners unto God, for which He has not sent down any authority. And their refuge shall be the Fire, and evil is the abode of the wrongdoers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turned Backs on the Road to Makkah**

The battle's coda — verse 151 — records the war's *after-outcome*, invisible to every chronicle but God's: *sa-nulqī fī qulūbi alladhīna kafarū al-ruʿb* — "We shall cast terror (ruʿb) into the hearts of those who disbelieve." The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī) anchor the clause concretely: withdrawing from Uḥud along the Makkah road, the victorious idolaters passed through a night of after-reckoning: they had killed seventy-two of the best men of Madinah, wounded the Prophet, stood at the threshold of the city — and *not entered it*; and as the order to turn and finish the work was debated among them, a terror not of men descended into the war-council: they doused the plan, and turned back to Makkah unfulfilled — the *khāʾibīn* of verse 127 exact. God names the operation His own: *sa-nulqī* — *We shall cast*: terror was not a derivative of facts on the ground (by every ledger of that evening they were the winners) but a *landed projectile* from outside the visible — one of the Qur'an's own named divine munitions, along with wind and rain and angels (8:9–12; 33:9; 59:2: "He cast terror into their hearts — they destroyed their houses by their own hands").

**Why the Terror: The Charge Laid to Account**

The reason-clause names the ultimate cause — not the Muslim spears but their own *dogma*: *bi-mā ashrakū bi-Allāhi mā lam yunazzil bihi sulṭānā* — "because they ascribed partners to God for which He has sent down no authority": the crime item list: shirk — deities devoid of any *sulṭān* (any warrant, any authorizing descent): a partnership forged in the void of warrant. The connection between *shirk* and *fear* is one of the Qur'an's most subtle arguments, and it is stated outright at 3:151's sister text: *"We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve because they associate with God that for which He has sent down no authority"* — and at 24:55's mirror-side: God grants the believers *tamkīn* — secure establishment — *replacing their fear with security* "because they worship Me, associating nothing with Me": *shirk terrifies its owners precisely because it is authority-less*: deep in every commission of a baseless system lies the knowledge of its groundlessness: idols cannot be defended; lies cannot consent to themselves; and armies resting on false ultimates carry, wherever they go, a hollow in the command-tent: the terror flies in through the hollow. The believer's doctrine of psychological war is written here: your best strategic assets are *not* your armaments but the *unshakeability of your premise*; every enemy of a true cause fights two battles — one with you, and one with the interior verdict that he has no authority for what he defends.

**"Their Refuge Shall Be the Fire" — The Terror's Terminus**

And the worldly terror's postscript is its final scale: *wa maʾwāhumu al-nār* — "and their refuge is the Fire" — *wa biʾsa mathwa al-ẓālimīn* — "and evil is the abode of the wrongdoers": *mathwā*: the residence-lodging: their terror's end-address. The word *ẓālimīn* (wrongdoers) replays the chapter's charge-file (vv. 86, 94, 128, 140): terror in the hearts today; abode-appointed tomorrow. The pastoral contrast, compiled across vv. 139–151, then stands in perfect order: to the believers — *do not falter... do not grieve* (v. 139): *their* hearts are carried by the two negations; to the disbelievers — *We cast terror*: the two camps walk away from the same battle with opposite interior conditions — and only one of the two interior conditions matters at the *nisba* of destiny.
**Ruʿb: Terror as a Deployed Weapon of Heaven**

*Sa-nulqī fī qulūbi lladhīna kafarū al-ruʿb* — "We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve": the future-emphatic (*sa-* of certitude) appoints an arm of God's war-fighting the believer never handles: *fear itself*, projected past walls and numbers into the enemy chest. The Book's registers show the munition's campaigns: at Badr the angels were told, *"I shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve — so strike above the necks"* (8:12); at the Confederates' ditches the terror arrived by wind and armies *unseen* (33:9); at Banū al-Naḍīr the God-cast *ruʿb* emptied a fortress-town without a battering-ram (59:2) — *"He it is Who expelled the unbelieving People of the Book from their houses at the first mustering... He cast terror into their hearts."* The commentators set the sūrah's verse within Uḥud's own aftermath: the Quraysh withdrawal stopped of its own confusion, Abū Sufyán's resolve cooling as his dead lay unburied — the cast fear having landed where the spears had not.

**Security Withheld: The Theology of Un-anchored Hearts**

The verse's charge — *bi-mā ashrakū* — "because of their shirk — *for which God sent down no authority"* — grounds the terror in metaphysics: the shirk-heart has *no anchor*, nothing beneath the mattress of its bravado; its gods cannot hold its pulse (16:54–56's idols who remove not the distress), so the first rumble breaches outward confidence into total interior panic. Belief's inverse register runs in 24:55's security-replacement promise: God *"will certainly change their state, after their fear, into security — they worship Me, ascribing nothing to Me"* — monotheism itself delivered as the only defense-system against the ruʿb-missile. Uḥud's lesson at the strategic depth therefore outlasts its battle: *castles, trenches, and cavalry reserve are all secondary armaments; the first is a heart whose doctrine has no cracks.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:152

> **And God certainly was true to His Promise to you when you were eradicating them by His Leave, until the moment you lost heart, and quarreled with one another about the matter, and disobeyed, after He had showed you that which you loved. Among you are those who desire this world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter. Then He turned you from them, to test you, and He certainly pardoned you—God is Possessed of Bounty for the believers—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Anatomy of a Victory in One Sentence**

Verse 152 is among the most psychologically penetrating battle-analyses ever written — a compressed account of the war's whole upper hour: victory, breach, collapse, and pardon, told in address to the believers themselves: *wa la-qad ṣadaqakumu Allāhu waʿdahū idh taḥussūnahum bi-idhnih* — "God indeed made good His promise to you while you were eradicating them by His leave": the morning's first phase is certified: God's promised reinforcement was real and running: the Muslim army was sweeping through the idolaters' camp (the verb *taḥussūnahum* — mowing them down, clearing them away) until the battle was, by all field-indicators, decided: the standard-bearers of Quraysh falling one after another (in the sīrah: nine men of Banū ʿAbd al-Dār fell holding the banner, Al-Qurṭubī's own detail), the enemy in headlong flight — *He had showed you what you loved* (*min baʿdi mā arākum mā tuḥibbūn* — after He showed you what you loved): victory *visible*: the promise kept so completely that the believers *saw it with their eyes*.

**"Until..." — The Four Verbs of the Fall**

The verse then pivots on a word as small as a hinge: *ḥattā* — "until": *ḥattā idhā fashiltum wa tanāzaʿtum fī al-amri wa ʿaṣaytum* — "until you lost heart, and disputed over the matter, and disobeyed": the fall is narrated in four verbs (fashil — wavering of heart; tanāzaʿ — dispute; ʿaṣā — disobedience; and fashil-tanāzaʿ-ʿaṣā are the sequence the commentators unfold): the archers' garrison — the order: hold the hill, whatever happens — watched the battle roll downhill and the enemy flee; and the four-verb sequence happened in their rank in real time: (1) some lost heart *for the command itself* — "the battle is over; why stay?" (2) dispute erupted in the ranks — the source's own record: some of the archers *insisted* on holding the post (the minority in the middle of the majority) — the *tanāzaʿ* was obedience against obedience's fatigue; (3) disobedience: the most descended the hill for the spoils; (4) and the hour turned: Khālid's cavalry — the Prophet's ﷺ own lifelong structure-of-tragedy before it became his famed rescue — wheeled around the undefended hill, surged into the Musklim rear, and the battle reversed in minutes: victory visible at 10 a.m.; the Prophet wounded before noon. Everything God had promised ran — the first clause; the *until* clause reveals what alone can interrupt heaven's help: not the enemy's power, *the believers' self*.

**"Among You Are Those Who Desire This World..." — The Bravest Diagnosis in Scripture**

God's own post-battle audit names the breach's root — *minkum man yurīdu al-dunyā wa minkum man yurīdu al-ākhirah* — "among you are those desiring the world; among you, those desiring the Hereafter" — and the report tradition's awe at the words is preserved in Ibn Masʿūd's own saying: *"I used not to believe that any of the Companions of the Messenger of God desired the world — until this verse came down"* (al-Ṭabarī's transmission, cited in the source-commentary): the men of Uḥud were not scoffers; they were the best generation of the religion; and among them was dunyā-desire *in its operational form*: grip loosened on command under the pull of spoils: the verse registers it *without hatred* (the "among you" is brotherly, not excommunicating) — diagnosis, not damnation — because the chapter's whole doctrine of the art of trials is at work: God turned you from them *li-yabtaliyakum* — *to test you*: the defeat was curriculum, and the pardon clause lands immediately: *wa la-qad ʿafā ʿankum* — "and He has indeed pardoned you" — with the seal: *wa Allāhu dhū faḍlin ʿalā al-muʾminīn* — "and God is possessed of bounty toward the believers." No army of God was ever told so gently that it had *disobeyed its prophet mid-battle* — told with the diagnosis of dunyā-pull in one breath and the pardon in the next — and no text reveals better God's pedagogic raison d'être of a morning of loss: the world-desirers identified, the Hereafter-desirers identified, the file of each read, and the pardon issued to all — with the lesson then bequeathed instantly to every army, every ministry, every community ever since: *your battles are lost in order: heart-wavering, dispute, disobedience — watch the first of the sequence* — and with the comfort bequeathed to every believer caught holding a hill-temptation in any hour of his own: *pardon precedes punishment whenever return beats persistence home*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:153

> **when you were climbing, casting a glance to no one, while the Messenger was calling you from your rear. So He recompensed you with sorrow upon sorrow, that you may not grieve over what escaped you or what befell you. And God is Aware of whatsoever you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Retreat Remembered: "To Me, O Servants of God!"**

The audit continues with the hour God preserved in narrative: *idh tuṣʿidūna wa lā talwūna ʿalā aḥadin, wa al-rasūlu yadʿūkum fī ukhrākum* — "when you were climbing, looking back at no one, while the Messenger was calling you from your rear": *tuṣʿidūna* (from ṣaʿada — ascending) — whether the climbing up the slopes of Uḥud in flight (al-Ṭabarī's register of the two readings and their terrain) or traversing insistently away — the image is single: upward is, in this moment, *away*: the routed soldier runs over whatever incline the ground gives him — away from the fight, away from everyone: *lā talwūna ʿalā aḥadin* — not looking back at *anyone*: the dear-men of a thousand days left unsearched: panic's complete narrowing of the field of regard to one's own skin; and against the blind backs, the sound the generation never forgot: *al-rasūlu yadʿūkum* — *the Messenger was calling you* — from behind — and the sīrah preserved his words verbatim (al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī): *"ilayya ʿibād Allāh! ilayya ʿibād Allāh!"* — "to me, O servants of God! to me, O servants of God!" — his own person the rallying standard: wounded, bleeding, a target in the open — and his voice the rope ringing out after fleeing friends: everything that made him God's mercy to the worlds in one cry.

**"Sorrow Upon Sorrow": The Multiplied Grief, and Its Un-Looked-For Purpose**

*Fa-athābakum ghamman bi-ghamm* — "so He recompensed you with sorrow upon sorrow": *athābakum*: recompensed — Allah uses *the wage-word* for grief: the sorrow was *payment*, earned currency: and the doubled *ghamm bi-ghamm* — grief joined to grief — the commentators enumerate the layers: sorrow for the Prophet's sorrow (al-Rāzī); sorrow of the false report of his death followed by sorrow of the casualties (al-Ṭabarī); sorrow of losing the battle and the spoils, then the enemy's gloating; or sorrow of the loss followed by the fear of the enemy's return: *a grief-stack, arranged*: and then the verse discloses the design: *li-kaylā taḥzanū ʿalā mā fātakum wa lā mā aṣābakum* — "so that you might not grieve over what escaped you nor over what befel you": the administered overdose of sorrow as *inoculation*: a heart already at the ceiling of grief — grief for *God-ward stakes* (the Prophet's face) — has no reservoir left for the small griefs (the spoils missed, the arms lost, the day spoiled): the great loss crowds out the little cures: by the time that evening descended on the field, the men could no longer identify what any worldly disappointment felt like — for they had just seen where true loss lives. Al-Rāzī's note on the consolation-form of God's discipline: He caused them sorrow *through* what He loves (the Prophet's wound and the martyrs' glory) to wean their inventory of sorrows off what He does not grieve for: *dunyā*.

**"God Is Aware of What You Do": The Seal of the Audit**

And the chapter's familiar watchman-name closes the account: *wa Allāhu khabīrun bi-mā taʿmalūn* — "and God is aware of all you do": the subterranean and apparent deeds both in His register: the wavering, the dispute, the descent, the climbing — and the rallying of those who turned back around the Prophet when the call reached them. The verse thus completes the Book's double register of Uḥud's poor hour: candid diagnosis — *disobedience, dunyā-desire, backs turned* — settled *inside* unbreakable covenant-love: God grief-pays them, and in the same sequence seals with the name of One who knows better than they themselves what hid in their slipping feet. Every believing reader since then finds in 3:153 the dark comfort of his own flight-hours — the pivot-moments where he, like the archers, *climbed, glancing at no one, with the call behind him still ringing*: and the knowledge that God can wrap even those in a design — "sorrow upon sorrow — so that you grieve no more for the little rooms": grief as God's anesthetic for grief.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:154

> **Then He sent down upon you—after sorrow—security, a sleepiness enveloping a company among you, while a company were anxious over themselves, thinking about God what is not true—the thinking of the Age of Ignorance—saying, "Do we have any decision [in this]?" Say, "The decision belongs entirely to God." They hide in their souls what they do not disclose to you, saying, "Had we any decision [in this], we would not have been slain here." Say, "Had you stayed in your houses, those who were destined to be slain would have gone out to their places of rest." And [this is] so that God may test what is in your breasts and so that He may assay what is in your hearts. And God knows what lies within breasts.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sleep Sent Down: Tranquility as Battlefield Miracle**

After the grief-stack, the verse records one of the most astonishing mercy-reports in all revelation: *thumma anzala ʿalaykum min baʿdi al-ghammi amanatan nuʿāsān yaghshā ṭāʾifatan minkum* — "then He sent down upon you, after the sorrow, security — a drowsiness enveloping a company of you": *nuʿās*: light slumber, the nodding of the first stage of sleep: on a battlefield, within the same day as the recompense of griefs, God sedated His army. The function is manifold in the commentators' careful inventory (al-Rāzī especially): (1) *psychological*: sleep is the nullifier of panic — one cannot sleep and panic simultaneously: the descent of drowsiness in a man terrified a moment before is thereby *tangible evidence* that God's amanah (security) has arrived: (2) *physiological*: an enemy could strike at any hour, and the army sleepless for a night would be routed at dawn — the nodding restored the men for the next phase; (3) *theological*: the hadith the source records — the Companion at Uḥud whose sword kept slipping from his hand as sleep took him, again and again — is elevated by Ibn Masʿūd's dictum (in al-Rāzī's preservation): *drowsiness in battle is of the trust of God; drowsiness in prayer is of the whispering of satan*: the hour-classifies the sleep: God's gift of sleep under the spears is the same gift in another dress as 8:11's before Badr: *"when He made drowsiness overcome you as security from Him"* — the text-verbatim twin. The army of God, after its one disobedient afternoon, is *tucked in* by heaven: the pardon's parole already operating (v. 152).

**"While a Company Were Anxious Over Themselves": The Two Sleep-Classes**

The verse divides the very field by chests: one company drowses: *wa ṭāʾifatun qad ahammathum anfusuhum* — "while another company were anxious about *themselves*": the hypocrites and the wobbly, God reports, could not sleep — for their dread was skin-dread: fear-for-self, not strength-surrendered: and the distinction is the verse's first diagnostic: sleep comes as gift to the hearts whose fear is in God; self-anxiety sleeplessly grinds in the hearts whose fear-principles terminate in the self. Then the deeper diagnosis is laid out — *yaẓunnūna bi-Allāhi ghayra al-ḥaqqi ẓanna al-jāhiliyyah* — "thinking of God other than the truth — the thinking of the Age of Ignorance": the *ẓann* — conjecture-thoughts, suspicion — of Jāhiliyyah: the mindset that judges God's truth by the day's deliverables: *if Muḥammad were a prophet, this would not have happened* (al-Rāzī's reading of their simmering thought): God and prophets, in pagan logic, trade protection for worship on a cash-register; prophets who bleed are, by the register, false: — precisely the thought-pattern the entire sūrah has been demolishing (v. 140's alternation; v. 144's "if he dies or is slain").

**"Do We Have Any Decision?" — The Rhetoric of Abdication**

Their exteriorized murmur is the petty accountancy of self: *hal lanā mina al-amri min shayʾ* — "do we have anything at all of the decision?" — meaning: *our counsel (stay in Madinah!) was overruled (v. 121); so look what counsel-cost*: God commands the Prophet's answer-total: *qul inna al-amra kullahū lillāh* — "say: the decision — *all of it* — is God's": *kulluh*: entire: not a partition of agencies (you plan, He ratifies), but *total* possession of *al-amr*: the exact sovereign-claim that v. 128 ("you have nothing of the matter") already established for the Prophet himself, now extended to all participants: Ibn Ubayy's block and the faithful both stand inside the same total *amr* — so no slope of "our plan would have spared us" exists to stand on.

**"We Would Not Have Been Slain Here": And God's Counterfactual Mathematics**

Then the verse unveils their hidden interior speech — *yukhfūna fī anfusihim mā lā yubdūna lak, yaqūlūna law kāna lanā mina al-amri shayʾun mā qutilnā hāhunā* — "they hide in their souls what they do not reveal to you, saying: had we any part in the decision, we would not have been slain here": the hidden syllogism of deserters: *our withdrawal would have spared our casualties*: the most durable sedition-line in war history ("stay-home logic"), utterable only by men willing to forget *the very rain that gave them life*: God's counter-address, commanded of the Prophet, is among the Book's most sovereign replies — *qul law kuntum fī buyūtikum la-baraja alladhīna kutiba ʿalayhimu al-qatlu ilā maḍājiʿihim* — "say: had you remained in your houses, those upon whom slaughter was decreed would have gone forth to their lying-places": the beds (*maḍājiʿ* — final lying-spots: graves-of-the-field) would have *come out to meet* their owners: death's appointments are not coordinates; they are *documents attached to souls* (3:145's *kitāban muʾajjalan*: the written term re-rung): no topology keeps them away. The bed you would have died in simply relocates. There is no *hāhunā* — "here" — to safety from it; nor any *there* that hastens it.

**"To Test What Is in Your Breasts": The Uḥud Curriculum's Final Ledger**

And the verse concludes by naming the battle's ultimate divine use: *wa li-yabtaliya Allāhu mā fī ṣudūrikum wa li-yumaḥḥiṣa mā fī qulūbikum* — "and so that God may test what is in your breasts, and assay what is in your hearts": the tamḥīṣ-word of v. 141 returning — refinery, at depth: *wa Allāhu ʿalīmun bi-dhāti al-ṣudūr* — "and God knows what the breasts hold": the chapter's signature-seal once more (vv. 29, 119, and here): the testing's work is to *make visible* — to the creation, to the watchers, to the souls themselves — what God already fully knows: Uḥud was, in the end, a massive chest-X-ray: drowsy faithful and sleepless hypocrites visible side by side; the Book its permanent print-out: every community since has had its own afternoon turn around; the lesson pre-printed: anxiety ends in the two negations of verse 139 — *no faltering, no grieving* — and the deep slepp of the God-fearing is the only nap worth waking from.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:155

> **Those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met—Satan alone made them slip because of part of what they committed. And God certainly pardoned them; truly God is Forgiving, Clement.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Satan Slipped Them": The Physics of a Fall**

The Uḥud audit now reaches its most delicate stratum — the complete aetiology of the rout, assigned precisely where revelation assigns it: *inna alladhīna tawallaw minkum yawma ltaqā al-jamʿāni innamā istazallahumu al-shayṭānu bi-baʿḍi mā kasabū* — "as for those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met — it was only that Satan slipped them, on account of part of what they had earned." The sentence contains three load-bearing facts.

(1) *The turn away was real* — *tawallaw*: they turned their backs — as vv. 153–154 recorded: the climbing, the no-backward-glance: the Book does not edit its saints' failures out; the best generation's worst afternoon is permanently published: the Qur'an's candor toward its own first saints is one of the miracles of God's pedagogy (God's friends are not wax figures; they are men who fall and are raised).

(2) *The slipping was Satanic* — *istazallahumu al-shayṭān*: *zalal*: slip, skid, stumble — not murder, nor wholesale inversion: a *slip*: the brake-off of a single step: satan's role in the whole event was exactly this: at the one moment of pressure he slid the foot: the sūrah's own identification of satan's method throughout (at v. 36: satan-touch; at 2:36: satan made them slip — *azallahumā al-shayṭān* — in the Garden): the word of Adam's fall returning in the battlefield's — the pattern is one: all human sin is *zall*: a slip in an hour of weakness, seized and deepened by the whisperer: satan cannot *march* a believer out of a formation; he can *oil the ground* under his one tired foot. Al-Rāzī's alternative syntactic readings add precision: *bi-baʿḍi mā kasabū* — *for/because of part of what they earned*: satan slipped them *in some matters* (only this slip — not their whole religion) or *on the occasion of some prior earnings* (the lingering faults, the earlier disobediences, that made the foothold slick): sin oils for sin: the archers' slip was lubricated by *prior small slippages*. One way or the other, the doctrine is: satan operates on *draft*: the draft supplied by *their own* ledger: the trust-in-self of a morning; the spoils-glitter of an hour; the accumulated debt of little disobediences: upon that draft the whisper works.

(3) *And God had already pardoned them* — *wa la-qad ʿafā Allāhu ʿanhum* — "and God certainly pardoned them" — with the double seal: *inna Allāha ghafūrun ḥalīm* — "truly God is Forgiving, Clement": *Ḥalīm* — forebearing, slow-to-punish, giving room: the pen-name that closes the case: satan slips; God pardons; the register keeps both entries. Al-Qurṭubī (with the commentators cited in the source) richly draws the lesson's continuity: God pardoned Adam when he slipped in the Garden (2:37: "then Adam received words from his Lord, and He relented toward him"): the same sequence across six thousand years: slip — return — pardon: the chain of transmission of grace from the first man to the warriors of Uḥud. The tafsīr-tradition is emphatic on this verse's ground of hope: the named men of the slip included (in one al-Ṭabarī option) ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān — the future third caliph! — with Companions of undisputed eminence: *they slipped on the earth of Uḥud; God pardoned; the community re-raised them to its highest offices*: God's way is not erasure — it is repair: the pardoned sinner is among God's greatest instruments.

**The Verse's Own Standing Ministry of Hope**

Every believer who has ever known the moment of *the turn* — the day he *climbed, looking back at no one*, whether from a battlefield, a duty, a refusal to forgive, a sin-clouded season — can recognize himself in this verse's three terms: satan slipped; part of what you earned oiled the way; God *ḥalīm* pardons. The Prophet ﷺ made the covenant with his universal formulation: *"all the children of Adam are sinners — and the best of sinners are the repentant"* (Ibn Mājah 4251; al-Tirmidhī 2499, from Anas). Slip-craft is human; return-craft is believing; and satan, at every turnback, plans his one choreographed move: whisper *that the pardon is exhausted* — the very suggestion verse 155 was revealed to demolish: after the worst afternoon in Muslim military history, God's own comment was *wa la-qad ʿafā Allāhu ʿanhum* — the accusative completed: *truly God is Forgiving, Clement*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:156

> **O you who believe! Be not like those who disbelieve and say of their brethren when they travel upon the earth or campaign, "Had they stayed with us, they would not have died and been slain," that God may make that a source of regret in their hearts. And God gives life and causes death, and God sees whatsoever you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Stay-Home Syllogism: A Forbidden Spectator-Logic**

The vocative returns — "O you who believe" — and outlaws a whole way of speaking that had spoken itself out after Uḥud across every council tent of the waverers: *lā takūnū ka-lladhīna kafarū wa qālū li-ikhwānihim idhā ḍarabū fī al-arḍi aw kānū ghuzzan law kānū ʿindanā mā mātū wa mā qutilū* — "be not like those who disbelieve, saying of their brethren, when they travel in the earth or campaign: had they remained with us, they would not have died and not been slain." The words are the exact formula of the stay-home party (identified by al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī with ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and his policied circle, though the grammar holds for the disbelieving in general): a counterfactual *analysis* masquerading as grief: *their fatalities were scheduling errors*: had they ignored the summons, stayed within the walls, inherited our prudence — they would be alive: the bitterness wrapped in the logic is insidious: it blames obedience itself for mortality: it makes the cause of death *religious response* rather than God's decree — and thus, in one idiom, attacks tawḥīd's entire sovereignty (v. 154's *al-amru kulluhū lillāh*; v. 145's *kitāb muʾajjal*).

**"A Regret in Their Hearts": The Boomerang Verdict**

The divine disposition upon this speech is verse-specific, and its beauty lies in its economy: *li-yajʿala Allāhu dhālika ḥasratan fī qulūbihim* — "that God may make that a regret (*ḥasrah*) in their hearts." Al-Rāzī cites two receivers of the ḥasrah: it can fall back upon the speakers — their own sedative-appeasing counsel converted into permanent heartache (for the martyrs' rank, announced in verses 167–171, proves the mid-day "loss" to be supreme gain — and the word-owners spend their worlds wishing their own sentence unsaid); or, as other commentators note, the words spoken in some households became grief in the hearts of the hearts-bereaved who had tried to prevent their kin from going out — a wound God administered in the wise by letting them taste the grief they had advised against facing honorably. And the commentators add the eschatological *ḥasrah*: on the day of the standing, the same speech will recur in their chests — there, where regret triples and never purchases. Either way, God retorts to the calculus of safety with the distribution of grief: *the speech itself becomes its disposition*: the Book's law — *sayings turn into conditions*.

**"God Gives Life and Causes Death" — The Sovereign Refutation**

And the final clause pronounces the doctrine that liquidates the whole stay-home arithmetic: *wa Allāhu yuḥyī wa yumīt* — "and God gives life and causes death" — *wa Allāhu bi-mā taʿmalūna baṣīr* — "and God sees whatever you do." Life and death are functions directly administered — not delegated to shelter-walls nor to battlefields: the household is not a ward against death, nor the field its forge: 3:154's own conclusive sentence (those decreed for slaughter would go out to their lying-places) is thus re-stated in *nominal* form: occupancy of danger does not *cause* death; God *causes* death: and God *causes* life: consequently the entire pragmatic passion for avoiding death's day is re-labeled by the verse as *misplaced agency-concern*: men's true agency applies to *conduct* — *God sees whatsoever you do*: not to outcomes. Al-Rāzī's spiritual extension of *yuḥyī wa yumīt* enlivens a further gallery: God *quickens* the hearts of His friends — the life of taqwā, maʿrifah, remembrance — and *deades* the hearts of His enemies: mourning-house detachments and battle-field companies alike: and thus the speaker of *"had they stayed with us, they had not died"* has diagnosed the wrong death entirely: there are dead-souled living in every council tent, quickened martyrs in every field-trench: 3:169's announcement arrives in eleven verses to make the reversal final — *deem not the slain in God's way dead*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:157

> **And indeed if you are slain or die in the way of God, truly forgiveness and mercy from God are better than what they amass.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Ledger Against the Hoard: Two Balance Sheets at Death**

The verse is a direct comparative bank-audit — the first of the Book's two great martyr-balance sheets (vv. 157–158 together, addressed in the imperative to arrive at vv. 169): *wa la-in qutiltum fī sabīli Allāhi aw mittum* — "and if you are slain in the way of God, or you die" — *la-maghfiratun mina Allāhi wa raḥmatun khayrun mimmā yajmaʿūn* — "forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they are amassing." The phrasing delicately cases the two exits: *qutiltum fī sabīli Allāh* — death *in the way* (battle-martyr); *mittum* — death of ordinary cause (every death — road-death, sickbed-death) *fī sabīli Allāh* per the wide traditional reading — the two doors of leaving are both annexed to the comparison; and what they purchase is weighed against *mā yajmaʿūn* — *what they amass*: the word of collecting-gathering: Ibn Kathīr's plain gloss: wealth-and-all-the vanities of the world: all the collecting the living are doing at this very moment — the granaries, the herds, the totals: it is put in one scale; and in the other: two words only: *maghfirah* — forgiveness — *wa raḥmah* — mercy — *mina Allāh* — *from God* — with the predicate: *khayrun* — *better*: the reversion of all the world's wealthism to what was defined within the chapter's own economy (vv. 14–15: the six banners of ornament vs. ḥusn al-maʾāb — the better return).

**Why Forgiveness-First: The Two Receipts of the Departing Soul**

The receipt-composition is matched to the moment of dying: a soul exiting a life arrives at the gate with two needs in front of everything else: first, *clearance* — the absolution of the ledger (maghfirah) — then, *welcome* — the active embrace (raḥmah): both from *God* — meaning both are *inflations-immune*: granted by Him, and therefore out of reach of any cancellation. With these the verse compares *all they amass*: and the comparison is intentionally absurd — nothing that can be gathered within the six banners (v. 14) travels one inch past the closing of the eyes: *"three things follow the dead: his family, and his property, and his deeds — two return, and one remains: family and property return, and his deeds remain with him"* (al-Bukhārī 6514; Muslim 2960, from Anas — the Prophet's own accounting-table of the funeral): the amassed literally *turns back at the cemetery gate*; forgiveness and mercy *proceed inside*. Better (*khayr*) is not even comparison; it is a different currency altogether.

**Why the Verse Offers This Here: The Cost of Obedience Answered**

Its precise placement in the Uḥud sequence is pastoral arithmetic: verses 156's stay-home party calculated the cost of going out as *seventy deaths*; verse 157 audits what those deaths *bought*: seventy eternal spoils — forgiveness-and-mercy *from God* — versus what stayed in the streets of Madinah: property which has since changed hands two hundred times and belongs today to no one. The deep pedagogy of the chapter is at high pitch here: *fear of loss* is the only emotion by which the hold-back logic ever recruits (obey us and lose nothing): against it God tallies *gain of a different magnitude*: *the slain in His way did not lose seventy; they gained seventy infinitudes*: and the grieving of verses 139–140 is finally made irrational at the root: what should the household weep that was *improved*? The believer's practice follows: at every moment of fearing-the-cost of an obedience (the risked livelihood, the risked reputation, the risked safety), run the same audit: *everything riskable is in the amass-class; everything at stake is forgiveness-and-mercy; better*: and decide accordingly.
**Forgiveness Before Mercy: The Sequence in the Reward**

*Wa la-in qutiltum fī sabīli Allāhi aw muttum la-maghfiratun min Allāhi wa raḥmatun khayrun mimmā yajmaʿūn* — "if you are slain in God's way or die — forgiveness from God and mercy: better than whatsoever they amass." The two-name sequence rewards a separate look, for the Book uses it as a fixed order of entrance: *maghfirah* — the covering and clearing — issued *first* as the gate's mechanism: dues cancelled, record hushed; *raḥmah* — mercy — following as the interior's furnishing: honor-abode, neighborhood of prophets, welcome. Al-Rāzī glosses the order from administration: debts must be cleared before dignities are conferred — the martyr arrives *cleared*, the messenger arriving after him find him *welcomed*. The slain-and-died pairing (*qutiltum... aw muttum*) is the chapter's standing widening: the promise covers *both exits* in God's way — battlefields and sickbeds alike — as v. 158's total-gathering will implement.
