**Mimmā Yajmaʿūn: The Amassed Mocked**

The comparative's object — *mimmā yajmaʿūn* — "than what they amass" — with its plural-pronoun carrying the amasser-class in general, totals the wealth-mockery already running since v. 14's six banners: everything the collectors collect — talent, estate, followings — is hereby weighed against *forgiveness plus mercy* and found the lighter tray. The Prophet's own teaching of the assembly registers the same ledger from the world's side:

> *"The world, compared to the Hereafter, is only like one of you dipping his finger in the sea — let him consider with what it returns."* (Muslim 2858, from al-Mustawrid)

The wet finger's drip is the whole amassed — for the forgetful among the readers, the amassed goods are the whole career — while the verse's *forgiveness and mercy* is the sea itself. Every risk-assessment at a Muslim's fork — safe shadow or God's exposed road — runs in grammar exactly this: *the cleared record outweighs the compounded assets.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:158

> **And indeed if you are slain or die, truly unto God shall you be gathered.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Destination Clause: Death as Application for the Throne**

The partner-verse to the ledger-audit is a single ninth-part-sentence whose whole content is *where you go*: *wa la-in mittum aw qutiltum la-ilā Allāhi tuḥsharūn* — "and if you die or are slain — to God you shall be gathered." The verb is the Book's great destiny-verb: *ḥashr* — gathering, mustering, massing — the Latinate *resurrection*: return-muster: the word used of the Day of Gathering (50:44: "the day the earth splits from around them in haste — *that is a muster easy for Us*"; of the tribes of creation assembled before Him (6:38; 81:5: "and when the creatures are mustered"); of the marshaled proceedings of the Standing. Death's true name in the Qur'an's grammar is not exit; it is *convocation*: souls are not dispersed; they are *assembled to God* — *tuḥsharūn*: the passive of perfect-ease: you have no taxis to hire, no quotas to meet, no thresholds to storm: you are *brought*: the divine haulage: the pilgrimage whose directions no man ever wrote because God is Himself the caravansary's Sender.

**Why "To God" Is the Whole Consolation**

The magic of the verse lies in its dative: *ilā Allāh* — *unto God* — not "unto the darkness," nor "unto the void," nor even "unto the Garden" as final — but *unto God*: the Here is God. The grief-analytics of the chapter (vv. 139–141, 153) now see the design complete: death, received as the end of persons, is terror; death, received as *arrival*, is a different morning: the Christian West's own poetry of the same verse ("departing to be with Christ is far better" — Philippians 1:23) lights on the same destination-grammar: arriving at What was desired all along: the Prophet's own deathbed matched the verse's exact architecture — in his final hours he gave himself the choice granted to prophets: this world or "the Highest Companion" — and chose: *"bal-l-rafīq al-aʿlā"* — "rather, the Highest Companionship" (al-Bukhārī 4435, 4586; Muslim 2443–44, from ʿĀʾishah): *ilā Allāh* as the *choice* over every other file — while in the same week the sūrah's own consolation was being read by the widows and orphans of Uḥud in Madinah: your men went *ilā Allāh*: the rest is administration.

**The Verse's Quiet Conversion of Fear**

The whole of 3:157–158 operates as the Book's definitive therapy on the fear of death — fear which the stay-home calculus (v. 156) had just exploited: therapy by destination-identification, not by denial: (1) if death terrifies because it is *annihilation* — the verse denies it: you are *gathered*; (2) if it terrifies because it is *exile* — the verse names the terminus: *unto God* — the Beloved of the prayer, the named in every bismillah: an arrival, not an exile; (3) if it terrifies because it is *unfair* — forfeited gains: v. 157 has just out-tallied the estate. The faithful's obituary-meditation ever since has run along a single sentence built exactly of these two verses: *dying defeats only the amassers; the muslim departs with maghfirah-raḥmah in hand and God's own muster at the door*: the fear dissolves; the longing is left; and the conducting of the life adjusts itself to the Jerusalem-clock of the destination: *we shall be gathered: let us build as those who know that*.
**Ḥashr: Gathering-Vocabulary in Its Own Register**

*Wa la-in muttum aw qutiltum la-ilā Allāhi tuḥsharūn* — "and if you die or are slain — to God you shall be gathered": *ḥashara* — gathering by muster, herding with inevitable drive — is the Book's appointed word for the Day's logistics, and the sūrah has been building its consonance since v. 9's *Jāmiʿ al-nās*: death and martyrdom both terminate in *muster*, none excused, none lost in transit. The Qur'an's own muster-gallery reinforces the term at its most total: *"the Day We gather the reverent to the Merciful in procession, and drive the criminals to Hell in thirst"* (19:85–86); and the animal-kingdom's own muster assures the logistics below them: *"no walking creature on the earth nor bird flying on two wings but are communities like you... then to their Lord they are gathered"* (6:38). Man's representative-files all arrive.

**Ziyārat al-Qubūr: The Practiced Reminder**

Uḥud's own dead gave the chapter its permanent visitation-ritual: the Prophet ﷺ used to stand at the graves of the martyrs and speak greeting, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar would keep up the visit — *"peace be upon you by what you patiently endured; how fair is the final abode"* — and the Prophet set the institution's general warrant for the whole ummah:

> *"I had forbidden you the visiting of graves — so now visit them; for they remind you of the Hereafter."* (Muslim 977, from Abū Hurayrah)

The muster-promise of v. 158 thereby receives its liturgy in every Islamic cemetery since: graves visited as *stations of the assembly*, the heart rehearsing its own gathering. And the believer carries the grammar home nightly — his sleep a death's brother, his waking a muster's rehearsal — until the evening the muster is his, and the gathering is to God.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:159

> **Then [it was] by a mercy from God that thou wert gentle with them. Hadst thou been severe [and] hard-hearted they would have scattered from about thee. So pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in affairs. And when thou art resolved, trust in God; truly God loves those who trust.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Diagnosis of the Greatest Heart Ever Placed in a Man**

Few verses of the Book have been more frequently cited across the ummah's entire ethical literature — the leadership manual in seven clauses: *fa-bi-mā raḥmatin mina Allāhi linta lahum* — "by a mercy from God you were gentle to them": *bi-mā* of causal emphasis: the gentleness is not a personality-trait of admirable luck but *raḥmah min Allāh*: a mercy *from* God, specially landed: the Prophet's softness is heaven-funded, as all his traits: *wa law kunta faẓẓan ghalīẓa al-qalbi la-nfaḍḍū min ḥawlik* — "had you been rough and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you": *faẓẓ*: coarse, harsh-grained, severe of manner; *ghalīẓ al-qalb*: thick-hearted, unyielding at the feeling-core: the two are paired deliberately: roughness of *conduct* and hardness of *heart*: both drive people off. *They would have scattered* (*la-nfaḍḍū* — the dispersal of a beads-string): the retention of a community around a leader is governed by *kindness-physics*: gentleness gathers; harshness scatters: God reveals to His Messenger, in immediate context of the Uḥud fault itself, the substance from which His gathering of humanity was built: not infallibility of the followers — they had just disobeyed catastrophicly — but gentleness of the shepherd: this is the hour for harshness, if any hour ever was — and God's instruction is precisely *softer*.

**The Three Commands: Pardon, Intercede, Consult**

*Fa-fu ʿanhum* — *so pardon them*: the ʿafw of verses 134, 152 now made the Prophet's personal assignment: *wa-staghfir lahum* — and seek forgiveness *for* them: two operations distinguished by the commentators (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī): pardon relates to the rights of *you yourself* as leader — the offense against your command (they left the post you had personally appointed); istighfār relates to the rights of *God* — the disobedience paid toward heaven: the Prophet is told to secure both dockets, his and His Lord's — descending to implement in person the ummah-forgiveness God had pre-signed (v. 152's *wa la-qad ʿafā Allāhu ʿanhum*): the Messenger begs for the men who had fled from him while he called *to me, servants of God*: no counter-page of prophetic conduct in any literature of the world matches the depth of this instruction. — And then the astonishing third: *wa shāwirhum fī al-amr* — *and consult them in the matter*: after a breach *in a matter of consultation* (the decision to go out, v. 121, made by shūrā, had issued in the breach), God instructs His Prophet to *again* consult the very men: not to cancel shūrā after shūrā had produced a catastrophe, but to *double it*: the institution is too princely to be a casualty of its own first failure: the Prophet is to consult them despite revelation — the commentators' own debate laid out honestly (some: shūrā for him was gracious allowance, for he needs no man's counsel; others, with al-Rāzī leaning this way: it was *institution-building*: the Prophet was knitting counsel into the ummah's blood: God was teaching a future people's constitution through His Messenger's practice: the Messenger consulted men and women alike through the whole sīrah — about war, about treaties, about release of captives at Badr's aftermath, about the Ḥudaybiyyah response: and when his companions asked him about the management of dates-palm pollination and his advice miscarried in a world-matter, his own words recorded the boundary: *"you are more knowing of the affairs of your world"* (Muslim 2364, and in the hadith-collections from Anas, Ṭalḥah, and others) — not abdication, but commission: prophetic infallibility guards revelation; technical knowledge is for consultation. The political-theory schooling of the whole Muslim world in the ages after has kept 3:159 beside 42:38 ("their affairs are counsel among them") as the twin pillars of shūrā — the Islamic principle of consultative governance: the verse's clear addressee being not only the Prophet but, through him, every leader in every age.

**"...And When Resolved, Trust": The Complete Operating Sequence**

And the fourth clause closes the loop with the complete decision-cycle: *fa-idhā ʿazamta fa-tawakkal ʿalā Allāh* — "when you have resolved, then trust in God": *ʿazm*: firm resolve, the binding-knot decision: after consultation converts into resolve, *the deliberation registers close*: no more meta-shūrā — the time of decision has come: and then — precisely at the instant of resolution — the soul is commanded *tawakkul*: to say: the counsel-humans and the resolve-human are done; the *outcome* is deposited with God: the verse thus legislates the whole sequence: (1) gentle gathering; (2) pardon the offenders; (3) carry their file upward; (4) counsel-them despite fault; (5) decide firm; (6) hand the consequence to God. The commentators note the exact symmetry of the fifth and sixth: resolve is your maximal *human* contribution; tawakkul is the *divine* assumption of consequence: between them no zone is left for anxiety: and the ending seals with the chapter's love-banners: *inna Allāha yuḥibbu al-mutawakkilīn* — "truly God loves the trusting" — the seventh "God loves" of the sūrah (muttaqīn, ṣābirīn, mutawakkilīn, muḥsinīn, muqsiṭīn, ṭāhirīn, and again ṣābirīn — the full love-catalog of tawḥīd's behavior-classes) — with the most beautiful of the ascriptions here: for it is addressed to the *Prophet* himself: even the man whose chest held revelation is told *trust in God* — for the Prophet's own heart was the first human heart this verse's love was promised to.

**ʿAlī's Retrospective — And the Verse's Afterlife**

Al-Rāzī preserves, on this verse, the saying of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib that Muslims have treasured ever since as a summary-history of the whole gentleness-principle:

> *"How good God has been to us! We were idolaters, and had the Messenger of God come with this entire religion all at once, and the Qur'an all at once, the responsibilities would have weighed heavily upon us, and we would not have entered. Rather he called us to a single word; and when we accepted it and tasted the sweetness of faith, we accepted what came after — word upon word, gently — until the religion was completed and the law perfected."* (al-Rāzī on 3:159)

Gentleness *was Islam's own generational method*: the religion of a stern prophet (God testifies) would have scattered the Arabs in a single season: taught by a man whose custom-ethos his wife summed in one sentence — *his character was the Qur'an* (Muslim 746, from ʿĀʾishah) — the new community learned the deepest lesson of leadership: *people follow those who love them*: and the love, per this verse's architecture, is planted by mercy, irrigated by forgiveness, disciplined by consultation, and harvested in tawakkul. Every parent, imam, manager, teacher, captain, and monarch ever since has had his conduct's whole curriculum written in 3:159: pardon, intercede, counsel, decide, trust — and *He loves the trusting*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:160

> **If God helps you, none shall overcome you. And if He forsakes you, who then can help you thereafter? And in God let the believers trust.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**First Principles of War in Two Clauses**

Verse 160 distills the entire Uḥud remedial curriculum into two conditional theses that have served as the battle-creed of Islam ever since: *in yanṣurkumu Allāhu fa-lā ghāliba lakum* — "if God helps you, none can overcome you" — *wa in yakhdhulkum fa-man dhā alladhī yanṣurukum min baʿdih* — "and if He forsakes you, who then is there that can help you after Him?" The two horns bracket *all* possibility of power: help and abandonment are God's toggles — forth and back of the one key: hence no third source of victory exists. Al-Rāzī reads the verse's own historical caption: God *helped* at Badr — and the outnumbered handful carried a day no arithmetic could hold; He *forsook* at Uḥud — and the army's own earlier momentum (vv. 152's *idḥ taḥussūnahum*) was pulled out from under it at the trigger of one disobedience: the two proofs lie three kilometers and thirteen months apart in the same sīrah: no commentary is needed beyond the Book's own record. And in *wa in yakhdhulkum*, the wording exacts a note of precision: *khadhl* is *letting-go*: dominion-withdrawn support — not betrayal: the covenant-forsaking is *ours*; His *khadhl* is proportionate withdrawal when the condition-key slips from the lock (v. 125's two keys: patience and reverence): the two conditional clauses then share one final clause — *wa ʿalā Allāhi fa-l-yatawakkali al-muʾminūn* — "and in God let the believers place trust": the third recitation of this refrain in the chapter (first at 3:122, admonition of the two wavering clans at the field's edge; again here; and again at final-closure at vv. 173's *ḥasbunā Allāh wa niʿma al-wakīl*): the trust-liturgy is thrice given in the sūrah because it is the whole hypothetical-matter of the entire campaign-curriculum: *in Him* — never in the handsome array of other horses.

**"None Shall Overcome" — The Whole Grammar of Invulnerability**

*Fa-lā ghāliba lakum* — no *ghālib* — no overcomer: the absolute negative at the superlative site: the statement's reach is total: no army, no technology, no conspiracy, no market, no geology, no demon: when God's help is assigned a thing, its *overcomer does not exist in existence*: the ḥadīth operating-code states the principle in reverse-bells: *"know: that if the whole community joined together to benefit you with anything, they could not benefit you except with what God had written for you; and if they joined together to harm you with anything, they could not harm you except with what God had written upon you"* (al-Tirmidhī 2516, from Ibn ʿAbbās — the "O young man" hadith, graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ): God's *naṣr* and the nations' whole parliament stand on the two tiers of causality: the lower is absolutely conditioned by the upper. From Al-Rāzī's own alternative reading of *min baʿdih*: the question can also run "who can help you *other than He*?" — yielding an even wider claim: help is not merely unrivaled; it is *singular*: monopolized (10:107's parallel question-form: "if God touches you with harm, none can remove it but He; and if He wills you good, none can set back His bounty"; 39:38's: "if God wills me harm, could they remove His harm — or if He wills me mercy, could they withhold His mercy?").

**The Verse's Domicile in Muslim Hearts**

No verse of this sūrah — after 3:26-27 (the kingdom-prayer), 3:8 ('our Lord, make not our hearts to swerve'), and 3:154 — is more inscribed on the memorial-cells of Muslims than this: memorized by every thirteenth-year enlisted man, whispered by plaintiffs entering courts they cannot win by law, recited by patients in the hour of diagnosis. The tawakkul-saint's strategy it codifies is the opposite of passivity: at verse 154 the army's own *feeblest* hour was followed by His bounty; at verse 151 the retreating idolaters were already *rotated* by terror cast: in between (v. 160) stands the instruction: none of the seen implements accounted for either; *trust in God* — the gate through which help descends upon the condition-holders: *if God helps you, none shall overcome*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:161

> **It is not for any prophet to defraud. And whosoever defrauds will bring what he obtained by fraud on the Day of Resurrection. Then every soul shall be paid what it has earned in full, and they shall not be wronged.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Red Cloak of Badr, and the Apostolic Integrity It Guarded**

The verse that descends upon the spoils-question of Badr and Uḥud is one of the great institutional guarantees of the religion: *wa mā kāna li-nabiyyin an yaghull* — "it is not for a prophet to defraud/purloin": *ghulla*: the secret taking from public trust — classically, the undistributed spoils. The occasion-rich commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī) hold the principal asbāb: at Badr, after the battle, a red garment (or burd-carpet) went missing from the spoil-camp, and voices of mocking suspicion — encouraged by the hypocrite-party — whispered *perhaps the Prophet has kept it*: heaven's response is constitutional: *it is not for any prophet to defraud*: the office-property of prophecy itself rules out trust-embezzlement: the man sent as certified trustworthy (*al-Amīn* — his very boyhood title among the Quraysh) is by covenant incapable of it: al-Ṭabarī's preferred reading is the general one: the verse *informs* — not merely commands: it states what prophets *are*, from Adam to Jesus to Muḥammad: trust-unbroken. And the second register of the asbāb anchors it to Uḥud's archers themselves: after the battle, when the men who had descended the hill for spoils were denied any share, they complained — and were answered: *your guarantee of fair shares lay in obedience, not descent* — while the general frame of the verse laid the whole discipline of ghulūl upon the ummah forever: spoils and public trusts are handled with prophetic rigor or God's own court steps in.

**"He Will Bring It on the Day of Resurrection": The Inventory-Visual**

*Wa man yaghlul yaʾti bi-mā ghalla yawma al-qiyāmah* — "and whoever defrauds shall come with what he defrauded on the Day of Resurrection": the commentators rich with the Prophet's own theatrical hadith of this scene, from Abū Hurayrah — full of sound and shame:

> *The Prophet ﷺ mentioned a man of ghulūl and said: "I would not want to see any of you on the Day of Resurrection carrying on his neck a camel he has grunting [or: a sheep bleating, a horse neighing], saying: 'O Muḥammad! intercede for me!' and I would say: 'I cannot help you — I conveyed to you.' ... And I would not want to see any of you carrying on his neck a garment rustling, saying: 'O Muḥammad!' — and I say: 'I cannot help you.'"* (al-Bukhārī 3107? — the fuller narrations: al-Bukhārī 6939 (ghulūl-account of the Day), 3079, 6979; Muslim 1830–1832 — from Abū Hurayrah and Ibn ʿUmar: the camel grunting, the sheep bleating, the horse neighing, the gold and silver strips rattling, the cloak rustling — each purloined thing carried *audibly* upon the neck of its purloiner: the public theater of embezzlement's audit: the Prophet's defense before God being, forever: *"I conveyed."*)

The wasp-poetry of the scene is total: the weapon against theft of invisible goods is the *converting of them into noise*: the gold his own voice; the cloak its own rustle: brought *on* — *yaʾti bi-mā ghalla*: not metaphor: the Qur'an's eschatology of audit runs on material evidence: what you frauded comes *with you*, as your indictment and your millstone (v. 180's collaring of the miserly by their hoard runs the same process).

**"Then Every Soul Shall Be Paid in Full" — The Settlement Doctrine**

*Thumma tuwaffā kullu nafsin mā kasabat wa hum lā yuẓlamūn* — "then every soul shall be paid in full what it earned; and they shall not be wronged": the sūrah's bench-verdict echoes (vv. 25, 57, 161): full payment, no ẓulm: the full-pay clause applying now in *both* punitive and rewarding directions: the fair leaders who carried the trust spotless — paid; the defrauders — collared: the Prophet's own standing jurisprudence of public office expanded the verse civilly: the hadith of the zakāh-collector (the man sent out to gather alms who returned saying *"this is yours — and this was gifted to me"* — to whom the Prophet replied):

> *"If you speak true, why did you not sit in your father's and mother's house, and see whether gifts would come to you? By Him in Whose hand is my soul — none of you takes anything of this [trust] woe-fully but he shall come with it on the Day of Resurrection carrying it on his neck..."* (al-Bukhārī 6974; Muslim 1832 — from Abū Hurayrah: the zakāh-collector hadith)

And from that line the Muslim civil law of office was built across the ages: officials' gifts treated as presumptive embezzlement; all tenders of public trusts audited at the source: *wa man yaghlul* — a single word-term that matured into an entire ethics of public money in Islam — from the Prophet's own example at the distribution at al-Jiʿrānah, when a rough bedouin pulled his cloak-line, demanding *"be just — for this is a distribution in which God's face is not sought"* — the companions rising in anger against him, and the Prophet restraining them with the immortal sentence of the verse's own countenance: *"woe to him — if I am not just, then who shall be just? I would fail and lose if I were not just"* (al-Bukhārī 4362-64; Muslim 1064 — the Khārijite's judgement: Dhū al-Khuwayṣirah's scene): integrity-outrage worn unhurriedly on the sleeve of the most wronged man in history, who had never touched a morsel of any public trust that was not written to his account in the sight of his Lord.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:162

> **Is he who pursues God's Contentment like one who earns a burden of anger from God, and whose refuge is Hell? An evil journey's end!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Whole Human Species Divided by One Question**

Verse 162 issues the chapter's most compact taxonomy — a single interrogative that sorts all humanity: *a-fa-mani ittabaʿa riḍwāna Allāhi ka-man bāʾa bi-sakhaṭin mina Allāhi wa maʾwāhu jahannam* — "is the one who pursues God's contentment like the one who incurs wrath from God — whose refuge is Hell? An evil journey's end!" *Ittabaʿa riḍwāna Allāh* — follows-after God's *riḍwān*: *riḍwān*: contentment, good-pleasure, satisfaction — the greatest of God's apportioned mercies: the Book's own ultimate prize: *"God is content with them, and they with Him"* (5:119; 9:100; 58:22; 98:8) — its dipláxis: God *contented*, the servant *contented* — 98:8's twin-reclosing: *raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhum wa raḍū ʿanh* — the Garden's exact paygrade: *"God has prepared for forgiveness and a great reward... for them Gardens of Eden, rivers running below, abiding therein forever — God's *riḍwān* is greater — *wa riḍwānun mina Allāhi akbar* — that is the great triumph"* (9:72): *riḍwān* outranks the Garden itself as its own content: the highest reply a whole life can receive. And *bāʾa bi-sakhaṭin min Allāh* — the opposite motion: *bāʾa*: came-home carrying, *returned laden with* — as at v. 112 ("they incurred wrath") and its parallels (2:61, 90): wrath as something *carried home as acquirement*: life as shopping-expedition whose bag is not bread but *sakhaṭ*: divine anger: and with the bag comes the lodging: *wa maʾwāhu jahannam* — his refuge is Hell — *wa biʾsa al-maṣīr* — "an evil the *journey's end*": *maṣīr*: the place finally come to ('arrival'): the measure of the whole march.

**The Question That Audits Every Hour**

The verse's interrogative structure — *a-fa-man* — "is he...?" — is the classical Arabic form of *self-evident inequality*: it expects no answer because the disparity is patent: two human beings live two biographies: one tracks God's contentment in every next act; the other tracks (with the same daily effort) his own appetites, edges, resentments: and at the day's end, the *travel-merchandise* of each has, by God's own receipt-book, been *riḍwān* or *sakhaṭ*: verse 162 says: *they are not alike* — a phrase the Book tires the rhetorical reader with across its parallel instances (32:18: "is the believer like the iniquitous? — they are not equal"; 38:28; 45:21: "or do those who work evil think We shall make them as those who believe and do righteousness...?" — the *not-alike* doctrine): since inequality-of-ends must be *earned* inequality-of-paths: the two roads cannot be averaged.

**Riḍwān, Sakhaṭ, and Maṣīr: The Three-Word Curriculum of Aqidah**

For the daily believer the verse installs the simplest of all worship-ethics: *every intended act is checked at a single window*: does this pursue riḍwān? — would the sight of it please the Lord whose face I seek (v. 13's promise)? The question is the practical field-equivalent of the entire theology of ikhlāṣ — for intentions parse quickest when measured by *Whose contentment* is being sought: God's — or one's own self, tribe, party, market, employer, or pride of name? The tradition's own generalship of this verse is in the Prophet's tall eighty-word inventory: *"Whoever seeks God's contentment by [what entails] the people's anger, God will suffice him against the people; and whoever seeks the people's contentment by God's anger, God leaves him to the people"* (al-Tirmidhī 2414, from Ibn ʿUmar/ʿĀʾishah — graded ḥasan): the exact e-commerceclauses of verse 162: riḍwān-pursuance purchases *divine sufficiency* (ḥasbī Allāh); sakhaṭ-purchasing purchases *abandonment* to the very hands that were being courted. — *Wa biʾsa al-maṣīr*: and the arrival shows the bag: journey's end reveals contentment or wrath: one verse at the end of Uḥud's curriculum, and the entire roster of the world's biographies is read in it.
**Riḍwān Superior to the Garden**

*A-fa-man ittabaʿa riḍwāna Allāhi ka-man bāʾa bi-sakhaṭin min Allāhi* — "is he who follows God's contentment like him who returns with God's displeasure?": *riḍwān* — from *riḍā*, contentment, in the emphatic weight-number of maximums — is the Book's summit-aim supernally, and the Book itself ranks the convoy: at 9:72, after the paired gardens-for-men-and-women and their everlasting abiding, God adds: *wa riḍwānun min Allāhi akbar* — *"and God's riḍwān is greater — that is the supreme triumph."* The Garden, with its rivers and its everlasting, is thus placed *under* the Lord's contentment — His being pleased — so that the inhabitants' final bliss is not in real estate but in relationship: the Ruler pleased with them. Verse 162's question-form (*a-fa-man... ka-man...*) thereby runs the highest stake the comparative-grammar can lift: two travellers, one pursuing *riḍwān*, one incurring *sakhaṭ* — and their ends: *wa maʾwāhu jahannamu wa biʾsa al-maṣīr* — his refuge is Hell, and evil is the journey's end.

**5:119: Contentment Reciprocated**

The sūrah's promise finds its reciprocal in the Blessed Table's closing scene — God's Day-speech over the truthful: *"God is content with them, and they are content with Him"* (5:119) — *riḍā* answered by *riḍā*, heaven's own symmetry — and its earthly rehearsal in the ḥadīth of the three-tasted faith: *"whoever is content with God as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad ﷺ as messenger, has tasted the food of faith"* (Muslim 34). Between 3:162's pursuit and 5:119's banquet the believer's whole economy is settled: pursue the Lord's pleasure down whatever track, Uḥud-morning or market-morning — for the pursuit's own sense ripen, faith's taste arrives early; and the Day completes it: God content, they content, riḍwān greater than the gardens.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:163

> **They are ranked in degrees in the sight of God, and God sees whatsoever they do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Darajāt": The Cosmos as an Ordered Ladder**

The next verse is a sentence of six words that completes the taxonomy of 162 with a section on *structure*: *hum darajātun ʿinda Allāh* — "they are degrees, with God" — *wa Allāhu baṣīrun bi-mā yaʿmalūn* — "and God sees whatsoever they do." *Darajāt*: stairs, grades, echelons — the concept of layered rank. The commentators (al-Ṭabarī first, al-Rāzī's fuller mapping) read the clause in two registers that are both true and mutually enriching: (1) *the two parties of verse 162 occupy different degrees here and now*: the contentment-pursuers are already at an altitude above the wrath-burdened, in truth's weight, honor, visibility before God — the world's mirrors often invert the heights, but *ʿinda Allāh* — *in God's sight* — the elevator-shaft is sorted; (2) *within each party, ranks vary infinitely*: the rewarded ascend through the degrees of the Garden — degrees as numerous as diligence levels ("for each are degrees according to what they did, that He may pay them for their deeds — and they shall not be wronged" — 6:132, and 46:19: "for each there are degrees for what they did, and that He may pay them in full for their deeds") — while the punished descend by similar stairs of sakhaṭ: some scorched in shallow outer pits (the Prophet's uncle Abū Ṭālib, in the famous mercy-report, minimally tormented in the shallows — al-Bukhārī 6564; Muslim 209 — his two sandals lifting his brain, per the narration, for his defense of the Prophet in his lifetime) and the Khārijites' depths beneath: *the entire theater of the Hereafter is raked*: no flat darkness, no uniform light: exactly-fitted floors.

**Degrees as the Deep Shape of Reality**

The commentators furthermore raise this clause to the level where the verse supplies Islam's anthropology of *order*: reality is not flat: *the cosmos itself is built in darajāt*: angels in degrees ("and there is none of us but has a known station" — 37:164), prophets in degrees ("those are the messengers — We favored some of them above others" — 2:253), knowledge-holders raised in degrees ("God raises those of you who believe and those given knowledge by degrees" — 58:11), the sky layered in seven floors (71:15), deeds ascending by degrees of weight (32:5). The verse thus installs the whole *vertical theory of being*: existence itself grades outward and upward — and the human wan is not exempt: man is the creature who *climbs his own code*: abase yourself before desire — you slide floors; pursue riḍwān — up you climb: God is *Baṣīr* — the Watcher — with the seal: *wa Allāhu baṣīrun bi-mā yaʿmalūn*: His watching means His *grading-criteria are perfect*: no rank is assigned on rumor: all ranks are set upon deeds *seen*.

**For the Reader, Climbing**

The verse's daily-use form of comfort is embraced by spiritual generations since: you are not bound to another's *darajah*: God's Book does not say *you* will reach the station of Abū Bakr or Mary (their darajāt are theirs); it says the ladder is *open*: today you can convert one hour into a grade-riser: one act of hidden charity, one prayer in the deep night, one pardon offered where you once kept score: *hum darajātun ʿinda Allāh* — degrees *in God's sight*: no worldly ranking affects it — the elevator-shaft of heaven is open all hours, and the One watching the deeds is the One whose +1 never mis-clicks.
**Darajāt: The Ladder That Stays Open**

*Hum darajātun ʿinda Allāh* — "they are degrees with God": the announcement stands as the pericope's (vv. 163–169) master-key: with God, persons are *ranked* — souls occupy steps of a ladder whose treads no census of titles could fake. The Book's ladder-system spans the whole creation-file: the angels disclaim rank-consciousness — *"there is none of us but has a known station"* (37:164); the prophets are graded among themselves — *"those messengers — We have preferred some above others"* (2:253); works and knowledge lift — *"God raises those of you who believe and those given knowledge by degrees"* (58:11). Placement of v. 163 — directly after the Uḥud ledger that had re-sorted every participant (archers, standers, counselors, martyrs) — transforms it from flattery to measurement: *your steps climbed were registered as steps.*

**The Hour-to-Degree Conversion**

The conversion-rate of days into degrees is the morals-economy the salaf preached from this verse-family: al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's saying runs in their number: *"I have met a people more stingy with their lives than with their dirhams"* — hours being the capital that purchases steps. The Prophet's own ascent through the Miʿrāj's seven heavens showed the ladder's architecture concretely — station above station, each landfall submitted before the next opened — and his constant request set the community's own application:

> *"O God, grant Your servant the loftiest of levels (al-darajāt al-ʿulā) of Paradise"* — the established wording of his supplication (al-Bukhārī 742: *"say among your prayers: O God, Lord of this complete call... grant Muhammad the wasīlah and the faḍīlah, and raise him the praised station You promised him"* — and al-Tirmidhī's degree-words in the ask for the *Firdaws, the highest of the Garden*, 3613 among the tirmidhī-requests).

Degrees are purchasable; the currency is deeds; the shop is open — v. 163's ladder-grammar having exempted no reader from its treads.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:164

> **God certainly favored the believers when He sent them a Messenger from among themselves, who recites His signs unto them, and purifies them, and teaches them the Book and Wisdom, while aforetime they were in manifest error.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Greatest Ledger Entry the Believers Ever Received**

Two verses after grades and ranks, God opens the chapter's final grace-enumeration — and names the supreme instance of the chapter's own deepest theme, *faḍl* (bounty): *la-qad manna Allāhu ʿalā al-muʾminīna idh baʿatha fīhim rasūlan min anfusihim* — "God indeed *was gracious* to the believers when He sent among them a Messenger from among themselves." *Manna ʿalā* — bestowed favor — the verb-gratitude's deepest scale: favor *mighty upon the believer* — and the appointment of the Messenger is presented *as the favor*: not victory, not spoils, not survival — *the Messenger himself*: if God had given this generation every battle and hidden this man, the account would have been bitter loss; having given them this man, every battle lost is still outright gain. — *Min anfusihim* — *from among themselves*: their own kind, their own speech, their own city: the irony the rest of the verse unpacks: what the idolaters held up as objection (54:24: "shall we follow a single human from among us?"; 11:12: "why has no treasure descended on him, nor an angel with him?"; 7:69; 38:4; 50:2 — the person's *human-ness* as scandal) is presented here as the blessing's own core: an angel-messenger would have supplied *excuse*; a *human* messenger supplies *possibility*: *what he does, you can do — the model must be of your species or it instructs no one.*

**The Messenger's Four Functions: Islam's Whole Education Ministry**

Then God lists the Messenger's work in four serial infinitives — the complete manual of what prophethood *does* upon a people: (1) *yatlū ʿalayhim āyātih* — *recites His signs upon them*: the Qur'an's own sound in their ears — revelation as living medium: he was the first radio of the unseen; (2) *wa yuzakkīhim* — *and purifies them*: *tazkiyah*: the growing-and-cleansing: the soul-craft: transforming appetite-ridden bedouin, quarrel-gridlocked tribesmen, pride-charged sons of chiefs into weeping, generous, disciplined servants: the generation-transformation that all historians hold is the Prophet's most matchless achievement (the same city that birthed the poets of tribal-fatwa bowed, within twenty years, beneath one dawn-call); (3) *wa yuʿallimuhumu al-kitāb* — *and teaches them the Book*: the scripture's contents made legible; and (4) *wa-l-ḥikmah* — *and Wisdom*: *al-ḥikmah* — the measured application: the Prophet's own approved practice and judgment: the sunnah-systematic comprehension of the Book: Word + Way — the two archives the Prophet left behind as his two-legged testament (the farewell hadith: *"I have left among you two things — you shall not go astray so long as you hold them: the Book of God and my sunnah"*). The complete formulation ratifies the exact prophetic job-description the Book seals elsewhere almost verbatim — 2:151 ("as We sent among you a Messenger... who recites Our signs and purifies you and teaches you the Book and Wisdom"); 62:2 — and, most beautifully, traces it to its *patriarchal root*: this verse is *the exact answer to Abraham's prayer at the raising of the House* — 2:129:

> *"Our Lord! Send among them a messenger *from among them* who shall recite upon them Your signs, and teach them the Book and the Wisdom, and purify them — You are the Mighty, the Wise."* — the nearly word-for-word petition of the Friend-of-God standing with Ismael at the Kaʾba's foundations: three thousand years between petition and fulfillment — and the sūrah's Abraham-cycle (vv. 33–34, 65–68, 84, 95–97) now declares its long-looped conclusion: God answers prayers of patriarchs over millennia — *the Messenger being the prayer's landing*.

**"While Aforetime They Were in Manifest Error": The Before-Photo**

The verse's closing phrase — *wa in kānū min qablu la-fī ḍalālin mubīn* — "though aforetime they were in clear, manifest error" — is written in ḍalāl's most unqualified grade: *mubīn*: evident, patent: no ambiguity shaded the Jāhiliyyah: daughters buried alive, tribes consumed in vendettas measured in decades (Aws–Khazraj of v. 103; the Basūs forty-year war of the she-camel), wine-marble *istiqsām* at the idols, usury doubling-and-multiplying (v. 130's own ban follows its practice), the child-brides, the slave-nudity circumambulations (in the sīrah's forensic inventory: men circumambulating the Kaʾba in the nude), mock-covenant and guest-lust: *manifest* — confirmed by the Arabs' own surviving poetry's own confessions of boast. God keeps the before-photo beside the cure so the medicine is properly graded: the Messenger's four functions converted *that* moral geology into the community of 3:110 ("best community brought forth") in twenty-three years — the civilization-engine of messengership executed where the whole earth's theological specialists had dismissed the terrain as unteachable. **The chapter's own crown runs here**: this sūrah, born in delegations and disputes, turns, in this verse, to vast gratitude: God's having blessed the believers with this one man exceeds, in the Book's own measure, every battle of the sequence just audited: *la-qad manna Allāhu ʿalā al-muʾminīn*: *the favor is Him.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:165

> **And when an affliction befell you, though you wrought an affliction twice its like, did you say, "Whence is this?" Say, "It is from yourselves." Truly God is Powerful over all things.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Whence Is This?" — The Question Every Setback Extracts**

The final diagnostic of the whole Uḥud curriculum is the most sovereign: *a-wa lammā aṣābatkum muṣībatun qad aṣabtum mithlayhā, qultum annā hādhā? qul huwa min ʿindi anfusikum* — "and when an affliction befel you — though you had afflicted twice its like — did you say, 'whence is this?' Say: it is *from your own selves*." The accounting of *mithlayhā* — *twice its like* — is the Book's own double-entry bookkeeping: al-Ṭabarī's lines: at Badr the believers had, in one morning, slain seventy of Quraysh and taken seventy captive — *140 total casualties inflicted*; at Uḥud Quraysh inflicted seventy: thus the muṣībah that *struck you* was exactly *half* of what you had struck them: your net stood +70 even on the combined ledger of both campaign-days. Al-Qurṭubī's articulation of the stricter reckoning accepted by the early commentators makes the ledger exact: slain-plus-captives equals a doubled affliction because captives could lawfully have been executed. Either way, the arithmetic is God's gentle sarcasm-of-perspective: *after inflicting two-on-one, you lost one, and your question — "whence is this?" — rose as though catastrophe had besieged an innocent house:* the Book's therapy for self-pity is not denial but *mathematics*.

**"It Is From Yourselves": The Sovereignty's Redirect**

And against *annā hādhā* ("whence this?") — the question whose tone insinuates God's abandonment — the commanded answer is monosemantic: *huwa min ʿindi anfusikum* — *it is from your own selves*: (1) the proximate chain — the archers' descent from the hill for spoils (vv. 152–153), the consultation's preference not heeded (Ibn Ubayy's withdrawal followed, v. 121), the world's-grease in some chests (v. 152); (2) the commentators' supplementary theories preserved faithfully (al-Rāzī: some said the affliction came because at Badr the believers had ransomed prisoners against the stricter counsel of ʿUmar and Saʿd — God testing whether the gentler or the stricter option would be chosen next time — the revealed discourse on Badr's ransom at 8:67–70 narrates the heaven-side deliberation itself; or that Uḥud's affliction came *because the rout had been yielded twice* — at Badr and at Uḥud's first hour — and once returned, in balance); (3) the deepest reading of *min ʿindi anfusikum*: your adversity within God's total sovereignty is causally routed *through your own act*: not as blame denied to God but as God's *system*: He gives you the moral engine, He hands you the laws of consequence, He watches what you feed into them: *the affliction is His decree — and your earning*: both true at once (theology's exact balance: Ashʿarī *kasb*: God creates, man earns; and the Book says both facts without contradiction: "from your selves" *and* "Truly God is Powerful over all things").

**"Truly God Is Powerful Over All Things": Sovereignty Sealed Above Cause**

The verse's final clause — *inna Allāha ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr* — seals the two-causalities in one sentence: your agency is *real* (the affliction came from your selves — yes: cause properly attributed); and God's *power over everything* (qadar) is simultaneously absolute: the Qur'an refuses both horns of all false dilemmas: the Jabrite (fatalist) horn — *nothing is from ourselves* — and the Qadarite (free-will absolutist) horn — *His power does not cover this*: at one stroke both ended. Uḥud *was* in God's power — His angels could have annihilated the Makkan cavalry by a word, v. 124–126's whole section; and Uḥud *was* from the believers' selves — God's own audit says so: a defeat-analyzed-in-heaven is worth a hundred victories trained-on-earth, and the chapter's final summary of the whole battle will arrive in its own two clauses: *so that God may know the believers and know the hypocrites* (vv. 166–167) — the *two groups' qualific-event*: which the next verses close.
**The Balance of Judgment: Qadar and Responsibility Held Together**

The double-entry audit — *for what you twice dealt the like as punishment... from your own selves* — is among the clearest of the Book's positions in the old dispute of Jabr and Qadar, and its phrasing refuses both half-schools: *the blow was real and measured* (twice-equivalence: exact, intended, deliberate) — God's administration precise; *its address was your ledger* (*min ʿindi anfusikum*) — your agency real, your choices chargeable. Al-Rāzī, whom the sects have never stopped claiming, here composes the mature reading: the decree frames the field; the *movements upon it* belong to the movers and are recompensed as theirs. The chapter's own instruction rehearses the balance domestically: Badr's ransom-debate (v. 152's failure-catalog opening the same topic in its passing) shows God's *permission* and man's *reckoning* running as separate entries at every action — and 42:30, the Ummah's own balance-sheet proverb, states the general law: *"whatever calamity strikes you is for what your hands have earned — and He pardons much"* — audit affirmed, overlay of mercy not forgotten.

**Min ʿIndi Anfusikum: The Hardest Word with a Door**

Buried in the arithmetic is the clause that alone makes recovery thinkable: the trouble is *from your own selves* — and therefore repairable at the selves themselves. Blame-site theology differs inwardly: if the blow were pure accident, there is nothing to fix; *because it is authored, the authors can edit.* The Prophet's ﷺ practice in every loss — istighfār at the very shock — modeled the reflex for the ummah: the burial-month after Uḥud was among the istighfār-seasons of Madinah. The believing reader of v. 165 undergoing his own small Uḥuds practices the sequence in miniature: no defense-brief to God first; no alibi-gathering — *my own self first; then ask; then stand* — the discoverer's morning always better than the look-away's.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:166

> **And that which befell you on the day the two hosts met was by God's Leave, and that He may know the believers,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Final Verdict of the War's Causality**

One short verse closes the long Uḥud audit — with the last stamp that settles the meaning of the whole day's trial: *wa mā aṣābakum yawma ltaqā al-jamʿāni fa-bi-idhni Allāh* — "what befel you on the day the two hosts met was *by God's leave*" — *wa li-yaʿlama al-muʾminīn* — "and so that He may know the believers." The *bi-idhni Allāh* clause is the completion of verse 165's double-causality doctrine: though it came *from your own selves* (instrumentally), the affliction *was by God's leave* (ultimately): no arrow in the field departed His jurisdiction: the two clauses together define Islam's whole theology of event: everything that occurs *both* is by God's leave and involves our own enjoying-of-causes: the poison arched by free hands and the wingspan of the same God permit it: Uḥud fell in *His* jurisdiction — hence *not tragic* in the pagan sense: it was an *allowed* lesson — like all events.

**"And That He May Know the Believers": Uḥud as a Great Illumination**

And then the final-other-cut of the *li-yaʿlama* purpose-clause (which we have already engaged at vv. 140, 142, 154): the battle existed *to know*: to bring into witnessable reality the *muʾminūn* and the hypocrites (the verse's next-half continues directly into v. 167 — the two-test audit is side by side). Battle-as-known: worth the whole grief: because God's plan for Madinah was to *found there a witness-community* — so it had first to be *seen* what its chests held: gold from chaff — a process the chapter has taught us to call *tamḥīṣ* (v. 154): seventy-two proofs of light-witness were extracted in the interim (v. 140's *yattakhidha minkum shuhadāʾ*); three hundred proofs of fog were identified around the departure-line (v. 167's scene); and the seven hundred who *stayed* — their wavering noted, their staying ratified — emerged the tested core of the next generation (by year 8, nearly every commander of the Muslim armies that brought the revelation across the peninsula had been at Uḥud: the battle's graduates). **The verdict-line of the whole war-curriculum is printed here**: not Badr's clean triumph but Uḥud's confused morning was *the* founding lesson of the new community — God knew the believers in it: and, as vv. 167–168 tell the matching end of the audit, He *knew the hypocrites* in the same light.

**The Believer and the Bi-idhn Allāh Clause**

The private application of *bi-idhni Allāh* is among the sūrah's great portable medicines: whatever your *Uḥud-day* is — the morning your plans died in one hour — hold it under the two registers the verse prescribes: (1) what befel you was *by God's leave* — no enemy overrode anything: it was *permitted*: therefore bitterness against God is incoherent; (2) it befel you in relation to *who you are*: God was then and there *getting to know you in the created sense*: your endurance, your faith, your state *revealed* through the pressure: therefore the day's testing was not a vanity: a known-heart is a harvested heart. And the whole audit joins hands with its sisters: 47:31 ("We shall test you until We know the strivers among you and the patient, and test your reports"); 29:3 ("We tried those before them — and God truly knows the truthful and knows the liars"): every day of your life is being *read*, and battles are simply reading-days of higher contrast.
**Bi-Idhni Allāh: Permission as Junction of Two Causalities**

*Wa mā aṣābakum yawma ltaqā al-jamʿāni fa-bi-idhni Allāh* — "and what befell you the day the two hosts met was by God's permission": *idhn* — leave, license, release-of-passage — is the Book's precision-term for the juncture where divine decree and human history actually meet: the event *passed* through God's permission (nothing eluding His government), while its *moral* ownership stayed with the actors. Al-Rāzī's treatise-note on the verse distinguishes the senses his school had spent generations over: *idhn* is neither command (*amr*) nor plea-*contentment* in the moral register — the disobedient event being under God's *decree* but never under His *legislative command* — and the junction is sovereign both ways: *nothing reaches pass without the permission; nothing passing is thereby approved.*

**Wa li-Yaʿlama al-Muʾminīn: To Know as Verification**

The verse's first purpose-clause — *and that He might know the believers* — binds the permission to revelation: God, whose knowledge does not learn, appoints the morning when *the hidden contents appear* — as 47:31's program unrolls the standing rule: *"We shall test you until We know the strivers among you and the patient, and test your reports"* — the *knowing* of manifestation, not discovery. Read side by side, 3:165–166 deliver the complete mathematics of Uḥud: the blow's arithmetic from the selves (v. 165); the blow's passage by His permission (v. 166a); its purpose the revealing of hearts (v. 166b); the hypocrite-set unmasked (v. 167). Every later morning of the believers re-runs the same four columns: authored, permitted, revealing, sorting — and the salient verb for the tested stays one: *verify, then verify again.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:167

> **and that He may know the hypocrites. And it was said unto them, "Come, fight in the way of God or defend [yourselves]." They said, "Had we known there would be fighting, we would have followed you." That day they were closer to disbelief than to belief, saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts. And God knows best what they conceal.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Withdrawal on the Field's Edge: Three Hundred in One Man's Wake**

The *other* class God's battle-audit made visible is now named directly: *wa li-yaʿlama al-munāfiqīn* — "and so that He may know the hypocrites." The scene is preserved by the whole of the tafsīr (al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī's record, the sīrah's own detail): when the Prophet came forth with the Muslims and passed through Mina/the outskirts toward Uḥud, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl — he who had attended the council, advised the city-defense, been overruled — called away his party, and about *three hundred of the thousand* wheeled back toward Madinah with him — openly, at the army's rear. To the Companions riding after them with the call — the words God preserves verbatim: *qītalaw? qīl lahum taʿālaw qātilū fī sabīli Allāhi aw idfaʿū* — "it was said to them: come, fight in the way of God, or drive [them off]": the minimum of their commission is carefully recorded (per al-Ṭabarī's and al-Qurṭubī's elaborations): even if a party would not fight *in* God's way, they might yet *make up numbers* — stand in the rank, mass the visible strength: *dify* — repel by presence: the softest possible assignment to men unwilling to hazard themselves: turn strength into deterrent: *and even on those terms they would not* — their answer, preserved in heaven's register: *law naʿlamu qitālan la-ttabaʿnākum* — "had we known there would be fighting, we would have followed you": and al-Rāzī's philological excursus exposes the wick: their objection is not pacifism (Uḥud's counsellors had been ready to fight *within* walls); it is the refusal to risk themselves when the *kind* of fighting on offer was open-field war: "we thought there would only be a stand-off *or* — knowing there would be a massacre — we hold off": their chilling erudition about what they expected God to do with the Muslim war is laid bare by God Himself.

**"That Day They Were Closer to Disbelief Than to Belief"**

God's verdict-seal follows: *yawmaʾidhin hum lil-kufri aqrabu minhum lil-īmān* — "that day they were nearer disbelief than belief": and the commentators land on the legal weight of the phrasing (al-Rāzī): God *could have* named them *kāfirūn* outright — had they been out-and-out deniers, He would have; why *aqrabu* — *closer*? Because their *outward* status — the testimony spoken, the rows prayed — remained contested: their confession genuine in its vocal-cords absence: *outward Islam, inward fog*: in the social register still among the Muslims; *near* kufr as the arrow is near the mark: the verse thereby becomes one of the principal texts Muslim scholarship has used to guard the community's own juridical door (the great hadiths about not declaring an apparent Muslim kāfir on suspicion; the hadith of the man appointed to kill at Khaybar who slew a man *after* his testimony — and the Prophet: *"did you split his heart open?"* — Muslim 96; cf. Usāmah's case: al-Bukhārī 4269, Muslim 96): *whoever keeps the testimony open in the world deserves his most cautious reading*; the inward-exposure belongs to God: *yaqūlūna bi-afwāhihim mā laysa fī qulūbihim* — "saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts" — and God seals it: *wa Allāhu aʿlamu bi-mā yaktumūn* — "and God knows best what they conceal": mouths mis-describe chests; God reads chests directly: the final audit-print of Uḥud's fog has its permanence precisely here: *nothing was hidden*.

**The Verse's Standing Diagnostic of Hypocrisy's Dialect**

And the chapter collects, in the hypocrites' quoted sentences of vv. 154, 156, 167, 168, the *complete grammar of religious de-commitment* — data worth a whole treatise: (1) *the sovereignty-complaint*: "do we have any decision at all?" (v. 154); (2) *the stay-home counterfactual*: "had they stayed with us — they would not have died" (vv. 156, 168); (3) *the conditional loyalty*: "had we known there would be fighting — we'd have come" (v. 167); (4) *the mouth-heart split*: "saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts." Notice: *every clause is some true-patriot's vocabulary misused*: decommitment speaks in entire form-words of prudence, calculation, and mercy-mongering: the hard-won immunity of the saint (v. 12's taqwā) is parodied in the coward's dialect: the whole of the Uḥud curriculum thus reads: the true believer and the dodger use the *same vocabulary of caution*, differ at one joint: whom they finally *obey*; and battle-days are those *open-book moments* when the two legibilities split for an hour — before the city's daily fogs close in again. For every community since Madinah, verse 167 remains a field-manual on the speech-patterns of *the turn-away*: watch the counterfactuals; listen for the conditionals; note, above all, where mouths go when hearts stay.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:168

> **Those who said of their brethren, while they were sitting [at home], "Had they obeyed us, they would not have been slain." Say, "Then ward off death from yourselves, if you are truthful."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"They Were Sitting": The Word That Fixes the Speaker's Posture**

The counterfactual-party receives one more diagnosis, and it opens on a participle that calmly indicts: *alladhīna qālū li-ikhwānihim wa qaʿadū* — "those who said of their brethren, while they sat": *qāʿidūn* — seated, sitting-out: the post-position is not geography but accusation: *they sat*: they never took the field; from their seats they issued analysis of the sacrifices of those standing. Ibn Ubayy's own faction are the direct subjects (al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī), and their formula is the re-issued stay-home line of v. 156 in exact register: *law aṭāʿūnā mā qutilū* — "had they obeyed us, they would not have been slain": *obedience* — their own — now erected as the summum of wisdom ("they obeyed *us*" — not God's command, note: the sedition-syntax of addressing the dead as though the summoner's superiority to heaven). And God answers the counterfactual on the only terrain that cannot be cosmetically staged: *qul fa-draʾū ʿan anfusikumu al-mawta in kuntum ṣādiqīn* — "say: then fend death off from your own selves — if you are truthful": *fa-* — *then* — the particle of logical extraction: if sitting-schedules determine slaughters, *demonstrate*: ward off your own deaths: the argument is deliciously totalitarian: *you have your own appointments;* sit all you like; move all you like; when the *kitāb muʾajjal* (v. 145) comes to term, *fa-draʾū* — push it back — here is your blank form: and if you cannot, then retire the analysis forever: appointment-data overrides sitting-data.

**The Counterfactual's Theology: Why the Book Hates This Argument**

Verse 3:168 is the Scripture's most concentrated dissection of a whole civilizational fallacy — and its engine is exactly the one the source commentary highlights (al-Rāzī): the counterfactual implies *changing God's decree by changed circumstances* — that God's knowledge-of-what-happens is a *rule whose outcomes vary by my choice of venue*: the Qur'an's own rebut-program has now all assembled: v 145 (every soul dies by leave — written, appointed); v. 154 (had you stayed in your houses, the decreed-slain would have gone forth to their beds); v. 156 (God gives life and causes death); and here — v. 168 (fend off your own): the four together declare: *not one martyr at Uḥud* would have lived one extra hour on the sitting-line: which converts verse 168's very sentence into its most devastating corollary: the sat-down did not *save themselves* from death by staying off the field; they *deferred* it — and ruined their portfolios meanwhile: the Prophet's own hadith in its own complete form spells the whole epistemology: from Abū Hurayrah, the long-standing Muslim doctrine of decree:

> *"The strong believer is better and more beloved to God than the weak believer — and in each is good. Be eager for what benefits you, seek God's help, and do not be helpless: and if something befalls you, do not say: 'If only I had done such-and-such, then such-and-such would have been' — but say: 'God decreed — and what He willed, He did' — for *if-only* (law) opens the work of satan."* (Muslim 2664 — complete: the Prophet's own ban of the counterfactual-particle: sitting-analysis banned forever)

**Seated Analysis vs. The Sacrifice's Witness**

And the reader notices the commentaries' own footnote: their "brethren" (*ikhwānihim*) — blood-relatives among the slain (al-Qurṭubī): kin-of-fathers in the same clans — the seated critiquing the fallen within one genealogy: no greater final irony: the men they said would not have been slain *were in the fire-smoke of God's receiving* before the seated finished their sentence — vv. 169 onwards will now open the files of the *true after-existence* of the dead of Uḥud: their travels and their feasts: the sitting-parties' *analysis*; the martyrs' *status* — the next two verses of the sūrah swing upward from the scorners' syllogism to the heaven-docket's own printed statement: the *living* dead.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:169

> **And deem not those slain in the way of God to be dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Most Prohibited Prohibited Misidentification**

With verse 169 the sūrah enters its summit — the verse that has, since the day it descended, redefined for Muslims what "dead" means: *wa lā taḥsabanna alladhīna qutilū fī sabīli Allāhi amwātan* — "do not ever reckon those slain in the way of God as dead" — *bal aḥyāʾun ʿinda rabbihim yurzaqūn* — "nay — living! — with their Lord, provided for." The Book here pulls off the full science apparent-contradiction it began at 2:154 (its first issuance: "and do not say of those who are slain in God's way, 'dead' — nay, they are alive, but you perceive not"): what the senses perceive (a corpse) vs. what God declares (life): the declaration overrules. And crucially — as al-Rāzī argues, pressing the grammar — the text says *aḥyāʾun* — living — *now*: not "will be revived at the Resurrection" (which is true of everyone, believer and obstinate alike, and would render the verse's prohibition without specific content — as al-Rāzī's argument runs rigorously); but a *present, in-barzakh* life — a kind and rank of aliveness *with their Lord* — *ʿinda rabbihim*: in His nearness, at His court: *yurzaqūn* — supplied: drawing rations: a living with *metabolism* of bounty: the body lies at Uḥud's foot; the man is on stipend in the Prefect presence.

**"Provided For": The Green Birds and the River**

The tradition supplies the full tour: from Ibn ʿAbbās (and in Muslim's Ṣaḥīḥ text from Masrūq, who asked ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd about this verse — *"the souls of the martyrs are in the bellies/interior of green birds, having lanterns suspended from the Throne, roving in Paradise wherever they will; then they take lodging in those lanterns; and their Lord looked upon them and said: 'Do you wish for anything?' They said: 'What could we wish for, wandering in Paradise wherever we will?' He asked them three times; and when they saw they would not be left without being asked, they said: 'we wish that our souls be returned to our bodies so we may fight for Your sake and be slain again.'" And when He saw that they had no need beyond, they were left.* (Muslim 1887 — the long narrative: complete: *ḥibāl*: interior/nests of green birds): their one wish, from inside bliss: *to die again in His cause*: testimony of the sweetness of the exact death the living most fear. At Uḥud's immediate descent, too, the night of the funerals saw the Prophet himself stand over the martyrs' graves, and later years' standing obituary practice — the Prophet visited Uḥud annually and said *"peace upon you for what you endured — and excellent shall be your everlasting residence"* — while the tradition preserved his answer on the martyrs' state with 3:169's recitation itself (and from Qatādah's report on Anas's chains, in Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī 3010: when the Prophet was informed of the slaying of Ṭalḥah's brother? — the narrative-event of seventy martyrs at Biʾr Maʿūnah: the *qurrāʾ* slain and God informing His Messenger of their state, and they said: "tell our people that we found our Lord true and pleased").

**The Doctrine This Verse Established**

Everything Islam teaches about the *barzakh* — the isthmus-life between death and resurrection — stands on the arch of 3:169 (and 2:154): (1) death is not extinction — a present-tense state of life is conferred; senses *do not perceive it* — but it is *more* real; (2) it is a life *in station* — *ʿinda rabbihim*: directional proximity: ranked presence; (3) it is nourished — *yurzaqūn*: ongoing provision, a fully-active economy; (4) its occupants are *aware of the world behind* (v. 170's *yastabshirūna bi-lladhīna lam yalḥaqū bihim* — rejoicing over those who have not yet joined them — as the next verse makes explicit) — news flows *up*, as at Badr's well the Prophet said of the dead enemies: *"do not think they do not hear: they hear now as you do"* (al-Bukhārī 3976; Muslim 2875, from Ibn ʿUmar) — the tomb is not silence; (5) the life among martyrs' lives has *tiers* — from the green birds to the lantern-lodgings to the chosen link of the direct heavenly river-bank described in Aḥmad's narration on al-Khālid? — on Jābir: *"the souls of the martyrs are at a river at the gate of Paradise — in green dome-pavilions: their sustenance comes out to them from Paradise morning and evening"* (Aḥmad 14821, and similar reports): *yurzaqūn* — provision-scheduled twice daily, from the gardens themselves. All of it derivable, in the sages' reading, from the verse's three loaded words: *aḥyāʾ* — *ʿinda rabbihim* — *yurzaqūn*: *alive — at their Lord — being fed*.

**And for the Living Left Behind**

The verse was revealed into streets full of widows and orphans: seventy-two households of Madinah learning, by God's direct certification, that their men are *not* gone from sustenance and scene: the tears had just been composèd into taqwā-conduits (the Prophet at Ḥamzah's bier — "I shall not be saddened after today" — his own grief exclamations in the sīrah; and heaven's auditing directing the mourners to this verse's logic): and the instruction to the grievers remains the same as the instant it descended: *do not reckon them dead*: not sentiment — *fact*: they are being *provided for* in a life you cannot see: the channels that carry your peace-salutations to them remain open, and the anniversary visits — the practice of the Prophet at Uḥud, of the caliphs after him, of the entire ummah ever since — are transactions between two live populations on the two sides of one veil: the martyr's economy is fully running; the mourner's is to be made worth their pride.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:170

> **exulting in what God has given them from His Bounty, and rejoicing in those who have not yet joined them from among those who remain behind—that no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Emotional State of Heaven's Already-Entered**

Verse 170 continues the living martyr's portrait with his two joys: *fariḥīna bi-mā ātāhumu Allāhu min faḍlih* — "exulting in what God has given them of His bounty" — *wa yastabshirūna bi-lladhīna lam yalḥaqū bihim min khalfihim* — "and rejoicing over those who have not yet joined them, from behind them" — *allā khawfun ʿalayhim wa lā hum yaḥzanūn* — "that no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve." Three facts in sequence, composed like a living dispatch from beyond the veil.

(1) *Fariḥīn*: they are *joy-receivers* of God's apportioned *faḍl*: the chapter's signature-word lands, at final pitch, in the martyr's register: faḍl (bounty) — after having been tracked as God's empowering of prophets, of the covenant, of the forgive — now stands as the name of the entire martyr-estate: all they now have is God's *bounty*, and all of it is reported by themselves as *farḥ* — glee. The Prophet's reportage of their own words, in the complete narration (Muslim 1887, given at v. 169): we wish nothing — except one thing: *to return, and be slain again in Your cause*: the joy is *this* kind: not erasure-of-memory but clarity-of-value: they now see *what the falling at Uḥud purchased* — and their estimate is joy.

(2) *Yastabshirūna*: they *give and receive good tidings* — over the ones behind them who have not caught up: the verse unfurls, in God's own account, the martyr's *benevolent watchfulness* over the living: the men who died on the hill and around the flag know the ones still fighting and still governing, still weeping their names at graves: news flows upward: and the good news they keep receiving makes them *glad* — not lonely, not miserable with longing: they are *report-receivers* issuing happiness down: al-Rāzī's graceful note on the whole scene: the martyr's relation to the living is *pastoral*: they *care about* their people; they cheer their toward-coming; and the joy flows in both directions: the living blessed by the thought of the blessed dead; the dead gladdened by the states of the living beloveds: person-continuity across the barzakh is not only real; it is *social*: one family, one ummah, still exchanging news across one wall.

(3) *And the warranty over those coming behind* — *allā khawfun ʿalayhim wa lā hum yaḥzanūn* — "that no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve": the *no-fear/no-grief* clause that the Book runs upon its beloved classes at every major seal (2:38, 62, 112, 262's reward-clause; 6:48; 10:62: "behold, the friends of God — no fear upon them, nor do they grieve"; 46:13): God issues the martyr, for his people, a *certificate of exemption from the two master-negatives*: no fear-of-the-future arrives; no grief-at-the-past arrives: the double protection over both time-directions of sorrow's whole empire — God's own feast-suite, first promised to the first exiles of Eden (2:38) and now issued in the green-dome dwellings of the martyrs.

**The Verse's Counseling of the Left-Behind**

To the women and sons of the seventy-two of Uḥud, the verse was the first true funeral-oration: your men are *not in the earth*: they are in loft-economy of joy — and *they are watching you*: cheer them by your endurance: not that they *pity* your durability — rather — their good-news-circuits run on your fidelity: persevere, and their banquets sharpen: fail, and no joy of theirs diminishes — for God Himself is their Direct Host: the conduct the verse prescribes the living-moster is thus exactly the religion's own balance: grieve as long as grief needs — the Prophet wept hugely for Ḥamzah — and *then honor them by building*: the martyr's entire kingdom is joy *forward* — he is already at rest *allā khawfun ʿalayhim*: his one remaining nature-interest is *your welfare*: hence the purest memorial any Muslim can pay any martyred beloved is *his own taqwā-flux over the rest of his own days*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:171

> **rejoicing in Blessing and Bounty from God, and that God neglects not the reward of the believers,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third "Fariḥ": Gift, Continuance, and God's Own Credit Line**

The martyr's joys stack one more level — and the verse expands its register to *all* believers: *yastabshirūna bi-niʿmatin mina Allāhi wa faḍlin* — "rejoicing in blessing from God and bounty" — *wa anna Allāha lā yuḍīʿu ajra al-muʾminīn* — "and that God lets not the believers' reward go to waste." The joy's referents are now three: (1) *niʿmah* — blessing: God's given good; (2) *faḍl* — bounty: God's *above-deserving* overflow (the sūrah's signature ledger-term at last use: after 74, 152, 170 — the bounty-word's final hoard in the chapter); (3) *the standing general clause*: *God does not waste the believers' reward*: *lā yuḍīʿu*: He loses not, misapplies not, lets not slip: the *trustworthiness* of God Himself securitizing the wage: as the Prophet's famous inventory-audit hadith pronounces the same doctrine in address to all deeds: *"whosoever comes with a good deed shall have ten times its like, and more"* (echoed at 6:160 and the qudsi khsoij: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen" — al-Bukhārī 3244-3246; Muslim 2824) — with the loss-clause stating the category-law: *nothing a believer worked is ever left un-registered*: the ledger cannot leak from God's side: only from the owner's side (by nullifiers: riyā — and the verses 22's own habṭ).

**The Generalization From Martyrs to All Believers**

The clause's movement is designed: from *the slain* — *alladhīna qutilū* — outward to *al-muʾminīn*: all believers: what God manifested in extremity at Uḥud is the *pledge carrying over all believing labor*: God's holding of the wage-account is not a martyr-only concession: the martyr simply receives it spectacularly, in documents of joy visible as parables across One veil; the sleeper at home in fidelity receives the same *lā yuḍīʿu* — the Prophet's own shop-saying for every lawful striving in the Book: *"you will not spend anything seeking God's face thereby but you will be rewarded for it — even the morsel you place in your wife's mouth"* (al-Bukhārī 56; Muslim 1628, from Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ?), and His own hadith on ḥadīth: *"God has written the full reward of the ummah's works..."* through to *"each deed of the son of Adam is multiplied — one good act by ten, up to seven hundred"* (al-Bukhārī 42; Muslim 115): the *reward-infrastructure* of Islam is a God's-own bank without leaks. The Uḥud dead showed its working from the inside. The living believer takes the same document, with the Prophet's discounting of dunyā-regret: *the fear-that-God-loses-your-work* — a fear the anxious pious have always nursed — is retired by this verse in three words: *lā yuḍīʿu* — He does not *cause to be lost*: the Arabic iḍāʿah is the *mal-operation* of a store: intentionally or neglectfully: both off the Base vector: the loss not: He preserves.

**From the File of Uḥud to the Files of the Reader**

Thus, at the chapter's descending cadence, the Uḥud audit finally closes with a complete inventory before every believer: (1) joy exists — active, nourished — beyond the veil, *now*; (2) the living and the dead exchange good news; (3) every believer's work is *custodied* at God's no-loss account. With those three framed, grief over any cost, and fear of any calculation, become irrational at the root — *which is exactly the disposition God has been growing from v. 139 onward* — and which now turns to the bookends of the whole sequence: verses 172–176's narrative of the wounded who answered God again, and 200's final pastoral call: * God does not lose the believers' wages.*
**Lā Yuḍīʿu: The No-Leak Wage-Bank**

*Wa anna Allāha lā yuḍīʿu ajra al-muʾminīn* — "and that God wastes not the wage of the believers": the verse's third room (after the blessing they rejoice in and the bounty they await) is its seal-assurance — the ledger kept against every leak. *Iḍāʿah* — wasting-apart, mislaying — is negated in the emphatic: the God of the martyr-file does not misplace entries. Its sibling-refrain runs at 18:30 with the wage-word of the measure-men: *"Those who believed and worked righteousness — indeed We waste not the wage of one who works well"* — the same *lā nuḍīʿu* sealing the workers' register end-to-end. The Prophet's own expansion of the doctrine into numbers trained the community's hope:

> *"God does not wrong the believer a single good deed: he is provided for it in the world, and it is reserved for him in the Hereafter; and the disbeliever is fed for his good deeds until, when he meets God, there is no good left for him to be requited."* (Muslim 2808, from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh)

— the wage-manifest running in both directions: the believer paid twice-bank (present provision and future reserve), the disbeliever once-bank — spent before arrival.

**Fasting-Month Budget of the Dead**

The month of fasting's own ledger repeats the no-leak bookkeeping at the horizon of the grave — the Prophet's good-news custom: *"For the fasting person are two joys: a joy when he breaks his fast, and a joy when he meets his Lord"* (al-Bukhārī 1904&ndash;; Muslim 1151) — and the standing burial-comfort appended by the salaf: the works sent before (*the works sent on ahead*, per 75:13's *mā qaddamat*) meet the arriving worker as a provision-caravan greets — v. 171's *they rejoice* and 9:124's rejoicing-believers being two hours of the same clock. For every laborer of God's projects grieved by shrunken outcomes, the sūrah's seal holds the one reassurance that cannot be under-issued: *nothing deposited in this bank wastes.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:172

> **who responded to God and the Messenger after being afflicted by wounds; for those among them who have been virtuous and reverent there shall be a great reward,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Ḥamrāʾ al-Asad: The Day the Wounded Marched**

Verse 172 records, in one clause, the most heroic morning-walk of the whole battle-sequence: *alladhīna istajābū lillāhi wa-l-rasūli min baʿdi mā aṣābahumu al-qarḥ* — "who answered God and the Messenger after the wound had smitten them": the *wound* — *al-qarḥ* — the very word of v. 140's wound-parity document now carried in the responder's own flesh. The event preserved in the sīrah (al-Qurṭubī's account supplied within the source) is among Islam's decisive shows of morale: the morning after Uḥud, with the dead of the day before still freshly buried, with most of the survivors bandaged, with the Prophet himself incisor-broken and helmet-marked, intelligence came that Quraysh — encamped a few miles out along the Makkah road at Rawḥāʾ — were debating a *return to Madinah to finish the work*: whereupon the Prophet ﷺ ordered the *same battered roster* — wounded, grieving, many at the edge of fever — to march after the enemy: and read to them the hadīth-consign rule (*no one rides with us except he who was present yesterday* — deliberately *limiting the levy to the wounded*, one of history's choicest symbolic acts); and the seven hundred came out — on leaning-slanted saddles, on make-shift dressings — and marched some eight miles out to the place called *Ḥamrāʾ al-Asad* ("the red slopes of the lion") — and made camp in sight of the enemy's road: and there the Prophet set the theater that completed the retreat's rout: *hundreds of campfires* ordered lit at nightfall — the valley-flanks ablaze as with a new levy of thousands; and through the agency of Maʿbad al-Khuzāʿī — a man of Khuzāʿah, an ally-tribe not yet Muslim, whom the Prophet briefed — word reached Abū Sufyān's camp in the night: *the Madinans have come out against you in numbers you never saw — their entirety, and more, enraged*: whereupon the terror of v. 151 landed *agains*: Abū Sufyān ordered the baggage out before dawn: the army of wounded men had, with fire-pots and steadfastness, *conquered by posture*: God had cast the second wave of ruʿb; the *deen*-narrative closed: Quraysh came home to Makkah saying *we did not win; tomorrow they will be upon us*: v. 151's fulfillment-visible.

**"Those Among Them Who Were Virtuous and Reverent": The Response-Tabulation**
