God then issues the reply-grade of the fire-march: *lilladhīna aḥsanū minhum wa-ttaqaw ajrun ʿaẓīm* — "for those of them who did good (*aḥsanū*) and reverenced — a reward magnificent": the *minhum* ("among them") is the commentators' point of scrutiny — and the consensus's tenderness: not *all* responders received the *ʿaẓīm* designation; God singled out *those among them who answered with iḥsān and taqwā*: the grading-differentiations of v. 163's *darajāt* in real-time: same march, same campfires — differential *intention-and-manner*: some went out of duty; some went out of iḥsān — the "as-though-seeing-him" register — and it is they whose wage God names *great*: and thus does the Book distinguish, forever, between *movement-with* and *belief-level-therein*: the band of the wounded-to-the-marched was no longer uniform; but all who answered — whatever their interior altitude — were secured *honorable mention in God's own ecclesiastical* record: the word *istajābū* — *answered*: the mood-theme of the whole sūrah from 3:104's callers to 3:168's "come, fight" — God calls; man answers: or not: Uḥud's two dawn-parties both *answered* — and the grades of the answer were not lost upon the Judge.

**The Verse's Standing Model of Trauma-Loyalty**

The pastoral payload to every believer since is written into the story's timing: *the answer arrived after the wound*: the easy *istijābah* — enthusiasm in comfort — was v. 121's; the priceless istijābah is day-after pain-obedience: flat-footed, bleeding-carrying, two-days-bereaved, humiliated in the paragraph the world writes — and *rising at the summons*: this is Islam's deep-choice constitutive act: *loyalty after loss*: for it contains, whole, the answer to the verse 3:144 knocked — *if the messenger dies or is slain — ?* — and to the conditional-faith of the wavering (v. 167) and the sitting-critique (v. 168): here are the men who did *not* demand a reason for the defeat; did *not* lodge a counterfactual; *responded when called, wounded*: — and God tells the whole human species — for those of them who acted beautifully and feared Him: *ajr ʿaẓīm*: a great reward: the sīrah's own historians add the fitting period: two years later, at the appointment of Badr II — the "lesser Badr" — Abū Sufyān's own promised re-match failed of courage in identical weather: *and the Muslims came home from the waiting-field with market-gains* — the commentators' record preserved in al-Qurṭubī: the wound replied-to becomes, within the Book's exact count, *nūn*: bounty: *fine* of the whole arrangement closes in v. 174-175's report.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:173

> **to whom the people said, "Truly the people have gathered against you, so fear them." But it increased them in faith, and they said, "God suffices us, an excellent Guardian is He!"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Intelligence Designed to Scatter — And Its Opposite Effect**

Verse 173 preserves the exact words of the warning-minuet at Ḥamrāʾ al-Asad: *alladhīna qāla lahumu al-nāsu inna al-nāsa qad jamaʿū lakum fa-khshawhum* — "those to whom men said: 'the people have gathered against you — so fear them'": *al-nās* twice — men said of men: the classical popular-voice move: anonymous authority ("the people say") invoked to fuse terror: the commentary (al-Qurṭubī) locates the speakers among travelers who had seen the Makkan contingents, and/or the hypocrite-party of Madinah itself, who had all along peddled this same counsel ("do not march out: their numbers!"). The warning's structure is the off-the-shelf kit of de-legitimization across every century: *numbers, gathering, consequence, fear* — four items meant to detach a smaller loyal party from its principle (the Prophet's ﷺ ummah received the identical warning at every stage: Makkah's own Meccan years: "your people have gathered against you"; al-Aḥzāb's confederated army: "the people have gathered"; and down the generations wherever the path of right is walked by smaller persons than the mobs' — the Sufi commentary cited in the source (Abū ʿAlī al-Daqqāq's line) catches its trans-temporal force: *let the spiritual man never be dismayed at the world's gathering against him — the repudiation is the sign of the truth of his attainment*: the gathering *of* the people is often the exact measure of the flame they fear).

**"But It Increased Them in Faith" — The Alchemy of the Demoralizer Reversed**

Then the verse unveils the effect — and it is *the opposite of the design*: *fa-zādahum īmānan* — "and it increased them in faith": terror-warning converted, inside chests trained by months of tawakkul-training, into a *faith-catalyst*: the very phrase of exaggeration ("they have gathered!") making God's own guarantee more valuable in contrast. This reversal is among the chapter's final lessons: *the intimidator's weapon only fires on the unprepared chest*; inside the God-holding chest it ricochets into conviction — he who had believed with half his chest believes *more* when threatened, for threat is precisely the scene of the proof the Book promised (v. 186's own prophecy: "you shall hear much hurt"); the believer reads threats *as annexes of the promise*: they came true: hence they steady him: hence faith rises.

**"Ḥasbunā Allāh wa Niʿma al-Wakīl": The Creed-Formula That Rules the Ummah's Fears**

And then the formula the wounded men uttered — the six words that have since entered Muslim life as the one all-purpose talisman at every danger: *wa qālū ḥasbunā Allāhu wa niʿma al-wakīl* — "they said: God is sufficiency for us — and excellent the Guardian!" *Ḥasab* — sufficiency-arithmetic: *He counts, for us, for everything needed*: wakīl — trustee, attorney-guardian: one entrusts to Him the case (*wakālah*): *niʿma* — excellent, blessed, perfect-of-the-superlative-form. The lineage of the formula in the Book is chosen-family: Abraham spoke it at the catapult-moment of Nimrod's fire — per the Companion Ibn ʿAbbās's report:

> *"'God suffices us, an excellent Guardian is He' was said by Abraham when he was cast into the fire, and by Muḥammad when they said: 'the people have gathered against you, so fear them.'"* (al-Bukhārī 4563-4564 — from Ibn ʿAbbās: the areal coinage: two prophets, one phrase, at the two great gatherings: the pire-builders of Babylon and the regroupers of Quraysh — and God answered both: to Abraham, the fire made coolness and safety (21:68–69); to the wounded outriders of Madinah, v. 174's return with blessing and bounty)

The phrase-of-sufficiency landed so deeply in the ummah's communicational bloodstream that it is recited at every funeral caisson, at every family crisis, at every publi threat, at every examination-hall doorway, scratched into the front pages of countless books of devotion: nine Arabic syllables that contain the entire tawakkul-theology: agent-sufficiency identified (*ḥasabī*); the trust-entrust declared (*niʿma al-wakīl*): *and no third clause needed*: after those two admissions, there is nothing left in one's own hand but Islam — the handing over. Read within the Uḥud-sequence, the men had just lost 72, carried wounds, marched eight miles — and had nothing left but the sentence — and God, faithful all along, grants the next verse His own verdict: *so they returned with blessing and bounty from God, untouched by evil.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:174

> **So they returned with Blessing and Bounty from God, untouched by evil. And they pursued the Contentment of God, and God is Possessed of Tremendous Bounty.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Return: A War Won in Posture, Paid in Bounty**

God closes the file of the wounded firemarch with His own four-branched verdict: *fa-nqalabū bi-niʿmatin mina Allāhi wa faḍlin* — "so they returned with blessing from God and bounty" — *lam yamsashum sūʾ* — "untouched by evil" — *wa-ttabaʿū riḍwāna Allāh* — "and they pursued God's contentment" — *wa Allāhu dhū faḍlin ʿaẓīm* — "and God is possessed of tremendous bounty." The return-*fa-nqalabū* echoes the khāʾib-return of their enemies (v. 127: *yanqalibū khāʾibīn* — the disappointed reverse) in opposite keys: they *also returned* — but with *niʿmah and faḍl*: with the battle *not refought* — untouched by *sūʾ*: al-Ṭabarī's plain-sense: no new wound, no second casualty: a military outing whose whole gain accrued without blood: terror served along the Makkan road, the war-party shattered of confidence, Madinah's morale re-erected: the Merciful Lord having designed that the wounded should, without a single blow, *accomplish the battle* Quraysh had wanted to fight.

**Niʿmah and Faḍl: The Two Receipts Auditor-Confirmed**

The paired coinage recurs (v. 171's own *bi-niʿmatin mina Allāhi wa faḍlin*): commentators (al-Rāzī) partition exquisitely: *niʿmah* — blessing — the visible-world good: safety, standing, the spirit-lowing of the enemy, the market-profit of their next trip (the Lesser Badr's episode of the traders' fair in the alternative routing of vv. 172-174 al-Qurṭubī preserves: the appointment where Quraysh failed to appear and the Muslims bought and returned loaded); *faḍl* — bounty — the *above-and-beyond* good: the heavenly credits stored — the standing of *shuhadāʾ-companions echoing to every barzakh*: in sum, world-wage and reward-wage — delivered *simultaneously*: the wounded-obeying men were not told "defer it to the Garden"; they were paid *on both channels* at once: the Book's law of 2:201 operating in sunlight.

**"They Pursued God's Contentment": The Engine Clause**

The heart of the verdict is the last condition clause: *wa-ttabaʿū riḍwāna Allāh* — "they followed God's riḍwān": the same currency-word of v. 162 ("he who *follows God's contentment* vs. he who incurs wrath") — the verse now ratifies the latter's *fulfillment*: the marchers who went out wounded did not go out for spoils, vengeance-recovery, or reputation-repair: God testifies: *riḍwān-pursuit*: theirs was the heart-taxonomy of the first of v. 162's two men: and so the Book's own closure-seal lands: *wa Allāhu dhū faḍlin ʿaẓīm* — God's *faḍl* is *ʿaẓīm* — enormous: the pay-grade of the wounded men recalibrated as *God-sized*: and the chapter's fifth explicit instance of its deep theme (God's bounty) rings its final bell before the sūrah turns to the final teachings: *faḍl* — God's bounty — has now been testified four times in fifteen verses: *because the healing of the whole chapter all along has been the re-direction of the human soul from earning-comparisons to bounty-reception*: *lam yamsashum sūʾ*: *the very battle* was bounty found on a morning after wounds.
**Fa-nqalabū: The Return-Blood of Two Campaigns**

*Fa-nqalabū bi-niʿmatin min Allāhi wa faḍlin lam yamsashum sūʾ* — "so they returned with blessing from God and bounty — no harm having touched them": the return-verb *inqalaba* tolls a deliberate rhyme against v. 127's *fa-nqalabū khāʾibīn* — the enemy's return *disappointed* — thus folding Ḥamrāʾ al-Asad's little campaign into the war-ledger of the chapter as counter-entry: the Quraysh went home emptied of their boast; the believers went home *loaded*. The commentators' report of the sequel completes the parable: the two caravans agreed to re-meet at the Lesser Badr appointment of the next year — Abu Sufyan failing to show, the Muslims keeping it, and the market that accompanied the mustering ground filling the appointment's days with trade — so that the community returned with the world's fairest margin: *soldiers' honor and merchants' panniers both full.* The blessing *niʿmah* and the *faḍl* bounty are thereby read by al-Rāzī's neat partition: the blessing of souls-and-faith; the bounty of world's fair-measure — God's love-registered generosity dropping a shade of 3:74's *faḍl ʿaẓīm* seal upon the running men of Uḥud's painful eight days.

**Sūʾ Un-touched: The Ruse and the Campfires**

*Lam yamsashum sūʾun* — "no harm touched them" — is the verse's quiet marvel, for their pursuer's army had in fact been in striking days' reach, and God prevented the meeting itself: the pursuit's report — Abū Sufyán's dissuasion-scheme turning back under Nuʿaym's rumor-lance — shows harm *postponed upward* and then cancelled. The salaf of the campaign loved the image that remained: Madinah's thousands of camp-fires left burning the night through on Ḥamrā's plateau so the scouts below would read a host ten-fold — ruse and reliance clasping in the same act. Between Ḥamrā and Lesser Badr the chapter's *faḍl*-line is complete: pursued, uncaught, enriched, and loved by God — v. 174 as the war's fair copy of its own psalm.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:175

> **That is only Satan, sowing fear of his friends. So fear them not, but fear Me, if you are believers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**De-Masking the Fear-Caster: "That Is Only Satan"**

God now X-rays the whole dread-campaign — verses 173's "the people have gathered against you — fear them" — and names the screen: *innamā dhālikumu al-shayṭānu yukhawwifu awliyāʾah* — "verily *that* is only Satan, causing fear of his friends (awliyāʾ)." The sentence's anatomy is precious: (1) *innamā* — *that is only*: the restricting particle: *when the fright-surge arrives, look at its address-of-origin: satan* — not truth, not fact-value, not wisdom's risk-analysis: the *shape* of the dread bears the whisperer's fingerprint (swelling the enemy's numbers, contracting your own, hollowing the heart with projection-visions of defeat); (2) *yukhawwifu awliyāʾah* — he *frightens* — but notice: the direct-object of his intimidation-as-God-puts-it is *his own friends* — *he frightens you *of* his friends* (the reading both plain-sense and classical: he makes you fear his party) — though the additional register the commentators preserve (al-Rāzī: satan *may also be* the disbelieving and hypocrite humans themselves — for the Qur'an calls even humans *shayāṭīn*: 6:112 — "and thus We made for every prophet an enemy: satans of men and jinn, inspiring one another with adorned speech") — both readings land at the same final analysis: the war of dread has a *signature*, and the signature is satanic: God's arithmetic for its defusing follows, in two perfect imperatives.

**"Fear Them Not — But Fear Me": The One-Quantity Doctrine of Fear**

*Fa-lā takhāfūhum wa khāfūn, in kuntum muʾminīn* — "so fear them not — but fear Me — if you are believers": the zero-sum theory of holy fear: human hearts do not vary in total fear-capacity; they vary in the *allocation*: fear assigned to the creatures' gathering is fear *subtracted* from God's dread; fear re-assigned to its one true Object leaves no supply for the creatures — the Book's own twin texts ringing: *"fear them not — but fear Me"* (2:150, 5:3 — identical clause-structure) and 33:39's praise-form — *"who convey God's messages and fear Him, fearing none but God — and sufficient is God as Reckoner."* The fear-exchange is thereby codified as a *spiritual finance*: the heart's treasury of khawf is *finite and spendable* — spend it on God and the vault is empty for every creditor army that ever gathered: the chapter's own long drill — from 3:103's heart-joining to 3:120's *their plot shall not hurt you*, to 3:160's *if God helps you none can overcome you* — was all along **training the heart's treasury-transfer**: Uḥud's wounded receiving the warning "they have gathered!" and replying *ḥasbunā Allāh* was its graduation-ceremony in practice: v. 175 finds the whole mechanism *named*: satan frightens with his clients; *fear Me* — one scroll-relocation of the fear's address.

**Fear, Applied: The Faith-Condition**

And the conditional outer-clause — *in kuntum muʾminīn* — "if you are believers" — carries the verse's own diagnostic: fear-allocation *is* īmān: its resettlement-choice shows the register: the man still fearing the gathered *people* above God has, by definition, not yet installed the belief-structure; and the workshop-day-to-day running of v. 175 in every believing life is massive and usual: fear of losing the job if truth is told: *there is satan, sowing fear of his friends*; fear of the crowd when a deception needs refusing: *satan sowing*; fear of the enemy's own rage when the commandment's path runs across it: *satan* — every dread is thereby cashiered at the same barred window: *fa-lā takhāfūhum wa khāfūn*: and the verse ends, on its own account, as one of the sūrah's crowned jewels — the whole psychology of God-centered courage in eighteeen words of translation.
**Fear's Monopoly Broken**

*Innamā dhālikumu al-shayṭānu yukhawwifu awliyāʾah* — "that is only Satan frightening his friends": the verse's restrictive *innamā* strips the terror-episode of v. 173's market-report to its source: the rumor-army was not a force but a *voice* — Satan's scare-machinery raising shouts through his own clients. The refuge-grammar then commands the fear-reallocation: *fa-lā takhāfūhum wa khāfūn* — "so fear them not — and fear Me" — *in kuntum muʾminīn* — "if you are believers": fear assigned back to its single licit object, monotheism's old law running through the pilgrimage-liturgy (*fa-lā takhāfū al-nāsa wa khāfūn* — 5:44, and 5:3's own day-of-perfection clause: *"this day I have perfected for you your religion... so fear them not — fear Me"*): God claims the monopoly of the frightened.

**The Skin-Test of News**

The sūrah's diagnostic for every rumor-season since runs in the grammar the verse installs: *fear that paralyzes is of the whisperer; fear that readies is of the Lord.* The Prophet's own prophetic practice armed the community with the rumor-filter's standing hadith:

> *"It is enough of a lie for a man that he relates all that he hears."* (Muslim 5, in the Muqaddimah's chain-custody)

— and the Book's verification-law completed it: *"if a corrupt person comes to you with news, then verify"* (49:6). The market-cry of Ḥamrā thereby stands as the ummah's training pattern for every panic engineered since — financial, medical, political, digital: ask whose interest the scream serves; if the answer is *awliyāʾ al-shayṭān*, then the verse's own imperative fires: *lā takhāfūhum* — fear them not — and the heart's single permissible dread returns to its throne: *wa khāfūn in kuntum muʾminīn.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:176

> **And let not those who hasten unto disbelief grieve thee. Truly they will not harm God in the least. God desires to give them no share in the Hereafter, and theirs shall be a great punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prophet's Mercy-Heart, and God's Permission to Be Consoled**

The sūrah draws to its close with one of the series of heaven's consolations addressed directly to the Messenger's own tender chest: *wa lā yaḥzunka alladhīna yusāriʿūna fī al-kufr* — "and let not those who hasten into disbelief grieve you." The grief-ground the verse's occasion supplied in the Madinan theater is mapped by the commentators: the speed-runners of kufr — idolaters of his own kin striving after his hurt (al-Rāzī), the obstructing parties of the People of the Book racing to outrun his evidence (al-Qurṭubī's range), the hypocrites subverting from inside — the Prophet grieved *for them*, not merely from them: his sorrow was missiological: he watched men court ruin while holding the rope they might grasp; and the Book's whole consolation-canon addresses the grief in identical key (5:41: *"let not grieve you those who hasten into disbelief"*; 10:65 and 36:76: "let not their speech grieve you"; 31:23: "let not his disbelief grieve you"; 35:8's full pastoral sentence: *"so let not your soul waste away in regrets over them"* — *fa-lā tadhhab nafsuka ʿalayhim ḥasarāt* — do not *spend your soul* in grief-spasms over them: even grief has a budget.) The series of consoles *does not deny the grief* — Jesus was told to preach on; Moses was told to deliver the word — it *relieves the grief of responsibility*: outcome-mission was never theirs.

**"They Will Not Harm God in the Least": The Dear Point of All of It**

The second clause returns the consolation's doctrinal base — once more, the recurring immunization the chapter itself first installed at 3:144 and 3:161's region: *innahum lan yaḍurrū Allāha shayʾan* — "truly they shall not harm God *at all*": Oh — say — the whole commotion of denial, blasphemy, slander, mocking the Prophet's face and blood at Uḥud *does not reach*: God's majesty lies above any creature-campaign (the chapter's own interlinked lessons: 97's *ghaniyy ʿani al-ʿālamīn*; 144's "he harms God not"; 175's satanic fright-campaign): accordingly the comfort for the Prophet's grief is *not* "they will be destroyed soon" — although that is true; it is: *what they harm is themselves: nothing you deliver is ever defrauded by their refusal*: the loss-event is not in heaven's records; it is in their own: a post-emission truth of the Prophetic office that releases the caller from its bearing: he is still charged with delivery (v. 20's *thine is only to convey*), never with persuasion-yields.

**"No Share in the Hereafter": The Partitive of Desire**

The verse's final-clause issue is powerfully-shaped in the classical debates the source records (al-Rāzī's overview): *yurīdu Allāhu an lā yajʿala lahum ḥaẓẓan fī al-ākhirah* — "God wills to allot them no share in the Hereafter": *ḥaẓẓ* — share, portion, lot: what is *withheld* is their portion of bliss — the commentators clarify: not *experience* of the Hereafter (they will be raised and judged) but share *of its good*: and the pronoun-slant questions — the syntax of a God *willing-the-absence-of-a-share* among His own rational creation way-marked here in parallel of v. 178 — squares with the chapter's whole two-causal doctrine already closed at v. 161–165: God's will runs *through* men's choices: their kufr being their purchased commodity (v. 177's market-words next), its share-consequence His allotment: *the causation runs at their end; the justice runs at His*. And then the tafsiric close: *wa lahum ʿadhābun ʿaẓīm* — "and theirs is a tremendous punishment": the *ʿadhāb ʿaẓīm* file opened at v. 105 closes at v. 176: the same fate-word assigned to schism, to concealment-labor, to the taunt "God is poor" (v. 181's own account runs adjoining) — and to speedy kufr whenever maintained: *hastening into disbelief is the only race on Earth whose finish-line is loss*: while the believers' race (v. 133's *sāriʿū ilā maghfirah*) stands, a few verses from the close, as its exact opposite-track: *each runner is headed somewhere; check your course*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:177

> **Truly those who have purchased disbelief at the price of belief will not hurt God in the least, and theirs shall be a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Mercantile Language of Faith-Loss**

The consolation of v. 176 continues into the third clause-cycle of the chapter's closing movement, now in the Book's signature commercial grammar: *inna alladhīna ishtarawu al-kufra bi-l-īmāni* — "those who have bought disbelief *with* belief": *ishtarā X bi-Y*: purchased X giving Y in exchange: a trade — not an accident, not a theft: a trade: kufr acquired, īmān handed over as payment: and the Qur'an's whole economy of moral choice stands on this verb: 2:16: *"these are they who bought error with guidance — so their trade profited nothing"*; 2:86: bought the world at the price of the Hereafter; 2:175: bought error at guidance's price, punishment at forgiveness's. What does the barter-model teach? (1) *agency* — no one gives up īmān involuntarily: it is *sold*: a decision-event: (2) *received price* — the seller gets *something* — the commodities of this world (approval, persistence in office, tribal release-relief, the unbrowed ease of unfenced license) — worth, precisely, what the seller took it to be worth: (3) *finality-of-clearing* — the deal closes: and on inspection, the purchase immediately shows its nature — the earlier exchanges having been already written: 2:16's own audit — *fa-mā rabiḥat tijāratuhum* — *their trade gained nothing*: the kufr bought is not even a good; it is a *bill*: *lan yaḍurrū Allāha shayʾan* — they'll not hurt God a whit — *wa lahum ʿadhābun alīm* — *and theirs a painful punishment*: *alīm*: *pain-bearing*: the chapter's fifth fate-signature: after *ʿaẓīm* (105, 176), *muhīn* (178), the Fire's *mathwā* (151), the curse (87): the inventory of bad endings: all purchased at one price: a once-held belief.

**To Whom the Trading Clause Applies**

The commentators range over the referents as the phrase deserves — because the wording is magnificently due-universal: (1) the apostates of the chapter's own chronos (vv. 85–91; the al-Ḥārith party of v. 89's) — they had īmān and sold it; (2) the concealed-deniers of the hypocrite party — outward commodity pretended, inward īmān null — a double-falsified account: the outward purchase being pretense, the inward sale genuine; (3) the knowing refuseniks of the People of the Book, whose *bought-kufr* was peculiarly costly — for they purchased with a coin of the rarest denomination: *illumination previously given*: the evidence of their own texts: v. 199 — the sūrah's own corrective — will answer the ledger for the exception-choral of their upright remnant; (4) and the universal warning — every Muslim in every later time who priced his īmān against any currency: office, comfort, vogue, fear of the crowd (v. 175's), or the old securities of verses 14, 116 — the trade-window is always open; the Book's remedy is the inspection-habit: *what am I selling my accounts for today?* — and the trade-consult: *whoever sold his Islam never later found a bidder whose valuation exceeded God's*: for God's own purchase-offer was announced in 9:111 — *"God has purchased from the believers their selves and their property, in exchange for which theirs is the Garden"* — the only *mubāyaʿah* whose first payment arrives already.

**"Hurt God Not": The Sovereign Sealer Again**

The clause we have met at 144 and 176 is stamped for the third time in thirty verses — which insistence is itself doctrine: God's security over His own cause is *three-times certified*: not needing defense: the harm-channel runs entirely on the other side. The believer thereby inherits a standing-mood toward all exhibitions of proud unbelief: not panic (the faith is safe); not hatred; but pity — the Prophet's own grief (v. 176) disciplined by God's own console: seller's ruin does not bend God's road: *wafā?* rather — the faith's honor does not rest upon all customers; God's road rolls through every defection to its destined ends, per the alternation of days.
**The Commerce-Inventory of the Soul**

*Inna alladhīna ashtarawū al-kufra bi-l-īmān* — "truly those who purchase disbelief in exchange for faith": the sūrah's commerce-imagery reaches its bleakest transaction, and the Book's ledger of the *ishtarā* (purchase-exchange) verses deserves its rows: guidance sold at loss — *"they purchased error with guidance — so their trade profited not"* (2:16); the Hereafter priced below the world — *"they purchased the world-life with the Hereafter"* (2:86); covenants and oaths priced at paltry goods (3:77, 3:187 coming); and now the direst: *faith itself* bartered outward for disbelief — the whole treasure sold, the whole debt taken. Al-Ṭabarī reads with the pericope the apostate-momentum of the war-years; al-Qurṭubī the standing jurisprudence: the exchange-verb presumes a *valuation* — a believed price received — and Heaven's verdict follows in the verse itself: *lan yaḍurrū Allāha shayʾ* — "they will not harm God a thing": the sale damages only the seller.

**Lan Yaḍurrū Allāh: Impotence Declared Above the Acts**

The harm-impossibility clause (with its brothers at v. 120's *they will not harm you save annoyance* and v. 144's *he does not harm God a thing*) composes one of the chapter's quiet rock-themes: the cosmos's management is beyond sabotage; every anti-God labor's invoice returns to the laborer. The clause secures the worshipper in his winter-hours as firmly as God's own promise of support secures him in his service-hours — *victory to the helpers of God* (22:40), *no bargain to the bargainers against Him*. And the verse's seal — *wa lahum ʿadhābun alīm* — painful punishment theirs — closes the file: the sold went cheap; the returned came heavy; the audit is complete.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:178

> **And let not those who disbelieve suppose that the respite We grant them is good for them. We only grant them respite that they may increase in sin, and theirs shall be a humiliating punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Deceptive Democracy of Extra Time**

The third consolation in the closing triptych unveils, in turn, the strategy of God's forbearance: *wa lā yaḥsabanna alladhīna kafarū annamā numlī lahum khayrun li-anfusihim* — "let not the disbelievers suppose that what We grant them of respite is good for their selves" — *innamā numlī lahum li-yazdādū ithman* — "We only grant them respite that they may increase in sin" — *wa lahum ʿadhābun muhīn* — "and theirs a humiliating punishment." *Imlāʾ*: to give *rope* — the word of extending-leash: the Qur'an's own term for God's long-range strategy with the defiant (7:182 — "those who deny Our signs — We shall lead them on by degrees, from whence they know not; and I grant them respite — *surely My plan is firm*", and 68:44: "leave Me to deal with those who deny this discourse — We lead them on *from where they know not*"). *Istidrāj* — the sages' own term for this march — is among the deepest and most unsettling divine dispositions in the Book: extra time, continued success, widened markets, undamaged health, prolonged regime — *conditioned upon* the user's *usage*: if used for return, it is pure mercy (v. 89's door remains open until the throat); if used for defiant accumulation — it is *condemnation advancing undetected*: the sinner is accordingly caught between two inversions: his *adversity* may be God's refining (v. 141's assay); his *prosperity* may be God's rope.

**"That They May Increase in Sin": The Theological Debate and Its Resolution**

The plain sense — *li-yazdādū ithman* — has generated among theologians the exact debate the source records under al-Rāzī's eye: do God's purposes *include the increase of sin*? The Muʿtazilite — for whom God never wills disbelief and disobedience (since He created mankind for worship, 51:56) — leans to readings that soften the purpose-particle (causal, not intentional: respite *ends up* in increased sin) or narrow its scope (respite at the battle, allowing the living-in-wickedness state itself — which is its own punishment); the Ashʿarite replies with the text's plain purpose-clause: God's act of respite *intends* what respite yields — and the clearing-up the later sages almost uniformly delivered: *God does not create their love of sin nor is He pleased by sin* (39:7: "He is not pleased with ingratitude from His servants"); He *extends the arena they chose* — decreeing *existence-and-usage*, not approval: the chosen road is lengthened because the lengthening is justice: no man, on the Day, pleads that his rope was too short. Al-Rāzī's own careful summation (preserved within the source) drives the doctrine home: *kufr* as a *condition* — directionlessness, guidance-lack, meaning-void — *is itself suffering*, and its continued operation generates further sins which are further suffering: God's respite is thereby already double-terror even on the interior register: *more time = more of the illness*: the Qur'an's exact psychology at 2:7–10 ("God has sealed their hearts... and *increase* for them except error... and theirs a painful punishment for what they used to lie"): heart-conditions progress by use.

**"A Humiliating Punishment" — The Final Title**

The fate-clause borrows the rank-word: *ʿadhāb muhīn*: *muhīn* — humiliating, bringing-low: the chapter's final catastrophic signature had appeared at v. 112's *ḍuribat*: abasement struck upon the obstructers: here the full eschatological edition: not only pain but *abasement*: the rope-receivers end in the position furthest from their self-picture: pride-ground spent a lifetime building a height, and the air it rests on is pulled: the proud polities of the Jāhiliyyah carry this sentence to memory each time a successor clambers over their ruins: from Nimrod's tower to Makkah's plutocrats to our own century's humiliations of the proud: the *muhīn* watch is long, and the paper-trail of respite exists simply to be *exhibited at the end*: merciful delay was the rope; and the gallows was the rope's field-use at the end: the option remains open always while the rope is being fed out: *the rope doubles instantly into the ladder of return when the soul turns* (v. 89): *that* is what the respite was for.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:179

> **God will not leave the believers as you are till He separates the bad from the good. And God will not apprise you of the Unseen, but God chooses from His messengers whomsoever He will. So believe in God and His messengers. And if you believe and are reverent, you shall have a great reward.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Promise of Separation: God Does Not Leave Chaff in His Wheat**

Verse 179 opens with one of the Book's most quoted statements on why trials exist: *mā kāna Allāhu li-yadhara al-muʾminīna ʿalā mā antum ʿalayhi* — "God would not leave the believers in the state you are in" — *ḥattā yamīza al-khabītha mina al-ṭayyib* — "until He separates the foul from the wholesome." *Mayza*: to sort, sieve, extricate: *khabīth* (rotten, foul) and *ṭayyib* (sound, wholesome): God will not leave His harvest-field unwinnowed: while believers and hypocrites remain indistinguishably mixed — the same mosques, the same rolls, the same ṣalāt-rows: the *admixture state* is intolerable *to His plan* — though no occasion for human panic: *He will do the sieving*: He will not deputize angels with name-lists nor provide the generality of men with chest-reading instruments: His tools are — as the whole Uḥud audit just taught us — *events*: wars, trials, callings, calamities: *life-phenomena by which each side eventually outs itself*: al-Ṭabarī's direct reading: hypocrites separated from sincere; al-Qurṭubī's: the answer to whoever asked how they might be told apart — *events tell them apart*. The verses 140–141, 154, 166–167's four-stage purpose-clause system (*li-yaʿlama / li-yumaḥḥiṣa / li-yabtaliya / li-yamīza*) is here given its theological lectern: *this is why Uḥud happened* — this is why every crisis-period of the ummah happens: **sorting is immediately underway**.

**"God Will Not Apprise You of the Unseen" — Chest-Reading Is Off-Limits**

Then comes the great boundary-law of religious epistemology: *wa mā kāna Allāhu li-yuṭliʿakum ʿalā al-ghaybi* — "and God would not acquaint you with the Unseen": no man is given *direct access to another's inner state*: men will remain believers in propositional mutuality — judged only by their opened profession-behavior — while God's registers hold their truth. Two entire ministries of Islam are built on this ban: (1) the *juridical*: you treat men per their outward: the Prophet's own jurisprudential furnaces on Usāmah's case ("did you split open his heart?" — Muslim 96) and his acceptance of Ibn Ubayy's funeral garment-and-prayers (al-Bukhārī 1333? — the funeral prayer by the Prophet over the well-known chief-hypocrite, silenced by revelation later: 9:84: "never pray over any of them who dies"): men act by outward signs even regarding the worst-suspected; (2) the *spiritual*: do not strut about souls' verities — your own *included* (no one knows his own *ending*: the hadith of the Book — "a man works with the deeds of the people of Paradise for seventy years... until there is between him and Hell only a cubit — and the record overtakes him" — al-Bukhārī 6594; Muslim 1122, from Ibn Masʿūd): certainty of eternal *classification* belongs to God — hence the believer's interior posture is *fear-and-hope*, not membership-pride: the ummah's greatest saints died uncertain of their own end.

**"But God Chooses From His Messengers Whom He Wills": The One Exception**

*Wa lākin-Allāha yajtabī min rusulihi man yashāʾ* — "but God singles out from His messengers whom He wills": *ijtibāʾ*: selection, choice: by *exception to the boundary-law*, God reveals *some* unseen matters to *some* messengers: the Prophet did receive classified exposure of the hypocrites of his own time (the hadiths of Ḥudhayfah — "the keeper of the secret of the Prophet" — naming their list in the reports, and ʿUmar's lifelong habit of asking Ḥudhayfah at every funeral: *was this man one of them?* — with Ḥudhayfah's granted silence as his answer); and the Sufi commentary of the chapter (the "Aj" note in the source) directs the boundary-law back into the seeker's own soul: *you also* are not granted all Unseens — not even your own grade in God's book: seek God, not secret knowledge: the ladder of spiritual travel is walked by intention, not by access.

**"So Believe": The Practical Close**

The verse's end legislates three clauses — *fa-āminū bi-Allāhi wa rusulih* — "so believe in God and His messengers" — *wa in tuʾminū wa tattaqū fa-lakum ajrun ʿaẓīm* — "if you believe and reverence, yours a great reward": belief to be *chosen* (not classification-knowingly, not experiential-certitude first) — the exact posture respecting both the boundary (Ghayb withheld) and the promise (reward assured) — with *ajr ʿaẓīm* the eighth God-paid paygrade of the chapter — the Book's benediction after the theology: match your inner to your outer, believe and shield yourself, and the reward sits *in God's own assets*: *ʿaẓīm*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:180

> **And let not those who are miserly with what God has given them from His Bounty suppose that it is good for them; rather, it is evil for them. On the Day of Resurrection they will be collared by that with which they were miserly. And unto God belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth, and God is Aware of whatsoever you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Let Them Not Suppose": The Hoarding Arithmetic**

The final warnings of the chapter begin by flipping another false valuation — this time of the pocket: *wa lā yaḥsabanna alladhīna yabkhalūna bi-mā ātāhumu Allāhu min faḍlih* — "let not those who are miserly with what God has given them of His bounty suppose" — *annahū khayrun lahum* — "that it is good for them" — *bal huwa sharrun lahum* — "nay — it is evil for them" — *sa-yuṭawwaqūna mā bakhilū bihi yawma al-qiyāmah* — "they shall be collared by what they withheld on the Day of Resurrection." The structure is the same deception-dialectic as verse 178's: the thing most immediately kept is most ultimately *used against*: the hoarder sees *his* wealth as *his goods'* custody; God's audit reads it as *the evidence accumulating*: *bukhl* (withholding) differs from its virtuous twin *iqtiṣād* (good management): the wealth from God's *faḍl* carries its social assignments (zakāh, kin, guests, travelers, causes) — skimming them converts what was blessing into *encumbrance*: evil *for them* in the world (anxiety-veined guarding, alienation from every neighbor) and in the next. The portrait of the collaring the Prophet painted — the fullest trust-embezzlement hadith of judgment — completes the image in the most unmistakable zoology of the grave:

> *"Whichever man is given wealth by God and does not pay its zakāh — on the Day of Resurrection it is made for him a bald-headed serpent (shujāʿ aqaʿ) with two black spots over the eyes, and it is coiled around him as a collar (yuṭawwaquhu), and it seizes him by the jaws and says: I am your wealth — I am your hoard (ana dhanubak? no — ana ḥashshak? — the wording: **ʾanā māduk — ʾanā kanzuk** — I am your wealth, I am your treasure)."* Then the Prophet recited the verse. (al-Bukhārī 1403, 4565 — from Abū Hurayrah)

The bald venomous serpent — the body plucked hairless by a lifetime of accumulated leanings-leaning on its head, per the commentators — is *the feelings-of-the-hoard itself* given body at the resurrection: the man meets his money.

**Wealth *and* Knowledge: The Two Hoards**

The commentators (al-Ṭabarī) deliver the verse's second theater of application: the withholding of *spiritual knowledge*: the hoard of the learned — which the sūrah's own history has been citing against the People of the Book from vv. 71, 78, 94 onward: the scholar whose wealth was scripture and who *collared himself* with his own monopoly: the tafsīr-chronicle detains one more Prophet-said corroboration now standard across the hadith-codes: *"whosoever conceals knowledge from his own people — God will bridle him with a bridle of Fire"* (Abū Dāwūd 3658; al-Tirmidhī 2649 — from Abū Hurayrah): the Fire-clause applying precisely at the two branches of hoard: *gold* and *sophia*: one God watches both ledgers (the chapter's signing: *wa Allāhu bi-mā taʿmalūna khabīr* — "God is Aware of whatsoever you do" — the watchman-name v. 154 closed with).

**"God's Inheritance": The Clause That Makes All Clutching Foolish**

And then the verse lands the crown-law of the whole chapter's property-doctrine: *wa lillāhi mīrāthu al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍ* — "and unto God is the *inheritance* of the heavens and the earth": not just possession (v. 109's *mā fī* and v. 129's) — *inheritance*: *mīrāth*: the receiving of an estate after its prior holders expire: God's title to the universe is *inheritance-law*: He outlives every owner: every owner *will* leave: the whole horizon of property collapses to *one Owner at the back of all owners*: 19:40's own formula — *"We inherit the earth and all upon it, and to Us they are returned"* — with 21:89's-"heir of heirs" and 2:116's own seals: *your* will-and-testament is *your* sole true part within the economy of an inherited-with-you cosmos: write it as He would have it written — for readers of the whole chapter now know what makes a man rich or poor on this earth: what he has *sent forward*, not what he has held: al-mawārīth all run God's way at every closing of the book.

**The Chapter's Thunder-Roll of Closure**

Within eleven remaining verses (181–200) the sūrah will now move with few blessings-wasted: open indictment's final history ("God is poor, and we are rich" — v. 181), the martyr-transcendence of v. 185's *every soul shall taste death* — the Book's most-quoted rationalization of death — and then the *ūluʾl-albāb* section (vv. 190–200): the portrait-crown of the reflecting believers, their exhaustive prayer-suite, God's direct answer in v. 195, and the sūrah's own seal *ṣbirū, ṣābirū, rābiṭū* — the command the chapter has been *training for* across one hundred and eighty verses — *be patient, vie in patience, keep your station* — born, as all final horses were born, in the foaming dust of Uḥud back at verse 121: the sūrah's last command is exactly the command its own narrative sealed: *stay at post*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:181

> **God has certainly heard the words of those who said, "God is poor, and we are rich." We shall record what they said, and their slaying of the prophets without right, and We shall say, "Taste the punishment of the burning."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Taunt That Heaven Overheard**

Among the chapter's most intense record-clauses, this verse documents the outermost boundary of speaking-against-God reached by any faction of the People of the Book: *la-qad samiʿa Allāhu qawla alladhīna qālū inna Allāha faqīrun wa naḥnu aghniyāʾ* — "God indeed heard the words of those who said: God is poor and we are rich." The occasion (al-Qurṭubī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr recording the same reports from the first generation: from Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Bakr's direct engagement in the counter-exhibit): when the verse *"who is it that will lend God a goodly loan, which He shall multiply for him manyfold?"* (2:245; 57:11) was recited in Madinah, some of the Jews of the city — the tafsīr names Banū Qaynuqāʿ's circles, and in more solemn accounts a deputation by name — scoffed: *your God is poor, and asks for loans — while we are rich*: they did not *believe* this, per the commentators' own philology: they spoke it to scoff, to unsettle the weaker hearts, to mock the call's very grammar (making God the *applicant* of his slaves): and Abū Bakr's own response — the historical material known through the reports of the later battles with Banū Qaynuqāʿ: his striking the man who said it (*Finḥāṣ the Jew*, per the detailed account in the tafsīr of the verse — the heir of 4:53? No — the specific report: Abū Bakr raised his hand against a Jew of the Banū Qaynuqāʿ who uttered this, and the man came to the Prophet complaining, and the verse descended: in the variant reports on 4:60 and this verse the report is organized in the tafsīr literature of Ibn Kathīr on 3:181) — and heaven answered the dispute with its own courtroom summation: *la-qad samiʿa Allāh* — God *heard*: the headphones are planted everywhere, even in the Qaynuqāʿ market-corners — the entire ground of God's *shahīd*-function (this chapter's own vv. 81, 98) roaring to life.

**"We Shall Record" — The Book Against the Taunters**

The divine answer proceeds with two ledger-clauses: *sa-naktubu mā qālū* — "We shall write down what they said" — *wa qatlahumu al-anbiyāʾa bi-ghayri ḥaqq* — "and their slaying of the prophets without right." The book-keeping is paired: (1) *the speech*: the very sentence, duly entered (for every slander-attempt in Scripture passes into the record — 17:13's "We have fastened every man's fate about his neck; We shall bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a book he will find spread open — read your own book"; 18:49; 69:19–25); (2) *the slaying of the prophets*: the chronic charge resumes (v. 21; v. 112; v. 183's shortly) — and the commentators note (per al-Qurṭubī's reasoning, with the Prophet's own rule in the hadith): the present generation inherits that indictment by *approval*: the hadith the source records:

> *"When a sin is committed on the earth — whoever was present and deplored it is as one absent; whoever was absent and approved it is as one present."* (transmitted in the Sunan — Abū Dāwūd 4345, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, and in others — graded ḥasan)

—the consignment principles of the law: what your fathers killed, you may not adopt as heritage: for applause flows backward into complicity.

**"Taste the Punishment of the Burning": The Answer at the Last Day**

And the furnishings of the charge end with the sentence heaven's own herald will read to them: *wa naqūlu dhūqū ʿadhāba al-ḥarīq* — "and We shall say: taste the punishment of the burning": *ʿadhāb al-ḥarīq*: the punishment of *the Burning* — the intensive-substantive: not merely of fire, but of the burning-event itself — ascribed to the mouth-hour throughout the Book (8:50: "taste the punishment of the burning"; 22:22): their taunt against God's *faqīr* is met by the precise scope of their own estate on that Day: the chapter's own 47:38's counter-text echo the most beautifully: *"and God is the Rich, and you are the poor"* — *wa Allāhu al-ghaniyyu wa antumu al-fuqarāʾ* — every proud account of "we are rich" settled on the day all exchange-alchemy is unrolled: God's *ghanī* never owed anyone anything; their "rich" was His entirely bestowed — and either banknote at the Day will be matched against the one ledger kept since the day the sentence was *heard*: *la-qad samiʿa Allāh*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:182

> **That is because of what your hands sent forth, and because God wrongs not His servants.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Shortest Verdict-Clauses in the Book — and Why They Answer Everything**

The verse is thirteen Arabic words, and it is the whole sentence-jurisprudence of the Resurrection: *dhālika bi-mā qaddamat aydīkum* — "that, because of what your hands have sent before" — *wa anna Allāha laysa bi-ẓallāmin lil-ʿabīd* — "and because God is not one to do injustice to His slaves." Each clause is a full academy.

**Clause one — *bi-mā qaddamat aydīkum*: the "sending-ahead" grammar of deeds.** The Book speaks of works as things *dispatched forward* in time — *qaddama*: to send in advance: the sinner's ay year-by-year mailings of his own hands, arriving at the Hereafter before him: his taunts written; his covenants sold; his killings ratified *by nod* — the *ābāʾ* of the previous verse. Nothing at the Day comes *to* him from outside; everything comes *back* to him from his own outgoing courier-service: the Book's images of this domesticity of results are one of its most arresting motifs: "whosoever is done an atom's weight of good shall see it, and whosoever is done an atom's weight of evil shall see it" (99:7–8); "on the Day every soul shall find present before it whatever good it did, and whatever evil — it will wish there were a wide space between it and that" (3:30 — this chapter's own opening-ledger verse, now ringing in its final ring); "read your book! — your own self suffices you today as Reckoner" (17:14).

**Clause two — *laysa bi-ẓallāmin lil-ʿabīd*: the innocence of the Judge.** The account-name God takes here — *ẓallām*: an habitual wronger — is *negated with emphasis in the predicate-place*: it is not possible for God: the chapter's own propositions (v. 108: "God wills no wrong for the worlds"; v. 117: "God wrongs them not"; v. 161: "they shall not be wronged") receive their collective sealer: punishment comes by mailed-deeds (clause one) — never by whim. The aqidah-ramifications the scholars unfolded from this clause are the middle-way of Islam's own theology: (1) justice with God is *real* — not arbitrary decree: the fire's door opens upon *files*; (2) God's *power* remains universal — for the wrong was never in His capacity but in His *Ḥikmah* and wisdom-will: what the Lord would *deserve* — *was*, in the later Ashʿarite expression, another's property and another's due outside His own absolute ownership (v. 129): wrong *cannot* hold; and (3) the *consolation* implied is the most immense deduction of them all: **no one will be in the least degree punished who did not hand his own sentence in**.

**The Two Clauses as the Chapter's Doctrine-Complete**

3:182 is, thus, the verse on which the chapter's entire moral cosmos stands *at summary*: deeds determine; God is beyond injustice: the forwarding-post of the creature, the incorruptibility of the Judge: the taunters of Banū Qaynuqāʿ who cried "God is poor" (v. 181) will, on the Day, find their sentence was *mailed* by themselves and *read* by One incapable of adding a single line of unfairness to it: *your hands sent it — God never errs*: and the believing reader is, on his own account, counseled in the very same sentence: to look at the horizon he fears most with these two words assembled: *qaddamat aydī* — what have my hands mailed? — and *laysa bi-ẓallāmin lil-ʿabīd* — and the postmaster is infallibly fair: a wake-up and a soporific in one scroll, depending on what the mail contains.
**Qaddamat: Forwarded Goods**

*Dhālika bi-mā qaddamat aydīkum* — "that is for what your hands have forwarded": the retribution-scene (the fire-taste of v. 181's perch) arrives self-addressed as a *parcel*: what strikes them had been *mailed ahead* by their own hands — the verb *qaddama* (sending before, forwarding) being the Book's matchless image for deeds as shipments dispatched to the Resurrection's depot, arriving there precisely at the addressee. The chapter's own forwarding-lines ring the same bearing: "whichever good you forward for yourselves, you shall find it with God — better and greater in reward" (73:20's extended-order wording, its kernel in the sūrah's own v. 30's *yawma tajidu kullu nafsin mā ʿamilat... mā qaddamat*), and the Day's individual report-card at 99:6–8: *"whoever works an atom's weight of good shall see it; and whoever works an atom's weight of ill shall see it."* No item mislaid either way.

**Mā Allāhu bi-Ẓallāmin li-l-ʿAbīd: The Negation That Is the Book's Relentless Creed**

*Wa anna Allāha laysa bi-ẓallāmin li-l-ʿabīd* — "and that God is never unjust to the servants": the name-gloss *ẓallām* — intensive-wronger — is *denied of God* in His own words (with its sisters at 4:40's not-a-weight, 10:44's *God wrongs them not*, 18:49, 41:46's *your Lord does not wrong*), and the Prophet's Sacred-Report sets the theology in God's own first-person:

> *"O My servants — I have forbidden injustice for Myself, and I have made it forbidden among you: so do not wrong one another."* (Muslim 2577, from Abū Dharr, in the long qudsi serial)

The dust-scenario of vv. 181–182 — the impoverished imprisoned in their imagining of God's equal poverty — is thereby arraigned on their own mail-book: the deprivation they suffered came by their own forwarding; the Owner of all pays none wrong. Let the Muslim of every audit-season learn v. 180's stinginess-diagnosis beside it: *hoardings are collars; the forwarding-hand lightens the neck.*

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:183

> **[As for] those who say, "Truly God has committed us to not believe in any messenger until he brings us a sacrifice consumed by fire," say, "Messengers certainly came before me with clear proofs and with that whereof you speak; so why did you slay them, if you are truthful?"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Fire-Consuming Sacrifice: A Challenge Set on the Procedure-Rule**

The chapter's last long-file against the obstructionists re-opens with the most technical of their challenges: *alladhīna qālū inna Allāha ʿahida ilaynā allā nuʾmina li-rasūlin ḥattā yaʾtiyanā bi-qurbānin taʾkuluhu al-nār* — "those who say: God committed us not to believe any messenger until he brings us a sacrifice which fire consumes." The commentators (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī recounting the delegation) preserve the account: rabbis of Madinah advanced to the Prophet the claim that the Torah — or God's own covenant with them — had stipulated the miraculous *fire-test*: a true prophet's offering accepted by heaven by a fire descending from above to consume it: the altar-challenge was real and had its foundation in the older scripture's own episodes — the commentators and the source note the Biblical roll: Elijah on Carmel with the bullock of Baal's rivals (1 Kings 18:22–38 — the fire fell, and consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, the dust, *and the water*); David at Ornan's threshing-floor (1 Chronicles 21:26); Solomon at the Temple's consecration (2 Chronicles 7:1); Gideon's offering (Judges 6:21); Manoah's (Judges 13:20). To this library of precedents they had *appended their own covenant* — *God covenanted us not to believe* — alleging revealed restriction on faith's door to everyone not passing their stipulated spectacle.

**God's Answer: The Precedent-Counterprecedent**

And the Prophet is instructed with the comeback that tears out *both* the stipulation's foundation and its selectivity: *qul qad jāʾakum rusulun min qablī bi-l-bayyināti wa bi-lladhī qultum* — "say: messengers came to you before me with clear proofs *and with that which you describe*" — *fa-lima qataltumūhum in kuntum ṣādiqīn* — "so why did you kill them — if you are truthful?" The argument is forensic: (1) the fire-test you require *was* brought to your fathers by prophets of their own — *with that whereof you speak* — God's certified prophets performed it before your nation's own eyes (and al-Rāzī and others add the blunting marginal note: many listed prophets of Israel did *not* even perform that sign — it was not the covenant-credential you claim); (2) *and your response, per your own chronicle, was slaughter*: Zachariah sawed in the tree (in the tradition's own reports), John beheaded on a platter, Isaiah martyred, and *"a prophet between two wars — killed"* per the reports— the prophets list-v: the verse has already memorized the indictment at v. 21 ("killing the prophets without right"), v. 112, and v. 181's ("their slaying of the prophets"); (3) *therefore the demand is not a standard but a device*: had fire-hunger been the honest test, your own past would have ended in believers; your history shows that test-appeals of this shape are *post-mortem excuses*: *we will believe — if our own laboratory-certification is supplied*: the standard whose operational use is only to *exclude at will*. The Sufi glosses the source cites (Abū Bakr al-Wāsiṭī etc., the "Aj" register) extend the verse inward, as always: the soul itself continuously manufactures *fire-consuming-sacrifice specifications*: I would follow the truth *if* my teacher were more illustrious, the times more convenient, the sign more exact — a private Makkah-of-conditions where the heart decapitates each prophet its own Lord sends.

**The Prophet's Own Miracle-Encyclopedia as Closed Answer**

And the answer's agriculture is, for the sūrah's whole polemic, the closing one: Muhammad's certifications did not run by the fire-slot; they ran beyond it: the whole sūrah has described his evidences as more encompassing: a book miracle unread in history; transformation of a continent; the moon; the horses; hearts. The Men of the Fire-Sacrifice found themselves, in years after, facing a religious inheritance-man whose work *outshone the fire-slot sufficiently* to be a judge of it: and history's final note: within the lifetime of the delegation's own children, Islam had outdisputed, outargued, out-accommodated, and finally *converted-in* more of their posterity than the First Temple's sons ever converted outside their nation: the covenant-Clause challenged in the prelude is *fulfilled by becoming the plaintiff's heir*: their demand generated, in the very vocabulary of 3:193's coming prayer, the call they may yet still answer: *our Lord — truly we heard a caller calling to faith — and we believed*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:184

> **So if they deny thee, they certainly did deny messengers before thee, who came with clear proofs, scriptures, and the luminous Book.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Consolation-Lineage: They Always Denied**

The consolation-strain of v. 176 now receives its final perfected form, addressed — as all the finest ones were — to the Messenger's own heart: *fa-in kadhdhabūka fa-qad kudhdhiba rusulun min qablika* — "so if they deny you, indeed messengers before you were denied" — partners of your rank, bearers of your office, exactly at this same station of rejection: the verse's genealogy-of-burden runs from Noah's nine centuries to Moses' scorn to Abraham's furnace to Joseph's accusations to John's platter to Jesus's cross-station: the denial of the chapter's own hearsay (v. 33's family of ʿImrān; v. 61's mubāhalah; v. 65's disputation of the Scripture-claimants) is delivered into perspective: *your case is not singular; the road is the highway of the prophets*: the power of the clause for a Messenger's daily living is recorded across the sīrah: at the worst hour of Makkah's persecution the Prophet ﷺ was told (and told others) the same roster — from the long, famous account of Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt's complaint at the Kaʾba ("will you not pray to God for us?"):

> *"Among those before you a man would be taken and a pit dug for him in the earth, and a saw brought and placed on his head, and he would be sawn in two — and that would not turn him from his religion... By God, this matter shall certainly be completed, until a rider travels from Ṣanʿāʾ to Ḥaḍramawt, fearing none but God — and the wolf upon his sheep — but you are a hasty people."* (al-Bukhārī 3612, 3853, 6943 — from Khabbāb)

**"Clear Proofs, Scriptures, the Luminous Book": The Triple Kit of Prophethood**

And the verse completes the picture by inventorying what the denied messengers carried — God's full equipment-manifest for prophets — in three clauses: (1) *bi-l-bayyināt* — *with clear proofs*: the ipsissima-indications: substantive evidences: miracles, signs, demonstrated coherence (denial's class, per Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī: every genuine proof of truth); (2) *wa-l-zubur* — *and the scriptures*: *zubur* — plural of *zabūr* in its generic sense: *written documents* (the root's precise base: something written) — per al-Rāzī: any divine book containing wisdom — applied broadly across Dovid? — David's Psalms, Abraham's sheets (87:18–19: the *ṣuḥuf* of Abraham and Moses, confirmed at 53:36–37), and each community's texts; (3) *wa-l-kitābi al-munīr* — *and the luminous book*: the *illuminating* book: in tandem classed within the zubur and emphatically of them (al-Rāzī's note: the wa-*and* here is explicative — the shining book *is* the scriptures in their quality: *munīr* — from nūr: the light-bearing quality of revelation: it does not merely inform; it *illuminates*: the description echoing the Chapter's own signature imagery — the Qur'an at this sūrah's beginning named the kht? — al-kitāb (v. 3) and 42:52's nūr ("so We revealed to you a Spirit of Our command... and made it a *light by which We guide whom We will*") and the final 7:157's attestition: "those who follow the Messenger... the light that was sent down with him"): prophecy's kit is *combination*: miracles in the realm of event, text in the realm of transmission, *light* in the realm of radiance — all three present in the last Messenger: the Qur'an *as* bayyinah, *as* book, *as* munīr.

**"They Certainly Did Deny": The Precedent Standing Ready**

The verse thereby delivers, to every caller after Muḥammad, the chapter's final stance-formula: the denial that seems the caller's special hurt is *inheritance*, not anomaly: Noah's century-denied century; Abraham's fire; Christ's elders; Muḥammad's own city: the denial-cadre has never been absent; but the *cause* has never been lost thereby: **and precisely so** — the consolation closes its loop — the denial is to be read *diagnostically, not personally*: if they deny *you*, they join the party that denied *them*: the verse's next move — v. 185 — will then take leave of all parties at once and sound the one truth under everything: *every soul shall taste death* — after which, the distanced-from-Fire are the winners, whichever century they preached in.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:185

> **Every soul shall taste death, and you will indeed be paid your reward in full on the Day of Resurrection. And whosoever is distanced from the Fire and made to enter the Garden has certainly triumphed. And the life of this world is naught but the enjoyment of delusion.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verse on Ten Million Tombstones — And Why**

Few verses of the Qur'an are more frequently inscribed on Muslim graves, spoken at deathbeds, or learned by heart than 3:185 — and its hold on the genus of grief is earned phrase by phrase: *kullu nafsin dhāʾiqatu al-mawt* — "every soul shall taste death." Every: no class of souls excepted — the martyrs' dying defined (v. 169), the disbelievers' dying registered (v. 91's thirsters of ransom), the Prophet's own dying sealed (v. 144's "if he dies or is slain"), and one day the readers' too. But God chose the verb *taste*: *dhāʾiqah* — from dhawq: to taste — the delicate verb of sensation: death arrives not as obliteration but as *taste*: an experience the soul *has* — a sip of a cup: al-Qushayrī's famous mirror-image the source retains: the cup of death has been placed in every living hand: you may drink it well — and find bliss — or drink it with grimace and wail: the *taste* is yours to season by all the years of preparation. And the narrative-depth of the Arabic verb allows the subtle reading the commentators discuss (the source preserves): the present-future *dhāʾiqatu* is durative: every soul *is ever tasting* death — now, daily: life itself is the slow fore-sip of the taste — each sleep (the Qur'an itself names sleep death's twin — 39:42) a rehearsal of the flavor: the day the full cup comes will have been met before.

**"Paid in Full on the Day of Resurrection": The Wage That Completes the Meaning**

*Wa innamā tuwaffawna ujūrakum yawma al-qiyāmah* — "and only then will you be paid your wages in full": death is not *settlement*; it is *passage to payroll*: the Book's own full-pay clause (vv. 25, 57, 161) stamped once more: *tuwaffawna*: fully-paid: nothing clipped; everything to scale; on the *day of faces* (v. 106's whitening and blackening). The coupling of *tasting* and *payroll* is the whole eschatological administration: no faith-wage is paid *this* side of the grave (whatever is paid here is *advance* — v. 145's two of-its); no labor is omitted *beyond* it: the grave is the *border between work-season and pay-season* — and every man's death is, thereby, his last work-shift.

**"Distanced From the Fire — Then the Garden — Has Triumphed": Islam's Complete Definition of Success**

Then comes the single most consequential one-sentence definition of success in the religion: *fa-man zuḥziḥa ʿani al-nāri wa udkhila al-jannata fa-qad fāz* — "whoever is removed from the Fire and admitted to the Garden — has triumphed." Note the two passive-voices: *zuḥziḥa*: *distanced*, dragged away — a verb whose image is of *removal* from the fire's very lip (the sages likened zahzahah to being dragged back by the collar); *udkhila*: *made to enter* — someone *pours you in*: both domains are *fates*: human tone - rather — in both clauses the man is *acted upon*, because in his own strength no one survives the fire's gravity nor enters the garden's gate: the two rescues are divine. And the copula unites them: deliverance *and* admission together constitute *fawz* — triumph — the word's v-fawz has the dynasty of 4:13, 9:72, 98:8: *fawz ʿaẓīm* — the *great* triumph — but only of the pair complete: *not the mere rescue*, nor *semi-paradise*: *both* pulls are required: the definition *rules out* (1) the hedonist's triumph of accumulated banners (v. 14); (2) and the merely *escapist's* — bare survival isn't triumph: Heaven's entry *is*. The Prophet's own noted hadith that the source retains measures the garden's true scale against the world's, precisely: *"the spot of a whip in the Garden is better than this world and everything in it"* — *mawḍiʿ sawṭin fī al-jannati khayrun mina al-dunyā wa mā fīhā* (al-Bukhārī 6568, 6586-87; Muslim 1881? — from Abū Hurayrah and al-Mughīrah in the narrations on 3:185: indeed told in the *context* of this verse per several reports): a whip-width of Garden > the whole planet and all it contains: the fawz is defined by comparison-unfair to every scale man knows.

**"The Life of This World Is But the Enjoyment of Delusion"**

And the verse crowns everything with its final and most quoted phrase: *wa mā al-ḥayātu al-dunyā illā matāʿu al-ghurūr* — "and the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion." *Matāʿ*: provision-enjoyment, supply-use: yes, enjoyment — real enjoyment, not fictitious: yet *al-ghurūr*: of deception — the noun of delusion, vanity's own decoy: the dunyā as legitimately enjoyable *and* structurally deceptive: it cheats not by *falsity* (its pleasures are real) but by *framing*: presenting itself as the *stakes*, when it is only their *waiting-room* — the verse's twin at 57:20 tracing the six stages: *"know that the life of the world is but play and diversion, adornment and mutual boasting among you, and competition in wealth and children — like rain whose greenness pleases the farmers, then it withers, you see it yellowing, then it turns to chaff"* — the ghurūr decomposed in the life-span of a harvest. Al-Rāzī's earlier amplification (v. 142) operates here too: the heart either *occupies* this matāʿ — and the Garden-dimension evacuates; or *uses* it — as provision, fuel, tafakkur-material — and the dimension fills. The theology of death, wage, triumph, and delusion — in a single verse — standing among the ten most recited consolations of the entire human engagement with dying.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:186

> **You will surely be tried in your wealth and your souls, and you shall hear much hurt from those who were given the Book before you, and from those who are idolaters. But if you are patient and reverent, then that is indeed a course worthy of resolve.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Trial-Table Announced Before Final Parole**

Just before the chapter's great benediction-cycle (vv. 190–200), the believers are issued their standing forecast — *la-tublawunna* — with the doubled-emphatic (the od ll? — the doubled *lām* of oath and the *nūn* of emphasis: *by God, you shall be tried*) — *fī amwālikum wa anfusikum* — "in your wealth and your souls" — *wa la-tasmaʿunna mina alladhīna ūtū al-kitāba min qablikum wa mina alladhīna ashrakū adhan kathīrā* — "and you shall *hear* — most assuredly — from those given the Book before you and from the idolaters — *much hurt*."

The prophecy is exacting in inventory. *The trial-fields are named*: property and self (al-Ṭabarī's note extends *anfusikum* also to your own kin — your near-people — and to the body's person); the *forms* of trial are the whole spectrum of loss-and-risk — confiscations, deaths, wounds, dispossessions: the chapter's own permanent rehearsal-file (2:155's parallel Inventory: "We will test you with something of fear, and hunger, and diminution of wealth, lives, and fruits — and give good tidings to the patient"). *And the hurt-suppliers are named*: the People of the Book — oblique: the scholars' envy-contexts already audited through vv. 69–112; and the idolaters — open hostility: the two humanities-of-refusal with which Madinah contended daily. *Adhan kathīrā*: *much hurt* — *adhā* again, the verse of 111's term of classification — *taunts, slanders, slights, the denigration of God-and-Messenger*: al-Ṭabarī's own range includes blasphemy-speak: the command is made unmistakable for the Muslim congress of the ages: *your posture toward these senses' assaults is decreed long before the assaults*.

**"If You Are Patient and Reverent": The Two Keys Again — and the Badge They Earn**

And the verse seals with the chapter's repeated covenant-pair — *wa in taṣbirū wa tattaqū* — "if you are patient and reverent" — *fa-inna dhālika min ʿazmi al-umūr* — "then that is indeed a matter of firm resolve." *ʿAzm al-umūr*: the binding-matter grade: the *highest class of affairs*: the language the Book uses of the ʿazm-designated prophets themselves (46:35: *uulū l-ʿazm of the messengers* — Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, Muḥammad) and of the greatest moral exertions (31:17's own formulation in Luqmān's counsel: endure what befalls you — that is among the matters of firm resolve; 42:43: he who is patient and forgives — that is of the firm resolve): *patience-under-hurt while staying within God's bounds is thus listed among the affairs of highest classification* — the taunter thinks himself clever-higher; God lists his target's restraint among the ʿazm. The exact structure of the Prophet's own conduct under provocation is the repository's exhibit: he heard "poison upon you" (al-sāmm) from a Jewish delegation at his own gate and answered *wa ʿalaykum* — with ʿĀʾishah's outburst corrected — *"ʿĀʾishah — God loves gentleness in all matters"* (al-Bukhārī 6928; Muslim 2165/2166) — while at every permitted line he turned to forgiveness — and the corrective proofs the scholars cite (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī insisting that 3:186 is NOT abrogated by the sword-verses: *patience under speech-hurt was the Prophet's method even at the height of military authority*): the Prophet's own conduct *with* hurt remained this verse to his deathbed: five-day grace-periods of patience procured, still, in a thousandth of the hurt's volume.

**"Worthy of Resolve": The Resolve-Premium**

And the phrase *min ʿazmi al-umūr* closes the whole pre-benediction forecast on a note of unknowable pride for every small believer: *your quiet endurance of the next slander at your workplace — your swallowing of the next communal slight — your polite response to the next sneer at your Lord* — sits, in God's Book, *on the same index* as the great firm-resolves of the prophetic line: *patience and reverence under provocation is ʿazm al-umūr* — there is no higher class of thing you could be caught doing at the moment of offense.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:187

> **[Remember] when God made the covenant with those who were given the Book, "You shall make it clear to the people, and not conceal it." Then they cast it behind their backs and sold it for a paltry price. Evil indeed is their selling!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Publication Covenant: Scholars' First Commandment**

The sūrah's closing indictment picks up the thread first woven at vv. 71–72 and again at v. 94 — and lays it now in the vocabulary of *contract*: *wa idh akhadha Allāhu mīthāqa alladhīna ūtū al-kitāba la-tubayyinunnahu lil-nāsi wa lā taktumūnah* — "when God took the covenant of those given the Book: *you shall make it plain to the people, and not conceal it*." The *mīthāq*-word is the mighty covenant-term the chapter has raced through prophets and Israel and believers (vv. 77, 81): its filing here places on the *scholars-and-learned* of every revealed community the standing law of *publication*: religious knowledge is *commons* — issued by God *to the people at large* (*lil-nās* — the phrase is universal — not "to your clergy" — not "to the initiated") — and its concealment (kitmān) is breach of *the covenant*, not mere etiquette-fault. Al-Ṭabarī's chain narrates the covenant's instrument — the prophets transmitting it to their learned (they bear the appointment in His name); al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī name both the general object (the Book *itself*, undiminished and undistorted — the teaching requirement) and the specific object much of the commentary runs on (the prophecies of Muḥammad in their texts — 7:157's "the unlettered prophet whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel"): in either case the *imperative-contract* is one: publish-and-teach, always.

**Cast Behind Backs and Sold for Crusts: The Twin Mechanics of Suppression**

Then God's audit of what they *did* with the covenant is drawn in two strokes of the chapter's own economics-and-grammar: *fa-nabadhūhu warāʾa ẓuhūrihim* — "so they cast it behind their backs" — the *nabadh* of the Book's more famous indictment at 2:100–101 ("every time they made a covenant, a party of them cast it off — nay, most of them believe not — and when a messenger came to them from God confirming what was with them, a party flung the Book of God behind their backs as though they knew not"): behind-the-back treatment being, in the source's own glosses, not so much *burning* the Book as *vacating it* — dis-enable it from life: they read; they did not render *manifest*; and — *wa-shtaraw bihi thamanan qalīlan* — "and sold it for a little price" — v. 77's own selling-grammar-recurring: v. 199's opposite profile (the remnant *not selling God's signs for a paltry price*) standing one verse-cycle distant as its plain counter-case: for what does the Book-of-God *sell*? the commentators' markets: stipends of establishment, favor of princes, keeping the crowd in dependency upon keepers (the priestcraft-tariff), and the silentest market of all — *the price of comfort*: the omission-of-teachings that would have troubled one's own class. *Fa-biʾsa mā yashtarūn* — "evil indeed is what they sell": the Book's double-damnation form (*biʾsa* + pronoun + verb: at v. 151's "evil the abode"; at v. 162's "evil the journey's end"; at v. 187's "evil the selling"): the sale-docket of the concealed text is the *worst commodity-exchange on record* — price little, merchandise incalculable.

**The Hadith's Fire-Bridle — and ʿAlī's Quid Pro Quo**

The tradition supplies the enforcement-clause: not only the collaring of v. 180's hoarders, but a pride-of-place torture-accessory for concealers of *knowledge* — the Prophet's own hadith the source recording:

> *"Whosoever conceals knowledge from his people — God will bridle him with a bridle of Fire on the Day of Resurrection."* (Abū Dāwūd 3658; al-Tirmidhī 2649 — from Abū Hurayrah)

And alongside it, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib's sentence (kept in al-Qurṭubī's and the classical corpus as a legal principle of the religion): *"God has not tasked an ignorant person with learning until He has tasked a learned person with teaching"*: the learned's teaching-duty *precedes* — logically — the ignorant's learning-duty: civilization's sole immune-condition against the loss of its Book is that its readers *speak*: the unblocked flow: every madrasah, every translation, every commentary in the whole sweep of Muslim intellectual history — including the thousands who penned tafsīr on this sūrah itself — is an act of raw obedience to 3:187; the internet-age explosion of Quran-word in every world language as its latest — its content proliferating with no custodians at all: the covenant's pre-requisite running without collars: *and the knowledge of God passed even around its concealers*.

---
## Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:188

> **Do not suppose that those who exult in what they have brought about and love to be praised for what they have not done—do not suppose that they are delivered from the punishment; theirs is a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Disorders of the Immodest Soul**

The final habit-verse before the sūrah's crown turns to the believers (v. 189) is the Book's most exact portrait of the spiritual vanity-class: *lā taḥsabanna alladhīna yafraḥūna bi-mā ataw wa yuḥibbūna an yuḥmadū bi-mā lam yafʿalū* — "do not think that those who exult in what they have brought about and who love to be praised for what they did not do" — *fa-lā taḥsabannahum bi-mafāzatin mina al-ʿadhāb* — "so do not think them in a place of escape from the punishment" — *wa lahum ʿadhābun alīm* — "and theirs is a painful punishment." Two linked disorders are anatomized.

(1) *Al-farḥ bi-mā atāw* — *exulting in what they brought*: the pride-glee in attained deeds: not gratitude (the shukr of verses 145, 147), which points upward; but *farḥ*: the self-applauding joy that *consumes the deed's credit internally*: the man who *did* something good and immediately *boulders?* — builds its pavilion in his own imagination: al-Rāzī annotating with his physician's eye: they delight in *worldly things and passions* — yet want the *credit-ledger of the pious*: the deed thus manufactured becomes supposedly his own product — he *brought it forth* — and the praise owed to its Author is thereby *embezzled at the heart's customs*.

(2) *Yuḥibbūna an yuḥmadū bi-mā lam yafʿalū* — *loving to be praised for what they did not do*: the full hypocrisy-disorder: the claim-credit for unperformed devotion: the commentaries (Ibn Kathīr's, al-Rāzī's) fill the instances of occasions: hypocrites who absented themselves from expeditions on forged excuses and then, upon the Prophet's return, *sought his pardon — and praise* — as though their excuses had been missions; the concealers of truth (v. 187) desiring the *title* of the learned after smothering the text; religious performers of all ages who *desire their piety's label* — one of the Prophet's most-quoted terror-hadiths lands directly beneath this clause — the hadith on *al-riyāʾ al-khafī*:

> *"What I fear most for my community is hidden shirk." It was said: What is hidden shirk, O Messenger of God? He said: 'A man stands to pray, and beautifies his prayer because people are looking at him — that is hidden shirk.'"* — and the head-of-all-shirk warnings: *"shirk in my community is more hidden than the ant's footsteps on a black rock in the dark of night"* (Aḥmad and the books, from Abū Saʿīd and ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār with varying chains — and the long riyāʾ-hadiths at Ibn Mājah 4204–4206, graded from the Companions; the formula *"the lowest degree of riyāʾ is shirk"* occurring across the Companion-literature)

**"They Are Not at Any Place of Escape" — The Prohibition of Supposed Salvation**
